The Maytag Man is one of the most enduring characters in American advertising, lonely because no one needs his help repairing a Maytag appliance. The Maytag brand, too, has endured—dating back to the days when Frederick Maytag’s washers used wooden tubs and cranks. Maytag was the first company to put an agitator at the bottom of a washing machine, a design still in use today. It was also the first to stack a washer and dryer and one of the earliest adopters of smart appliances. But mostly, the brand has eschewed novelty and staked its claim on durability and reliability for its heavy-duty dishwashers, washers, dryers, refrigerators, and ovens. This is true even as Maytag came under the ownership of former competitor Whirlpool.
Maytag remains one of the few appliance companies to offer 10-year limited warranties on essential parts. But Maytag promo codes are more ephemeral, offering short-term deals on appliances that will hopefully last a decade. Here’s how to get a Maytag coupon code and Maytag promo codes, and to find closeout deals on last season’s Maytag appliances to save even more.
Save Big With Maytag Appliance Closeout Deals
A simple way to find discounts on Maytag appliances is to check out overstock and closeout deals, which feature substantial markdowns on last season’s models as Maytag clears space for new products. These deals don't need a coupon code but do require knowing the right place to look. Visit the Maytag outlet website for appliance closeout offers. Usually, these deals are available only until supplies last.
Select Customers Can Get a Special Maytag Promo Code
Like many big companies, Maytag offers professional discounts for military, first responders, health care workers, students, and teachers. To receive up to a 15% discount as an active military member, veteran, or spouse, you’ll need to create a Maytag account and verify your military status through the SheerID program. Maytag first responder and health care worker discounts also require SheerID verification. There’s also a discount program for students and teachers, including a teacher savings program and up to 15% off sitewide. Verified students can access student-specific pricing when moving into their first off-campus apartment.
Work Smarter, Not Harder With Maytag Smart Appliances
Maytag is also offering deals on select smart appliances. This includes a unique combination toaster-microwave that’s about $100 off MSRP, and a slide-in electric range with smart connectivity that’s steeply discounted to $1,260—hundreds of dollars less than even other recent sale prices. You can check out the special Maytag deals on connected and smart appliances by scrolling to the bottom of Maytag’s smart appliance page.
Get an Extra Year of Coverage With Maytag
If you’ve been wanting to upgrade your home with new appliances built to last, now’s a great time to do so. For a limited time, when you buy select Maytag appliances, you can receive an additional year of the standard one-year manufacturer’s warranty, bringing coverage to two years. Plus, this is on top of the 10-year limited parts warranty, so you get extra peace of mind. Eligible categories include: dishwashers, ranges, cooktops, microwaves, ovens, laundry machines, and refrigerators. This Maytag promo is valid only for purchases made directly from June 1 to June 30. For more information, visit the Maytag product warranty page.

Paramount said Friday it plans to start moving the listing of its Class B shares from the Nasdaq to the New York Stock Exchange in early October.
Noting the still-pending $110 billion merger with Warner Bros Discovery as a key variable, the company said in an SEC filing that the date of the shift could be subject to change. As of now, listing and trading of Class B common stock will end as of the close of the market on October 5 and begin on the NYSE the next day.
CEO David Ellison told employees on Monday after legal settlements were reached with state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America that the merger was tentatively on track to close about two weeks from that date. If that timeline holds up, that would put the close on October 5.
Watch on Deadline
Both the Nasdaq and the NYSE have media and entertainment listings. The Nasdaq long has been more weighted toward tech companies, including Netflix. The Walt Disney Co.’s shares are among those traded on the NYSE. It’s not uncommon for companies to switch exchanges.
RELATED: ParaBros Foes Urge Court To Reject Settlement In Midnight Filings: “This Merger Lessens Competition”
A federal judge is scheduled to preside over a hearing on Monday to review the settlement and hear from the parties in the suits, with the hearing pushed back from its original date on Thursday of this week. The Block the Merger coalition and other opponents of the deal have filed amicus briefs reiterating their objections. The judge can alter terms of the settlement or even reject it outright, though instances of the latter have been rare.
If the deal is not closed by October 1, Paramount has agreed to pay WBD shareholders a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee.” The fee was a sweetener it volunteered earlier this year as a way of outmaneuvering Netflix in its pursuit of WBD.
Since the legal truce was declared, the industry has been reeling given that the timing and the terms of the settlement were both surprising. The combination will redraw the Hollywood map, putting two century-old studios along with HBO and CBS under one roof and giving Warner Bros its fourth corporate owner in the past eight years.
RELATED: Dealmakers React To Paramount-WBD Settlement: “Tech Has Won”
To the surprise of many observers of the case, Paramount is not being required to sell assets or make structural changes as part of the takeover. They are instead making financial commitments to domestic production, worker retraining as well as pledges regarding the number of annual theatrical releases and conducting separate pay-TV negotiations with distributors. The consent decree governing those commitments, which lasts five years, has prompted criticism in recent days given the perceived leverage of the plaintiffs since they filed suit in mid-July. Federal regulators had already approved the transaction.
Paramount said in Friday’s filing that its board of directors on Friday had authorized the stock move. The company expects to distribute warrants to purchase Class B shares on October 13, though that action will depend on the merger being closed.
The merger “is subject to further closing conditions, and the ultimate timing for the closing of the WBD merger, if any, is not yet certain,” the filing noted. As a result, the company said it may choose to cancel or postpone the move.
>If the deal is not closed by October 1, Paramount has agreed to pay WBD shareholders a $7 million-a-day “ticking fee.”
It’s going to be the California taxpayer paying that ticking fee btw.

Iran offers US plan to reopen Hormuz within 7 days
Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi says the ball is now in Washington’s court, after setting out conditions for ending the war
Iran’s Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on Friday that Tehran had offered Washington a plan that would see the Strait of Hormuz reopened to maritime navigation within seven days once agreed.
Araghchi met with US President Donald Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff for talks on Tuesday, and previously set out conditions for ending the war and reopening the vital energy shipping channel.
“Iran has conveyed to the United States, through Qatar, a concrete seven-day plan. If the necessary conditions are met, the strait can be reopened, and normal maritime passage restored within seven days,” Araghchi said at the UN on Friday.
“The choice now rests with the United States. Iran does not accept coercion, threats, or intimidation, and Iran will not surrender its sovereign rights under pressure.

One of the first things I did when I left my full-time job at WIRED was give Claude Cowork access to my email and calendar. After reporting on artificial intelligence for years, I was curious about what the technology could do for me. I had imagined Cowork as a hyper-capable digital assistant, but was let down to discover that it was more like interacting with a regular chatbot, albeit one with extra tools. What did I want it to do? I had no idea.
Then Instinct, an invite-only AI agent that communicates with users through iMessage and WhatsApp, started popping off in the Bay Area. It connects to your email, calendar, and messaging apps. Think of it as OpenClaw for normies. The company, which launched in private beta in February, is reportedly in talks to raise $1 billion on top of the $350 million it’s already raised, bringing its valuation to $10 billion, according to The Information.
Instinct’s moment in the spotlight comes as Meta is experiencing its own unexpected burst of popularity thanks to Muse, an AI assistant the tech giant launched earlier this month. As of writing, Muse is the most popular free app in Apple’s App Store, with more than 900,000 downloads, according to third-party estimates. The commentator class on X seems genuinely excited about it, despite the fact that it rolled out with a serious security vulnerability that would have “let attackers do ‘whatever’ they wanted on a victim’s Mac,” according to Ars Technica. I’m not about to give Meta a ton of my personal information, but if Muse can keep me logged into Bloomberg or unsubscribe me from Hot Yoga São Paulo, which has been emailing me once a week since 2017, I’ll reconsider.
Agent Provocateur
The divide between people who use AI agents for everything and those who have never tried one has never been wider. It explains, in part, why tech CEOs were largely caught off guard by the data center backlash. If you think agents can automate the majority of people’s administrative drudgery and turbocharge their productivity, the costs and disruptions associated with building data centers might look like an acceptable trade-off. But if you’re using chatbots as a fancy form of Google, that deal is probably much less appealing.
The overarching problem, as technology journalist Jasmine Sun writes, is that “most people’s problems are not software-shaped, and most won’t notice even when they are.” AI agents, like chatbots, still require a lot of input and direction from users. If you know what you want—help with your homework, a virtual girlfriend—the tools are eager to provide. But if you don’t, well, welcome to the permanent underclass.
I was eager to avoid such a fate. I may not be agentic, but I like to think I’m action-oriented. Surely I could identify a software-shaped problem in my life. I had used Claude previously to generate a few freelance invoices, saving me approximately 10 minutes. It was nice, but not life-changing. I decided to give Instinct a try.
If you talk to AI researchers about Instinct, you’ll hear the phrase “form factor” a lot. Instinct got the form factor right—no open text box, just iMessage, WhatsApp, and a few helpful prompts. It’s hard to overstate how important this is. Rather than trying to figure out for yourself how to make the chat experience more useful, you’re texting with an agent that’s suggesting things it can do for you, and then actually doing them. And unlike other agents in this space, it doesn’t text too much. I tried a competing agent called Lindy for a week and deleted it after it texted me each morning and started popping into Zoom meetings without my approval.
For its first project, I gave Instinct my itinerary for a work trip to Venice, Italy. I had it book reservations based on where I was going to be, including WhatsApping hole-in-the-wall spots. Success! Restaurant reservations appear to be a gateway drug for many agent-curious people, and I was no exception. (It’s worth noting that while Muse can also call restaurants to book reservations on your behalf, some of those calls are reportedly made by humans in call centers, according to reporting in 404 Media).
Next, I gave Instinct a more complicated task. I had already booked a trip to New York in November with my sister when WIRED asked me to attend the WIRED World Fair, which was taking place in Miami the day before. Unfortunately, I’d booked a saver fare, meaning I couldn’t move the ticket, and if I missed the first leg of the trip it would automatically cancel the whole thing.
Could Instinct cancel my trip and get a refund? To my surprise, it could. The agent detected that Alaska had moved my flight 90 minutes earlier, a fact I’d completely missed, which qualified me for a full refund. It canceled my ticket, saving me roughly $550, and rebooked my one-way return to San Francisco. I don’t know about you guys, but I’m starting to feel the AGI.
Unnatural Instincts
This is where I have to pause and acknowledge the risks of using Instinct. There are a lot. People have reported that when they tried to disconnect the agent from their email, they found out it was retaining a copy of their inboxes anyway. One venture capitalist said he was banned from Resy after the bot pinged its API roughly 200 times per hour while trying to make a reservation. Another tech investor said he deleted the app after determining that it would be trivially easy for Instinct to be phished.
Instinct’s Terms of Service are pretty far-reaching, allowing the company to use at least some of your conversations to train its AI models. I also experienced an annoying (if minor) snafu: One day, Instinct canceled a DoorDash order that was seriously delayed, forcing me to forfeit $64. (I’d explicitly told it to cancel only if I could get a refund.) This alerted me to another thing Instinct is very, very good at: profusely apologizing without offering to pay for its mistakes.
The company Instinct, which shares the same name as its flagship AI agent, did not respond to requests for comment from WIRED.
Instinct feels like a mildly chaotic personal assistant, and since I’ve never had a real human assistant, I’m sticking with it. Last week it told me “NOT TO OPEN” an email from a friend inviting me to a backyard BBQ—it turned out to be a phishing scam. Agents are a security nightmare. I get it! But I’m busy. I’m a mom. Everything feels like a security nightmare these days. For now, I’m willing to take the risk.

Nisshin: India will face Afghanistan in the men’s cricket quarter-finals at the Asian Games 2026 after Nepal topped Pool A following a rain-affected washout between Nepal and Japan in Nisshin on Saturday.
The quarter-final between India and Afghanistan is scheduled for September 28 in Nisshin, with Nepal’s first-place finish in the group determining the knockout-stage line-up. Japan’s abandoned match ended their campaign, while Afghanistan advanced alongside Nepal from Pool A.
The equation was settled after Japan’s chase against Nepal was completely washed out. Nepal had posted 149 for four in 15 overs after being put into bat, but persistent rain prevented Japan from beginning its pursuit.
Nepal’s innings was built around an explosive finish from Sundeep Jora and Lokesh Bam. The pair remained unbeaten and accelerated sharply after Nepal found itself at 84 for four at the end of 10 overs.
Jora, who came in at No. 3, finished with an unbeaten 57 from 32 deliveries, striking five fours and three sixes. Bam provided the late surge, smashing 52 not out off only 22 balls, including six sixes and a four.
Earlier, Aasif Sheikh provided Nepal with a brisk start to the middle phase, making 21 from 15 balls and sharing a 55-run partnership with Jora for the second wicket. Nepal had otherwise struggled to build momentum, with Kushal Bhurtel, Kushal Malla and Gulsan Jha departing for single-digit scores.
Japan were therefore left facing a demanding target in a severely shortened contest, requiring 150 from 15 overs. However, before their response could get underway, another spell of rain brought the match to a premature conclusion.
The washout proved decisive for the group standings, sending Nepal through as Pool A winners and Afghanistan into the quarter-finals as the other qualifying side.
Japan bow out after showing glimpses of promise during the tournament. They had impressed with the ball against Afghanistan in their opening match and had also competed well against India in the one-off T20I preceding the Games, but their batting ultimately proved a limiting factor.
For India, the focus now shifts firmly to the knockout stage, with Afghanistan standing between the side and a place in the semi-finals.

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

A nine-second long video clip is has gone viral on social media, showing a man assaulting a puffed rice vendor. In the video, the man is seen overturning the box hanging from the snack seller’s neck and pouring all the food items onto the vendor’s face before they scatter onto the street. As this purported attack unfolds, the vendor stares at the man helplessly.
The video was posted by X user Alka Maurya on September 16 and has garnered more than 2,85,000 views and shared over 1,500 times till publication time. The caption of the post, translated from Hindi, reads: “(He) must be feeling so proud after doing something like this.” (Archive)
कितना गर्व महसूस कर रहा होगा ऐसे करके हैं ना …… pic.twitter.com/F6upi4I2ZD
— Alka Maurya (@MauryaAlka76391) September 16, 2026
Apart from Maurya, film actor Kamaal R Khan posted the same video with the caption: “How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now.” (Archive)
How will you fix this mentality which has developed in last 10 years. India can’t be fixed now. pic.twitter.com/o2T2AJzGoj
— KRK (@kamaalrkhan) September 17, 2026
Other social media users circulated the viral clip with similar captions, condemning the man seen purportedly attacking the vendor.
As a billboard visible in the video reads ‘Welcome to Patna Junction’, the Patna police was tagged in the comment section of certain posts, requesting them to take stringent action against the man who allegedly assaulted the vendor.
Fact Check
To verify the authenticity of the viral video clip, we ran reverse image search on several relevant keyframes. It led us to a video posted by content creator Sonu Paswan on Instagram. With 1,79,000 followers, he posts scripted videos highlighting the helpless condition of the working class people in India. Paswan has a social media presence on Facebook and YouTube as well. And according to his social media bios, he is from Darbhanga, Bihar.
In all of his videos, accessible on his Facebook page, Paswan himself can be seen playing different “poor characters” being harassed and attacked by others as he helplessly accepts his fate.
On September 18, Friday, Paswan posted a video on his Instagram page, where he clarified that he enacts emotional scenes on poverty as ‘content’ on his social media platforms. He clarifies that the viral clip does not depict a real attack on him, but is in fact a prepared skit. “I want to tell you that in the video you are seeing, the vendor is me and the man who is attacking me is part of my team. I want to let you know that we, as a team, make emotional videos on poverty. I request you to take this video purely as entertainment, and not believe that this is real,” he said.
The caption of this video reads, translated from Hindi, “Because we make emotional videos on the poor…You all give me so much love…but you guys have taken this clip to heart.
I know I have hurt you guys with this video. Please delete the video from your channel…I request you not to share this video any further.”
View this post on Instagram
After the clip started going viral and attracted significant backlash, on September 17, most of his videos on YouTube and all of his previous videos on Instagram had to be deleted. In the aforementioned video, Paswan urges audiences to not share the viral clip and excerbate his situation even further. “I request you to not share the clip on your personal profiles, please do this much for your brothers,” he said. He shared the same clarification on his YouTube page.
Moreover, Paswan posted videos of the guy who is acting as the attacker in the video, also clarifying the viral clip is indeed a skit, on his Instagram and YouTube pages. “The video you guys are watching and getting emotional and taking to heart is just our content…its not real…please stop roasting this video. Because of you [sharing the viral clip as real] all my efforts have gone to waste, all my videos, over 300 videos…I have had to delete them all. I request you to keep supporting and loving us,” he states in the video.
View this post on Instagram
Given that their skit went viral, misleadingly as a real incident, the content creators said they received backlash and trolling, compelling them to remove their previous videos. At present, Paswan’s Instagram page only features the two clarification videos and his YouTube page features the same. However, his Facebook still displayed his earlier content. The description of his Facebook page, translated from Hindi, also reads: “I make emotional videos on poverty.”
True to the description, Paswan’s Facebook page contains videos similar in theme to the viral video. In these videos, visibly destitute people or poor vendors are seen being humiliated or suffering at the hands of others, while accepting their fate.
Paswan can be identified acting in all of these videos, and a visual match can be established, indicating that he was indeed the person seen in the viral video. Thus, it can be concluded that a scripted video made by a content creator has gone viral, leading netizens to falsely believe that it depicts a real incident of attack on a puffed rice vendor.

Elephants use medicinal plants to treat themselves, researchers find
- Published
African elephants use dozens of different medicinal plants to treat themselves and their families when they are sick.
This is the conclusion of a study which interviewed people who live and work alongside the elephants in the Mount Elgon region of Kenya.
These particular animals have long intrigued scientists with their extraordinary behaviour - they are known as salt-mining elephants, because they go into caves and scrape the rock with their tusks to extract minerals for their diet.
This newly published research suggests that the same elephants use several different plant species in the forest for medicinal purposes.
One of the lead researchers, Dr Elodie Freymann from Brown University in the US, said the study raised the question of whether destruction of forest habitat deprives animals - and humans - of the medicines they need to thrive.
"This shows just how entangled our medicines are with the non-human world," Dr Freymann told BBC News.
Medicine for baby elephants
The scientists collaborated with the conservation charity the Mount Elgon Foundation, external. They interviewed local people, including wildlife scouts and community elders.
Accounts described elephants selecting particular plants when they seemed unwell, and mothers reportedly giving medicinal plant material to their calves.
From this, the researchers concluded that the elephants use 35 different plant species, and that 25 of those are known locally to have medicinal uses.
The study, published in the journal Scientific Reports, external, did not name the interviewees - keeping participants anonymous so they felt free to share their stories.
Their accounts reveal some intriguing details. In one testimony, a wildlife scout described seeing elephants using a plant known as Angurweet "as medicine to give to babies".
Angurweet is used as a remedy for ailments including stomach ache. The scout, who described elephant mothers mixing it in their mouths - "removing the leaves and chewing it until smooth, along with the roots of some other trees".
He also recounted that he had seen mothers mix this plant material with their own milk. "They give it to the babies, who chew on it themselves and spit out the solids".
Professor Michael Huffman, a primatologist based in Japan, currently at Nagasaki University, said this particular account was "tantalising", but more evidence would be needed to prove that elephants provided bespoke medical treatment for their calves.
The scientists have already embarked on gathering that evidence - giving the local wildlife experts they worked with cameras to record the behaviour they witness.
They are also analysing plants that the elephants use - looking for new medicines that the elephants themselves may have discovered.
Another lead reearcher on the project, Dr Fabien Schultz from the Bernhard Nocht Institute for Tropical Medicine in Hamburg, told BBC News: "Local knowledge has given us a map".
"We [now] want to follow the elephants and investigate whether they select particular plants in particular health contexts, and whether those plants have relevant biological activity."
Natural medicine factories
Many animals treat themselves with plants and other natural remedies.
The earliest scientific accounts of elephants practicing "self-medication" date back to the early third century.
Roman author Claudius Aelian in his text De Natura Animalium (On the Nature of Animals) described an elephant that, after being wounded by spears and arrows, consumed flowers and oil from an olive tree. The elephant made a full recovery.
Centuries later, these scientists are delving into what we can learn from wildlife about the properties of plants in the forest habitats they evolved in.
"There are medicine-producing organisms on this planet that have this incredible capability," Dr Freymann told BBC News." Medicine factories that exist all around us."
Prof Huffman, who was not involved in this study, added: "We now know that mosquitoes and drosophila (flies) self-medicate, bees self-medicate, as do many other species all the way up the evolutionary ladder to the great apes of Africa and Asia.
"WIth each new species studied, we have gained a greater understanding of our medicinal past."
For Dr Freymann, the findings also contain a lesson for our future.
"So many of the medicines we buy in a pharmacy were derived from compounds from trees, algae, from fungi, from coral reefs.
"It's a win-win for us to protect these forests and keep those natural pharmacies around... long enough that we can discover new natural products that could save us down the line."

The Pacific is churning with hurricanes. The Atlantic is quiet. Blame El Niño
It's been an extreme hurricane season in both the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans — but for vastly different reasons.
The Pacific Ocean has seen 18 hurricanes so far and 41 named storms overall, which are unusually high numbers for this point in the season.
The Atlantic Ocean is experiencing the exact opposite.
For the first time in over 100 years, no full-blown hurricanes have formed in the Atlantic as of September 25. Only seven named storms have formed, all of which were less-intense tropical storms.
"It's a tale of two basins," says Gabriel Vecchi, a professor of geosciences at Princeton University. "The Pacific: incredibly active. The North Atlantic: incredibly inactive."
Scientists say this is likely due to a powerful El Niño climate pattern. This natural pattern, which occurs every few years, tends to suppress hurricanes in the Atlantic while fueling more storms in the Pacific.
Hawaii is one place bearing the brunt of this shift.
Hurricane Nolo is expected to bring heavy rainfall and potential flooding to Hawaii this weekend, according to the National Hurricane Center.
It's the third hurricane to threaten the islands this year, following Hurricane Lala in August and Hurricane Lowell in early September.
The role of El Niño
Why is it such an unusual year? Climate scientists point to this year's record-breaking El Niño.
El Niño happens when water temperatures increase in the Pacific Ocean, near the equator. That warmer water provides fuel for hurricanes, driving bigger and more powerful storms. That means when a storm forms, it's more likely to reach hurricane strength.
It also affects weather patterns around the globe. In the North Atlantic, El Niño tends to increase wind shear, making it more difficult for hurricanes to form by tearing storms apart.
This year, El Niño is more intense than usual. Pacific water temperatures are already hitting record highs, even though the phenomenon won't reach its peak until later this year.
"We are headed toward what will almost certainly be the strongest El Niño on record," says Brian McNoldy, a senior research associate at the University of Miami. "It has exceeded expectations," in both the Pacific and the Atlantic, he says.
Warmer waters can also fuel more rapid intensification once storms form.
On Tuesday, Hurricane Polo, off Mexico's Pacific coast, strengthened from a tropical storm to a Category 5 hurricane in less than 24 hours.
Vecchi describes the intensification of Polo as "astounding."
Such rapid intensification can make storms more dangerous, in part by limiting the time people have to prepare.
What is the role of climate change?
Scientists are still trying to understand why some El Niño events are stronger than others. Some recent studies suggest climate change may be driving stronger El Niño events.
That science remains uncertain, Vecchi says, but the potential impacts of El Niño are well-understood.
El Niño generally raises temperatures globally and can make some areas around the world wetter and others drier.
In the immediate future, Paul Roundy, a professor of atmospheric science at the University at Albany, says he's watching for more storms to impact Hawaii along with droughts and fires in Central America.
El Niño could also bring a wetter winter for parts of the Southwestern U.S., where drought has persisted. But this could also increase the risk of floods.
These impacts from El Niño come on top of warming driven by human-caused climate change, which is already increasing the likelihood of extreme weather around the world.
"You can think of climate change as always acting in the background of basically everything we're experiencing in the ocean, in the atmosphere," McNoldy says. "So it tips the scales."

In this India Today Special conversation, filmmaker Meghna Gulzar and actor Prithviraj Sukumaran discuss their film Daayra, addressing thematic complexities surrounding sexual assault cases, extrajudicial encounter killings, and growing public disillusionment with the criminal justice system. The discussion explores how systemic bottlenecks and an overburdened judiciary with millions of pending cases lead to public frustration, often driving societal support for immediate retribution and police encounters over constitutional due process. Reflecting on landmark events such as the 2012 Nirbhaya case and the 2019 Hyderabad police encounter, the creators dissect the moral conflicts faced by law enforcement and citizens alike. Prithviraj Sukumaran elaborates on his role as DCP Raman, explaining how the narrative juxtaposes violent crimes against women with retaliatory police actions to prompt societal dialogue without validating vigilantism or offering simplistic moral conclusions. Additionally, Meghna Gulzar highlights the civic function of cinema in confronting uncomfortable social realities rather than relying on standard commercial tropes. The panel also covers casting decisions, the shifting dynamics between theatrical exhibition and digital streaming platforms, and the increasing convergence between regional and mainstream Indian film industries.

Sales of Chinese hybrid cars have rocketed in the EU in the past four and a half years, new data shows, underlining growing concerns in Brussels over the future of the European car industry.
In 2022, just 659 Chinese-made fully hybrid cars (vehicles in which the petrol or diesel engine charge the motor and battery) were sold in the EU. However, after Brussels imposed anti-subsidy tariffs on fully electric cars from China in 2024, sales of hybrids have shot up to 160,662 in the first seven months of this year.
Eurostat figures show that sales of Chinese-made plug-in hybrid vehicles – models popular for longer driving distances which can recharge via both the fuel engine and an external power source – have also soared, rising from 56,706 sold in 2022 to 217,764 from January to July this year.
The volume of Chinese hybrids on the roads is now spooking the car industry and Brussels, which has asked China to voluntarily reduce its hybrid exports to the EU or face safeguards, likely to be quotas.
According to new figures released by the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association (ACEA), hybrid cars now account for almost 37% of the overall market, with electric cars making up just over 21% of the market.
ACEA figures showed three Chinese manufacturers – BYD, Chery, and Leapmotor – making significant inroads with triple-digit growth in the EU.
A fourth firm, Geely, has had a steady 8% increase in the first eight months of the year, and remains the most popular Chinese brand in the EU with 205,000 cars sold in the first eight months of the year. Its brands include Sweden’s Volvo and Polestar, the EU’s only all-electric car manufacturer.
BYD is catching up with Geely with sales year-on-year rocketing 163% with 177,000 units sold.
Both firms, along with a fifth Chinese manufacturer, SAIC, are now firmly ahead of Elon Musk’s Tesla which sold 142,000 cars across the bloc in the first seven months of the year.
European car manufacturers still dominate with the Volkswagen group selling 2m cars in the first eight months of the year.
Sales of electric cars are also growing fast in parts of Europe including Germany, up 75% to 69,000 units in August, and in France, where sales are up by 112%. In Slovenia sales have increased by 266%. This compares with the UK, up 27% in August to 28,000 EVs sold and Ireland up just 7% to 2,200 units.
Earlier this month, the European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, described the now €1.18bn-a-day trade deficit between the bloc and China as having reached an unsustainable “tipping point”.
The EU’s trade commissioner Maroš Šefčovič and his Chinese counterpart Wang Wentao will meet on 8 and 9 October to try to build a truce.
Also hoping for a trade truce are Donald Trump and Xi Jinping who meet in their third summit in 12 months in Washington on Thursday.
Trump agreed in South Korea last October to drop tariffs on certain Chinese imports in exchange for a suspension of China’s export restriction on rare earths, critical to the car industry across the US, EU and the UK.
Some believe a deal may not have been reached yet and the suspension may not be announced until the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation conference next month.

Why the viral clip of 'multitasking mom' at a baseball game has enraged people online
Video of woman carrying baby, diaper bag, trays of food toward waiting man draws disbelief and scorn
A woman with a baby strapped to her chest, a diaper bag on her back, and her arms full of food at a Major League Baseball game has inadvertently become a metaphor for the disproportionate load mothers carry — in this case, literally.
The woman was singled out by two legendary broadcasters at Tuesday's game between the Giants and the Twins at Oracle Park in San Francisco as she sidestepped back toward her seat balancing three trays of food.
"Holy smokes, Mike! Look at this," Duane Kuiper says as the woman makes her way across the aisle.
"If there's ever a true definition of a multitasking mother, that is the deal right there," Mike Krukow responds in the broadcast.
The clip, which has since gone viral, shows the man in the seat next to the "multitasking mother" staring at his phone until the woman is nearly beside him, standing up to move a coat out of her seat, then digging into his food while the woman shrugs the diaper bag off her back, still holding the grinning baby and two full trays.
"Did I just hear that guy say, 'Did you forget something?'" Kuiper asks, as the two broadcasters joke that maybe he she didn't bring any ketchup.
The broadcast returned to her a few more times between pitches while Kuiper and Krukow expressed disbelief at the scene, exclaiming, "are you kidding me?" and "bless her heart" as the man popped some fried food in his mouth.
"Well, that’s mom of the year right there!" Krukow said.
"She’ll be the last one to eat, too," added Kuiper.
Neither the woman nor the man sitting beside her have been identified. CBC News has contacted the San Francisco Giants and NBC for comment, but has yet to hear back.
Visual of a familiar sentiment
Without hearing from the people involved, observers can't know the context of the situation — like whether the man is her partner, or whether or not help was offered.
But while some have argued you can't judge a situation based on a short clip, for many others, "multitasking mom" represents invisible labour, the mental load of motherhood, and weaponized incompetence.
"How do I divorce someone else’s husband?" one person asked in the comments of an ESPNW Instagram reel of the clip viewed 40 million times by Friday. The comment was "liked" nearly 115,000 times.
"Let us stop normalizing this," someone else commented.
- Despite gains, women still do most of the housework. Will this gender gap ever narrow?
- Did 'Marathon Mom' ignore her kids? Why a viral video is enraging runners and mothers
The clip is resonating because it gave a visual to a familiar sentiment — that women do more household labour and family management, explained Shana MacDonald, the O'Donovan Chair in communication at the University of Waterloo, who researches social and digital media.
"This showed that in a very direct but almost comical way," she told CBC News.
On a broader scale, the past year has seen a significant increase in conversations around motherhood, MacDonald added. Some parts of society are emphasizing motherhood as "womens' central calling," she noted, while in other spheres, we're hearing more concerns about burnout and lack of support.
That includes some of the recent conversations about Lindsay Clancy, the U.S. mom who was on trial for the deaths of her three children, MacDonald said.
Clip is triggering for many: sociology prof
The clip from the Giants game offers people a chance to voice their frustrations, Lisa Strohschein, a sociology professor at the University of Alberta and editor-in-chief of the journal Canadian Studies in Population, told CBC News.
She cautioned people against rendering judgments without knowing any of the context, while adding that the clip has tapped into the anger about structural inequalities in our society.
In the U.S., for instance, reproductive rights are being rolled back, she noted, and so-called "trad wives" that glamourize domestic life are on the rise.
In Canada, while some studies have found that fathers are taking on more parenting than they have in the past, others have found mothers are still generally the managers of the household. Women also still consistently take on a larger share of unpaid household work, including chores and child care, according to a 2022 Statistics Canada report.
All that to say, a woman balancing trays of dinner and a baby while a man next to her eats seems to be triggering for a lot of people, Strohschein said.
"Women, when they see this — I think it's kind of like the last straw."

Russian woman mauled to death by bear as attacks surge across Siberian region
The attacks have been attributed to climate change and human carelessness

A Russian woman has died after being mauled by a bear in her garden, making her the seventh person to be killed by the animals in her Siberian region this month, according to state investigators.
The attack comes amid a wider series of deadly encounters across Russia that experts attribute to climate change and human carelessness.
Video footage released by officials in the Krasnoyarsk region of Siberia, located approximately 3,000 km (1,864 miles) east of Moscow, showed team members walking through woodland to inspect the body of the brown bear responsible for the mauling.
State news agency TASS reported that the 51-year-old woman was killed in the village of Voznesenka after discovering the animal attempting to gain entry to an outdoor pen where she kept domestic livestock.
"The bear lunged at the woman. The predator was shot dead by a neighbour of the deceased," TASS reported.
Experts quoted in Russian media explained that brown bears - which have launched attacks in at least 11 regions across Russia this year, causing at least 20 deaths - have been compelled to search further for food because an unseasonably early and dry spring left a shortage of wild berries in September.
Human activity has also contributed to the problem, with people leaving food waste exposed outdoors where it attracts bears and ignoring safety protocols, according to experts. Authorities in at least one region have also been accused of failing to keep bear numbers under control.
Milder and shorter winters, among other factors, have led to Russia's bear population more than doubling since 1990, when it stood at 130,000.
Environment ministry figures show that Krasnoyarsk accounts for nearly 27,000 of the 308,000 brown bears nationwide. On Wednesday, investigators in the region launched a criminal case into the local environment ministry, accusing officials of negligence that resulted in the deaths of six people — a figure that reached seven following the attack on the woman in her garden — in September alone.
State bodies had a legal responsibility to track bear populations and intervene immediately if human lives were endangered, investigators said.
"Despite numerous warnings of danger, officials from the ministry and other authorised officials failed to take measures to regulate the predator population and prevent their appearance in areas inhabited by people," investigators said in a statement.
"Monitoring data show that the brown bear population in the Krasnoyarsk region has increased 2.5-fold, reaching over 26,000 animals. Residents... have submitted more than 120 reports of brown bears entering the boundaries of settlements in more than 15 districts of the region, as well as in the cities of Krasnoyarsk, Zheleznogorsk and Zelenogorsk," they said.
Investigators warned residents to stay clear of woodland and to delay plans to go mushroom and berry picking, a widely popular Russian pastime.
"If you encounter a large predator, you have virtually no chance of survival," the statement said.
Other fatalities in the Krasnoyarsk region this month include a 39-year-old male logger and two women who were gathering mushrooms.
In Siberia's Irkutsk region, an elderly male mushroom picker was killed by a bear this month, alongside two men gathering wild plants in woodland.
During one of the most high-profile incidents this year, a bear attacked two tourists in their tent in the Altai region in August. It dragged a 29-year-old female camper from the tent, killed her, and buried her body in the forest.
In the Siberian region of Tuva, ice hockey coach Alexander Kuzmenko — father of NHL player Andrei Kuzmenko — died this week after being attacked by a bear during a fishing trip.
The environment ministry has attempted to downplay the surge in fatal attacks.
"In recent years, around 20 to 30 cases of bear attacks have been recorded annually," it told the RBC news outlet.
"The only abnormal spike was in 2014, when there were 166 cases. The thing is, nowadays everyone has a smartphone, and information spreads quickly via the internet and social media, which creates the impression that the problem is widespread."

Calcutta HC division bench sets aside order protecting Congress candidate in Nandigram by-poll
A division bench also expressed surprise at the protection granted to Milan Pradhan, the arrested candidate, by a single Judge bench on Thursday.
A division bench of the Calcutta high court on Friday set aside an order of the single bench which had ordered that the Congress’ candidate for the upcoming by-election in Nandigram on October 6 should not be treated as arrested in a 2007 case.
The division bench, headed by chief justice Ravindra Vithalrao Ghuge, expressed surprise at the protection granted to Milan Pradhan, the arrested candidate, by a single-judge bench on Thursday.
“The division bench has set aside the single bench’s order. The single bench, while observing that Pradhan be allowed to campaign and contest the by-poll, had ordered that he should be not treated as arrested in a case registered in Khejuri police station in 2007, as it was not flagged during the last hearing on September 22,” said Ajitesh Pandey, advocate representing Pradhan.
The court also directed the state police not to take any coercive steps against Pradhan in the particular case till October 12.
The Calcutta high court had said on Thursday that Pradhan be allowed to contest the Nandigram bypoll properly, while holding that he would not be treated as arrested in a case for which he was sent to judicial remand by a lower court till October 7.
Milan Pradhan, the candidate, was arrested on September 18 in connection with a 2007 murder case and later shown as arrested in five other cases, all registered in the same year. Earlier this week, two lower courts at Contai and Haldia in East Midnapore sent him to judicial custody till October 7. With the by-election scheduled on October 6, Pradhan will not be able to campaign if he is denied bail. To be sure, arrest and judicial custody do not disqualify Pradhan from contesting the bypoll.
He moved the Calcutta high court seeking bail so that he may campaign for the by-election scheduled on October 6.
The bail petitions in four murder cases registered at Nandigram police station in 2007 were heard by a bench of justice Tirthankar Ghosh on Friday. The court is likely to hear the matter again on Monday.

A woman in a tribal village cut off by floods in Andhra Pradesh’s Alluri Sitharama Raju district died on Friday (September 25, 2026), a day after giving birth to a boy, because overflowing streams and a washed-away bridge kept her from a primary health centre about 6 km away, according to initial reports. The rain came with the deep depression that crossed the north Andhra coast on Thursday night.
Lavanya, of Gangavaram village in Darakonda panchayat in G.K. Veedhi mandal, went into labour on Thursday night and delivered a baby boy. She then fell unconscious and her condition deteriorated.
Villagers tried to take her to the Darakonda Primary Health Centre (PHC) but could not, because several streams on the route were overflowing after the heavy rain. The PHC is about 6 km from Gangavaram by the Narsipatnam-Chintapalli-Sileru road, normal conditions, according to Google Maps. A bridge connecting the village to the plains had also been washed away, and the village was cut off.
They looked for other routes to take Lavanya to a health facility, but no vehicles were available because of the continuing heavy rain and the state of the roads.
Lavanya died on Friday. The newborn boy is reported to be safe.
Officials in the district had been warned. On Wednesday, Joint Collector T. Sripooja directed officials across the Agency mandals to identify in advance the places where streams and seasonal waterways were likely to overflow, set up control rooms in every mandal and keep the district control room informed on road connectivity and essential services. Roads in G.K. Veedhi mandal were already damaged or washed away that day, The Hindu reported. In the neighbouring Parvathipuram Manyam district, the Collector on Friday ordered about 158 pregnant women in flood-hit tribal areas to be moved to hospitals and health centres.
