The offers had come in earlier that day. Paulina Borsook, 72, allowed herself a flash of excitement before returning to the question of what had ruined her life.
“I don’t know what to make of it,” she said as we drove to lunch. I’d picked Borsook up outside her home near Oakland, California, a basement unit that she calls “Ice Station Zebra” on account of the cold and the color scheme and the isolation. At least that’s how I was encouraged to picture it. Borsook didn’t want me to come inside, lest I pull the old magazine hack’s scam of investing the decor with symbolic significance. She wrote enough stories of this kind in her heyday, back when she was landing bylines in WIRED and the like, to know how the game gets played. Later, she explained over email: “this place i ended up in reflects me not at all. i lost all i owned when i couldnt pay for storage and this place is the best i could find that worked with my disabilities. so i feel it REALLY doesnt reflect me/my taste/my preferences. shame and aversion.”
What had happened to Paulina Borsook? The question was haunting her, even on a day when she’d gotten such good news. It’s haunted her for a quarter-century now. In 2000, after years writing about Silicon Valley, she published a book, Cyberselfish, that discerned within the tech utopianism of the era a dead-eyed, woman-hating social malevolence—what the subtitle called the “Terribly Libertarian Culture of High-Tech.” It was smart at a moment when the whole of the tech industry had gone dumb, and it was funny where Silicon Valley was at its most self-serious. Cyberselfish got warm, if occasionally baffled, reviews. It sold something like 5,000 copies in hardcover and another 2,000 in paperback, a respectable mid-list number, no blockbuster but not a dog, either.
And then … nothing. Editors stopped taking her calls. No fellowships materialized, no second book deal, no regular MSNBC spots for the dotcom Cassandra of the boom times. Borsook couldn’t get work. She began to wonder if she had been blacklisted. Her health, always wobbly, only worsened. She was living in other people’s houses. She went broke, a process she likened to a fire in which everything burns to the ground, and was getting by on a GoFundMe and support from friends. She’d taken to calling the book TDB. That damn book.
When Borsook and I first met, in December of last year, she was fully in the midst of what she terms “this resuscitation thing.” It had happened so quickly and altogether without her knowledge: a social media post here, another one over there, celebrated tech critics like Gil Durán of The Nerd Reich exhuming her book and waving it around as proof that, even in the go-go days of the dotcom bubble, some people saw where things were headed. “Instead of centering men who missed the boat (and still don’t seem to get it), let’s lift up the work of Paulina Borsook, who saw it all very clearly and tried to warn us 25 years ago,” Durán wrote in a widely shared post on Bluesky—in response to a 2025 WIRED essay by Steven Levy. Borsook was christened a prophet, unappreciated in her time but uniquely fitted to ours. Hadn’t she written of “testosterone-poisoned guys with chips on their shoulders and too much time on their hands” years before the manosphere? Hadn’t she recuperated the Luddites as “early protesters of de-skilling” back when “Luddite” was an epithet? Hadn’t she raised her eyebrows at the theorists of Sand Hill Road playing footsie with eugenics? Cyberselfish became a minor phenomenon without Borsook so much as saying a word about it. The New York Times profiled her, calling her “The Writer Who Dared Criticize Silicon Valley.” It’s like what a friend once told her: The universe isn’t done with you yet.
Publishers were now keen to get the book back in circulation. That day in December, five of them had sent their bids to her agent. (Eventually, Borsook would settle on Tin House, which published a new edition of Cyberselfish in mid-September, with a foreword by Durán.) The offers were validation, after all those years in the wilderness. Things were finally looking—
“It really kind of broke my heart in so many ways,” Borsook was saying now at the restaurant, as we waited to order. Her mind was back in 2001, wondering again what had happened to her career. Was it something she’d written? Could it have been an actual blacklist? Was it something as depressingly commonplace as sexism? “I really hate playing that card,” she said, “but I do have to wonder.” She just couldn’t figure it, even still, all these years later. In a way, the happy turn of events in the past few months had left her even more discombobulated. As she told me more than once, “I don’t know how to think about myself anymore.” She’d won me over in a matter of hours—a common enough phenomenon, I would learn, among people who find themselves in Borsook’s orbit. When I dropped her off that afternoon, I promised—only half in jest—to find the guy who killed her career.
Ok, but first I have to tell you about Dick Pick. Literally his name. Richard A. Pick. Went by Dick. It was the 1960s, and back then you could walk around with a name like that and no one would think to laugh, even if you were, as Dick Pick apparently was, something of a serial flirt.
Dick Pick was a software developer for a military contractor during the Vietnam War. The story goes that the Army needed a way to track spare parts for Lockheed’s Cheyenne attack helicopter. Alongside his business partner, Don Nelson, he came up with a database operating system that they called—and here you have to imagine two of the shit-eatingest grins you’ve ever seen—the Generalized Information Retrieval Language System: GIRLS. (What, you thought tech bros were a new phenomenon?) Like a lot of tech innovation underwritten by defense spending, GIRLS was soon put to commercial use. Eventually it came to be known as PICK, and it was with this latter name that the operating system found itself under the fingertips of one Paulina Borsook, an employee at a small software company in Marin County.
Before she became one of the sharpest media observers of early Silicon Valley, Borsook first learned how to see tech. That happened in the early 1980s, in front of one of those so-called minicomputers that were in fact big enough to be buried in. The company was called Construction Information Systems, and Borsook was doing some technical writing, documenting in the plainest language she could muster how the software worked.
She learned two important things at that job. The first is that tech is “infrastructure, not magic,” she wrote in a 2015 essay. The second is that the computer is a way of seeing into the mind of another human. It is, ineluctably, social. “Learning about PICK,” she wrote, “taught me that software was a human artifact; that is, I began to be able to think the way the creators of PICK thought … The dyer’s hand, the design sensibility, the cognitive blind spots: all evident and all human artifacts. Technology is idiosyncratic like the humans who devise it and the people who make it are just people.”
Everything Borsook would later write as a journalist covering the industry—the frisky pieces for Salon and Suck, the weightier profiles for WIRED, every barbed word of Cyberselfish—seemed to flow from a simple imperative drawn from her experience at that minicomputer: never lose sight of the human in the machine, the Dicks (as it were) behind the system. Once, she described her writerly voice as one of “agonized humanism,” and that’s it exactly. She was appalled by those in the industry who were determined to leave the human behind. “The most virulent form of philosophical technolibertarianism is a kind of scary, psychologically brittle, prepolitical autism,” she wrote in an especially pungent passage in Cyberselfish. “It’s an inability to reconcile the demands of being individual with the demands of participating in society … these technolibertarians make a philosophy out of a personality defect.”
Her own politics ran to the left, broadly speaking, though like a lot of political commentators of her time she seemed to cherish her own à la carte apostasies. She wasn’t embarrassed to say she agreed with the libertarians in their premises. More than anything she, too, wanted “to be left alone,” she wrote in Cyberselfish. But what Borsook brought to her journalism was an understanding of Silicon Valley as a social creation. Some of that can be attributed to growing up in Pasadena during the space-age boom. She remembers the “vaguely New Deal mentality” of the engineers and scientists at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory and Caltech, all of them beneficiaries of robust state investment in the war machine. In a place like that, there could be little mistaking the public’s role in the development of new technologies. Thus did Borsook receive an early inoculation against the basic fetishism that would come to define the culture of Silicon Valley—the idea that the power of technology is inherent and not derived from the social relations that produced it.
We shouldn’t overstate things. Not everyone who lived or worked in the shadow of the military-industrial complex drew the same lessons about the virtues of government. In his indispensable 2006 book From Counterculture to Cyberculture, Fred Turner reminds us that the research laboratories spun up during the Second World War were also sites of freewheeling collaboration across disciplines, liberated (so it seemed) from hierarchy—sites of what today we might call disruption. And believe it or not, all those earnest poindexters with their slide rules offered an organizational model for the libertarian communalists of the following era. This was the milieu that would eventually spawn the magazine you have in your hands now. When Borsook began writing for WIRED in the 1990s, it was something of a collision between two very different ways of understanding the political economy of the American midcentury.
Borsook grew up precocious and miserable, the daughter of “infanticidal” parents from whom, at one point, she sought legal emancipation. In 1968, when she was 14 years old, Borsook was shot in the head with a .45 Colt at a distance of 6 feet. She’d been with a couple of girlfriends, and one of them had fired the gun. The official story, the one they gave the cops, was that it was an accident, just dumb kids horsing around. The real story, as Borsook would tell it in 2013, as part of an art installation she called My Life as a Ghost, is that the friend had taken the gun out of a kitchen drawer—it was the friend’s house, and the friend’s parents were Birchers—and started waving it around. Borsook took cover behind the wall in another room. After a moment she popped her head out to see what was happening. Her friend pulled the trigger. Borsook remembers two things: a ringing, pulsing sound, and then silence. The bullet had ripped through her cheek and left through the back of her neck.
Borsook has no doubt the shooting was “accidentally on purpose,” some violent fugitive impulse escaping the tangle of teenage love-hate. She tells the story now without self-pity or sentiment, simply as a way of explaining why her brain works the way it does. Even in the moment, she refused any histrionics. She went to the kitchen and poured cold water on the hole in her face, told her friends to call the operator, and then somehow gave them to understand that now was the time to get their stories straight.
“I felt protective” toward the friend who shot her, Borsook explains now. “I know she immediately regretted it. And I said we need to come off as like we’re just a bunch of ditzy teenagers, as opposed to these alarmingly precocious, kind of scary young women that we were.” She says she refused to cooperate with any attempt to prosecute her friend. The two remained close for years.
It was the jolt from the impact, Borsook believes, that caused the most lasting damage. The effects soon began to present themselves. “That gunshot prematurely aged my brain,” she said in her presentation for My Life as a Ghost. She continued: “I flunked calculus three times and I had no idea why this happened. Ever after, I simply could not process texts of a certain density, such as a geology textbook or a legal opinion. It all washes out. My brain just cannot process and retain quantitative transactions and language of a certain abstraction—all of which are necessary to function as a symbolic-manipulator in a knowledge economy.” (It isn’t just an issue of cognitive function. She says her lifelong environmental sensitivities—so acute now that she can’t even wear a metal watch—were likely exacerbated by the shooting.)
Borsook got a degree in psycholinguistics from UC Berkeley, but even then, communication of any kind was difficult, an issue that predated the shooting. Whether in her speech or her writing, she had a tendency to be “gnomic,” “elliptical,” “highly condensed”—her words. “How my friends put up with it, I don’t know,” she says. She developed a conversational habit, still obvious today, of rounding off her sentences by asking if what she had just said made any sense. “I began to realize that a lot of the ways I think and speak about things don’t make sense to a lot of people,” she says, “so I have to check in with them.” She was still chatty, and nothing would seem outwardly amiss. But she knew something had fritzed out in her head. “Parts of my brain just shut down forever,” she tells me. “Does that make sense?”
One thing that helped, oddly enough, was the technical writing. “Imagine if your hands were really palsied,” she says, gnarling her fingers in front of her face. That’s what it was like in her head, all the words gone stiff and useless. But the precision and clarity required of technical writing forced Borsook to work at her sentences, to limber them up, until ordinary readers could grasp them. The technical stuff certainly had no long-term effects on her prose style—her writing for popular audiences, zippy and full of late-gonzo neologisms like “el stewpido” and “our fabu hyper-accelerated crashboombang economy,” was never, ever plain. To listen to her explain it, the change was more akin to rebuilding an atrophied muscle. She had rehabilitated the capacity to make herself legible to other people. “I could just feel things sort of unkinking,” she says, relaxing her fingers and pulling them from her face. “It was like Jane Fonda aerobics.”
She moved over to the technical end of journalism not long after, joining the staff of Data Communications magazine. That’s where Katie Hafner met her in 1984. Hafner had come on as the news editor; Borsook was the new products editor. The work was impenetrably abstruse. “I have to set the scene for you,” says Hafner, who went on to have a distinguished career in tech journalism. “Paulina was a psycholinguistics major at Berkeley. I was a German literature major at UCSD. This guy Peter Schmader [the managing editor] was some kind of philosopher. The two copy editors, Sue and Sandy, were also English-major people. And we were all complete fish out of water.”
Hafner was immediately taken with Borsook: “She was like the smartest, grumpiest person I’d ever met. And I was in total awe. I’d never met anyone like her. So blunt, completely honest, had something trenchant to say about absolutely everything around her.” Once Hafner set her up with a friend. “They went on a date, and the next day he was just furious,” she recalls. “And he said, ‘Your friend, she has a lot of opinions about everything.’ And I said, ‘Oh, yeah, what’s wrong with that?’”
It was Borsook’s brain that Hafner “worshipped.” She had the right phrase for anything. Hafner remembers a piece Borsook wrote about a chocolate shop in Berkeley in which she described customers who would arrive just after close and “piteously rap on the windows.” Hafner loved the phrase so much she used something like it in a story of her own, in The New York Times. There was the time the two of them went clothes shopping, and Borsook said, “Oh, are you like me—you’re like a sausage with a string tied around the middle?” Hafner laughs. “That is indelibly etched in my head.” When Hafner was living in Berlin, Borsook visited and stayed with her. Hafner paid her friend the highest of compliments a writer could ever receive, from a fellow writer, no less: She asked Borsook to read one of her short stories aloud, as a bedtime story.
The event was in San Francisco, and it was about women and the internet. This would’ve been sometime in the 1990s—Borsook can’t remember when or where, exactly. The commercial internet was in its infancy, and for all its promise of scrambling the dominant gender paradigms, it was also proving to be a fantastic means of shoring them up.
This was also true of the communes in the late ’60s and early ’70s, the ones that gave rise to Stewart Brand’s Whole Earth Catalog and eventually to WIRED itself—the men up front, leaders of the utopia, and the “women in the back having babies and putting bleach in the water to keep people from getting sick,” as Turner has put it. But computer work had belonged to women before it was regendered, in the span of a generation, from a type of clerical job to the domain of the charismatic autonomous man. Nowhere was that more evident than in the media dedicated to covering Silicon Valley. At the talk there were some 30 women in attendance. When they were asked if they read WIRED, they all raised their hands. “And when they were asked if they hated WIRED,” Borsook wrote in an essay, “they all raised their hands.”
The piece appeared in a remarkable anthology from 1996, Wired Women: Gender and New Realities in Cyberspace, published by Seal Press, a sort of consciousness-raising meeting in book form. One of the anthology’s editors, Elizabeth Reba Weise, stops short of saying it was the first book to examine the experience of women online, but it was certainly one of the early ones. “We called it cyberspace, for God’s sake,” Weise says—that’s how early this was. Over and over the contributors, a mix of academics and journalists and women working tech jobs of one kind or another, emphasize that the computer and the internet are tools for women, a way of enabling communication and connection—the gendered division of labor coming to roost now in the differing ways of being online. From Weise’s intro: “In my circle, computers aren’t fetish objects, but tools.” From Ellen Ullman’s essay: “We use the Internet as a tool, like the phone or the fax, a way to transmit news and make appointments.” Susan Clerc: “Like the TV and VCRs, the home computer is a tool that lets her participate fully in the community.” And Borsook: Women “generally are interested in the utilitarian value, not fetish-worthiness, of tools.” The Australian feminist Dale Spender has a pithy old line about computers that is applicable here: “Women use them, whereas men fall in love with them.”
WIRED from its start in 1993 was a magazine for falling in love with computers. Digital utopianism was the order of the day. One of the magazine’s founding editors, John Battelle, today calls the mindset a “naively optimistic libertarianism.” There were more circumspect voices in tech media—in particular the inspired and unjustly forgotten Processed World, which viewed computers from the perspective of the people who had to work with them. In 1995, a British magazine called Mute published an essay, “The Californian Ideology,” that laid out a “critique of dotcom neoliberalism” similar in some ways to Borsook’s. A decade earlier, Lenny Siegel and John Markoff published The High Cost of High Tech: The Dark Side of the Chip, an early criticism of Silicon Valley. Alongside the media were tech-dubious movements, like the mostly memory-holed Neo-Luddites of the 1990s, not to be confused with the new Neo-Luddites. But the critics weren’t breaking through. Processed World’s cofounder, Chris Carlsson, characterizes the era as “an unbelievable frenzy of boosterism and back slapping, we’re all getting rich, ha ha ha, isn’t this great, here, have another line, come to this fancy dinner, here’s a glass of champagne. Oh, you don’t want to be part of the party? Get the fuck out of here.”
In her essay for Wired Women, Borsook reviewed every issue of the magazine to that point and ran the numbers. “Women were the subject of about 15 percent of WIRED articles and only one cover out of twenty-five as of June 1995,” she reported. “There are vague in-house grumbling intimations by women on staff of likely accomplished females being shot down as article-subjects in WIRED editorial meetings and of no-account off-point numb-nut guys being celebrated instead—but that’s par for the course in any mostly-male arena.” She was even more dismayed to find that only 15 percent of WIRED authors to that point were women. One month, she was the only woman on the masthead.
Borsook had been writing for WIRED more or less from its inception. She’d bailed out of Data Communications at the end of the ’80s and had gotten her MFA at Columbia, and now she was making a go of it as a freelancer. One Friday in 1993, she emailed the magazine’s cofounder, Louis Rossetto, a self-styled radical libertarian, asking if he’d be interested in her fiction. Her agent mailed over her MFA thesis, whose concluding novella was a story about an affair that unfolds over email, in all the “perversions and evasions” of what was then a newish medium. It was smart and allusive and full of finely observed shifts in interpersonal weather. By Monday, as Borsook tells it, she was a contributor to WIRED. “Love Over the Wires” appeared in the magazine’s fourth issue.
In short order she was writing big-ticket features. There were profiles of super networker Esther Dyson and Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen. While an ethos of tech utopianism pervaded, writers were allowed to roam with their prose, and Borsook’s touch was unmistakable in her stories. She called Allen “a nerd nonpareil, resembling nothing so much as a manatee with dancey blue eyes.” He was apparently upset with the description, Hafner recalls. “And Paulina, she was so funny. She said, ‘But it’s really sweet! They’re really big and gentle!’”
The pieces weren’t necessarily critical of the tech world, not in the way that Cyberselfish would be, but neither did they go in for gooey panegyrics to the likes of Newt Gingrich, WIRED’s cover boy in August 1995. Despite the plum assignments, Borsook never felt like she belonged. In her Wired Woman essay, she describes herself as a token for the “editorial boykings” of the magazine. “If one is not interested in participating in circle-jerk exercises and paying homage to the alpha male of the moment,” she wrote, “what is there left to do at WIRED?” She bickered with Kevin Kelly, WIRED’s founding executive editor, over a section in her Dyson profile in which she addressed how gender might have shaped her subject’s career. She’d been surprised by how many people asked her, in the course of her reporting, about Dyson’s dating life—surprised as well by the “personal quality of what her detractors had to say,” the snide stuff about her clothes and manners. Kelly, in Borsook’s telling, didn’t think it was relevant. They went back and forth. The section stayed in. (Kelly remembers a narrower dispute. He writes in an email: “My recollection was that she was asking Dyson if she was gay/lesbian and she wanted to report Dyson's response [which I think was ‘negative’], and I thought it was all immaterial to Dyson’s contributions.”)
“I mostly want to be left alone to do my work, to get at that still silent voice within, and not be fighting ideological battles my editors at WIRED might not even consciously realize they are engaging in,” Borsook wrote. “Progress means exchanging one set of problems for a more interesting set of problems—but my struggles with WIRED have been generating problems of ever-decreasing interest. I strive to have other, better, more rewarding and less stupid battles to fight.”
“I always had a fondness for Paulina,” says Battelle. “I mean, I generally have a fondness for difficult people. Like most of my good friends are extremely difficult people. I never was like, ‘Oh, this woman, oh my God, now I’ve gotta deal with her.’ I enjoyed working with her. And yeah, it was difficult. And I did feel like she seemed to sort of arrive besieged, you know?”
Battelle says he “got the sense she didn’t completely buy into some of the core premises and values” of WIRED in that era. He goes on: “She was very critical of the political philosophy that was evident in the magazine.”
In a sense, Cyberselfish is a continuation of Borsook’s criticisms of early WIRED. In the mid 1990s, her agent, Stuart Krichevsky, started pitching the book around under the pulpier title Deadly Embrace, a computer science term for when processes get stuck because each is waiting for another to release a resource. (It became Cyberselfish after Mother Jones published an essay by Borsook under that headline.) Nothing about it came easy. A deal with WIRED’s publishing arm fell apart after Borsook gave an interview in which she recited some of her criticisms of the magazine. Another publisher proved a bad fit. Eventually, Lisa Kaufman at PublicAffairs rescued Cyberselfish from publishing oblivion, and the book landed just as the dotcom bubble began to deflate.
If sales were modest, the book was “a reputational success” for the publisher, Kaufman says. The New York Times sang its praises. Turner goes so far as to call it “the first actual from-the-left critique of the tech world that I’m aware of” and “one of the first clear articulations of some of the really nasty conflicts that are built into some of the cybercultural thinking of the period.” He adds: “The thing that Paulina got right off the bat: She just saw right through that, all the way through. She saw that these firms were commercial firms. They were seeking market positions. They were seeking standing.”
Not everyone had such glowing reviews. Battelle, broadly sympathetic to the book’s premise, recalls thinking Cyberselfish was a “pretty thin deconstruction” of tech libertarian utopianism. One tech journalist recalled similar grouching among colleagues about the lack of reporting, by which they presumably meant investigative legwork. Cyberselfish was full of reporting in the most basic sense—conversations over dinner, dispatches from conferences, information gleaned from others and related to readers—but it was all of the “soft” variety, cultural and thus dismissible.
The work dried up after the book came out—though it was drying up for a lot of people in the first decade of the new century. Borsook couldn’t seem to catch anyone’s eye. She wrote an essay for Processed World in 2001 on “the disappeared of Silicon Valley,” about failure in the time of the dotcom boom, the piece itself a narrative of Borsook’s own failure to write the story she had set out to tell. She tried other subjects. Borsook was sure she could scare up some interest in a story about a grassroots campaign she was working on, Stop the Spray, which was agitating against the use of pheromone pesticides in the Bay Area targeting the light brown apple moth. Nothing. For a time she lived as an Airbnb superhost in return for free rent. All her worst suppositions about not belonging were being confirmed. “The universe is just telling me to go jump off a pier,” as Borsook puts it.
Maybe she was catastrophizing—or maybe catastrophe was just a normal state of affairs for her. “There was always this sort of Calamity Jane thing about Paulina,” Hafner says. “She’d go through stuff, and you’d go, ‘Oh, my gosh.’” She would go on a work trip, and someone would break into her room and steal her prized watches. Or she would show up to the office one day with an enormous bandage on her leg, the victim of a burst hot-water bottle. “I just thought, how does this woman endure what she endures?” Hafner says.
Could an actual blacklist have been among her torments? I put the question to a number of people.
John Battelle, who was gone from WIRED by the time Cyberselfish came out: “I think it’s conceivable. Whether or not it’s factual, I can’t speak to … WIRED was a quasi-religious community. And while we were OK with people debating fundamental principles of the community, we weren’t OK with people, you know, with ad hominem attacks. My sense is if someone kind of wasn’t on the WIRED train, then, you know, they’re not gonna be invited to write for the magazine. That doesn’t strike me as an unusual thing.”
Gil Durán, whose angry thread on Bluesky helped kick-start the Borsook revival: “It’s likely. At the same time, one of the ways you get blacklisted in journalism is just nobody’s interested in you, right? Doesn’t have to be a conspiracy or something. As we’ve seen, there was not much of a hunger for real criticism of tech in Silicon Valley. “
Katie Hafner: “I would lean heavily on the side of there was no conspiracy. She was grumpy. She didn’t want to write suck-up stories, which was a lot of what was happening back then. That doesn’t mean she was blacklisted. It’s just that she had a lot of opinions.”
Steven Levy, longtime contributor to WIRED: “I’d push back against the word blacklist—especially [given] the connotations of it, the horrendous things of the McCarthy era. It may very well be that what she was pushing in the core of her writing was an unpopular theme which now people see maybe there was something to it, but back then led to people thinking, we don’t have an appetite for that kind of story.”
John Markoff, tech reporter for the Times until 2016: “There are stories people don’t want to hear. It wasn’t so much about Paulina but that the things she wanted to write didn’t have a market.”
Hafner again: “It was just because she’s Paulina. I mean, it’s hard to be Paulina.”
“I don’t even know if the blacklist existed,” Borsook was saying. “I don’t think it existed.” This time I was the one who’d brought up her years in exile. We were sitting in the shade in her friend’s backyard in Berkeley. It was August, and she was waiting to be photographed for this very magazine, the one that had handled her roughly for a time and then, maybe worse, had decided not to handle her at all. The new edition of Cyberselfish was no longer notional. The paperback had arrived in the mail that day, and when she pulled it out of the padded envelope and held that damn book up, it was as if she were displaying an award. Her agent, Stuart Krichevsky, told me that when the Tin House offer came in, Borsook practically squeaked.
“I—this sounds weird—I don’t think TDB was important enough to be blacklisted,” Borsook said. She had come to see her own exile as part of a larger process. No conspiracies or blacklists were needed to render her disposable. “It was such a changed media landscape,” she said. It was more than the media, too. From the vantage of 2026, Cyberselfish reads a little like Borsook’s account of her own encroaching obsolescence—she was describing a campaign, ultimately successful, to root out a whole way of understanding tech. There could be no seeing the dyer’s hand, no perceiving the Dicks in the system, not in the utopia the technolibertarians were building for us.
Earlier we had been talking about ghosts, the way they seem to pop up in different corners of the story Borsook tells about her life. Even before her friend had shot her, she had this spectral sense of herself, a compulsive feeling of not belonging that only heightened with the violence done to her brain. “Hmm, maybe I really am not supposed to be here,” as she put it in 2013, “and my life ever since has been an accident.” She was standing on a deck now, white hair blowing this way and that in the wind, white scarf wrapped around her neck. A photographer was snapping away, an assistant holding up a bounce board, redirecting daylight toward Borsook’s face. A strange but happy image suggested itself to me: an old ghost in a warm sun.
Does that make any sense?

Why this break has come at the worst time for De Zerbi & Spurs
- Published
Big spending always means big ambitions, but shelling out so much money on so many players the way Tottenham did this summer produces problems for any manager, and there is no quick fix.
If I was given a bundle of cash and asked to buy an outfit for a wedding, and I spent every penny of it on pink shoes, brown trousers, yellow shirt and orange tie, then I am sure you would all say that just doesn't work.
That is similar to what has happened at Spurs, where the board backed Roberto de Zerbi to the hilt with an outlay on new players of around £400m.
It was an almost unprecedented occurrence from a club that has always been renowned for being careful with investment in their team, and it sent expectations from many Spurs supporters through the roof.
The club had just avoided relegation two seasons running, finishing 17th twice in a row, but suddenly some fans were looking forward to a season competing for trophies and a top-four finish.
Their early results and performances have been disappointing, of course, but fans have to understand all the different factors that affect you when you are building a team - and it is ridiculous to suggest De Zerbi should be under pressure already, especially after he kept them up last season.
Let's give De Zerbi a chance
Finding a way for your club to win takes a manager in lots of different directions but they all involve time - on the grass or with social interaction with the players.
Not only has De Zerbi not been given that early time and opportunity, the majority of his players have now been taken away from him for another three weeks on international duty.
De Zerbi has many other issues to deal with, from Tottenham's poor home form to their inability to recover from conceding the first goal in games.
But his biggest challenge right now will be to fit those players who have just arrived in with the ones already at the club, into a unit that plays as a team and produces results so that the money the club has spent is justified.
All of this will take time, and patience, and all the kinds of little detail that supporters never see.
In my day, we were given time to create a team, and a family. For today's managers, time seems more limited than ever.
We are only five games into the season but there are already some Spurs fans who seem to think De Zerbi is the worst manager in the world, even though he has proved elsewhere how good he is.
I like De Zerbi's passion, and his approach. That will count for nothing if Spurs don't eventually produce, but let's give him a proper chance.
Combinations can take time to click
De Zerbi is a very passionate, straight-talking and ambitious manager who demands total commitment and backing from his board.
He has definitely had that at Spurs, which has left people wondering why he has made such a slow start.
But, before the season started, I thought his biggest challenge with so many different types of players arriving would be to put players together that fit as a team, not as a group of individuals.
I've been in that situation myself, for example in my early days at Stoke, when I signed Gerry Taggart and Michael Duberry to play together, two centre-halves who were complete opposites in relation to how they dealt with space on the pitch.
Gerry always wanted to drop off deeper because he wasn't overly quick, whereas Michael was fast and didn't ever worry about leaving space behind him.
I couldn't make Gerry any quicker, so common sense locked in and I had to convince Michael that he would have to take a step away from his main strengths of pace and power and work along Gerry's lines instead.
We spent a great deal of time on the grass in training until we finally got both working in unison. Both were different, but they understood the importance of working together as a pair for the benefit of the team. Even so, it still took time for it to click.
For any manager trying to build a successful team by developing combinations like that, the main thing you need is time with your players.
It can happen where a lot of new players settle in quickly at the same time and the team starts well - like Sunderland last season, or Brighton pretty much every year when they have lost several key players - but the difference is that while those clubs might also have changed their manager, they have not changed their identity.
Whether it is Sunderland and Brighton, or Brentford and Bournemouth, they all have a set identity so that when they look for a player to fit in a certain position, he has to have certain strengths.
When you don't have that solid base behind you, knowing exactly what is needed for certain positions, then bringing 10 new signings and all in one window like Spurs have just done, is going to create many issues for the coach.
Each player has a different personality and needs different amount of time to settle in, not only to a new environment but also to adjust to the demands of a very single-minded and demanding coach like De Zerbi is.
This settling-in period would have been covered if all the players had had a pre-season together, to get up to speed with their team-mates and what De Zerbi is asking of them, with his front-foot style of play.
That did not happen, and then even after the season started, Spurs were still adding to their squad.
Finding out who understands importance of teamwork
Coaching a team to be a team takes time, patience and a sound idea of the strengths of all your players.
Even when you have got that, trying to knit every player together takes time, and that is still De Zerbi's issue now.
For starters, he was always playing catch-up. Because all of his players were not in place when the season began, he missed the opportunity to assess his squad and impose his own principles on his top group of players.
He is a coach at heart and will want to be out on the training pitch conducting a system of work for the team, in and out of possession, that he believes will bring success to the club. This international break means he cannot do that with all his players.
Another issue De Zerbi has is that he has only been in the job a few months and he is still getting to know the existing players, not just the new ones, on and off the grass.
On it, you need to find out who understands the importance of teamwork and who doesn't, to iron out shortcomings and and see what works and what doesn't.
An example of when you realise something doesn't work was my experience at a club who had just bought a right-back from a top Premier League team, for more than £1m which was big money at the time.
We were struggling at the bottom of the league when I came in and needed a direction on the pitch that would bring better results.
During the defensive work we were doing in training, the full-back kept picking up what were, in my opinion, poor positions while covering from the opposite side to where the ball was.
I must have stopped the session on at least four occasions to remonstrate with him and give my view, but in the end the lad told me that this is not what he believed was right.
I immediately replaced him with a young full-back from the reserves who had been playing for the opposition in the drill, who understood his role was for the team, and not for himself.
Getting to know your players' characters too
Getting things right off the pitch is so important too, and that involves getting to know what your players' characters are like, finding out what they are like as individuals, and understanding their lifestyles.
I had three South American players at West Brom who were fantastic lads but we still had to look after them.
I spoke to my assistant, David Kemp, about taking them and their families out for dinner, and by spending time with them and their children and their wives I believe we won a degree of respect and trust that we would never have had if we had not bothered to meet them all together as a family.
You have to realise that players from different cultures can be used to living a different lifestyle, and this can make a difference to how quickly or how well they fit in.
I had one player in the Premier League whose routine I just could not believe, yet he became such an integral part of keeping a struggling club up.
His 24 hours typically played out like this - training from 8.30am to 1pm, home and bed until 9 or 10pm and then up and out again for dinner and then a casino or whatever, until the early hours.
Then he would be up for training, and he would go again.
It took me a few weeks to get to the bottom of this but, once I confronted him, he was adamant that his routine suited his lifestyle. He certainly knew the best restaurants around town, but his performances were always of the highest quality on the pitch.
Did he heed my advice? I think he did, but he was such a great lad, top player and a great team member that he wasn't a problem anyway.
He had been a bit isolated from the rest of the squad at first, but it just took him some time to integrate.
Again, finding out about him as an individual and making personal contact with him, was important, and it was something I always saw as vital with all my players.
Tony Pulis was speaking to BBC Sport's Chris Bevan.

Students strike across Germany in protest against military service
- Published
School strikes are taking place across Germany to protest against the possible reintroduction of compulsory military service.
One of the organisers of the strike, Bela Breitner, from School Strike Against Compulsory Military Service said the federal government was "serious about gradually reintroducing compulsory military service".
At one protest in Hamburg, demonstrators waved flags and held up banners emblazoned with the words "We won't take part in your wars".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made boosting Germany's military a priority following Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
A new law introducing voluntary military service came into force in January, with the aim of recruiting volunteers to increase the number of soldiers.
However, if the security situation worsens or if too few volunteers come forward, a form of compulsory military service could be considered by Germany's Parliament, the Bundestag.
Under the law, all 18-year-olds in Germany are being sent a questionnaire asking if they are interested and willing to join the armed forces.
One protester, 16-year-old Elias Bernhard, from Hamburg, said that the responses to the questionnaires "show that young people do not want to join the Bundeswehr [Germany's army]".
"That is why I am out on the streets today. That is why we are serious about striking until compulsory military service is off the table. We will carry on."
The questionnaire is mandatory for men and voluntary for women. All 18-year-old men will have to take a medical exam to assess their fitness for possible military service.
The organisers of the protests, say the trigger came after some 18-year-olds in the northern German towns of Kiel and Flensburg, were sent official invitations for medical exams, even though they expressed no interest in joining the army on their registration forms.
The group says over a hundred demonstrations are planned across Germany, including in Kiel, Hamburg, Berlin and Frankfurt.
A spokesperson for the Defence Ministry told the BBC that under the law, the obligation to undergo a medical examination applies "to all men liable for military service who were born after 31 December 2007".
This also applies to people who have stated that they have no interest in compulsory military service. The spokesperson said that since July around 1,000 18-year-old men, who showed no interest in the army, have had the medical exam.
During the Cold War, Germany, like many other European countries, had a large army. But it reduced its armed forces during the 1990s after the fall of the Iron Curtain.
Germany's former Chancellor, Angela Merkel, ended compulsory military service in 2011.
But now, in the face of perceived threats from Russia and heavy pressure from Germany's traditional ally, the US, Merz has vowed to transform the Bundeswehr into Europe's strongest conventional army.
The Bundeswehr currently has around 186,700 troops. By the early 2030s, Germany wants to raise the number to 260,000, supplemented by around 200,000 reservists, in order to meet new Nato force targets and strengthen Germany's defences.

Japan’s Financial Services Agency is stepping up its scrutiny of financing for AI data centers by the country’s biggest banks and life insurers, as major financial institutions increase their exposure to the rapidly expanding sector.
The regulator will examine areas including the lenders’ risk-management frameworks, according to a senior FSA official, who asked not to be named. The official said he’s talking about data center projects mainly in the United States.
In its policy priorities announced earlier this month, the agency identified project finance — including that for data centers — as an area for enhanced monitoring, along with lending to the domestic real estate sector.
Regulators around the world have been increasing their focus on financing for data centers and other AI-related infrastructure. The European Central Bank examined the risks faced by banks in the region from the artificial intelligence industry, Bloomberg reported in February. In Asia, Singapore’s central bank has warned that uncertainty over sustaining massive AI investments is a key challenge for global growth and financial markets.
The FSA has no intention of discouraging financing to AI data centers, which it sees as a growth sector, the official said. Still, regulator needs to pay closer attention to the risks surrounding such lending, citing uncertainty over whether hyperscalers can generate adequate returns on their massive spending, as well as the debate over the rapid pace of development and its safety.

In 1961, there was no measles vaccine. Jewel Murray remembers when one of her siblings caught it. Then another. And then her. Her siblings quickly recovered. But Murray, then a kindergartner, vividly recalls her father carrying her to their station wagon and rushing to the hospital, where she stayed for a month, partly in a coma.
“Since I survived rather than dying, why is my story worth repeating? The answer is simple: Children who die don’t grow up to tell their own stories,” said Murray, an internist and epidemiologist at the Dell Medical School at the University of Texas at Austin. “The current surge in measles cases should worry all of us.”

All Food Items in Ride A Pet
Food is the easiest option for upgrading your pets in Ride A Pet. Keep in mind that food stock is always limited, and if you don’t have solid late-game eggs in Ride A Pet, it is better to stockpile them. As each food item costs money, only use them on your best pet in the ranch.

Drinking at football matches - would fans welcome it?
- Published
When UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham embarked on his trip to the United Nations in New York, he might not have been expecting a question about football fans drinking alcohol in grounds.
Burnham firmly believes the law that prevents supporters from having a beer at their seat during a match is outdated.
It's a position the Everton supporter has long held, and when asked was happy to reaffirm.
"I do believe there is a case to remove that discrimination," said Burnham, who feels football fans are singled out compared to those of other sports and events.
There is no suggestion this is about to become official government policy, and last year MPs rejected a Conservative amendment to the Football Governance Bill that would have forced ministers to launch a formal consultation on scrapping the rule.
That was, of course, before Burnham returned to Downing Street.
It is a complicated and divisive issue, about not just safety. But it it something that match-going supporters actually want?
What the law says
Drinking alcohol at football grounds in England and Wales has been strictly controlled since the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act was introduced in 1985.
It was brought in to counter escalating hooliganism through the 1970s and into the 1980s.
The ban impacts clubs in the Premier League down to the National League. While beer can be sold, it must be consumed in areas that do not have a view of the pitch.
Yet fans who support teams in the National League North and South and below can drink alcohol around the pitch.
The ban is more strict in Scotland, with a law in place since 1981 that alcohol is only available in hospitality areas and not for other fans.
It was initially imposed following a riot during the 1980 Scottish Cup final between Rangers and Celtic at Hampden.
However, attitudes have been changing in recent seasons.
It was lifted as part of a pilot scheme last year, with several Scottish clubs selling alcohol in clearly defined, monitored areas of the stadiums. It started with lower-level clubs, eventually being extended to the Premiership.
The Scotland national team joined the trial for the friendlies against Japan and Curacao earlier this year. It has been extended to games against Switzerland on 29 September and Slovenia next month.
The Women's Super League in England has just completed two seasons of successful trials and the rule preventing drinking in the stands has now been removed by the league's governing company, WSL Football.
The women's game is not governed by the Sporting Events Control of Alcohol Act, enabling the competition organiser to make the change.
Is there support for the move within English football's corridors of power?
Premier League chief executive Richard Masters said in August the competition had not "got a specific view" and "we'd need to give it some really careful thought".
The English Football League, however, issued a statement on Thursday that said it would be "receptive to discussions around reviewing the current legislation".
It added member clubs had already provided "a mandate to lobby for appropriate reform" which had "not kept pace with significant developments in stadium management, safety and stewarding".
Fans' views differ on drinking in stands
The Football Supporters' Association has for some time backed changing the law.
Like the prime minister, it considers it to be unfair on football fans.
"I think it is outdated," FSA chairman Tom Greatrex told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme.
"If you go to watch football in Germany or in other places around the world, then it's perfectly acceptable.
"It is civilised and appropriate. There's no reason why that shouldn't be the case for football fans, as it is for fans of rugby league, watching Oasis, or anything else that happens often in the same stadiums in the same seats."
The FSA's position is that clubs should have the choice, in consultation with supporters, to sell alcohol.
Clubs might want to offer it in all stands, others in designated areas, while a few might choose not to do so at all.
Other sports offer designated alcohol-free sections, something that football clubs may wish to copy for some families and supporters who do not consume alcohol because of their religion.
The FSA acknowledges this, but believes having the option to make such decisions is important.
It believes relaxing the law would be more popular the further down the leagues you go, where alcohol sales could potentially provide a crucial additional income stream.
The UK Football Policing Unit rejected the suggestion, arguing alcohol plays "a significant part in violent and disorderly behaviour" and that "other sports simply don't see the violence and criminal behaviour" that football does.
Yet for Greatrex, there is already proof police are not open to ideas through their previous opposition to safe standing.
Before it was introduced four years ago, Mark Roberts, who has been the national lead for football policing since 2014, told the BBC it would make it "easier to throw missiles, engage in hate chanting, racism, sneak alcohol in, take cocaine".
"[The police] were telling everybody that we couldn't have standing at football again, that it would jeopardise safety, " Greatrex said.
"Actually, what we saw then was a controlled, managed pilot projects to get that re-established.
"There hasn't been the level of disorder that some of the police sources were saying there would be. I think the police should have more of an open mind and engage in this in a sensible and mature way."
For many match-going fans, however, the prospect of beer being thrown and potential anti-social behaviour outweighs the opportunity to watch a game with a pint.
Dave, a Chelsea fan from Twickenham, told Nicky Campbell on BBC Radio 5 Live, that he was "100% against it".
"Have a look at some of the footage you see on social media at Boxpark, for instance. A goal goes in and there is beer and lager thrown everywhere," he said.
"I don't want to go round stinking of other people's beer and there is a fashion among certain supporters to throw their beer everywhere.
"If people can't go without drink for a 45-minute period there is something the matter with them."
Adrian, from Leicester, claimed it would be the "worst idea you could come up with".
"There is enough trouble with other things in football, with the flares, drug taking and other things," he added. "You throw the alcohol in as well. Football is tribal whereas other sports they aren't."
But Ryan, a Wolves fan in Banbury, said "a solution that suits everybody" is to provide designated areas for drinking in stands.
What is it like in other sports and different countries?
Football is in the only sport in the UK which faces restrictions on the consumption of alcohol.
Some of these sports have issues with alcohol-related and anti-social behaviour, but none have the same reputation as football.
The restrictions differ around Europe.
There is a strict ban in the top two divisions of Spanish football, where only alcohol-free beer can be sold outside of hospitality areas. It can, however, be taken to seats.
In the German Bundesliga, there is no ban on drinking at your seat. So relaxed is the approach to alcohol at games that you will even find people selling bottles of beer from shopping trolleys outside grounds.
In the Italian Serie A it is similarly as relaxed, though to a limit of 5% ABV. Some games which are designated "high risk" have sales suspended in and around the stadium.
In France, the Evin Law was introduced in 1991 which is pretty much in line with Scotland, as far as football is concerned. Alcohol cannot be sold at any sports event, other than in VIP areas.

As Apple’s Tim Cook era draws to a close, we’re seeing more experimentation with the iPhone’s design than we’ve seen in a long time, but you wouldn’t know it from the iPhone 18 Pro. This absurdly fast, full-featured handset might be eclipsed by the hype around the iPhone Duo this year, but it’s still just as good as its immediate predecessor.
Of course, not too much has changed since the iPhone 17 Pro. There’s the new variable aperture and other camera controls for those who want to get granular with their mobile photography, a welcome addition given the iPhone’s reputation for inflexibly opinionated computational photography.
Beyond that, though, all the most important changes are under the hood: a new chip, better battery life, and much-improved thermals that both give the phone better sustained performance and make it cooler to the touch in many situations.
I think we’re seeing something of a transition for the “Pro” iPhones. They may still be the flagships in a sense, but Apple is at least for now saving its flashier design ideas for new products like last year’s iPhone Air or this year’s iPhone Duo.
The Pro phones aren’t the sexy, cool ones right now; they’re the everything-and-the-kitchen-sink, cover-for-every-kind-of-obsessive-user workhorses. I think that’s a great space for them to occupy, and this year’s iteration is no exception.
Design
The iPhone 18 Pro mostly looks and feels like last year’s flagship. It’s a function-over-form design (at least compared to something like the iPhone Air) with good materials.
I’m not normally one to care too much about color in these phones. For my personal phone, I’ve always just grabbed whatever was closest to black. (Apple says this year’s black is the blackest yet, of course.) But I have to admit the new burgundy color of my review unit is appealing, even though it’s quite the fingerprint magnet, in a long tradition for iPhones.
The main design difference this time around is a smaller Dynamic Island, that cut-out at the top of the screen that houses the front-facing camera and sensors. Apple has achieved this by moving the IR camera underneath the OLED panel, now in the top-left corner of the screen.
A new pixel arrangement allows infrared light to pass through in that spot, while the pixels in this region operate at twice the brightness to compensate for lower density, so there’s little visible effect on the image on the display. You can tell there’s something subtly going on in that corner if you know what to look for and look closely, but I don’t think most people will notice.
As I wrote when the Dynamic Island was first introduced, the way Apple combines the per-pixel brightness and absolute blacks of the OLED panel with creative software to turn what should be something of an albatross—a big, chunky hole in the screen—into an appealing feature by displaying live activities and other information around the sensors is one of the company’s more impressive design ideas in recent years. The execution is excellent and remains so.
Now, that hole is less big and chunky, making it sensible for Apple to now show up to three live activities at once in the region, not just one. The middle one has more information, while those on the left and right are basically dots with just enough to tell you something useful.

It’s also now possible to show more information on a second live activity when there are just two being displayed; I found this even more appealing than showing three live activities.
This isn’t enough of a reason to upgrade from an earlier Dynamic Island phone, of course, but it has made a good feature a little bit better.
Performance and thermals
Let’s talk specs, performance, and the main story with this phone—heat management. For most specs, this is last year’s iPhone 17 Pro. But the A20 Pro chip has some improvements that make this one of the more notable performance steps in a while.
A20 Pro
First up is the new A20 Pro chip. Apple has gone from a 3-nanometer process node in the A19 Pro to 2 nm here. It has a 6-core CPU with four efficiency cores and two performance cores—nothing new there. The GPU has seven cores, each with a Neural Accelerator that Apple says helps improve GPU-based AI workloads. (There’s hardware-accelerated ray-tracing support, too, though few games or apps utilize it.)
Also for local AI features (which are a big emphasis for this year’s iOS 27), there’s the dual 16-core Neural Engine.
Apple also says the A20 Pro has “the widest memory interface ever shipped in an iPhone” (naturally) with 50 percent more bandwidth. Based on what Apple has said so far about it, that seems to be mainly to improve AI performance. I’m speculating here, but given that Apple Intelligence and Siri AI features work fine on other recent iPhones, I imagine that’s a bit of padding to enable support for future AI features that won’t work on the 16 Pro or 17 Pro.
Unsurprisingly, and as the 3DMark benchmark chart below shows, that could make a big difference in graphics performance, too. It’s not like many people were complaining about the 17 Pro’s frame rates in Genshin Impact or Diablo Immortal, but hey, they definitely won’t be now.
Improved heat management
The chip has been re-architected in a couple of ways. New chip packaging promises improved heat management, thanks in part to a design that puts the system-on-a-chip next to the memory instead of stacked on top of it.
The most notable improvement is arguably a larger vapor chamber. Last year’s iPhone 17 Pro introduced the vapor chamber as an additional cooling measure, meant to help the phone sustain good performance for longer and distribute heat more sensibly. A copper material on the display plate helps keep the display cooler, too.
Apple promises up to 40 percent better sustained performance compared to last year’s Pro and up to 100 percent better than the iPhone 16 Pro before that. That’s neat, but sustained performance wasn’t a big problem for most users before. The main benefit is that the phone feels cooler and is less likely to overheat.
In my view, the better thermals are the most welcome addition to the iPhone 18 Pro. Many of us who have tried to use our phone as a GPS on the car dashboard on a hot summer day know the frustration of features shutting down when the phone goes into crisis heat-management mode. And even in normal use, like during online gaming or web browsing while streaming video, iPhones from a couple of years ago or earlier tended to get quite hot.
It’s been quite cool and overcast in Chicago this week—fall is here at last—so I haven’t been able to test the former of those extreme cases, but I’ve used the phone enough to be able to report that there is noticeable improvement in the more day-to-day scenarios. It still gets warm in some situations, like when I read the 3DMark benchmarks, but most of the time, it subjectively seems better than a couple of generations ago.
It’s normally hard to notice the absence of a problem, but my own iPhone 16 Pro has gotten hot frequently enough over the past couple of years that the contrast has been real and felt.
We’ll leave the camera specs to the cameras section of the review, but there are a couple of other spec changes worth noting.
A beefy battery (and other updates)
First off, there are further battery life improvements. Apple has long used offline video playback as one of its measures, and it says the iPhone 18 Pro can offer up to 36 hours of that on a single charge, compared to 33 for its predecessor. (It’s up to 45 for the 18 Pro Max and 39 for the 17 Pro Max.)
Subjectively, I’m impressed by the battery performance here. My personal daily driver is an iPhone 16 Pro Max, which is currently sitting at 86 percent maximum capacity per Apple’s battery health panel in the Settings app.
I have no complaints; I charge it for about an hour in the morning, then do whatever I want with it (other than maybe intensive 3D gaming) with the brightness cranked up until the next morning, when I charge again.
I noticed the iPhone 18 Pro showing higher percentages when I wake up in the morning than my 16 Pro Max with similar use, which is impressive for a smaller phone—even though my 160 Pro Max’s battery has aged a bit.
In terms of other additions, Apple has put its proprietary C2 cellular modem in the 18 Pro, which uses less energy than the Qualcomm modem in the 17 Pro, so that’s part of the battery life story here, too.
And if you’re inclined to charge wirelessly rather than with a USB-C cable, the iPhone 18 Pro has wireless charging at up to 25 W.
Cameras
If you’ve read my iPhone reviews before, you may recall I am not a photography geek. This is not the review to read if you want a deep dive on optics or how well this thing will work in a professional photo shoot scenario. (I’ll leave it to more skilled and knowledgeable people to assess the phone from that perspective, as there are already many such reviews out there.)
I’m a point-and-shooter. Thanks to both new hardware features and developments in computational photography, that’s actually where some of the more interesting and fastest-moving developments have been happening in the iPhone and its Android competitors over the past few years.
Sure, the iPhone 18 Pro is “pro” in the sense that it will be used by content creators and others who approach snapping photos or capturing videos far more seriously and creatively than I do. But really, it’s the phone that sometimes lets non-pros like me produce quasi-pro-looking images despite ourselves.
Take the new variable aperture feature, which got the most fanfare when this handset was announced. The ability to tweak this setting manually is a niche proposal, really; many people will rarely, if ever, touch it. That said, it adjusts automatically based on what’s in the scene by default, so in many cases, even folks like me will get slightly better photos.

There’s also Photographic Styles 3, the latest generation of Apple’s set of non-destructive presets for the general appearance and vibe of the photos you’re taking. Think Instagram filters, but less blunt-force. Previously, Photographic Styles were basically just color balance settings, but Photographic Styles 3 allows for texture tweaks, too.
This includes four texture options: film, glow, soft skin, and standard. These options—especially the film one—allow the iPhone’s built-in Camera app to compete with some third-party apps that tried to give photos warmer, more film-like looks. I won’t say it’s enough to make everyone drop those alternatives, but it’s good to have more options for those who are loyal to the main app.
Apart from these and a few other minor tweaks, it’s the same triple-48 MP rear camera system that we reviewed in last year’s iPhone 17 Pro, paired with the same front-facing 18 MP camera.
With the variable aperture and the other custom camera controls that are now accessible in the built-in Camera app (all the others are available on other recent iPhones), Apple has finally done plenty to address long-standing complaints that iPhone cameras were a little too opinionated for some users’ tastes.
Yes, these new features enable better point-and-shoot photos in some narrow situations, but user control seems to be the main pitch for the cameras this year.
For those who just want a good phone
This was Tim Cook’s last year as Apple’s CEO, and the iPhone 18 Pro is the quintessential iPhone of the Tim Cook era: practical, pricey, loaded with features to cover ever-more niche edge cases, and not especially bold in its design or ambitions—all to a high standard of quality.
This is the formula that has made it the world’s most popular flagship smartphone. There’s nothing wrong with that formula. Its recent predecessors were all great phones, and this one is, too.
But we all know the era of buying a new smartphone every year or two to enjoy amazing new features has passed. (Which is also great, by the way—for our pocketbooks, for the environment, for a whole bunch of reasons.) If you have an iPhone 17 Pro, there’s little reason to upgrade. Yes, we’re seeing some notable performance improvement year-over-year here, but I don’t think too many of us were complaining about the A17 Pro’s performance to begin with.
My personal daily driver is an iPhone 16 Pro, and I won’t be pulling the trigger this year, either. In fact, I think you’re still in great shape with your iPhone 15 Pro, if that’s what you have, provided your battery is still holding up.
Go further back than that, though, and all these little things start to accumulate into something enticing. That’s where we’re at, and that’s where we’ve been for a while now.
I wouldn’t go so far as to say the modern flagship smartphone is perfect in all respects; Apple and its competitors still find small ways to refine it and up the ante for specific types of users year after year, and I expect that to continue. And last year’s base iPhone 17 is still more than good enough for almost everybody.
But after almost two decades of competition and iteration, it’s at least directionally perfect. The basics are all here, and they don’t need to change. I wish the price hadn’t risen, but I suppose that’s the reality we live in right now.
If you want something new and flashy to impress your friends or to satisfy your brain with a novel experience, hold out for the iPhone Duo next month or venture into the slightly more energetic Android market. But if you just want a good phone that leverages all the latest technological progress without overdoing it for attention or progress’ sake, the iPhone Pro line is a good fit.
The good
Greatly improved thermal management has added up over two generations
Ditto for battery life
Very strong graphics and AI performance
New custom camera controls and photographic styles help you get (a little bit) out of the typical Apple processed look
The bad
Some might find it a little heavy
This isn’t really a bad thing, but there’s not much here to excite you or to inspire an upgrade if you already own a recent iPhone

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Kingdom of the Netherlands have renewed their strategic partnership in addressing the growing impacts of climate change on global health.
The Netherlands is providing a new allocation of €500 000 for 2024 to WHO, reinforcing its commitment to climate resilience and sustainable healthcare systems worldwide. This allocation supports WHO’s ongoing efforts to strengthen the Alliance for Transformative Action on Climate and Health Secretariat and advance climate change and health programmes globally.
This contribution builds on the partnership established in 2023 between the Netherlands and WHO to collaborate on climate change and health. Together, they have supported African, Asian and Eastern Mediterranean countries in advancing the implementation of integrated climate and health surveillance and early warning systems, enhancing capacity to deliver on COP26 health commitments, helping harmonize early warning systems for health-related climate risks, and empowering countries to advance climate-resilient health system readiness.
This partnership along with the support from other organizations is pivotal in assisting Member States in developing climate-resilient and low-carbon health systems. Engaging with relevant partners, including civil society, Multilateral Development Banks, UN Agencies, and health professionals in concerted action on climate change and health, is also a core activity.
The Netherlands has been at the forefront of advocating climate action in health, aligned with the Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030 which emphasizes the intersection of climate change and health. In addition, the Netherlands, together with Peru, led the adoption in 2024 of the World Health Assembly 77 Resolution on Climate Change and Health at the to renew the current one from 2008. Recognizing the increasing urgency and the need for accelerated efforts, the resolution calls for a WHO global action plan, increased national efforts and mainstreaming of climate change and health in WHO’s new Fourteenth General Programme of Work.
The partnership’s renewal brings the total support from the Netherlands to WHO activities on climate change and health to over €1.1 Million since 2023 and comes at a crucial time as countries face increasing health challenges from climate change and as the global health community gears up for discussions on climate change and health at COP29 in Azerbaijan in 2024. Climate change will continue to be a key priority area in the new GPW, and where WHO’s work in collaboration with Member States and partners will result in 7.5 million lives saved in the next four years, as estimated in WHO’s latest Investment case.
The Netherlands and WHO will continue to leverage their partnership to ensure that health remains central to climate negotiations and actions. A focus on building resilience in vulnerable regions and empowering countries to implement sustainable, low-carbon healthcare solutions remains central.
