If the Beijing meeting between Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in May was the “stalemate summit”, the second round of talks between the presidents of the US and China this week seemed to give up entirely on the idea of breakthroughs.
Instead, it was described as a celebration of “diplotainment” rather than diplomacy, where pomp prevailed over progress and where one of the main outcomes was the news that two giant pandas would soon be sent from China to Atlanta zoo.
Trump rolled out the red carpet for Xi’s arrival on Wednesday and broke with decades of precedent to meet the Chinese leader at Joint Base Andrews. Thus began a three-day state visit that involved a tour of Trump’s new helipad and the Marine One helicopter, and a 90-minute meeting that Trump described as “great” and that revealed, according to Trump, that Xi “has great interest in granite”.
“The biggest takeaway is that Trump has been displaying an extraordinary degree of deference to Xi Jinping,” said Julian Gewirtz, who served as a senior China official in the Biden administration.
But what of actual substance? Expectations going into the summit were low. But the outcomes somehow still fell short.
One of the biggest issues in the US-China relationship is trade. Last year, as Trump unveiled successive rounds of tariffs on Chinese goods, the White House accused China of unfair practices that it said contributed to the loss of 3.7m US jobs and inflated the trade deficit. The tariffs were supposed to suppress the volume of Chinese imports to the US and put pressure on China.
To some degree, they worked. The US trade deficit with China in 2025 fell to $200bn, down from nearly $300bn in 2024. But experts have noted that some of this shortfall is made up for by Chinese goods being shipped to the US via third countries, a trend underlined by the fact that China’s trade surplus surpassed a record $1tn last year.
With the US and China accounting for 43% of global GDP, their trade war has far-reaching implications for the world economy. So it was a relief not just to Beijing and to US consumers when the two countries agreed a temporary truce in Busan last year.
That truce is due to expire in November. China, where the economy is heavily reliant on exports, was reported to be pushing for the truce to be extended until the end of Trump’s term, in January 2029.
On Thursday, it was revealed that Xi’s first state visit to the US in more than a decade had resulted in a mere two-month extension. That reflects “the lack of preparation for this summit beyond the pomp and circumstance”, said Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society.
William Yang, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group, said: “This summit largely achieved symbolism and ritualism over substance. That is very clear.” The short extension “reflects the level of fundamental differences that still exist between the two countries over a variety of issues”.
China’s most powerful response to Trump’s tariffs was the decision to block the export of rare earths, critical minerals vital to US manufacturing and military supply chains. That seemed to skewer Trump’s leverage over China.
Gewirtz said: “Beijing’s retaliation … seems to have had a profound effect on [Trump] and his administration’s willingness to take risks vis-a-vis China.”
Apart from the trade war agreement, the summit failed to achieve any meaningful progress on thorny issues in the US-China relationship such as artificial intelligence, Taiwan, the wars in Iran and Ukraine, and human rights.
On Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be the most important issue in the relationship, Xi put pressure on Trump to weaken the US’s support for the self-governing island that China claims as its own. According to the Chinese readout of the Xi-Trump meeting, Xi told Trump he hoped “the US side will adhere to the correct position of opposing Taiwan independence”.
For the US to state that it “opposes” Taiwanese independence would be a rhetorical shift from the current position of “does not support” such a claim, and would be a move welcomed by Beijing. Trump has not yet commented on whether he agreed to such a statement. But it does seem he is no closer to approving a $14bn arms sale package for Taiwan, a sale that Beijing would like to see disappear completely.
On Thursday, US Senate Democrats lambasted Trump for opting for “pageantry over purpose” and for failing to deliver agreements on “the economic and security issues that will shape America’s future”. Trump ignored recent warnings about the dangers posed by AI, writing on social media on Thursday: “I want to leave it exactly where it is,” adding: “That is China’s position also.”
For China, the lack of big news from the visit is a win in itself. “The summit went excellently from the Chinese perspective,” Thomas said. Xi “got a huge amount of respect from the American president, the full state visit treatment [and] really great images beaming back to China of the Chinese and the American presidents interacting as peers on the global stage, without having to make any meaningful concessions or compromises.”

Shortly after the IPO lock-in expiry, SEDEMAC’s institutional investors A91 Partners, Xponentia, NJRN Family Trust and Mace Pvt Ltd have cumulatively offloaded shares worth ₹1,456.38 Cr via multiple bulk deals today. As per NSE data, A91 Partners, via holding entity A91 Emerging Fund II LLP, sold 16.10 Lakh shares of SEDEMAC at an average price of ₹3,010 apiece, netting ₹484.9 Cr. Xponentia sold 16.85 Lakh shares across three bulk deals to rake in ₹507.4 Cr. Meanwhile, Mace Private Limited sold 7.28 Lakh shares worth ₹219 Cr, NJRN Family Trust offloaded 4.5 Lakh shares worth ₹135 Cr. Meanwhile, HDFC Life Insurance sold 3.63 Lakh but picked up 4.02 Lakh shares. The shares that flooded the market were picked up by Government of Singapore (10.23 Lakh shares), Amansa Holdings (4.63 Lakh shares), Invesco Mutual Fund (3.54 Lakh shares), SBI Mutual Fund (5.25 Lakh shares), Monetary Authority of Singapore (2.37 Lakh shares), T Rowe Price International Discovery Fund (2.32 Lakh shares). This is the second instance when these investors have lightened their holding in SEDEMAC after paring stake via its initial public offering (IPO) earlier this year. The IPO comprised solely of an offer for sale (OFS) component and saw SEDEMAC’s investors offload 80.43 Lakh shares, netting a cumulative ₹1,087 Cr from the issue. Investors like Xponentia Capital Partners, Mace, IIT-Bombay’s SINE, 360 One, HDFC Life Insurance, among others, were some of the selling shareholders in the IPO. While A91 Partners netted the highest return at ₹325 Cr, Infosys cofounder Nandan Nilekani’s family office NRJN Family Trust made the highest gains at a 14.2X return on investment. Founded in 2007 by IIT-B professor Shashikanth Suryanarayana and his students Pushkaraj Panse, Manish Sharma and Amit Dixit, SEDEMAC designs and manufactures electronic control systems for mobility and industrial applications. The mobility segment brings in nearly 86% of SEDEMAC’s revenue. On the financial front, SEDEMAC Mechatronics’ net profit zoomed 95.1% to ₹33.3 Cr in Q1 FY27 compared to ₹17.1 Cr in the year-ago quarter. A study by Chennai-based diabetologists has attempted to find out how India has managed to reduce the prices of new and expensive diabetes drugs and what lessons this could possibly hold for other low- and middle-income countries (LMIC). The study, ‘Making Modern Diabetes Medications Affordable and Accessible: Lessons from India for Other Countries’, was led by V. Mohan, chairman, Dr. Mohan’s Diabetes Specialities Centre, Chennai, and was published in the journal Diabetes Care.
What did the study find?
Of the 589 million adults in the world with diabetes, 80% live in LMICs, the study noted. Modern diabetes therapies such as GLP-1 receptor agonists as well as SGLT2i (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors) improve cardiovascular and renal outcomes, while analogue insulins help reduce the risk of hypoglycaemia. However, affordability remains a barrier: diabetes requires lifelong care and management of complications.
India’s ability to maintain low medication prices is closely linked to its role as a major pharmaceutical exporter, the paper stated, noting the strategic legislative history of maintaining critical safeguards to prevent ‘patent evergreening’ and allowing for generic manufacture of drugs. It also found that the country has increasingly focused on strengthening domestic manufacturing capacity. There are concerns over global trade policies affecting prices and the availability of raw materials. A government incentive scheme has been introduced to promote domestic manufacturing of raw materials, and as of 2025, production has commenced for 26 molecules that were previously imported.
The paper notes that metformin and sulfonylureas continue to form the foundation of type 2 diabetes management in India - both are included in the National List of Essential Medicines (NLEM). While DPP-4 (dipeptidyl peptidase 4) inhibitors, SGLT2i and GLP-1 RA have all been introduced, they are not currently in the NLEM. Initial uptake of these drugs was constrained by pricing. Following the competitive entry by multiple domestic manufacturers, the price of semaglutide, for instance in India, has dropped considerably now, and there has been a huge increase in sales; however, absolute monthly costs remain high relative to the household income in India, and, crucially, these are not covered by insurance, as they are, to a great extent, in the U.S.
Quick availability of generic and biosimilar drugs, deliberate regulatory and distribution strategies such as the government’s Jan Aushadi Kendras, and market competition have allowed for affordable drugs in India, the paper highlighted.
What does it propose for other LMICs?
Building local manufacturing capacity as a strategic public health investment, balancing patent governance that encourages easier access to newer molecules, predictable and structured price regulation, good distribution networks at reasonable retail prices and aligning pharmaceutical policy with health financing and ongoing monitoring of medicine quality, prices, prescription patterns and patient access can all help with improving access to affordable medicines, the paper noted. These core principles could also apply to high-income countries facing drug prices, the paper said.
Challenges ahead
Challenges that remain include urban-rural disparities in distribution and availability of medicines; tight regulations potentially affecting chances of drug innovation; differences in quality between generics and difficulties in maintaining strict pharmacovigilance; as well as limited formal evaluation of government schemes to look at their long-term impact on clinical outcomes.

Newcastle University is facing a backlash from conservationists over the appointment of the heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune who runs a controversial mega-zoo as a professor of sustainability.
The university announced that Anant Ambani had been given a professorship of practice for “his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship” and “significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future”.
Ambani is the son of India’s richest person, Mukesh Ambani, who made his fortune primarily in oil and gas, owns the world’s largest oil refinery and has close ties with the ruling Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). Mukesh Ambani has enthusiastically praised BJP policies, and firms linked to his Reliance conglomerate have recently made significant donations to the party. The prime minister, Narendra Modi, attended Anant Ambani’s lavish 2024 wedding in Mumbai.
Anant Amabani, 31, who is leads on renewable energy on the Reliance Group’s executive board and is worth an estimated £90bn, has set up Vantara, a 1,400-hectare (3,500-acre) private zoo near the family’s oil refining facilities in Gujarat, which reportedly has more than 150,000 animals including 200 lions, 250 leopards and 900 crocodiles, and where he hosted his opulent pre-wedding celebrations attended by celebrity guests and politicians.
Conservation groups have previously raised questions about how some of the animals were sourced, given many were endangered species. Vantara has never been found guilty of any wrongdoing.
The university’s announcement was met with incredulity and derision from academic staff and Indian and international conservationists and environmentalists.
Ramachandra Guha, a leading Indian public intellectual and the author of the book Speaking With Nature: The Origins of Indian Environmentalism, said: “I must say that it is a rather mystifying choice. As a scholar of Indian and global environmentalism, I can name at least 50 – perhaps 100 – individuals who are far better qualified to be thus honoured. They include soil scientists, energy scientists, water conservation experts, community forest workers, ecologists, pollution abatement experts etc who have made real and tangible contributions to a more sustainable future for India and Indians.
“I wonder on whose advice Newcastle University has acted, and whether it did due diligence on what has and has not been done in these fields. Its appointment of Mr Ambani is puzzling in the extreme, and is likely to adversely affect the university’s institutional credibility and intellectual standing.”
Bhuvan Mangalore, an Indian investigator into illegal wildlife trade who is completing a dissertation on Vantara at Anglia Ruskin University, asked: “Is this a joke?”
Prof Matt Perry, the chair of the University and College Union branch at Newcastle University, said staff members had objected to the appointment citing environmental concerns.
Prof Lyla Mehta, the head of the climate, environment and sustainability department at the University of Sussex’s Institute of Development Studies, shared concerns that “as public funding for universities falls, there is a real danger that billionaire and corporate money begins to shape academia”.
She said: “Universities are supposed to be places that question power and hold corporations to account, not give them academic legitimacy.”
In April, Anant Ambani launched Vantara University, billed as the world’s first global university dedicated to wildlife conservation and veterinary science.
Lorne Stockman, a research co-director at Oil Change International, said: “At a time when the climate crisis demands an urgent phaseout of oil and gas, we must demand our publicly funded institutions do better.”
In 2025, an investigation by the German newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung found that many animals delivered to Vantara arrived through countries with opaque wildlife trading networks such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Arab Emirates, raising concerns that endangered species may have been illegally trafficked.
In August last year, an investigation by India’s supreme court, which lasted less than three weeks, cleared the zoo’s operators of any wrongdoing. A subsequent fact-finding mission into the zoo by Cites, the UN body that regulates the trade of endangered species, found that some of the permits used to bring animals to Vantara were probably forged.
Its report said: “There is a need for caution to ensure that imports of large numbers of animals by these facilities are not inadvertently creating a demand for illegally sourced animals.”
Cites recommended restrictions on India’s imports of endangered wild animals. However, it subsequently reversed its decision after objections from India, the US and Japan at a Cites meeting after they argued there was not enough proof of illegal imports.
In August, the zoo launched a “reset” in its operations by appointing a former Cites head to oversee its operations and said it would voluntarily pause all wildlife imports until June next year.
Vantara has declined to comment. The Ambani family and Vantara have previously denied the allegations of wildlife trafficking. They have said: “Our mission and focus continues to be the rescue, rehabilitation and care of animals.”
A Newcastle University spokesperson said: “The award of a professorship of practice recognises Mr Ambani’s contributions to conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare and environmental stewardship through his work with Vantara, a wildlife rescue and conservation initiative, and as the executive lead for the Reliance Group’s transition toward a green energy future.”

AI superpower ambitions take centre stage as Trump and Xi meet
- Published
"Whoever wins AI, WINS!"
US President Donald Trump has been blunt about his AI ambitions, as well as about who he considers the US's main rival to be: China.
His Chinese counterpart, Xi Jinping, has not said anything so forthright - but it seems he holds a similar view.
"China very much sees it as a race, they very much think China should be the leading force in AI - they see AI as a power maximiser," says Rebecca Arcesati, from the Mercator Institute for China Studies.
You can look beyond the rhetoric for evidence of this: AI has been a cornerstone of China's technological ambitions for more than a decade, whether Xi emphasises it publicly or not.
For Trump, beating China to AI supremacy outweighs any risks of the technology to humans - something he has described as "a hoax".
China's foreign ministry warned that "narratives of threat" and confrontation hinder global AI governance, calling for cooperation to ensure it benefits all.
It means when the two presidents sit down on Thursday there will be few more important topics than their AI ambitions - and what they say and decide will matter to the whole world.
Is the US in the lead?
There's no doubt the US and China are global leaders in AI but who is ahead depends on how success is measured.
American companies lead on so-called frontier models, with the highest-performing systems on most benchmarks coming from firms such as Anthropic, Google and OpenAI.
In February 2025, an AI model by China's DeepSeek "briefly matched the top US model" and as of March 2026, Anthropic's top model led the pack "by just 2.7%", according to researchers at Stanford University, external.
Part of the US advantage stems from the vast sums being invested in leading AI companies as the frontier labs burn through mountains of cash to build the infrastructure to train new models.
The stock market is booming and a large part of the US economy's expansion relies on the enormous growth - and projected profitability - of AI companies.
So that might partly explain why President Trump sees AI as key to US success.
Another factor limiting China's ability is the sweeping government restrictions placed on US companies that prevent them from selling advanced microchips to Chinese firms - these are crucial for developing cutting-edge models.
China's advantage
Despite the chip restrictions, new AI models are coming out almost monthly in both countries and it's unclear what "winning" the AI race would actually mean, or whether there is a finish line at all.
Many companies are racing to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI), a theoretical form of AI capable of learning, reasoning and performing a wide range of tasks at or above the level of humans.
The Chinese AI industry has so far focused not on creating frontier models but releasing what is known as open weight models - downloadable and tweakable in a similar way to open source software.
This contrasts with the approach taken by many US firms, which largely focus on proprietary models accessed through paid subscriptions or company platforms.
Chinese open weight models are being released at a rapid pace, with benchmarks showing the country's top models trailing US rivals by only a few months.
Models such as Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 have become popular in China and overseas because they perform close to the frontier models while remaining freely downloadable and adaptable.
Beijing's focus is more about deploying the technology across its economy, China analyst Lizzi Lee from the Asia Society Policy Institute said.
"AI isn't the moon landing," she said. "The US may lead at the frontier, while China could still gain enormous economic and geopolitical leverage by making capable AI cheap, open and ubiquitous."
AI is also very energy hungry, and China is very well placed there, Rebecca Arcesati told Tech Life on the BBC World Service.
"Chinese AI companies are able to access the electricity they need for a much lower cost and that really is an advantage," she said.
In robotics - a field of AI that some believe will be world-changing - China has become the world's biggest manufacturer of robots, with more than two million working in the country's factories, the International Federation of Robotics estimated.
The nation is also the world's biggest maker of humanoid robots, accounting for more than nine-tenths of global shipments in the first half of the year, according to independent policy institute Chatham House.
Chinese AI developers have showed "remarkable resilience and innovation" in spite of the shortage of advanced American chips, analyst Lian Jye Su from tech research firm Omdia said.
But US officials and AI firms have also alleged that Chinese developers closed the gap by using distillation - a technique that enables models to learn from more advanced platforms.
China's foreign ministry said in response that AI development was "fuelled" by the country's "vision of extensive consultation and joint contribution for shared benefit".
Safety concerns?
China and the US may be in fierce competition, but their governments' approaches to safety concerns are markedly different.
While some in the industry have recently warned that AI could pose an existential risk to humanity, Chinese researchers seem less concerned about that and are more worried about potential misuse of the technology and cyber war.
Responding to concerns over AI, Trump has said the US already has sufficient rules in place and that the only guardrails AI needs are a "high IQ" president.
"We're leading now over China by a lot, and everyone else, and we're going to keep it that way," Trump said this week, adding that the US was not going to "stifle the growth of something that will be bigger than the industrial revolution".
Washington has prioritised innovation and sought to reduce regulation in an effort to "keep American labs ahead", said information security officer Jayant Dave from cybersecurity firm Check Point Software Technologies.
Beijing has taken a different strategy to the US hands-off approach.
Xi urged the country's leaders to keep a close eye on AI's risks and ensure the technology was always "under human control".
"China has taken a relatively cautious and centrally-coordinated approach," introducing guides on data usage and algorithms before many other countries, helping to address many underlying concerns, Dave said.
The use of guidelines, though not legally binding, sets expectations while giving developers room to innovate, said National University of Singapore AI ethics lecturer Jonathan Sim.
Will they cooperate?
Despite calls for international cooperation, it remains unclear how the AI superpowers plan to address the technology's potential dangers - if at all.
The two countries have previously cooperated on existential threats such as nuclear weapons, but that was based on a shared understanding of the threat, which is not currently the case with AI, Dave said.
"Washington worries about capability escaping control. Beijing worries about capability threatening domestic stability," he added.
Trump has dismissed proposals for an industry-wide slowdown, arguing that it could allow Chinese developers to close the gap.
Ahead of the Trump-Xi summit, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng discussed establishing a notification mechanism for serious AI incidents.
While the messaging from Trump on China in recent weeks has been "more antagonistic", the fact that AI is expected to be on the agenda was a "good start", said policy analyst Leia Wang from the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.
What we don't want, he added, was for an "unhealthy version of the race narrative to perpetuate", potentially escalating an already fierce rivalry in AI.

Warrington edge past Leeds to reach Grand Final
- Published
Betfred Super League play-off semi-final
Leeds (12) 12
Tries: Hall, Connor Goals: Connor 2
Warrington (12) 14
Tries: Bentley, Yates Goals: Irwin 3
Warrington Wolves have reached their first Super League Grand Final in eight years with a thrilling victory against Leeds Rhinos at AMT Headingley Stadium.
In a tense and topsy-turvy semi-final the sides traded two first-half tries each and were locked at 12-12 at the break, before the Wolves were awarded a contentious penalty which was slotted nervelessly by 18-year-old Ewan Irwin to nudge them ahead.
Half-back Jake Connor scored 10 points for an injury-depleted Rhinos, including a first-half try which he inventively created in midfield, and attempted a goal-kick from 62 metres out with the final play of the game but the ball landed short of the sticks.
The Wolves will face the winners of either Wigan Warriors or Wakefield Trinity in the showpiece final at Old Trafford next Saturday, as they stand just one win away from a first league title since 1955.
Leeds limped into the semi-final missing a number of key players including the league's top try-scorer Maika Sivo, captain Ash Handley, and Man of Steel nominee Lachie Miller.
The Rhinos were dealt with a further injury blow moments before kick-off when Chris Hankinson pulled up in the warm-up and had to be replaced by Ned McCormack in the starting line-up.
Warrington breached Leeds' inexperienced backline after five minutes as England captain George Williams' pinpoint kick was met by Matty Ashton, who helped find former Rhino James Bentley to slide over for an early score.
Brodie Croft's cut-out pass found Ryan Hall to score his 358th career try to draw level with former Wakefield legend Neil Fox in the all-time scorers list, as Connor nailed the extras from touch to drag Leeds level.
Connor was then involved at the other end of the field, teaming up with young full-back Fergie McCormack to usher Albert Hopoate into touch as he threatened to score and moments later Arron Lindop collided with team-mate Hopoate as the Wolves again squandered a certain four points.
Leeds made the Wolves pay soon later as they raced down field. A delicate kick over the top from Connor bounced kindly for McCormack, and once Kallum Watkins found Connor he was not to be denied by Ashton's scrambling defending, using his momentum to spin and crash down.
Moments before the break, prop Luke Yates pirouetted elegantly past Cooper Jenkins to slide in next to the sticks as Irwin levelled the scores with the boot as half-time approached.
The game's decisive moment came after the break when James McDonnell was adjudged to have challenged Williams off the ball under a high ball and Irwin stepped up to the tee to notch Warrington two points in front.
A charge down from Keenan Palasia near his own line kept Leeds in the fight but a great tackle from Bentley forced a knock-on as both defences were on top in the second period.
Connor's sensational 40/20 with two minutes remaining ultimately was in vain as Palasia's ball-carrying arm had already hit the floor in the build-up.
A block off the ball gave Connor the chance to be the hero and force the game into golden point but, at the wire, he was unable to find the distance required and Williams kicked the ball into touch to the relief of the travelling supporters.
'A soft penalty decided a big game' - reaction
Leeds Rhinos head coach Brad Arthur said:
"I've not whinged or complained the whole time I've been here. I'm extremely proud of our team and our club and players.
"I don't know what more we could have really done. We got a couple of bits and pieces wrong but so did they. It just would have been really nice if the game was decided by an individual or a piece of skill.
"We're talking about a field goal or something like that rather than a soft penalty to decide such a big game. It is a soft penalty.
"Ned got escorted four or five times tonight on kicks and I wasn't expecting penalties for them. But that's a soft penalty to decide such a big game."
Warrington Wolves captain George Williams told BBC Radio Merseyside:
"Nerve-wracking, mad game, just pleased we've came through the other side.
"Credit to Leeds, they gave it a good crack. They've been a great team all year but we rode the waves and the main thing is we're through to the big dance next week.
"They were probably dominant for the first 20 [minutes], we came home strong in the back end [of the first half]. It's no good for the nerves but sometimes it's better when you're out there, you can do something about it."
[On earning the match-winning penalty] "People think it might be a bit controversial but I was chasing the ball and I got a little nudge. I was off balance and nowadays, with the escorts, they give them. Luckily, it went to us and that was the game."

India had the highest number of children with no sanitation service in schools, with 50 million out of the world total of 244 million as of 2025, according to a new global report. Only Nigeria (34 million), Ethiopia (26 million), the Democratic Republic of the Congo (11 million) or Indonesia (8 million) had a comparatively large number of schoolchildren who had no access to sanitation service.
The data from ‘Progress on drinking water, sanitation and hygiene in schools 2015-2025’ shows the progress as well as the challenges India is facing in meeting the water, sanitation and hygiene goals that are part of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDG) set for 2030.
14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service
The report can also be seen as a decadal report card on the Swachh Bharat Mission, which was launched in India on October 2, 2014. The report cites the achievement of India which saw a 14% reduction in schools with no sanitation service.
Lack of hygiene service
The WHO/UNICEF report that is part of the Joint Monitoring Programme (JMP) for Water Supply, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) shows that globally, 362 million children still had no hygiene service at their school in 2025. Of these, 20 million were from India.
It is not just lack of access that the WHO report flags about India but also gaps in data. “There is now sufficient data to estimate trends in basic hygiene coverage between 2015 and 2025 for all SDG regions except Central and Southern Asia where there were insufficient recent data to generate estimates for India, and therefore the region, beyond 2024.”
Drinking water
On the brighter side, India is among the 28 out of 62 countries that are on track to achieve universal coverage of basic drinking water in schools by 2030.
As of 2025, there were 258 million children who still had no drinking water service at their school. The number of children from Indian schools made up 12 million of this number or about 1 out 20 children in the world. The report shows that India has made a big progress in basic drinking water services in 2025 and average rates of change between 2015 and 2025. India, Panama, Syrian Arab Republic, Togo and Tuvalu increased coverage by over 4% per year, “demonstrating that rapid progress is possible”.
However, the report found that while gaps in basic water coverage persists between school levels and between rural and urban areas, this did not apply to India, Cambodia and Fiji.

Supreme Court allows Trump to use controversial database to check voter citizenship
- Published
The US Supreme Court has lifted restrictions on the Trump administration to use a controversial federal database that uses citizenship information and other sensitive data to identify voters suspected of being non-citizens.
Critics have questioned the reliability of the data, warning it could result in US citizens being wrongly removed from electoral rolls.
In June, a federal judge ruled that the system was illegal and violated the privacy rights of Americans.
But the top court's conservative majority ruled that the National Voter Registration Act prohibits broad purges of voter rolls in the weeks before an election, which limits any "potential impact" of the decision ahead of the midterms.
The three liberal-leaning liberals on the Supreme Court dissented from the decision.
One of the dissenting Supreme Court justices, Ketanji Brown Jackson, expressed concern that this could mistakenly revoke the voting rights of eligible voters.
"The harm caused by burdening or disenfranchising even a few lawful voters outweighs the non-existent harm that the government experiences when it is prevented from taking an action that it likely lacks the authority to take," she wrote.
The Department of Homeland Security programme, known as Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, allows officials to verify the eligibility of voters on their rolls.
The database was first created in 1986 to help officials verify the citizenship or immigration status of those applying for public benefits.
But the Trump administration last year expanded its search capabilities by allowing bulk searches using sensitive information from Social Security rolls.
In June, however, US District Judge Sparkle L Soonnan - a Biden-appointee - ruled that the revamped system shows that the federal government "knowingly trampled on the privacy rights" of US citizens "in a manner that threatens the sacred right to vote".
A federal appeals court allowed her ruling to stand, only to be overridden by the Supreme Court on Friday.
The top court ruled that a 1996 law allows DHS to seek citizenship and immigration data from federal agencies, and has "an obligation to respond" to states seeking that information.
The use of the Save programme by individual states is voluntary.
The previous judge's order, the Supreme Court ruled, "prevents the federal government from using the programme it believes is best suited to the task".
Lawyers for the Trump administration have long argued that the system is lawful and necessary to prevent non-citizens from voting. A total of 27 states currently use the system to check voter citizenship.
Critics, however, have pointed to a number of cases of the system already having led to mistakes.
For example, officials in Travis County, Texas, found that of nearly 100 voters identified as non-citizens, at least 10% of them - and potentially more - were US citizens, according to US media reports.
Since the state began checking its voter rolls with the Save system last year, only three non-citizen voters have been charged with illegally voting in Texas.
Since returning to the White House in January last year, the Trump administration has sought to reform the US electoral system, a process that has included a bid - rejected by the Supreme Court - to reign in mail-in ballots.
In 2024, for example, Texas Governor Greg Abbott announced that 1,930 people with a "voter history" had been removed from electoral rolls out of a total of nearly 18 million registered voters.
The figures are far below the hundreds of thousands of non-citizen voters that Trump and the Department of Homeland Security have previously suggested were on voter rolls.

SpaceX Starship's first orbital flight test on track after successful launch rehearsal
The vehicle is scheduled for launch on September 28.
SpaceX has successfully conducted a wet dress rehearsal for Starship, making sure it's in working condition for its next test flight that's bound to become a major milestone for the vehicle if everything goes according to plan. "Launch rehearsal complete ahead of Starship Flight 14," the company has announced on X.
In a wet dress rehearsal, the rocket goes through a full launch simulation. It's loaded with liquid propellants and powered on before it goes through final checks to ensure its fuel lines, software and communications with the ground team are all working. The launch team even runs it through the full countdown sequence, demonstrates procedures for scrubbing launches in the event of poor weather conditions and then drains the fuel to simulate offload procedures. In other words, the rocket goes through the whole launch sequence without actually lifting off.
With the success of this rehearsal, Starship is on track to launch for its 14th test flight scheduled for September 28, with a 75-minute launch window opening at 8:15AM Eastern Time. It will be the vehicle's first orbital flight after multiple suborbital tests. Starship will be orbiting our planet six times within the course of 10 hours before re-entering our atmosphere and crashing into the ocean. It will also ferry 26 Starlink V3 satellites to orbit, which will be the first next-gen models to be added to SpaceX's satellite internet constellation. You'll be able to watch the Starship launch on September 28 on X.

Trump is bracing to lose his latest fight with the press
Trump’s lawyers said he barred three news outlets from the White House on security grounds. A judge seemed skeptical.
A hearing on President Donald Trump’s White House press ban ended without a ruling this afternoon — an admittedly anticlimactic outcome, but one that will likely change very soon.
The Trump-appointed judge in the case, Timothy Kelly, appeared skeptical of the administration’s arguments for banning CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds last week. Kelly said he would rule “as soon as possible.” Until then, the ban remains in place.
By all accounts, Trump’s case is a feeble one. While the Justice Department attempted to argue on Wednesday that the three outlets’ reporting jeopardized national security, Trump himself kind of gave the game away last week when he said he had singled these organizations out over what he characterized as negative and inaccurate stories.
The move sat poorly even with people and institutions you’d expect to be sympathetic to Trump: Fox News was one of several outlets that boycotted White House events this week to protest the ban, for instance.
And ahead of today’s hearing, Trump himself seemed primed to lose. In a Truth Social post on Monday, he promised he would “almost without question” appeal any decision against him.
Go a little deeper
This is all emblematic of how Trump has escalated his attacks on the news media in his second term: not just by insulting and demeaning the press, but also by weaponizing otherwise neutral-seeming rules.
Every administration has policies that regulate who can access the White House grounds and under what conditions, for instance. But in early 2025, the White House took control of the press pool — the rotating group of reporters that frequently travels with the president — and soon sought to exclude disfavored organizations.
More insidiously, Trump has mobilized regulatory agencies like the Federal Communications Commission against his perceived critics, in some cases even threatening to revoke the licenses of local TV stations that air coverage and commentary he disagrees with.
While no licenses have actually been suspended, the FCC has mysteriously pulled some up for unscheduled review. And just the prospect of government retaliation has been enough to force some content off the air: Just two weeks ago, the late-night comedy host Jimmy Kimmel said his show wouldn’t air a scheduled interview with Texas Senate candidate James Talarico because of the FCC’s new scrutiny of political content.
This playbook isn’t a Trump original, as my colleague Zack Beauchamp has explained. In fact, weaponizing broadcast regulations was also a favored technique of former Hungarian Prime Minister (and infamous strongman) Viktor Orbán, who successfully used licensing rules and other bureaucratic technicalities to force independent media outlets into submission.
Likewise, revoking the press credentials of critical reporters has long been a favorite tactic of Russian President Vladimir Putin, Nico Perrino, the executive vice president of the nonprofit civil liberties group Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, said in a briefing on Wednesday: “These are things that are done by regimes that we do not want to emulate.”
Lest these comparisons get you down, however, recall that neither Hungary nor Russia has all the defenses that the US does. Defenses like, for example, an independent court system.

Walmart CEO John Furner wants to clear the air about how the retail giant is using new pricing technology.
"We don't set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won't," he said in a memo to employees and customers on Friday.
Furner said he was responding to questions he's received this year about how the company is implementing new digital shelf labels and the AI-powered shopping assistant, Sparky.
"When you engage with Sparky, that's an invitation to serve you better not to use your personal information to set a personalized price," he said. "We've never used the relationships our associates have with customers to charge more, and we won't do that with AI."
Furner also said that any form of personalized pricing would violate the company's decades-long commitment to being an everyday low-price retailer.
"We price the product, not the person," Furner said.
Walmart and its competitors have faced growing public scrutiny over the rollout of both online shopping assistants and in-store digital tech that critics say could be used to selectively hike prices on individual customers.
The company has said its focus on using the tech is to improve the efficiency of its stores and deliver a better shopping experience for customers.
Read the full memo from Walmart CEO John Furner:
To our customers and members, For more than 50 years, our pricing principle has been Every Day Low Prices (EDLP): low, consistent prices you can count on without guessing whether Monday or Tuesday is the better day to shop or wondering if someone else is getting a better price than you. Prices can change. We lower them when we can pass savings along. Sometimes they rise because an item costs more to buy or transport. But using someone's income, shopping history or moment of need to charge them more would violate the EDLP promise our business model is built on. We won't do it. YOU are at the heart of our WHY and our relationship with you has always been built on trust. For decades, our associates have built that trust, one interaction at a time. So, as technology improves, we're putting the same attention on trust and serving you as we do when you walk into our stores and clubs. I've heard concerns about companies using that information and technology to charge you more. I want to tell you where we stand: We price the product, not the person. Many of you have seen the digital shelf labels in our stores and some have asked why we have them. A shelf price should match what rings up at checkout. Digital shelf labels help us do that more consistently by displaying the right price. They also save associates time replacing paper tags. It may sound like an easy task — but as someone who has had to change those paper tags by hand over the years, I can tell you it's a time-consuming and unrewarding task. Our associates would much rather be helping you, our customers. AI has added incredible new ways for us to serve our customers and members, and it rightfully also raises questions about the information it has access to. Understanding our customers and members is what makes us special and allows us to better serve them. For years, that has taken place in our stores and clubs as we help each customer with their individual needs. We want to offer that same level of personalized care when our customers shop online with Sparky, our AI shopping assistant. When you engage with Sparky, that's an invitation to serve you better not to use your personal information to set a personalized price. We've never used the relationships our associates have with customers to charge more, and we won't do that with AI. With that in mind, I want to share three commitments you can count on as technology changes: 
- We don't set different prices based on who you are or the time of day, and we won't. Your income, shopping history, urgency or what we think you could pay won't change the price. And whether you're buying groceries or electronics on a hot afternoon or in a sudden rush for an item, it's never a reason to charge you more.
- We'll hold our shopping tools to the same promise. We won't use the information you share with us on Sparky or otherwise to raise your price or hide lower-priced options that meet your needs.
- We'll continue to use your information responsibly and respect your choices. You decide whether to share additional details for more personalized help. We'll continue to be clear about how we use that information, protect it and honor the choices you make. When you do share, we will focus that data on ways that better serve you.
Our people will continue to oversee pricing, and we'll monitor and test our technology against these commitments. Thank you for trusting us with part of your family's budget. If there's one thing I hope you take from this note, it's how much we value the trust you place in us. Technology will keep changing. Our responsibility to earn your trust and help you save money and live better won't. John Furner President and CEO, Walmart Inc.

Ngetich breaks women-only half-marathon record
- Published
Agnes Ngetich broke the world record for a women-only half marathon as she took gold at the World Road Running Championships in Copenhagen.
The Kenyan claimed victory in one hour, five minutes and 15 seconds as she took a second off the previous record, which her compatriot Peres Jepchirchir set in winning the World half marathon gold in 2020.
Ethiopia's Letesenbet Gidey holds the overall women's half-marathon world record with a time of 1:02:52.
"My coach believed in me and told me that I could do it, that I could win the gold medal," said Ngetich, 25. "So, I am very happy and very grateful to now hold the world half marathon record, too."
In April 2025, Ngetich set a new 10km world record when she clocked 29:27 to become the first woman to run the distance in under 30 minutes in a women-only race.
She also broke the 10km world record in Valencia in 2024, becoming the first woman to run the distance in under 29 minutes when she won a mixed road race in 28:46.
Ngetich added: "I am now going to discuss with my coach what is ahead of me. But I know I am coming back to track races in 2027, because there is a World Athletics Championships.
"It is my dream to win a gold medal on the track. It is the only one I am missing."
Sweden's Andreas Almgren won the men's half marathon as he broke his own European record by 35 seconds, crossing the line in 58:06 in Copenhagen.

Two days before she helped India win its first shooting gold medal at the Asian Games, Suruchi Singh sat alone in her hotel room in Nagoya, trying to figure out how she was going to pull herself back from the lowest point of her international career.
She couldn’t think of anything, so she did what made sense to her.
She slept. For 13 hours.
When she woke up, she knew what she had to do.
The 20-year-old parted her hair neatly down the middle, kept her nails unvarnished, and wore modest earrings. Churma or malpua made for a special treat. She liked ghar ka khana, with ghar being the village of Sasroli in Haryana’s Jhajjar district.
There were no stickers on her pistol bag of countries she had travelled to, something many of her compatriots flaunted as a flex.
Suruchi wasn’t the sort of person who liked to stand out in a crowd.
The one thing she cared about, though, was pistol shooting.
And she was very good at it. Put her in the middle of a shooting range and she would show just how prodigious her talent is.
On Friday, at the Aichi Prefectural Shooting Range, that’s exactly what she did. Competing in the 10m air pistol mixed team event at the Asian Games, she and Kamaljeet Singh topped qualification with 587, equalling the Asian record.
Then, in the final, they led from start to finish, setting a new Asian record of 484.6 and beating South Korea by 6.6 points to win India’s second gold medal of the Asian Games in Nagoya.
This was India’s first shooting gold medal at these Games, and Suruchi’s role in it was instrumental. She shot 296 in qualification, more than anyone else in the field. In the final, only three of her 24 shots were outside the 10-ring. There was just one series in which she was outshot.
It was simply impressive.
But over the last couple of years, that was exactly what you had come to expect from Suruchi.
The daughter of a former wrestler, she had become one of the world’s leading 10m air pistol shooters, winning five ISSF World Cup gold medals as well as the World Cup Final. She had gone into Nagoya as India’s top-ranked shooter in the event, ahead of Esha Singh, the silver medallist at the previous Asian Games, and Olympic bronze medallist Manu Bhaker.
She was expected to lead India’s challenge for team gold and compete for the individual title herself.
However, she failed to qualify for the individual final, finishing well outside the top eight.
She had shot just 568.
“I don’t even know the last time I shot that badly. It was unacceptable,” she would say later.
National coach Samresh Jang tried to console her. “It happens. It’s your first time at the Asian Games,” he told her.
But it didn’t help.
Suruchi wasn’t the only Indian pistol shooter to struggle in Nagoya. None of India’s six men’s and women’s 10m air pistol entries made the individual final.
But perhaps no one was expected to do as well as her, which made the failure that much harder.
Coaches recalled that she tried to make a joke about how badly she’d done. No one bought it, although, of course, they wouldn’t tell her.
“She was absolutely distraught,” said national coach Ronak Pandit.
Samresh, who had worked with her for the past couple of years, since she made her senior international debut, knew what had gone wrong.
Suruchi had started smoothly but then shot two consecutive 8s.
“They had both gone to completely different ends of the target. That broke her. After that, instead of shooting freely, she started shooting defensively,” he said.
It was the worst thing that could have happened.
“When you are shooting freely, you are shooting without thinking. When you are defensive, you are only thinking of what can go wrong. You are cross-checking every small element,” he said.
Suruchi knew this as well.
She was normally a very fast shooter.
Now she overthought every shot.
She routinely finished her qualification round in around 40 minutes. On Wednesday, she raised and lowered her gun repeatedly, unwilling to pull the trigger. She eventually struggled through to the finish, taking an hour and 13 minutes to fire her 60 shots — just two minutes less than the maximum permitted time.
But there was no point talking about technique at that moment.
Maybe with a more experienced shooter, yes. But, certainly not with someone making her debut.
“Sometimes all you can do is give them space. Let them get over it on their own,” Samresh said.
For Suruchi, the hard reset came in the form of a long sleep.
She got up bleary-eyed but clear-headed, knowing exactly what she had to do.
As India’s best shooter in the selection trials, she had one more chance in the mixed team event.
Her partner was Kamaljeet Singh, another debutant. He had failed to make the final of the men’s event by a solitary point.
Unlike Suruchi, he couldn’t sleep at all.
Suruchi, though, was raring to go. She had a point to prove.
She slept for a more reasonable eight hours the night before the mixed team event.
“I got up aaram se, I prepared myself. I left on time, not even a minute late,” she said.
It wasn’t as if a switch had been flicked and suddenly everything became easy.
Although her score didn’t suggest it, she still had to grit her way through qualification.
“There were times when I made a bad shot and right after that I didn’t have the confidence to release the trigger for my next shot. That happened a few times,” she said.
But she made her way through that round.
In the final, her confidence surged with every shot she made.
After the first series of 10 shots, India led South Korea 103 to 98.1, with 52.7 of India’s points coming from Suruchi’s gun. There was still some way to go, but the contest had already begun to tilt decisively in India’s favour.
“When I saw that score, I felt relaxed. I was very happy. Wow, acchi khaasi lead hai (it’s a very good lead). No tension! Now I can shoot relaxed,” she said.
She shot exactly as she had hoped, even compensating for Kamaljeet, who had a more up-and-down final.
“I knew that when Suruchi was shooting so well, I could even shoot a couple of bad shots and we would be fine. When you have a teammate like that you feel more confident,” he said.
Towards the end of the competition, the long faces from just a couple of days earlier were long forgotten.
Coach Samresh Jang even called for a timeout before the final couple of shots, for no other reason than that he had one and wanted to tell his team they were going to win gold.
With the gold secured, Suruchi still had a long day ahead of her: media commitments, dope-control tests and then the journey back to her hotel room.
After everything that had happened over the previous two days, there was only one thing she wanted.
“I’m looking forward to sleeping,” she said.

Super El Nino report: Co-author explains methodology behind '451,000 excess deaths' estimate
New Delhi, The University of Chicago's Energy Policy Institute's report that claimed that the 'super El Nino' might cause around 15,800 additional heat-related deaths in India over the next six months, was measured using two components, seasonal temperature forecasts, and temperature-mortality relationships, a co-author of the study said.
Emily Grover-Kopec, a co-author, told PTI that temperature-mortality relationships were assessed using "one of the most commonly referenced seasonal forecasts" from the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts .
The recently published report claimed that the climate phenomenon could push global land temperatures 1.2 degrees Celsius above normal in the coming months, resembling the higher temperatures that climate change is projected to deliver in the next 20 years.
"When considering a wide suite of seasonal forecasts that are available, the ECMWF SEAS sits in the middle in terms of the projected temperature anomalies, so this presents a relatively moderate view. We also used temperature-mortality relationships that were peer-reviewed and published in one of the most rigorous economics journals, the Quarterly Journal of Economics in November, 2022," Grover-Kopec, who is also a director at the climate and energy practice at the Rhodium Group, said.
She said that the earlier study used the same formula to predict deaths far into the future based on climate models, adding that this time it was used differently for shorter-term seasonal forecasts.
Asked why a specific window of 1996 to 2025 was chosen for the report, she said that the goal was to keep the numbers relevant to how decision-makers currently plan and act, as the projections are meant to inform how resources are used, and when early action is taken to save lives.
"Using a long baseline period of 30 years in climate science is common and often considered best practice. We therefore referenced the most recent 30-year period as our baseline: 1996-2025," Grover-Kopec told PTI.
Speaking about the findings in the report, Abhiyant Tiwari, who leads the climate resilience and health team at Natural Resources Defense Council in India, noted that it is a useful early warning and underlines the call to action.
"The study is a useful early warning, but its mortality estimates should be treated cautiously as model-based projections, with the full methodology yet to undergo peer review. The findings nevertheless underline the call to action," Tiwari said.
He said that India's experience with Heat Action Plans and stronger institutional frameworks offer a foundation to scale sustained preparedness, protect vulnerable communities, and share valuable lessons with the Global South and the wider world.
Meanwhile, Harshal Ramesh Salve, a public health professional and faculty at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences , stressed that the report provides an opportunity to act swiftly with clear intention for mitigation strategies such as implementing Hs at all levels.
"The report further cements the current knowledge regarding heat impact on human health in the form of mortality and morbidity. As expected, the South Asia region is getting one of the worst estimates of mortality. However, it also provides us an opportunity to act swiftly with clear intention for mitigation strategies such as implementing Hs at all levels, data driven policy making, and developing data-sharing mechanisms at national and local levels," Salve told PTI.
According to the public health professional, an equity-driven approach focusing on the most vulnerable, such as the elderly, people with comorbidities, children, pregnant women and occupational workers, is essential to tackle the situation.

'I have never felt heat like that' - a survivor on watching 33 cellmates die in Nigeria
- Published
Usman Muhammad pauses by the entrance to a tiny Nigerian prison cell and leans his forehead against the wall unable to speak.
The day before he had been trapped inside the stifling room, measuring roughly 6m (19.7ft) by 3m (9.8ft), with more than 50 other prisoners.
Thirty-three of his cellmates died in the cramped conditions in the prison in Minna, the capital of Nigeria's Niger state - and four died later in hospital.
The mass deaths caused an outcry and sparked protests, including attacks on public buildings, as relatives and locals demanded answers.
Federal officials had initially blamed the deaths on a diphtheria outbreak but exactly what happened is now the subject of an investigation.
"I have never felt heat like that in my life. When we touched each other's bodies, it felt like fire burning," Muhammad tells the BBC once he is able to gather his thoughts.
When he was locked inside, there was standing room only amid humidity levels of more than 90%, which in some circumstances can be dangerous to human health as it prevents the natural cooling mechanism of sweat drying on the skin.
The temperature outside was above 25C and the only ventilation came from a small, high-up window.
"One of us fainted and we started knocking at the [cell] door. When [a guard] came we asked him for water. He looked at the guy that fainted and closed the door. That's how they started dying one after the other," Muhammad says.
Like the others who had been detained, the young man, in his 20s, is an artisanal miner, eking out a living searching for precious metals at mine sites.
The federal government has tried to crack down on this alleged illegal activity as it says it costs the country revenue, damages the environment and can be linked to wider criminal activity.
Officers from the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC) had arrested a large group of miners near Minna last Tuesday and Wednesday.
The prisoners were held at its detention centre in the city, but the NSCDC has not shared either the names or the number of those it was holding.
As the hours inside the cell wore on, the heat and dehydration became unbearable and Muhammad says some of the detainees began drinking their own urine and collecting sweat from their bodies to try to stay alive.
He describes seeing people in distress and struggling to breathe.
"People were calling for help, some were already very weak."
But no-one came to help, he and others allege.
"While in the cell, we were shouting and telling them that people were dying," another survivor Adamu Isah told the Reuters news agency.
"We tried to break down the door when they refused to open it… At one point, a security officer came to the door.
"We were shouting and telling him that people were dying, but he said it wasn't his problem if people died."
Finally, on Thursday, the cell door was opened and the guards saw the dead bodies.
The NSCDC has not directly responded to the accusations of neglect and maltreatment but has said that 24 of its personnel are now in custody in connection with the deaths, including its suspended Niger state commandant Suberu Aniviye.
"The people who were killed are not flies. How can this go unlooked? We will get to the bottom of this," Niger state Governor Umaru Bago told the BBC.
As the organisation involved is a federal body rather than a force under his jurisdiction, such as the police, the governor is unable to exert direct influence but he welcomes the investigation that has been ordered by the government in capital, Abuja.
A 10-member committee has now been set-up to determine exactly what happened.
It has two weeks to establish the causes of the deaths and identify who was responsible and can recommend legal action against anyone found culpable.
No officer, regardless of rank, would be protected and any attempt to obstruct the investigation would be taken seriously, Interior Minister Olubunmi Tunji-Ojo said.
As he leaves the cell after talking to the BBC, Muhammad says he hopes that by speaking out he can help find justice and bring some closure to this traumatic event.

The United States’ withdrawal from key aid programs has put has put healthcare in Africa and the Global South “under growing strain” a new report warns.
The report says the Trump administration’s cuts to programs such as US Agency for International Development (USAID), as well as the Covid-19 pandemic and rising costs of living globally have brought “new urgency” for the need to reform healthcare in the region.
The report, titled A Sovereign Future For Health, was created by the Accra Reset, a global health initiative led by John Dramani Mahama, Ghana’s president, that believes countries in Africa and the wider global south should have greater control over their health development rather than being dependent on aid from western countries and international institutions.
A key statistic cited by Mahama and Accra Reset is that Africa produces less than 1% of its vaccines while carrying about 25% of the global disease burden.
The report cites how abrupt changes to global health financing, such as the US withdrawal from several global health initiatives, forced countries within the global south to urgently restructure their finances. The report points to the Trump administration’s decision to dissolve USAID, which pushed Nigeria to absorb the 28,000 health workers who were previously employed by the agency at a cost of $200m.
External financing for health in Africa contracted by close to 70% between 2021 and 2025, the report notes, meaning that African countries historically dependent on aid were forced to adapt quickly.
The withdrawal of the US Emergency Plan for Aids Relief (Pepfar) funding for South Africa, which provided over $400m a year annually and is credited with saving 26m lives globally since 2003, led to HIV clinics closing across the country. That left 1.4 million people living with HIV to face uncertainty about their treatment.
Such funding cuts caused “severe and devastating” disruption globally, according to research presented at the 26th International Aids Conference in Brazil earlier this year.
At the World Health Assembly in May, Mahama said Ghana lost $78m following the closure of USAID programs which affected maternal healthcare, the treatment of malaria, nutrition and HIV/Aids interventions.
The initiative’s latest report, published on Monday, comes amid these major cuts to international aid and growing pressure on countries to take greater ownership of their health systems. Mahama refers to these aid cuts as a clear example that donor dependency is not sustainable.
“The Accra Reset is not an argument for traditional donors to do less on global health. It is an argument for doing it differently and doing it better. As countries take greater ownership of their health futures, donor countries should step up to support that transition – following the lead of countries that set their own priorities, and work alongside them to determine where outside support is most valuable,” said Naveen Rao, senior vice-president of the health initiative at the Rockefeller Foundation. “The Accra Reset shows how we can evolve to back country-led solutions while advancing our shared health and economic interests.”
Mahama notes in the report that the “past few years have shaken global health cooperation to its foundations”.
“The Covid-19 pandemic exposed the risks created by concentrated production and unequal access to essential health products; rising debt and fiscal pressures have constrained national health budgets; and declining development assistance is placing programs and services under growing strain,” he continued, adding: “These shocks have brought new urgency to reform debates that have continued for years with limited progress. It was in this context that we launched the Accra Reset and its Sovereign Health Agenda – to give renewed political force to the reform agenda and place the agency of countries of the Global South at its centre.”
The report comes alongside a recent survey revealing the progressive attitudes many US citizens have towards foreign aid. Some 75% of Americans – including more than one in two (52%) who primarily support Donald Trump – agree that the US should restore disease prevention aid to contain the Ebola virus, according to polling of over 2,000 US adults commissioned by the Rockefeller Foundation.
The polling also revealed that 65% of US adults support international cooperation even if it means compromising some national interests; 64% also believe Americans have a shared responsibility to others, including people in other countries whom they do not know.
The Guardian has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) for comment.

Step Curry has agreed to a two-year contract extension worth $116m (£88m) that would take him through the 2028-29 season as he backs up his longstanding commitment to finish his career with the Warriors
Saturday 26 September 2026 08:00, UK
The Golden State Warriors have signed star guard Steph Curry to a two-year, $116m (£88m) contract extension, according to ESPN.
The deal includes a player option in the final season (2028-29), according to sources.
On top of Curry's final year on his previous contract, he'll be earning up to $178.5m over the next three seasons.
Golden State general manager Mike Dunleavy said last month he was optimistic of getting something done with the two-time MVP and NBA career leader in three-pointers.
Curry, who turns 39 this season, will complete a $62.6m extension he signed for the 2026-27 season in August 2024 before the new contract takes him through 2029 - which would be his 20th season.
His contract will dip to $55.7m for the 2027-28 season and a player option for $60.2m in the 2028-29 season.
"We're in a very interesting situation," Curry told ESPN earlier this week. "All the different salary cap conditions of whether I sign for a max or less or whatever it is, I want to be on a competitive team. I want to have an opportunity to have some flexibility because we haven't had that in years past, the recent past. This team should have flexibility to make necessary moves if things happen. Those are always just the considerations.
"For me, information and patience is key. It's just a very unique situation all the way around based on where we've been the last four years, where I'm at in my career, what our team looks like this year and the absolute desperation to win. Trying to balance all that.
"The idea of getting back to work is exciting," Curry added. "I feel like I've taken advantage of the offseason. I feel like there's no hesitation about where I'm at physically going in. But I'm excited about getting back to work."
Curry averaged 26.6 points, 4.7 assists and 3.6 rebounds but was limited to 43 games last season because of injuries. He has won four NBA titles with Golden State, most recently in 2022.
The extension brings Curry's career on-court earnings to $652m, making him the first player to eclipse $600m in NBA history.

When I first heard of Life360, my first thought was that I knew I never wanted to use the app to track my two kids, despite its popularity among parents. Almost a decade later, I still feel the same.
But it wasn't until my oldest got his driver's license in 2020 that I realized my decision to opt out of this trend was helping to build trust with my teenager. And now, my relationships with both of my kids are better for it.
I prefer conversations to spying
Life360 is an app advertised as a way to coordinate within families, from keeping up with busy schedules to checking everyone's locations. The app also boasts safety features that are likely to appeal to parents of new drivers.
But as a mother, I only saw it as a way to spy on kids, something I had no intention of doing.
Of course, it's important to know where they are and who they're with. And I'm sure they occasionally didn't tell me the truth about their whereabouts, and though that's not ideal, it's been fine. I know I wasn't always honest with my parents about these things when I was a teen.
Instead of seeing where my kids are via an app, I prefer to have face-to-face conversations about their friends, jobs, after-school activities, and their everyday lives and interests.
A therapist's advice helped me
The issue of tracking came up when my son started driving and again when my daughter got her license three years later. As I contemplated whether or not to track them as most of their friends' parents did, I recalled advice a therapist gave me years earlier as we discussed parenting during the pandemic.
"Remember what it was like to be their age," the therapist said. "Try to recall your mindset and think about how you would feel going through what they're going through."
That advice served me well in many parenting situations, including the Life 360 decision. I reflected on my emotions and thoughts at their ages, remembering how I wanted to be independent, learn to make decisions, and trust my own judgment. My parents didn't have the ability to track me, and if they had, I'm certain I would have figured out ways to get around it, just as teens do today.
More on child independence
For instance, when my son was in high school, the mother of one of his friends called me because her son wasn't answering her calls, and the app pinpointed him at my address. He wasn't at my house. But apparently his phone was.
Another mom acquaintance once told me she tracked her son at college and discovered he was skipping classes.
The app didn't prevent these teenagers from lying to their parents or from making poor choices.
We have a zero-tolerance policy
My agreement not to track my teens did come with rules. Text me when leaving a location and when arriving at the next. Text me if plans change. Return texts from me promptly. And this deal ran on the zero-tolerance policy. If I caught them in a lie or they otherwise abused our arrangement, the app would immediately go on their phones.
My son is now 22 with a college degree, and my daughter is almost 19 and a college sophomore. I never had to follow through on that threat.
I often heard other moms talking about how tracking gives them peace of mind that their kids are safe, which sometimes made me second-guess my decision.
However, when I look at my children who aren't children anymore, I'm thankful I opted out. I respect my young adults and love our close relationships. I trust them to use good judgment, though I know sometimes they won't. But they'll learn from their mistakes, and that's part of becoming an adult, more so than their mother monitoring their every move.

Iran has proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz to traffic within seven days if certain conditions are met, as the cost of the seven-month conflict begins to weigh on both sides.

US and Iranian negotiators were also exploring a possible ‘phased’ solution to the crisis, prioritising the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports, per Reuters.

Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey discuss aid for Riyadh in New York
The foreign ministers of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met on the sidelines of the UN general assembly to plan a meeting to discuss aid for Riyadh in its fight with the Houthis, the Saudi Gazette reported on Friday.
The ministers were said to have reviewed ongoing preparations for a chiefs of staff meeting, which will look at their respective responsibilities under their defence pact.

The Iran-backed Houthi rebels have ramped up attacks on Saudi ships and infrastructure in recent weeks, seizing land on the Red Sea coast to squeeze the Bab el-Mandeb strait, through which Riyadh exports oil with the Strait of Hormuz closed.
Saudi Arabia has a joint defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey - under which an attack on one is considered an attack on all - but neither have yet offered material support.
The latest: Iran suggests Strait of Hormuz could reopen within a week
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said in New York on Thursday that his country’s mediators have submitted a plan to the White House that would pave the way for the Strait of Hormuz to reopen within a week.
“We have introduced a plan to the United States through the mediators that if certain conditions are met ... the strait will be open in seven days”, he said.
Should both sides reach an agreement, they could restart negotiations for a final deal, Araghchi added.
Reuters reportedly separately on Thursday that US and Iranian negotiators were exploring a possible ‘phased’ solution to the crisis, prioritising the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the US blockade on Iranian ports.
A senior Iranian official said the most plausible way to end the impasse would be a phased arrangement, with Iran allowing navigation through Hormuz in return for the US lifting its economic blockade and Tehran potentially gaining access to frozen assets.
Iran’s motivation to end the crisis is a recognition of the economic cost of prolonged confrontation, officials said, noting that neither side wants to be the first to back down.
A phased agreement would involve Donald Trump accepting another temporary fix after the interim Islamabad Memorandum collapsed in July.
A central challenge facing the negotiators is not just to sketch out a deal but also to ensure any concessions are durable enough for both sides to trust, the sources said.
Yemeni VP says weapons, technology should be kept from rebels' hands
Arguing that protecting the strait "is the responsibility of every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation," Yemen’s vice president Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer urged the international community to keep weapons and technology from getting into the rebels' hands.
For years, the UN Security Council has imposed an arms embargo on the Houthis and an asset freeze and travel ban on their leaders and top officials.
Iran denies arming the Houthis, but smuggled Iranian weapons and parts have been seized from numerous shipments bound for Yemen, and a report by UN experts in 2024 documented extensive military ties between the Houthis, Iran and its other allies.
Al Alimi-Bawzer contended on Thursday that the rebels wouldn't have been able to maintain their position for a dozen years without Iranian weapons, expertise and military technologies.
The Houthis claimed on Thursday to have fired dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia's southwestern Jazan province. A Saudi military spokesperson, Major General Turki al-Malki, said the kingdom intercepted six ballistic missiles targeting its Red Sea port of Yanbu and the southwestern city of Taif, blaming the Houthis.
His statement followed alerts by Saudi civil defence authorities, who later noted the danger had passed.
Yemen tells UN that Houthi rebels' moves on key strait threaten global economy
Yemen's internationally recognised government pressed world leaders anew on Thursday for help defeating the Houthis, saying that their new perch along one of the world's busiest waterways presents an international economic risk.
The Houthis — who have controlled Yemen's capital, Sanaa, and much of the country's north for over a decade — stormed down Yemen's coast this month and seized the crucial port city of Mokha and key Red Sea islands.
That gives them better surveillance of ships passing through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, at the sea's southern end. About 12 per cent of the world's trade usually passes through the waterway.
The rebels have declared a blockade on Saudi shipping. While asserting there's no other threat to commercial shipping on the Red Sea, they have warned other nations not to get involved.
But the vice president of the internationally recognised government council urged world leaders at the UN General Assembly not to trust the Houthis' assurances and to see a bigger picture in the strife around the strait.
Russian, Iranian foreign ministers say only diplomatic solution to conflict around Iran
Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov and his Iranian counterpart met on Thursday and Moscow said both agreed that only a diplomatic settlement could end tension in the Middle East sparked by the US-Israeli war against Iran.
"Current regional and international issues were discussed with emphasis on the situation around Iran," Russia's foreign ministry said in a statement after Lavrov and Iran's Abbas Araqchi met in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.
"It was stressed that there is no alternative to a diplomatic settlement of the crisis provoked by the illegal actions of the United States and Israel."
Russian president Vladimir Putin and his Iranian counterpart Masoud Pezeshkian signed a strategic cooperation partnership in 2025 which provides for a deepening of bilateral ties and closer defence cooperation, but includes no mutual defence clause.
Each side has provided the other with military know-how and equipment.
Pezeshkian thanked Putin earlier this month for Moscow's position on the Iran war and said together, Moscow and Tehran can resist what he called US "unilateralism".
Netanyahu praises Trump during his UNGA speech
Benjamin Netanyahu was making a short visit to the US for his UN address and, unusually, without a planned meeting with US president Donald Trump, whom he praised during his speech.
"We will continue to defend our state. We will continue to win because we have no other choice. In this battle against the barbarians, we've had no greater partner than President Trump. I thank him. I thank him for his bold leadership," he said.
UN delegates walk out of Netanyahu speech
Delivering a defiant address to the United Nations on Thursday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu mounted a firm defence of Israel's regional military actions, attempting to push back against deepening global isolation ahead of upcoming domestic elections.
