- Published
Five senior military officials have been detained in Kazakhstan following the death of 14 service members who were taking part in military exercises.
Those who died were among a total of 17 who were swept into the Caspian Sea as they were disembarking from a boat on Thursday. Officials say the incident occurred "during a combat training mission due to a sharp deterioration in meteorological conditions and increasing winds".
Three were rescued.
Those detained include the chief of staff and first deputy commander of Kazakhstan's Naval Forces, two military unit commanders, and the commanders of a marine company and a boat. They are suspected of criminal negligence.
An interior ministry committee has been set up to investigate the incident, which occurred some 43km (27 miles) from the city of Aktau in south-western Kazakstan.
Deputy Interior Minister Sanzhar Adilov said a pretrial investigation into the deaths was being conducted.
The investigation was looking into the decisions made during the organisation and execution of the military training exercise, whether safety requirements had been observed, and weather conditions had been taken into account - in addition to technical specifications of the boat.
More than 500 military personnel, warships and coastal units were participating in the Caspian Defense 2026 military exercise, according to the Kazakh ministry of defence.

Five baby orangutans have been found in a forest in India, prompting authorities to investigate if they were trafficked into the country from south-east Asia.
The orangutans, native only to the islands of Borneo and Sumatra and known for their shaggy red fur, were found in Balasore district of Odisha state, thousands of kilometres away from their natural habitat.
Odisha’s environment minister, Ram Singh Khuntia, said wildlife investigators were trying to establish how the rare apes reached India.
“We suspect that an international racket might be involved in this,” Singh said.
International commercial trade in orangutans is prohibited under Cites – a global agreement governing trade in endangered wildlife.
The five babies were found by forest department officials who were patrolling in the Jaleswar range in Balasore district.
Officials believed the orangutans had been in the area for just a few days, and they have now been placed in quarantine at a zoological park in Odisha.
According to the World Wildlife Fund, about 104,000 orangutans remain in Borneo and Sumatra, down from more than 230,000 a century ago.
The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis), a third species, is classified as critically endangered, with fewer than 800 believed to survive in the wild.
In November, conservationists found the Tapanuli population had been reduced by 7% after severe flooding in Indonesia.
Between 33 and 54 Tapanuli orangutans were estimated to have been killed in widespread floods and landslides in North Sumatra province.
Previous research has suggested annual losses of 1% of the Tapanuli orangutan population would be sufficient to lead to eventual extinction.
The entire Tapanuli population dwells solely in the West Block of the Batang Toru, a forest threatened by mining, palm oil plantations and a large hydropower project.

Three infants died after a fire broke out at the Special Newborn Care Unit (SNCU) ward of Rajiv Gandhi Institute of Medical Sciences (RIMS) in Telangana’s Adilabad district late on Monday (September 21) night. The incident occurred around 11.40 p.m. As many as 25 other infants being treated in the ward were safely rescued and evacuated in time.
According to Adilabad District Medical and Health Officer (DMHO) Sadhana, the fire was caused after an air-conditioner in the reception area of the SNCU burst into flames.
“The SNCU has two flanks, one with 11 beds, and another with 13 beds, while the Kangaroo Mother Care area located opposite the SNCU has four beds. The sections are enclosed and have glass windows. When the fire broke out, smoke accumulated inside the unit. As soon as the fire was noticed, the attendants of patients broke the glass windows and evacuated the babies from the affected areas,” the DMHO said.
The rescued infants were subsequently shifted to nearby private hospitals for further treatment. The two infants who died, aged five and four days respectively, were preterm babies. One of them died immediately after the incident, while the other succumbed four hours later. The third infant, a two-day-old girl who was born prematurely at 28 weeks and weighed 1.1 kg, was in a critical condition and died while being shifted to a nearby hospital, confirmed Director of Medical Education (DME) N. Vani.
Upon receiving information about the fire, a fire tender was rushed to the hospital and the blaze was brought under control. The exact cause of the fire was is yet to be ascertained. The police have registered a case and launched an investigation into the incident.
Adilabad Superintendent of Police (SP) Akhil Mahajan said the incident occurred at around 11.40 p.m., and police teams reached the hospital within three minutes, by 11.43 p.m. “Although Ganesh immersion processions were under way and a large number of police personnel were deployed, our teams were able to reach the spot within three minutes and assist in evacuating the children,” he said.
CM conveys condolences
Chief Minister A. Revanth Reddy expressed grief over the incident and conveyed his condolences to the families of the infants. He stated that the death of infants was extremely tragic. The Chief Minister directed officials to ensure better medical treatment for the children undergoing treatment at the hospital and to continuously monitor their health condition.
Mr. Reddy ordered an inquiry into the incident and directed officials to submit a report on the causes of the fire. He further instructed authorities to strengthen fire and other safety measures in hospitals across the State to prevent similar incidents in the future.
Govt. support
Health Minister C. Damodar Raja Narasimha, who inspected the fire incident site, expressed grief over the deaths and conveyed his condolences to the bereaved families.
The Minister also reviewed the rescue and relief measures undertaken following the incident and the arrangements made to safely shift the infants undergoing treatment in the SNCU to other wards. He also sought updates from doctors on the condition of the infants and other children receiving treatment and directed them to provide the best possible medical care while closely monitoring their health. The Minister later met the families of the affected children and assured them of the government’s support.
“The condition of other children who were in the ward at the time of the incident was stable and none have developed any complications,” said a note from the Minister’s office.
He was accompanied by Adilabad MLA Payal Shanker and Principal Secretary, Health, Medical and Family Welfare, Dr. Christina Z. Chongthu.
A preliminary inquiry indicated that an electrical short circuit in an air-conditioning unit may have triggered the fire, causing plastic components to burn and filling the SNCU with thick smoke, the Minister said. A detailed enquiry by an expert committee would ascertain the exact cause and identify any lapses in safety standards, he added.
The Minister said RIMS staff, district officials, Fire and Police personnel acted swiftly to disconnect the power supply, evacuate the infants and provide emergency medical care.
He said a 150-bed Mother and Child Health (M&CH) Building would be established at RIMS, taking its bed strength from 800 to 950. Plans were also under way to develop the institute into a super-speciality hospital, besides setting up Hematology and Emergency Trauma Care wings.
The Minister said steps were being taken to increase postgraduate medical seats in Paediatrics, Gynaecology, Radiology and other departments and strengthen the out-patient and in-patient services at RIMS.

Mention Rui Pinto's name to Manchester City fans outside Etihad Stadium, and you mostly get blank faces.
But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work.
Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City.
Through his website Football Leaks, he published a cache of confidential club documents, including internal emails about sponsorship deals and payments.
That ultimately led to the Premier League charges for breaching of financial rules and Friday's news that the club had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 counts.
For some, 37-year-old Pinto is no more than a criminal who stole information with sinister intentions.
To others, though, he is a bastion of truth who has shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.
BBC Sport has been on a journey across Europe to find out more about the mysterious figure who was the catalyst for so much controversy.
We spoke to one of Pinto's former teachers, a Portuguese politician fighting for him to be protected as a whistleblower, journalists who published the leaks, and a former financial adviser at Manchester City.
And we sat just a few feet from Pinto in the latest of his court cases.
'Maybe he felt the need for justice'
With his cherubic face and spiky hair, Pinto is instantly recognisable. And it seems he hasn't changed.
It is how Mario Falcao, his former geography teacher, remembers him.
In a small courtyard garden in Portugal, we got a glimpse of what Pinto was like as a boy.
"Rui was a perfectly normal pupil. He was nice, with his spiky hair, he was quite sociable but not extrovert," Falcao said.
"He had a good relationship with the teachers, although he did miss these classes quite often. His father was always on top of things, so in the end he passed quite easily."
Did he spot a strong interest in computers in a young Pinto?
"Certainly he was very good in computers. All the work that he did for various courses were very good, when he put his mind to it," his former teacher explained.
The now-retired Falcao speaks fondly of Pinto, who he says behaved just like his friends and would "go to the gym, go to McDonald's".
Pinto had a modest upbringing. He grew up in an area called Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the Douro River from Porto, Portugal's second-largest city. We visited the road where he used to live, which featured tile-fronted houses with terracotta roofs.
His school, Escola Secundaria Almeida Garrett, was well-regarded and was known by locals as 'the university'.
His father, Francisco, worked in a shoe factory and later as an antiques dealer. His mother had died when he was 11.
Falcao said he never predicted what was to come of his former pupil.
"We were very surprised," he said of the moment Pinto was named as the founder of Football Leaks in 2019.
"We weren't imagining anything like this could happen, that he could have problems with justice.
"I certainly wouldn't wish him and his family to be in this situation. Perhaps it was a question of the excesses of youth, his ability with computers, and maybe an excess of club-ism."
"So, you know, the fact that he supported FC Porto prompted him to commit some acts, but maybe he also felt the need for justice that young people very often do feel."

'One of most important whistleblowers in Europe'
Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football".
Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John".
"It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important."
Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums.
"We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela.
"You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion."
It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted.
The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto.
Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar.
Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him.
It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen.
Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team.
"In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said.
"If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work.
"It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context and you can see if there's any reliability issues.
"We always need to make sure that it's authentic material and whenever we publish something about it, it needs to be in the public interest to start writing."
Winterbach finally met Pinto in person in 2019, when he was being held in prison in Lisbon awaiting his trial. He conducted another interview with Pinto in witness protection, in a secret location with high security, describing the arrangements for getting there as being "like a Hollywood movie".
He said: "Rui Pinto is not very tall. He has very distinctive hair, like spiky hair. He usually has red cheeks and he's a youthful, cheeky, funny character. He's friendly and warm when you meet him.
"He's a very impressive character, he's very focused, he's very concentrated. He's very, very intelligent. He's very idealistic about the topics that he uncovered.
"He's one of the most important whistleblowers that we have in Europe or maybe the world."
In all, Pinto provided more than three terabytes - equivalent to about 3,000 copies of the Encyclopedia Britannica - of information to Der Spiegel and other outlets in the European Investigative Collaborations consortium.
A 'hero' or a 'thief'?
We encountered stark contrasts in perceptions of Pinto wherever we went.
Former Portuguese politician and diplomat Ana Gomes has also met Pinto in prison and testified on his behalf at one of his trials. She is firmly of the view that he deserves to be protected, not prosecuted.
"What he has exposed is very important. In Portugal, definitely he is by far the most important whistleblower," the former Member of the European Parliament told us in Lisbon.
"He should be made an ally of our judicial and criminal investigative authorities. He has helped the authorities of other European countries in going after the corrupt and the criminals, instead of being the subject of this judicial prosecution by the choice of our public prosecutors."
When asked what she would say to Manchester City, who had their emails hacked by him, her answer is blunt.
"I couldn't care less. If they have nothing to hide, what's their problem?"
Jose Carlos Freitas, a retired journalist, said Gomes's sympathetic view is not a widely held one.
"For the majority of the people, they look at him as a thief," he said. "For some people, he is a kind of hero, a Robin Hood, you can say because he was exposing the dark side of the business of so many clubs, but unfortunately for the majority of the people, he is not a good person."
Varela is on the fence. "Nowadays, I think I put him in the middle [between whistleblower and criminal hacker] because he got the information illegally. But he gave us, all of us, a view, a dark view of European football, so he did a job to the society illegally."
Wherever you sit in the debate, he has faced serious consequences for what he did. As Winterbach puts it, Pinto "has powerful enemies through the work that he has done".
Pinto's life has been far from normal for six years
For the past six years, Pinto's life has been far from normal.
Having been arrested in Hungary in 2019, he was extradited to Portugal and has at various points been in solitary confinement, under house arrest and in witness protection.
Following his first trial in Portugal, in 2023 he received a four-year suspended sentence having been found guilty of attempted extortion, illegal access to data and breach of correspondence.
A separate trial in France resulted in a six-month suspended prison sentence a few months later.
And in January last year, Pinto's latest trial began in Lisbon. The opening day at the Central Criminal Court encapsulated the realities of his life and the difference in opinions of him.
Pinto arrived with members of his witness protection team, two of whom stayed in the courtroom throughout the hearing, along with an armed police presence.
He was dressed casually in a blue, long-sleeved top, jeans and brown boots, and had his distinctive spiky hair and some facial hair. He was fairly expressionless throughout, aside from the occasional shrug of the shoulders or glance at his team.
We sat just a few feet from him, as he conversed with his legal team in hushed tones and spoke to the judge purely to confirm details like his name and age. When asked for his address, he said he could not give this for security reasons.
Local journalist Miguel Dantas explained the security arrangements were scaled back compared with the first trial, when he wore a bulletproof jacket and there were snipers on the roof.
Rui Patricio, the lawyer representing Benfica, told the court Pinto was "no more, no less than a burglar", that he had obtained the information by "illegal and condemnable methods" and that the ends did not justify the means.
Outside court, Patricio added: "Our argument is very, very simple. He's a hacker, period, just like that. What he did is not allowed - it's a crime and there are no excuses. It's very, very simple. Very, very straightforward."
In his statement in court, Francisco Texeira da Mota, representing Pinto, accepted that his client was "not a hero and not a saint" but said he had brought "advantages for society".
What is the impact of Football Leaks?
The impact of Football Leaks is still being felt a decade on.
The Premier League's case against Manchester City has been one of unprecedented scale and significance.
From speaking to his legal team after the court hearing, it became clear Pinto has been closely monitoring that case from witness protection since the Premier League brought the charges in February 2023.
Asked if the outcome mattered, Texeira da Mota said: "I think it's important for him because it's very difficult to be like he is, living a very difficult life, more or less hiding, because he made some revelations, he whistle-blowed lots of important things, namely about Manchester City.
"So it would be important for him to feel vindicated that it was useful, that something happened, because what of what he said."
Speaking before the announcement of the decision in the City case, Stefan Borson, a former financial adviser to Manchester City, said: "I think for City, really, the whole of the Sheikh Mansour era is at stake if the core allegations are proven against the club.
"I think the consequences could be very far reaching for the club, and it would be a very difficult thing for them to deal with.
"Over time, clearly there would have to be some kind of reset. I think in many ways the Premier League is a loser either way."
Borson's view was that Pinto should not be seen as "some kind of warrior for freedom".
He said: "We know that what he carried out was a criminal act and he's been prosecuted for it.
"We also know that hackers of that nature do try and reframe themselves as part of the defence process as purveyors of freedom of speech. But, once those documents are in the public domain, then I think it's for the authorities to act."
For some, Rui Pinto is a criminal hacker who stole information with sinister intentions. To others he is a heroic whistleblower who shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.
What is undeniable is that one Portuguese man on his computer in Budapest has had a seismic impact on global football.

A payments business that operates across Africa and is ultimately controlled by an Indian billionaire has announced its intention to float on the struggling London Stock Exchange.
Airtel Money, the mobile money arm of Airtel Africa, is planning one of the biggest UK listings in years, in a boost for the shrinking London market that has faced a string of recent departures.
The company is understood to be hoping to raise about $800m (£601m) from the initial public offering (IPO) and is targeting a valuation of $8bn to $9bn, which would make it one of London’s largest listings in recent years.
Airtel Money has 53 million monthly active users across 13 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, including Uganda, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of Congo.
It operates through a network of branches and kiosks, which enable customers to load money on to their phones, withdraw cash and access other money services, and the company generated revenues of just under $1.4bn in the last financial year.
Airtel Money’s parent company is Airtel Africa, a telecoms provider that is part of the Indian conglomerate Bharti Enterprises, which is ultimately controlled by the billionaire Sunil Bharti Mittal. Airtel Africa is already listed on the FTSE 100 but said it wanted Airtel Money to be listed separately.
“From a company perspective, [the listing] gives us flexibility for the future,” said Airtel Money’s chief executive, Ian Ferrao.
“We evaluated multiple [stock] exchanges, including the Middle East because we’ve got a headquarters in Dubai, along with European and North American exchanges. Ultimately, shareholders felt that London was the right choice. We still believe there is deep capital available … all the global institutional investors are here.”
Ferrao added: “Most importantly there’s a deep understanding of emerging markets in the London market and Africa specifically.”
Airtel Money said it would announce more details about the float in early October, including the indicative price range and number of shares to be offered, with final pricing to follow later in the month.
Airtel Africa had originally targeted a listing in the first six months of 2026 but delayed it to the second half of the year, blaming unfavourable market conditions as a result of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Several other companies also pushed back planned IPOs amid the market volatility caused by the conflict.
Airtel Africa owns just under 78% of Airtel Money and will remain a long-term investor after the IPO. Minority stakes are held by TPG, Mastercard, the Qatar Investment Authority and Chimetech Holding.
Revenue in Airtel Money’s most recent quarter to 30 June climbed 38% to £399m, according to Airtel Africa.
The decision to float Airtel Money in the UK could mark a turning point for the City, which has struggled to attract listings in recent times and has also been hit by departures, partly as a result of overseas takeovers of UK companies.
Airtel Money’s planned listing could be one of the biggest debuts since the international payments company Wise floated in 2021 with a valuation of £8.75bn. Wise has since moved its main listing from London to New York.

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending approved by Congress, the White House announced on Friday, using a rare and contested power to axe funding for immigrant services and diversity-focused initiatives.
Trump’s Office of Management and Budget described the funding cut as focused on “the most harmful government spending.”
Most of the cuts are focused on Health and Human Services programs that serve refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration says the funds are no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have diminished considerably.
Also targeted for cuts were a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Department of Justice office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, housing counseling services from the Housing and Urban Development Department and a series of grants from the Health and Human Services Department that the administration called “outright harmful and blatantly ideological.”
A White House press release announcing the funding rescissions notes that some of the organizations are led by people who worked in the administration of Democratic President Barack Obama.
Trump’s move was condemned by Sen. Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican in a tough reelection campaign and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
Collins said in a statement that the action came without warning or consultation. She also said she would work to address with colleagues “these illegal actions.”
“Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress’s appropriations powers,” Collins said. “OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding.”
Under federal law, Congress has 45 days to review the president’s proposed spending cuts before they take effect. But Trump made that all but impossible by announcing them with just five days left in the federal fiscal year and the House out of session through the November election. The Government Accountability Office, which is an arm of Congress, says the maneuver known as a “pocket rescission” is illegal.
Collins called it the latest attempt by OMB to “undermine Congress’s Constitutional power of the purse.”
A year ago, Trump issued a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years by blocking $4.9 billion in congressionally approved foreign aid. The U.S. Supreme Court declined to block those rescissions, saying that Trump’s authority over foreign affairs weighed heavily in its decision. This year, Trump is targeting domestic spending.
The use of a “pocket rescission” fits into a broader pattern by the Trump administration to exert greater control over the U.S. government, eroding Congress’s power.
What was essentially the last pocket rescission occurred in 1977 when then-Democratic President Jimmy Carter rescinded it, and the Trump administration argues it’s a legally permissible tool, despite some murkiness, since Carter had initially proposed the clawback well ahead of the 45-day deadline.
The administration has also fired federal workers, imposed a historic increase in tariffs, and started the war in Iran without going through Congress, putting the burden on the judicial branch to determine the limits of presidential power.
Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the lead Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, described the White House action as “theft from the American people, plain and simple.”
“These are funds Congress has delivered on a bipartisan basis and should be helping people—not cut off by a president more focused on building a ballroom than investing in families,” Murray said.
Murray said that in recent spending negotiations, Democrats fought to include language to prevent the administration from usurping Congress’ power on spending decisions, but Republicans have declined to go along.
“While Trump spends tax dollars on ads promoting himself, Congress needs to reassert its powers to help people, and it’s past time Republicans join us in that fight,” she said.
In addition to immigrant services, the White House said it was rescinding $70 million for what it called “woke” international education programs, $28 million in grant funding for Health and Human Services research programs, and $9 million in debt relief for foreign countries that fund climate change policies. Another $10 million was being withheld from a minority business development program.
— Kevin Freking and Jonathan J. Cooper

A court in Sri Lanka has convicted 15 men on terrorist charges for their involvement in the deadly 2019 Easter bombings and sentenced them each to at least 220 years in prison.
The terror attacks, which targeted luxury hotels and churches as they held Easter services, left 267 people dead and wounded almost 600. The bombings, which were inspired by Islamic State (IS), were among the deadliest terror attacks in Sri Lanka’s history and sent shockwaves through the country.
Two Sri Lanka-based Islamist militant groups were believed to have orchestrated the attacks. A video, recorded by the suicide bombers the day before the bombings, showed the attackers with their faces covered, armed with rifles and swords and pledging allegiance to the then-IS leader Abu Bakhr al-Baghdadi to make Sri Lanka an Islamic nation and wage war.
The attacks were carried out by nine suicide bombers who died in the blasts. None of those who directly participated survived.
Those on trial were accused of conspiring and aiding the bombings, which had deliberately targeted the minority Christian community and foreign tourists. The proceedings had spanned nearly five years, with the slow pace of justice frustrating victims and their families.
In 2021, authorities filed 23,270 charges against 25 suspects whom they accused of planning or inspiring the attacks: three at churches, three at tourist hotels, one at a motel where an attacker killed himself, and two others after aborting a plan to attack a fourth hotel. The charges included murder, conspiracy to commit terrorism, and firearms and explosives offences under the Prevention of Terrorism Act.
The verdict was finally delivered on Tuesday by a three-judge high court amid tight security, with hundreds of police deployed around the courthouse.
In total, 15 defendants, who were all from Sri Lanka’s minority Muslim community, were sentenced to more than 200 years each. The judges also ordered the property of the defendants to be confiscated.
Nine defendants were freed after the court found that the charges against them were not proven. One other died before their case reached trial.
“Finally, we have justice,” said Catholic priest Jude Fernando. “It has taken a long time to get to this point.”
However, the completion of the trial is unlikely to offer full closure for some. Sri Lanka’s Catholic church has long alleged that perpetrators put on trial were not the masterminds behind the bombings.
Since Sri Lanka’s new government was elected in late 2024, there have been renewed investigations into allegations that elements within the Sri Lankan state – tied to former president Gotabaya Rajapaksa and his powerful family dynasty – may have had links to those responsible for the attacks.
Investigators have alleged the Easter bombings were part of a conspiracy to manufacture a security threat, that would create chaos and help bring Rajapaksa, a former defence chief, to power.
Rajapaksa was elected as president just a few months after the attack, on the back of a campaign that portrayed him as a strongman leader who was tough on terror.
A parliamentary committee found that police and intelligence officials failed to act on repeated intelligence warnings of the attacks. In July, a former police chief and a former senior defence ministry official were sentenced to death for failing to act promptly on foreign intelligence warnings of possible attacks.
Earlier this year, police also arrested Suresh Salley, a former intelligence chief and retired army major general, alleging he had prior knowledge of the attacks and worked with Islamist extremists before the bombings were carried out. He remains in custody but denies the charges.
The country’s defence ministry and the Rajapaksa family have denied any involvement in the attacks.

The Indian women’s kabaddi team secured the gold medal at the Asian Games 2026 after defeating Iran 37-34 in a thrilling Women’s Team gold medal match in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan. The defending champions held their nerve in a closely fought contest to overcome a determined Iranian side and add another Asian Games title to their impressive record.
India entered the final with strong momentum after producing a dominant run throughout the tournament. The defending champions had earlier defeated Bangladesh 42-21 in their opening Group A fixture before overcoming Iran 37-23 in the group stage. They then stormed into the final with a commanding 48-24 victory over Nepal in the semi-final.
The gold medal clash against Iran proved to be a far tighter contest than their earlier group-stage meeting. With the stakes significantly higher, both teams battled hard for every point as India looked to maintain their grip on the women’s kabaddi title. Iran, meanwhile, entered the contest determined to challenge the defending champions after previously denying India gold in the 2018 Asian Games final.
India ultimately managed to hold off the Iranian challenge, finishing the contest with a 37-34 victory. The three-point margin underlined the intensity of the final, with the Indian team showing composure when it mattered most to secure the gold medal.
The triumph further strengthens India’s remarkable record in women’s kabaddi at the Asian Games. The Indian women had won gold at the 2010, 2014 and 2022 editions, while Iran had ended their title-winning run in the 2018 final. With another victory over Iran in the 2026 gold medal match, India have once again emerged as Asian Games champions in women’s kabaddi.

Inside the FBI hack: Agents fearful and angry after 'dangerous' data breach
- Published
Current and former FBI agents have spoken to BBC News of their shock, fear and anger following a hack that appears to have exposed the private and personal information of the agency's entire workforce.
"This is really bad for our undercover agents," says one former FBI agent, who fears for the safety of his colleagues.
The former cyber investigator is in a group chat with current agents who are worried their personal information could soon be freely available online to criminals and hostile nation-state hackers.
He says staff fear they could be targeted, or that criminals could use the data to create highly convincing phishing attempts, scams or demands for bribes.
The hacking group ShinyHunters is threatening to publish the stolen databases and documents within four days unless its demands are met.
Some agents are also concerned about the risk of physical attacks from cyber criminals they have investigated.
"One of the things we are discussing in the group chat is 'violence-as-a-service' attacks from young online gangs," says the former worker.
"They could use this information to harass an FBI agent who has worked on their cases."
Personal concerns
Groups similar to ShinyHunters - believed to be an English-speaking gang - have in the past been linked to swatting incidents, and even petrol bomb attacks against law enforcement officers and rivals.
The group claims it breached FBI systems on Monday and later posted details of the attack on its darknet site.
The FBI has not responded to requests for comment.
However, on Wednesday the agency acknowledged the breach - saying it was "aggressively investigating" how it occurred.
For Michael McPherson, a former FBI agent who is now senior vice president of security operations at cyber firm ReliaQuest, the hack presents "a security threat which cuts to the core of agent safety, particularly their families".
He says agents understand the "inherent risks" that come with the job.
"But this incident reportedly includes personal data such as home addresses and contact information, which could expose family members who are normally insulated from the threats associated with such a career," McPherson says.
ShinyHunters shared samples of the alleged stolen data with reporters, along with an extortion demand.
The samples appear genuine and include names, addresses, phone numbers, badge numbers, job titles and information about spouses.
The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.
The criminals also appear to possess highly sensitive medical information relating to thousands of special agents.
BBC News has seen samples of stolen "fitness-for-work" medical examinations containing information such as blood and urine test results, along with doctors' notes mentioning conditions including a "shellfish and banana allergy".
Agents' full names and addresses, as well as references to medical issues including "blood in the urine" and "high cholesterol" are now in the criminals' hands.
Cynthia Kaiser, who was the Deputy Director of Cyber at the FBI and now leads the Research Centre at Halcyon says ShinyHunters appear to already have lost control of some of the data which is circulating in various online groups of cyber researchers and could lead to harm even before the main tranche is published.
"A lot of the damage may already be done, and as we have seen in past FBI data breaches, that information continues to circulate the dark web years later," she said.
There are also concerns about the breach's national security implications, such as staff becoming targets for recruitment efforts by hostile foreign intelligence services.
Fallout fears
Alongside fear, many of those who spoke to the BBC expressed anger at the FBI for allowing the data to be stolen.
The hack is particularly embarrassing from a technical perspective because ShinyHunters is not generally regarded as a highly sophisticated hacking group.
One former cyber agent said FBI staff were furious about the "sloppy and lazy security failures" that allegedly enabled the breach.
There is also confusion about how to handle any fallout if data is published next week, as threatened.
The FBI appears unlikely to comply with the extortion demands, and the hackers have indicated they intend to post the information on their darknet site.
Unusually, the group is not demanding money. Instead, it wants the FBI to retract an advisory published in May, which it claims "offended" them.
"The agency leadership is lost," the former cyber investigator tells me.
He says staff have been advised to sign up to a service called DeleteMe, which helps remove personal information from data broker websites - a response he feels is inadequate.
According to another former agent, there is widespread shock that such a breach could happen at one of the world's best-resourced law enforcement agencies.
"You would think this information would not be internet-exposed. It's disturbing, actually," he says.
'Kicked a sleeping lion'
There is also embarrassment that a prolific group of young cyber criminals has repeatedly managed to evade law enforcement while carrying out a string of high-profile hacks.
ShinyHunters has been linked to numerous extortion attacks, including on Rockstar Games and the education platform Canvas.
The group regularly communicates with reporters via Telegram, where members often boast about their activities.
"The bureau doesn't know what to do with teenage cyber criminals," one former agent says.
McPherson says there is no doubt the FBI is taking the incident extremely seriously.
He expects the agency to draw on its extensive network of partners and resources "to make this group suffer the consequences for this brazen and taunting attack".
Kaiser added that the hackers have been "reckless and foolish" and warned them to expect "a significant effort by the FBI to quickly bring them to justice."

Airbus has detected a quality issue involving the surface protection coating on the fuselage of a number of its narrow-body A321neo aircraft, with around a dozen planes operated by IndiGo impacted, PTI reported citing sources.
The European aircraft manufacturer has identified the source of the issue and contained it, while a remedy is available, Airbus said on Friday.
 
Airbus says issue is not safety-related
An Airbus spokesperson said the issue was identified during standard rework involving a surface protection deviation on stringers located in the lower front section of the fuselage.
 
“The source of the issue has been identified, contained and a remedy is available. All newly coated stringers conform to all requirements,” the spokesperson said in a statement, according to PTI.
 
Airbus said the affected aircraft can continue to operate, describing the matter as “a quality issue, not a safety issue.”
 
IndiGo and Air India are the two Indian airlines operating the A321neo. Together, they have around 190 aircraft of the type.
 
The PTI sources said there is no impact on Air India's A321neo fleet.
 
There is no official comment from IndiGo or Air India on the matter.
 What does the repair involve?
According to the news agency's sources, some parts of the affected fuselage need to be repainted, with the work required to be completed within two years.
Airbus said the rework does not require the disassembly of the stringers.
“Once rework is applied, the aircraft is considered to be back as if at nominal design,” the Airbus spokesperson said, according to the news outlet.
IndiGo operates over 180 A321neo aircraft
IndiGo has a fleet of more than 430 aircraft, including over 180 A321neo planes, according to the information provided by PTI.
Air India, meanwhile, has around nine A321neo aircraft.
The A321neo is part of Airbus' A320neo family of narrow-body aircraft and is widely used for domestic and international operations.

Digby Campbell, 75, was on death's door when he was rescued off the Darwin coast last month
After a freak wave off the coast of Timor-Leste in July destroyed Digby Campbell's navigational equipment and much of his rations, what was supposed to be a six-day voyage to Darwin turned into a weeks-long ordeal.
The 75-year-old veteran sailor was found drifting in Darwin Harbour last month, sunburnt, dehydrated and disoriented aboard his trimaran the Singapore Sling, more than a month after he departed Dili in early July.
Maritime officer Chris Chridland was one of the three men who spotted the boat and approached to do a welfare check.
"It just looked tired, so we thought we'd better go and have a look," he said.
Launch master Rawson McCrae and crew member Joshua Witkin said the Singapore Sling and its captain were in a sorry state when they pulled up alongside it.
"I said, 'You alright mate?' And he said, 'Not really,'" Mr Witkin said.
Mr McCrae said Mr Campbell's ankles were "swollen like you would not believe".
The men learned Mr Campbell had been standing at the yacht's helm trying to steer the ship into port for a day and a half and had not eaten for three days.
"I was buggered," Mr Campbell said.
The trio helped Mr Campbell safely to shore and into a waiting ambulance, but not before they had organised to meet again for a beer, to hear the full tale of the Singapore Sling's voyage.
"He said, 'I wanted to make a Sunday sesh, it's what kept me going,'" Mr McCrae said.
"We said, 'We'll have one with you mate, you're a legend.'"
An angry harbourmaster, two backpackers and a pushbike
Mr Campbell said he had flown from Bundaberg to Dili in June to purchase the Singapore Sling, knowing the Val 31 trimaran to be a reliable vessel.
But he was held up in Dili, awaiting the handover of the boat's registration in the harbourmaster's office shortly before it closed for the day.
"All of a sudden [the harbourmaster] said, 'We gotta wait for someone,'" Mr Campbell said.
"Next minute this French backpacker shows up. He said, 'I want you to take this man with you.'
"Another French backpacker comes in and he's got a pushbike."
Mr Campbell said he was able to convince the harbourmaster that the boat was not equipped for three passengers and was also in worse shape than he had expected.
"He was angry but he gave me my stamp and away I went," he said.
Two days out of port in early July, the Singapore Sling ran into rough seas off Timor's east coast and began falling apart.
"The big outboard on the back broke part of the bracket away and went underwater," Mr Campbell said.
"And about the same time one chain plate broke — that holds the mast up — and the battens were flying out of the main.
"So I had a motor in the water, the headsail was tangled up, and then another big wave come up over the back and took out the tablet and my phone."
Faced with a choice between returning to Dili and pushing on to Darwin, Mr Campbell said he was only really left with one option.
"I thought the smart thing to do was turn around and go back, but I couldn't — I got the port captain and these two French backpackers on a pushbike. There was no way I was going back," he said.
At that point Mr Campbell had given Australian authorities four days' notice of his expected arrival into Darwin for what he thought was a six-day voyage.
During what turned into a four-week trip, Mr Campbell said he was given supplies and radio equipment by Australian Border Force personnel and received a welfare check in the dead of night from a Royal Australian Navy warship.
"I said, 'Convey my thanks to the captain, I'm OK,'" he said.
But by the time he reached Australian waters Mr Campbell's supplies were running dangerously low.
"I had one can of beer and two cans of Red Bull," he said.
"I thought, 'When I see Australia, I'm going to have that can of beer.'
"I actually drank the can of beer when I saw the lights of Darwin. I never saw land, but I thought, 'There's land there under the light.'"
Mr Cridland said when Mr Campbell was eventually rescued in waters off Darwin Harbour there was barely any wind and that his boat was only moving at about 1.5 knots per hour.
"It would've taken him two days to get into harbour with wind like that," he said.
An unexpected connection
When Mr Campbell was able to reunite with his three rescuers after recovering from the harrowing journey, one of them discovered he had his own connection to the Singapore Sling.
"We were able to make contact and caught up at Dinah Beach for a beer [and] started hearing Digby's stories," Mr McCrae said.
Having grown up in Darwin's sailing community, Mr McCrae said a nagging feeling led him to ask about the Singapore Sling's previous owner and realised he had actually sailed on the decades-old trimaran himself as a 10-year-old boy.
"Wow! This is freaky," he said.
For their heroics, Mr McCrae, Mr Witkin and Mr Cridland were each given Distinguished Lifesaving Awards from the Australian Maritime Officers Union (AMOU) at an informal presentation at a pub on Darwin's waterfront this week.
"Their actions embody the very best traditions of the maritime profession and serve as a reminder that mariners look after one another, whether they are colleagues or complete strangers." AMOU president Matthew Jepsen said in a statement.
With the Singapore Sling repaired and given a fresh coat of paint, Mr Campbell said he was preparing to set sail for New Zealand, via Cairns, in a couple of weeks.
"I'll just wait for the wind to get the right direction," he said.

New Delhi, Sep 23: Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had flagged multiple issues, including deletion of names, in various states during the voter roll cleanup but the poll body was unanimous in its decisions related to the pan-India Special Intensive Revision of voters' list, officials said on Wednesday.
The officials made the remarks in the wake of a media report that the two Election Commissioners had objected to the Election Commission's steps 14 times in 10 months amid the SIR.
Responding to queries, the officials said the two commissioners had flagged decisions related to deletion of names in various states during the poll roll cleanup and handling of voter database.
EC sources maintained that all decisions of the Election Commission of India, including SIR, have been unanimous and with the approval of both the Election Commissioners and the Chief Election Commissioner.
Officials said the law governing the functioning of the Election Commission and a Supreme Court judgment underline that as much as possible, decisions should be taken unanimously and if need be, majority view should prevail.
The Indian Express reported that questions were raised on issues related to the SIR of electoral rolls within the three-member Election Commission (EC) itself, time and again by two of the three Election Commissioners, Sandhu and Joshi.
The national rollout of the SIR has been under the supervision of all three Commissioners. But Sandhu and Joshi have formally objected, on record, at least 14 times over the last 10 months -- four times on a single day -- to decisions taken and orders issued, they say, without their knowledge, the report in the English daily said.
Opposition parties have slammed the EC over the SIR, claiming it was meant to target electors not aligned to the BJP and its allies.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.

With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

The sell-off in insurtech stocks continued for the second straight session today as the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) proposed overhaul of insurance distribution commissions rattled investors. Shares of Policybazaar parent PB Fintech fell as much as 7.8% to touch a fresh 52-week low of ₹1,115.10 on the BSE. Meanwhile, Turtlemint shares opened at their 20% lower circuit of ₹87.30, which was also the stock’s fresh all-time low. The stocks later pared some of their losses. At 12:21 IST, PB Fintech was trading 5.12% lower at ₹1,148.10, with a market capitalisation of ₹53,128.6 Cr (about $5.5 Bn). Turtlemint was trading 18.84% lower at ₹88.55, giving the insurtech company a market capitalisation of ₹2,607.6 Cr (about $272 Mn). At the prevailing prices, PB Fintech shares have fallen about 39% across the two sessions, while Turtlemint has declined about 35% from its level before the sell-off began. The rout began yesterday after IRDAI released a consultation paper proposing product- and channel-specific commission ceilings for insurance distributors. The proposed framework would reintroduce product-level commission caps more than three years after the regulator removed such limits in April 2023 and shifted to an expenses of management (EoM) framework. Under the proposed framework, commissions for insurance distributors would vary based on the product, distribution channel and effort involved in selling and servicing a policy. Open-architecture insurance distribution entities such as Policybazaar and Turtlemint’s insurance broking arm would generally face lower caps than individual agents and other distributors. For digital insurance distributors, the proposed changes could put pressure on revenue from health, motor and life insurance, while forcing platforms to rethink customer acquisition costs and sales incentives. PB Fintech cofounder and group chairman Yashish Dahiya said during an investor call yesterday that the proposals have “almost forced” the company to consider entering insurance manufacturing, which would allow it to design, underwrite, and sell policies itself, though it would wait for greater regulatory clarity. The proposals are not final, with IRDAI inviting stakeholder comments until October 25. ‘Much Worse Than Imagined’ As PB Fintech and Turtlemint extended their sell-off, brokerages began quantifying the potential impact of IRDAI’s proposed overhaul. Bernstein described the proposed commission cuts as “much worse than imagined”, warning that they could unravel PB Fintech’s unit economics, particularly in health and motor insurance. Jefferies retained its ‘Buy’ rating on PB Fintech but cut its price target to ₹1,540 from ₹2,050. It estimated that a 10% reduction in new business commission rates could translate into a 10%-12% decline in earnings. The brokerage also flagged the proposals as a risk for Turtlemint. Bank of America retained its ‘Neutral’ rating on PB Fintech but cut its price target to ₹1,410 from ₹1,970. It described the proposals as directionally negative for online insurance brokers, though it expects the impact on Policybazaar’s life and term insurance businesses to remain manageable. Morgan Stanley said that the net present value of PB Fintech’s health insurance business could fall 60%-70% under the proposed framework, while the impact on its life insurance business could be relatively limited. HSBC downgraded PB Fintech to ‘Hold’ and cut its price target to ₹1,150 from ₹2,100. It also slashed its FY28 and FY29 earnings per share estimates by 56% and 17%, respectively. Motilal Oswal Securities said that the proposals could reduce PB Fintech’s FY28 core online insurance revenue by 30%. Without cost reductions or additional revenue streams, this could translate into a 46% cut to its earnings estimate. Citi said distribution economics could compress by 70%-90% across several high-margin insurance categories if the proposals are implemented in their current form.

The story so far: The Union Health Ministry has said that stem cell therapy for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) cannot be offered as routine or commercial treatment and can be used only as part of a duly approved clinical trial. The advisory, issued on September 16 to States and Union Territories that have adopted the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, follows a landmark Supreme Court judgment in January that examined the use of stem cells for autism.
What exactly has the government said?
The Health Ministry has reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for disease conditions or indications included in the Ministry’s approved list. Autism is not among those indications.
For ASD specifically, the Ministry has said that therapeutic use of any type of stem cell must remain restricted to duly approved clinical trials, following the National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research, 2017, and other applicable regulatory requirements. It should not be offered as a routine, standard or commercial clinical service.
The advisory is an attempt to ensure enforcement of an existing regulatory framework, particularly after the Supreme Court ruling.
Why is this significant for autism?
Autism is a neurodevelopmental condition. There is currently no established stem cell treatment that has been shown to cure autism or to provide sufficient evidence of benefit to make it a standard treatment.
The Indian Council of Medical Research (ICMR), in its evidence review on stem cell therapy for ASD, examined the available scientific evidence and concluded that it did not support using stem cells in addition to behavioural and supportive therapies. It recommended that stem cell therapy for autism should not be offered as standard or routine therapy and that its therapeutic use should be restricted to approved clinical trials.
This distinction is important — a treatment being investigated in a clinical trial does not mean that it has been established as an effective treatment. A clinical trial is the mechanism through which safety and efficacy are tested.
What did the Supreme Court say?
The issue came before the Supreme Court in Yash Charitable Trust & Ors. v. Union of India & Ors., decided on January 30, 2026.
The petition raised concerns about the commercial promotion and administration of stem cell “therapy” for autism. The court examined the scientific and regulatory position and held that, given the evidence available at present, stem cell therapy for ASD could not be offered by medical practitioners as a clinical service outside an approved and monitored clinical trial or research setting.
The court also said that, until further research establishes stem cell therapy as a sound and relevant medical practice for ASD, offering it as routine clinical treatment would not meet the reasonable standard of care expected of medical practitioners.
The court recognised the difficult situation faced by families of people with autism who may look for experimental treatments when conventional interventions do not produce the hoped-for results.
It therefore also addressed patients who were already undergoing such treatment before the judgment. Rather than abruptly discontinuing treatment, the court directed the Health Ministry to work out a mechanism, in consultation with AIIMS and the National Medical Commission, to provide the best possible solution and facilitate their continuation until they could be redirected to institutions conducting clinical trials.
So is all stem cell therapy prohibited in India?
No, that is not what this latest advisory states. The latest advisory does not say that stem cells can never be used clinically. It draws a distinction between approved standard care and experimental use.
The Ministry’s current approved list covers 18 adult and 14 paediatric indications. These include several blood cancers and blood disorders, as well as conditions such as multiple sclerosis and systemic sclerosis. For these indications, the relevant treatment is haematopoietic stem cell transplantation performed appropriately; the Ministry’s list specifically states that mesenchymal stem-cell transplantation is not recommended for any disease condition.
Autism is not on this list.
The 2017 National Guidelines for Stem Cell Research also make a fundamental distinction between established haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation and experimental applications. They state that, apart from approved indications, stem-cell use in humans must be within an approved and monitored clinical trial.
What is the way forward for use of stem cells in children with autism?
The advisory states that this therapy cannot be simply prescribe or administer as a routine therapy/treatment.
If stem cells are being investigated for ASD, the treatment has to be part of a properly designed and approved clinical trial. Such research requires the appropriate regulatory and ethical approvals. Depending on the nature and manipulation of the stem cells, different regulatory requirements apply.
This is the key difference between research and treatment being that a clinic cannot describe an experimental intervention as an established therapy and charge patients for it as ordinary clinical care.
What about clinics already offering it?
The Health Ministry has asked State and District regulatory authorities to ensure compliance and to disseminate the Supreme Court’s directions to government and private clinical establishments involved in stem cell research, treatment, promotion or administration.
The National Medical Commission (NMC), in an advisory dated September 5, has separately reiterated that stem cell therapy can be offered as standard clinical care only for approved indications. It has said that unauthorised administration, prescription, promotion or advertisement beyond those indications would constitute professional misconduct. State Medical Councils have been asked to examine complaints and take disciplinary action where professional misconduct is established following due process.
There can also be consequences for clinical establishments. The Health Ministry has referred to Sections 32 and 40 of the Clinical Establishments Act, which provide for cancellation of registration and penalties in applicable jurisdictions.
What should parents understand from this?
The advisory does not mean that research into stem cells and autism has stopped. It means that such research has to remain research until there is convincing evidence that establishes safety and efficacy.
For parents, perhaps the most important distinction is between a clinic saying that stem cells are being studied for autism and saying that stem cells are an established treatment for autism.
The first is a legitimate area of scientific investigation, subject to approvals. The second is not supported by the present evidence or India’s regulatory framework. ICMR’s assessment remains that stem-cell therapy should not be offered as routine treatment for ASD.
The September advisory puts renewed emphasis on enforcing the distinction between an experimental intervention being tested under scientific oversight and a commercial treatment being sold to families as established care.

Since 2024, Microsoft has tried to sell “Copilot+ PC.” The marketing initiative was aimed at making it easy for people to know which Windows systems were approved to run AI-accelerated workloads locally.
But Copilot+ PC branding is nowhere to be found on the new Surface PCs Microsoft announced this week.
Speaking with Windows Central, Brett Ostrum, corporate VP of Surface, said that the new Surface computers “are not called Copilot+ PCs” despite meeting the label’s requirements.
“They do meet all the requirements of our previous bar for what Copilot+ devices are. We still lean into the narrative around AI on the edge and being able to have a hybrid solution out there,” he said.
Copilot+ PCs require 16GB of RAM, 256GB of storage, and an integrated neural processing unit (NPU) with performance rated at 40 trillion operations per second (TOPS) or better.
The Surface Pro 12-inch (2nd Edition) and Surface Laptop 13-inch (2nd Edition), coming out on October 13, both run Qualcomm Snapdragon X2 Plus processors and have a Qualcomm Hexagon NPU rated at 80 TOPS.
“[T]he purpose for Copilot+ PCs was to be able to deliver [NPU] experience,” Kedar Kondap, SVP of compute at Qualcomm, told Windows Central. “So, it was to define a certain category of devices with a certain bar and metric, like, for example, a 45 TOPS NPU. … So from that perspective, it’s more offering the same experiences, probably without just using [Copilot+ PC] terminology now.”
AI PCs are old news
Copilot+ PCs are “a class of AI PCs and laptops” that represent “the fastest, most intelligent Windows PCs ever,” according to a Microsoft marketing page that was up as recently as May, per Internet Archive’s Wayback Machine. That Copilot+ PCs landing page, however, now redirects to a page for “performance PCs” that still names “Copilot+ PCs” but features the label far less prominently.

When the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, sat down for an interview in the heart of Silicon Valley at the weekend he had known for two days that his was the first government known to have been attacked by a rogue AI agent.
He didn’t reveal the attack then, but he sounded a warning about the march of AI: “the risk is that AI develops in a way in which humans are no longer in control of what AI is producing.”
But Albanese noted, too, that two countries – the US and China – would dominate the world’s response to the new technology.
“The truth is they’re the big two giants here, and so we want to see cooperation,” Albanese said.
“The US is essentially ahead of China when it comes to the race that is on for the development of this new technology. But it is in the world’s interests that there be engagement.”
Days later, Albanese used the global attention of the United Nations general assembly meeting in New York to reveal that Australia’s government healthcare system, Medicare, had been attacked by an OpenAI agent in June, but that it was three months before his government was told.
Again he warned of “the potential risks of allowing frontier AI to develop too fast without guardrails”.
China’s president, Xi Jinping, skipped the general assembly in favour of a bilateral meeting with the US president, where he emphasised the responsibility to manage AI “for good, and ensure that the development of AI is always under human control and serves the wellbeing of the people”.
But the president of the United States – the nation which is the global leader in artificial intelligence – used his general assembly address to insist he would only encourage, not restrain, the AI race.
Alarms sounding
To little fanfare earlier in the week, the UN’s independent international scientific panel on AI warned a threshold had already been crossed.
There was, the panel, said: “no assurance that humans can reliably keep AI agents under control today, particularly as they become more capable, harder to monitor and better at finding loopholes or hiding their activity”.
The Australian government had known the reality of this for more than a week. OpenAI had known it more than a month.
Two days after the panel’s statement, the Australian prime minister belatedly revealed an OpenAI agent had hacked medical data held by Australia’s universal health care provider, Medicare.
No patient data had been accessed, but the agent had gained unauthorised access to “non-public files”.
OpenAI’s agent hacked the government sites in June of this year. OpenAI discovered its agent had gone rogue in August. It did not tell the Australian government until 10 September, and then only with a solitary email to a generic public email address not checked until the next day. The prime minister was informed on 18 September.
It was another week before the Australian people were told.
Australia has promised, if it is possible, to lay criminal charges, though this is complicated by the fact that OpenAI claims the hack was committed by an AI agent – apparently acting beyond its instructions (euphemised by OpenAI as “misaligned behaviour”) – not a person.
The hack on Australia’s Medicare statistics reporting service portal, as well as three other government sites, follows the Hugging Face incident in July, in which autonomous AI agents developed by OpenAI broke out of their isolated testing environments, coordinated themselves into a “swarm” and launched a cyber-attack on competitor AI platform Hugging Face.
The UN panel, investigating that attack, warned “the traditional method of safeguarding is unravelling” as AI agents act autonomously to breach protections.
“The default interpretation and immediate lesson is that basic cybersecurity practices were overlooked, and safeguards are not advancing at the pace of capabilities. The more insidious and grave concern is that current training methods can lead agents to adopt goals of their own, knowingly violate safety instructions, and conceal their actions.”
Twenty countries (including Australia) and the EU this week signed a statement arguing the rapid development of frontier AI models posed serious risks to safety and security if not properly managed.
“AI must remain under human direction, oversight and control. It must be developed and used in line with international law.”
Too soon?
Even those running AI companies have warned the technology is developing too rapidly for humans to control.
Appearing before the UN security council this week, OpenAI’s chief executive, Sam Altman, warned: “some of the things people working to build AI have said are so dystopian that they sound like the plot of bad science fiction movies”.
“As AI systems become more capable and more autonomous, they can move faster than our institutions … or make decisions that people no longer understand or control.”
But there are at least two – very loud – voices in opposition to any external regulation of the AI industry.
Elon Musk, who co-founded OpenAI with Altman before falling out with him, said in a recent interview the “smart move” would be to have the “leading AI companies at least just meet or have some sort of call once every few weeks and just discuss any safety and security issues”.
Musk said AI would probably be beyond the control of humans within a decade, and that humanity should “enjoy the ride”.
“I still think there’s risk associated with AI and robots. It’s not zero … my sort of philosophical conclusion is to look on the bright side. I can’t see any way to really stop this incredible momentum of AI and robots.
“If there was a stop button, we probably shouldn’t press it, because the most likely outcome is incredible abundance for all.”
Donald Trump used his speech to the UN general assembly to attempt to rebrand AI, and insist it should never be reined in.
“The United States also totally rejects any attempt to construct a globalist scheme to control for the artificial intelligence being spoken of so much now,” the US president said.
Trump wants to re-label artificial intelligence “superintelligence”.
“I’m not going to stifle growth of something that will be bigger than the Industrial Revolution.
“We’re going to encourage it, not rein it in.”
Trump said the US was “leading China by a lot” in AI, and would continue to do so “safely and responsibly”.
“Whoever wins superintelligence, wins.”

Trump once promised to feed Xi McDonald’s. He gave him a lavish state dinner and hearty serving of praise instead
The summit itself was the point of the visit, but Trump reveled in showing off his gilded DC in front of China’s president and a roomful of billionaires, Alex Woodward writes
