WASHINGTON — A key Senate committee on Thursday approved the nomination of top federal health official Chris Klomp to be deputy secretary of health and human services, clearing the way for him to be confirmed by the full Senate.
Klomp is currently senior adviser to HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. He was advanced by the Senate Finance committee in an 15-12 vote. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) joined all Republicans in supporting Klomp.
He will now go to the full Senate for a final vote.
The committee voted 14-13 to advance Ge Bai’s nomination to be HHS assistant secretary for planning and evaluation.
Klomp spent two days last week testifying before Finance and the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committees, where lawmakers highlighted the power Klomp wields at HHS and questioned how he might use that power. Klomp has already helped broker drug pricing deals with pharmaceutical companies, aided in high-profile hires, and acted as a liaison between HHS and the White House.
During his confirmation hearings, Democrats joined by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), who chairs the health committee, repeatedly called on Klomp to push back on his boss, Kennedy, and even President Trump, if he continued to undermine vaccine policy. Cassidy, in particular, pressed Klomp to address the CDC’s refusal to report certain measles-related deaths in Pennsylvania.
“People are dying. The American people should know that,” he said. Cassidy had previously threatened to withhold health care nominations if HHS continued its aggressive vaccine overhaul, but Klomp’s nomination was squarely in the hands of the Finance committee, which Cassidy sits on but does not chair.
Klomp, in his statements to the committees last week, acknowledged the outsized role he would play in influencing HHS.
“Part of my responsibility is to enable the smooth operations of the department. I’m responsible for personnel, among other things,” Klomp told Finance last week. “My job is to make sure that we have everything.”
Klomp joined the Trump administration to oversee the Medicare program, before taking on additional duties at HHS. He also advised the first Trump administration on health care matters. Klomp is a health care entrepreneur, and was previously the CEO of health IT company Collective Medical.

The United States has proposed a new trilateral meeting with Ukraine and Russia aimed at advancing efforts to end the war, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday (September 25), with the UAE suggested as a possible venue.
Zelensky said that Kyiv was waiting for the US to provide a date.
 
Kremlin signals possible trilateral meeting
The Kremlin has also said a trilateral meeting involving Russia, Ukraine and the US could take place in the near future, although it said there were no specific details yet.
 
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump had discussed the possibility of such a meeting during their call earlier this month. Moscow has previously indicated that it expects negotiations in a trilateral format to resume.
 
The latest proposal follows renewed US diplomatic efforts, including meetings by US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner with Russian and Ukrainian officials earlier this month. Ukrainian officials have described the effort as a restart of the diplomatic process.
 
UAE again emerges as peace-talk venue
The UAE has previously hosted US-Russia-Ukraine negotiations. Earlier trilateral discussions were held in Abu Dhabi, while another round took place in Geneva. Those talks did not produce a major breakthrough, with territorial and other core issues remaining unresolved.
 
The UAE's possible role comes as Washington seeks to revive negotiations after diplomatic efforts lost momentum during the escalation of the Iran conflict. Recent US proposals have also included a possible halt to attacks on energy infrastructure and reopening a Black Sea grain corridor.
 
Zelensky seeks China's help
Zelensky also said on Friday that he had asked Trump to encourage Chinese President Xi Jinping to use Beijing's influence with Moscow to help end the war.
 
Zelensky said he had not yet received feedback from the White House on Trump's discussions with Xi but expected to learn more.
 
He has also said he is ready to meet Putin as part of efforts to end the conflict, while continuing to seek additional US air-defence support for Ukraine.
 
Major hurdles remain
Despite the renewed diplomatic activity, the central disagreements between Moscow and Kyiv remain unresolved, particularly over territory and security arrangements. Previous US-led efforts have produced talks but no comprehensive peace agreement.

Antonelli 'comes back to earth' with qualifying crash
- Published
Kimi Antonelli says his crash in qualifying at the Azerbaijan Grand Prix was "stupid" and "a good way to come back to earth" as he pursues his first world title.
The Mercedes driver, who has been running away with the championship this season, hit a wall in first qualifying in Baku and will start Saturday's race 16th.
Team-mate George Russell, his closest pursuer in the title race, starts from pole after a dominant performance.
Antonelli said: "I misjudged with the grip being so different compared to the first lap. I hit the wall. Unnecessary mistake early on.
"So it's a good way to come back to earth and to remind myself I need to be on top of it every time because otherwise I do these mistakes and a very stupid one."
He added that he was "very mad about it".
The 20-year-old Italian has been on the back foot all weekend, fighting to make up for time lost to a reliability problem in practice on Thursday.
His Mercedes suffered a hydraulic leak halfway through the first session and the car was not ready for him to go back out on track until halfway through the second session.
Antonelli was 0.252secs behind Russell in final practice on Friday, 0.092secs quicker than the Briton after his first lap in qualifying and then made his mistake on his second.
His error brought back memories of last year's grand prix in Baku, which proved to be a turning point in the 2025 championship.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri appeared on course for his first world title heading into this race, leading team-mate Lando Norris by 31 points.
But the Australian crashed in qualifying, jumped the start and then crashed out of the race on the first lap, and his season came off the rails after that.
Antonelli's error gives Russell, who is 81 points adrift in the championship, a second chance in three races to narrow his deficit to the Italian.
But the Briton has sounded resigned to losing out on the title for some time and he referred back to Antonelli's stunning drive at the Italian Grand Prix, which he won after starting 19th on the grid because of a penalty.
Russell said: "You can't discount Kimi. You know, started 19th in Monza and now he's in 16th, so, yeah, he should be leading by a few laps early this time."
Russell also pointed out that this was the first significant mistake Antonelli had made in a competitive session all year.
Asked if he believed Antonelli's mistake was a result of "title jitters", Russell said: "When you look at every championship campaign, even for the winners, there are mistakes along the way.
"So, I still keep on believing and keep on fighting until it isn't possible any more. But I don't feel any pressure.
"I feel excitement every time I jump in the car now, purely because I feel more confident in myself.
"When that confidence starts to build, it's just like this upward cycle.
"On the flip side, when you're on the back foot, you start losing that confidence and then you start pushing the limits more, and that's when mistakes happen.
"But he's been flawless this season. It's the first mistake he's made in a qualifying or race this whole year."
Russell's pole margin was a massive 0.837secs, with Ferrari's Charles Leclerc second and Piastri third.
The Baku street circuit has a long straight that affords good overtaking possibilities and has a reputation for producing incident-packed races.

Asked about potential challengers in the race, in addition to Antonelli, Russell said Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who qualified eighth after a difficult session, "is going to be a threat".
Verstappen, who was quickest in final practice just ahead of Russell, suffered a string of problems that he said had stopped him taking a place on the front row alongside the Mercedes.
"The whole qualifying was not how it should be," he said.
"Already from Q1 the engine was 0.5secs down on the straight compared to my team-mate and they can't explain or understand why. So you're on the back foot.
"Then in Q3 on my middle lap my battery didn't charge to 100% so I had to abort the lap which means you lose tyre temp and around here that's killing.
"I tried to push... but being down on top speed and I had a yellow flag from Lando in front of me, [which] meant that's where we are."
The Dutchman added: "The whole weekend we were running really well and then we run into so much trouble in qualifying. It's not good enough.
"Looking at George's lap, I don't think we would have fought for pole but there is a big gap behind and we should have slotted in to that easily.
"But when you have that many issues you also don't deserve to be there. We need to be more robust and we need to be on top of these things."

Ontario regional police forces investigating threatening email sent to Muslim schools across Canada
Anonymous note threatened to kill Muslims, unless they are deported
A number of regional police forces in Ontario have launched an investigation into an email sent to Islamic schools across Canada over the course of this week, which threatened to kill Muslims unless they are deported.
The Muslim Association of Canada, which runs the eight private schools that received the email, said they alerted municipal police in Ontario, Vancouver and Montreal, as well as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, on Thursday morning.
The MAC schools follow standard provincial educational curricula, on top of Islamic, Quranic and Arabic-language education.
The email — which CBC News has seen — was fired off from a party identifying themselves as "Jehu, Citizen Vigilante" and came from an account titled "exposingNWO@protonmail.com." It was time-stamped last Sunday, Sept. 20.
Using dehumanizing language against Muslims, it says "millions on top of millions of people in the nation of Canada are ready to take up arms."
The email alludes to the upcoming Alberta referendum, which includes a question asking voters there to decide if the province should remain a part of Canada or eventually hold a vote on secession, and states Muslims will be "deported or slaughtered" once "Alberta becomes its own nation."
It then says this will happen "regardless of the election results," and "you won't be warned again."
Investigations underway
CBC News reached out to the RCMP and the six local forces where the eight schools are located.
In a statement, the London Police Service said it is investigating a threat to a local school and "collaborating with partner law enforcement agencies to gather information and assess any potential connections." Potential criminal code offences may include uttering threats, criminal harassment, or inciting willful hatred, the service said.
In the Greater Toronto Area, Peel Regional Police also posted a statement on the social media platform X, saying its hate crime unit is actively investigating. It said it beefed up officer presence overnight near local mosques and schools, and patrols will continue over the weekend.
Waterloo Regional Police said its officers visited a school after receiving notification of an emailed threat and conducted safety planning. The Ontario service's hate crime unit has launched an investigation, and are aware of emails sent to other jurisdictions as well.
The Ottawa Police Service confirmed it received a complaint and said it is working with law enforcement partners as part of an ongoing investigation.
"As a precaution, police visibility remains increased around religious institutions and the educational facility that received the complaint," the OPS said in a statement. "At this time, we have no information indicating a specific or imminent threat to religious or educational institutions in Ottawa."
Scope of threat unprecedented: MAC
Nabil Sultan, a spokesperson for the Muslim Association of Canada, said while the organization has received "hate comments and emails on social media" in the past, a single note targeting many of its schools is something it has never experienced before.
"Such a disturbing email to be received by teachers and administrators, and families and children, really makes it difficult for us to live as a community feeling good about ourselves, feeling that we are welcomed in this society," he said in an interview with CBC News from London, Ont., where two of the schools that received the email are located.
Sultan said it was hard not to think of the Afzaal family, which lost four of five members after a man deliberately drove his truck into the group while they were out on an evening stroll in June 2021. London police called it a hate-motivated crime and a sentencing judge said it was a terrorist attack.
"A part of you wants to move on, and a part of you wants to believe that it was a lone wolf incident, and that something like this should not happen again," he said. "And this is a reminder that that is not the case, and we're still under threat."
CBC News visited one of the two Ottawa schools that received the emailed threat, Abraar Elementary, on both Thursday afternoon and Friday morning, around the times parents were picking up or dropping off their children.
An Ottawa Police Service vehicle was parked outside the school on Thursday.
Sara Omar, who had just dropped her five-year-old daughter, spoke to CBC News outside the school on Friday.
"Definitely me and my husband, and other moms in group chats, we were worried and anxious. But at the same time, honestly, we won't be intimidated," she said.
"We have confidence in our schools, in our community. So we won't stop living and bringing our children to school because of these threats."
Omar said she and her husband are still trying to figure out how to have a conversation with their daughter about the threat.
"If there is a lockdown, what does that look like? How to listen to her teachers in that moment — in such an intense moment. How do you even have these conversations with a five-year-old?"
The school's principal, Mohammed Saleem, said getting the note in his inbox was a "total shock," given the "explicitly violent language" and clear threats to children in the email.
Parents at the school were notified by email and teachers were preparing to have classroom talks with students on Friday, he said.
Saleem said he is unsure how long heightened security measures, including police stationed in front of the school and patrolling the neighbourhood, might last.
"Usually, we will work with the police, consult with them to see, because they will let us know from time to time what they are hearing on their radar, what they're seeing," he said.
The school recently temporarily hired security guards, he said, after gunmen killed three people during a mosque shooting in San Diego last May in what police have called a hate-motivated crime.
Push for more government action
Statistics Canada reported in March that police-reported hate crimes in Canada more than doubled between 2018 and 2024, jumping from 1,817 to 4,882. Incidents involving Islamophobia in Canada nearly tripled, growing from 84 reported crimes to 229 over the same period.
The agency also noted a tripling of reported hate crimes targeting Jews from 2020 to 2024, rising from 331 incidents in 2020 to 920 in 2024.
Concerns over the email come on the heels of a shooting near the Sons of Jacob Synagogue in Belleville, Ont., which police have said was a deliberate, hate-motivated attack aimed at the Jewish community.
Saleem said the incident highlights a hole left behind when the federal government scrapped two offices — focusing on combating Islamophobia and antisemitism respectively — earlier this year. They were replaced with an advisory council that is meant to combat all forms of hate.
"It was the wrong move," Saleem said. "It's important that we kept that office to make sure that proper interventions, policies are being enacted to combat Islamophobia."
In an interview, Amira Elghawaby, the former special representative on combating Islamophobia, did not go as far as saying her office should be restored, but said that the federal government needs to continue to "meet and uphold its commitments on human rights, which includes making sure that Canadians of all backgrounds, including faith minorities like Canadian Muslims, have the protections and supports and the solutions they need to live lives of dignity in Canada."
She spoke to CBC News from New York City, attending meetings on the margins of the United Nations General Assembly, where she said it was clear to her that both Islamophobia and antisemitism continue to be dangerous at the global level.

Fall has officially arrived, which means you're likely swapping out sandals for boots and dresses for sweaters. But don't forget to spruce up your fragrance collection, too.
If you've been pondering the idea of finding your signature scent, now is the perfect time to be on the prowl. Business Insider spoke with three professional perfumers to get their expert-backed fragrance recommendations and tips.
From classic scents like sandalwood, vanilla, and honey to more unexpected notes of banana, rose, and tea leaves, here's what experts say are this season's must-haves.
It's a great time of year for woodsy scents.
Watching the leaves change colors and spending time by the fireplace are quintessential fall experiences. So, it makes sense that woodsy, earthy scents are popular during this time of year.
Darryl Do, a New York-based senior perfumer at Delbia Do Fragrances & Flavors, thinks sandalwood in particular will be huge this season.
Yes, Nós Temos Banana, a fragrance by Brazilian brand Granado, is one of Do's fall favorites. This scent combines sandalwood and cedar with banana leaves and fig for a tropical twist on woodsy scents.
If you're looking for something more traditionally earthy, Bryson Ammons, a New York City-based perfumer and founder of The Alloy Studio, recommends Somewhere but Nowhere by LORE. This fragrance features notes of cedarwood, cardamom, black tea, and vanilla cream.
He said it's a "great starter fall fragrance at a really accessible price point."
Gourmands are still on trend.
When fall rolls around, certain scents like pumpkin spice become all the rage — but there are other sweet, culinary-inspired fragrances that deserve a spot on your shelf, too, according to Ammons.
"A lot of different perfumes [...] are playing with that warm, autumnal spice and sweetness without literally being pumpkin spice," he said.
Teddy Haugen, a Bay Area-based perfumer, founder of Teddy the Perfumer, and creative director at House of Cosmo, recommends chocolate-forward scents as the season changes.
One of his favorites is Lust Oud Delice by Chris Collins, which Haugen called a "beautiful powdered-chocolate gourmand" that has notes of dark chocolate and hazelnut.
Warm yourself up with some spice.
As the weather gets colder, the fuzzy socks and heated blankets start to come out … and another way to exude warmth is by adding a spicy scent to your fragrance collection.
"In the fall, we often look for warm, sensual, resinous smells, like rich vanillas and spices," Haugen said.
For a resinous and spicy vibe, Ammons likes Nefer by Parfum Prissana, a scent inspired by ancient Egyptian perfumery. You'll find notes of saffron, cardamom, and nutmeg, alongside hints of amber, tangerine, and rose.
Another one of Ammons' favorites is Honey Body by Syd Botanica, a spicy, sensual fragrance that's perfect for fall. Although Sichuan pepper is one of its featured notes, Ammons said the honey and apricot give it a nice mix of spicy and sweet.
Let florals stick around this fall.
It's a given that many people reach for floral scents during the spring. To Miranda Priestly's surprise, though, florals for fall might actually be groundbreaking.
"It's fun sometimes to wear something unexpected because people associate fall and winter with sugar and spice," Haugen said.
One floral fragrance he recommends is Diptyque's Eau Rose. The fragrance features notes of damascena and centifolia roses, chamomile, and artichoke.
Do is also a fan of florals for fall. He recommends Anood's Sunny 7, which blends rose and tuberose with comforting notes like vanilla, pistachio, and blood orange.
Fruity fragrances aren't just for summer.
Just because summer's ending doesn't mean that refreshing, fruity scents have to leave, too.
"Spice plus fruit feels so right to me when it gets cooler," Ammons says.
One fragrance he reaches for in the fall months is Mirth by Herb Craft Perfumery, which blends fruity and spicy notes like Mexican grapefruit, lemon balm, apricot, saffron, and even cotton candy.
Dark and smoky notes are having a moment.
If you want the scent you're wearing to be a little moodier, consider notes like tobacco and leather.
Haugen said Epichron's Twin Peaks is "one of the most incredible smoked-tea fragrances ever created." Inspired by the Himalayas and the Wuyi Mountains, this fragrance involves the pleasantly intense scent of Lapsang tea leaves, which can mimic the smell of a campfire.
It's also balanced by other notes like black tea, honey, rose, and bergamot.
Meanwhile, Ammons suggests Tobacco Road by Ariana & Evans. This fragrance combines tobacco and smoke with other fall-friendly notes like sandalwood, amber, bay leaf, and hinoki.

The Trump administration is facing growing questions over its decision to abandon a fraud and bribery case against the Indian billionaire Gautam Adani after he promised to invest $10bn in the US.
For the second time this year, two Democratic senators have demanded attorney general Todd Blanche answer questions about the US Department of Justice department’s handling of the case – and raised concerns over its judgment under Donald Trump.
In August, a federal judge in New York agreed to drop the fraud case against Adani, one of the richest people in the world, at the request of prosecutors, despite having concerns about “irregularities” in the “highly unusual” decision. It has become the latest example of judges raising eyebrows at Trump administration prosecutors for pushing to dismiss criminal cases.
Now, more than a month later, senators Elizabeth Warren and Richard Blumenthal are asking Blanche to clarify whether people close to Donald Trump were involved in that decision.
It comes aftera New York Times report revealed that Adani, represented by one of Trump’s personal lawyers, admitted to offering a $10bn investment in the US to resolve the criminal case. The federal judge overseeing the case determined the investment played no role in the DoJ’s decision to abandon the case.
“These fresh details continue to raise concerns about the judgment of the DoJ, and the extent to which the DoJ is willing and able to prosecute white-collar criminals under President Trump,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in a letter sent on Wednesday, and seen by the Guardian.
Adani was indicted in 2024 in New York for allegedly participating in a bribery and fraud scheme in which he paid Indian officials to secure a contract for one of his companies. He denied the allegations.
Prosecutors suddenly moved to dismiss the case against Adani in May after he hired a new legal team, led by Robert Giuffra Jr, and offered to invest $10bn into the US.
Following the news, Warren and Blumenthal sent a letter to Blanche in June requesting information about the fraud case and raising concerns about whether the justice department dismissed the case in exchange for Adani’s investment.
However, the senators did not receive a response. Since then, new details about the case have emerged, including allegations that Boris Epshteyn, a member of Trump’s personal legal team who also served as an informal adviser, helped Adani.
Another report claimed Donald Trump Jr, the president’s son, met with Adani in November 2025, before the case was dropped. A spokesperson for Trump Jr said earlier this year that the conversation “had zero to do with DoJ’s actions in this case”.
A spokesperson for Epshteyn denied being involved in Adani’s “arguments, advocacy or efforts” to the Wall Street Journal in June. Epshteyn was never hired by Adani or his company, the Adani Group, nor did he maintain a relationship with Adani, the spokesperson added.
The Guardian has asked Epshteyn for comment.
The Democratic lawmakers are now asking the DoJ for more information about Adani’s alleged investment offer, including a list of employees who were present when the offer was made, the terms of the offer, when the offer was made and where.
They also want to know whether the DoJ employees knew Epshteyn was allegedly working on behalf of Adani, or if Epshteyn had any contact with DoJ employees regarding Adani, among other questions.
“We are also concerned about the involvement of two of President Trump’s personal lawyers in this case, and the extent to which they reveal potential political influence and special treatment for well-connected insiders at the DoJ,” Warren and Blumenthal wrote in their letter.
The Democrats also want to know if Trump Jr, or any person working on behalf of Trump Jr., had contact with a DoJ employee regarding Adani.
Warren and Blumenthal requested responses no later than 5 October. The Guardian has asked Blanche’s office for comment.

BEIRUT/LOUISVILLE, Kentucky – When governments impose economic sanctions, like the “economic D-Day” U.S. President Donald Trump is now imposing on Iran, they portray them as a precision instrument — a scalpel rather than a sword — capable of pressuring ruling elites while sparing ordinary citizens.
That narrative has been used to justify some of the most sweeping acts of economic coercion in modern history. The only problem is that the central premise is untrue.
The case against sanctions is not merely strategic — that they rarely achieve their stated foreign-policy objectives — but also moral. Sanctions, particularly financial ones, do not fall equally on a population. They fall hardest on those least able to bear them: low-income, wage-dependent and publicly employed people. Thus, anyone who claims to care about the ethics of coercive statecraft must confront its distributional realities with the same rigor applied to questions of military tactics.

Inside the real war games as Europe readies for an attack by Russia
As warnings increase about a Russian attack on a NATO country, real-world war-games, whether played out around a conference table or on the ground as military exercises, are happening all the time. But the real danger is the potential for hysteria, fear and miscalculation to turn a shadow war into something much worse, writes Owen Matthews

Rarely does a piece of television docu-drama land in the middle of an unfolding real-world crisis as squarely as Sky’s The Wargame. Even as the first episode opened with an all-star cast of former British ministers, generals and MI6 officers contemplating their response to a fictional Kremlin grey-zone attack on the UK, French President Emmanuel Macron summoned party leaders to an emergency meeting to discuss urgent intelligence warnings of possible Russian aggression.
Just days before, Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned his parliament that intelligence assessments suggested Russia might launch an attack with drones or missiles on Nato territory “in the coming months.” Poland’s veteran Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski doubled down, warning Russia that Nato’s air superiority could destroy Russia’s oil refining capacity within days in the event of any attempted invasion of the Baltics. Nato’s response would “not just be defensive,” warned Sikorski. “It would be offensive.”
The day after Denmark’s intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch a limited military attack against one or more Nato countries bordering Russia, Sweden and Finland scrambled fighter jets to intercept and identify Russian military aircraft over the Gulf of Finland, in their first such joint operation.
Sky’s The Wargame is a drama – but one based on years of research by the showrunner, Sky News' Security and Defence Editor Deborah Haynes. The cast is also made up of ministers, generals and MI6 officers with real, recent experience at the highest levels of the British and US states. Among them were General Sir Richard Barrons, Chief of Defence Staff, Kim Darroch, National Security Adviser, and Christopher Steele, Intelligence Chief. Former Nato Secretary General George Robertson plays himself, while former White House communications director Anthony Scaramucci takes the role of US Secretary of State.
Many elements of the drama ring very true. Most important is the fact that the Russian attack comes as an escalating series of hybrid operations – sabotage and assassination attacks that fall below an identifiable threshold for triggering Nato’s Article 5 collective security clause. Britain’s inability to deter a Russian attack, to defend itself when it comes, or to properly respond also tracks with reported reality.
Military chiefs tell the political leaders there is "bugger all" military capacity available because so many aircraft, destroyers and submarines are out of action or in maintenance. Another telling moment came as viewers watch the politicians gathered in the Cabinet Office Briefing Rooms – more dramatically known as COBR – backtrack on years of belligerent anti-Russian rhetoric the moment that words turn into sticks and stones; ‘Deputy PM’ played by Nicola Sturgeon instead blames ‘Foreign Secretary’ Jim Murphy's diplomacy for taking Britain to the verge of annihilation.
The entire show is based on a real-life April 2024 Sky News report by Haynes on the alarming fact that Whitehall officials were combing through the Cabinet Office’s Government War Book – Cold War-era records of Nato's biannual Winter Exercises and Civil-Military Exercise, discontinued in 1990 – for clues on how to transition Britain to war readiness.
Out in the real world, war-games, whether played out around a conference table or on the ground as military exercises, happen all the time. In the two most recent boots-on-the-ground war-games Nato forces were seriously put to the test by Ukrainian veteran drone operators playing the ‘Red’ – read Russian – team. In both the Hedgehog exercise played out in Estonia in May 2025 and Aurora 26, involving 18,000 Nato troops in Sweden this April–May, a handful of experienced drone pilots inflicted devastating damage. In this instance, Anatoliy Merkotun, commander of the Ukrainian Nemesis unit in Aurora 26, said Nato's habit of keeping vehicles and troops in compact groups looked “nearly suicidal”, a way of fighting both Russia and Ukraine had “abandoned years ago.”
Meanwhile a host of Western armies and military think tanks – notably the US Naval War College, the Pentagon's Joint Staff, and US European Command and Strategic Commands, plus the UK’s Defence Science and Technology Laboratory and the Defence Academy – constantly play out war-game scenarios to test readiness. A war-game exercise organised by the German newspaper Die Welt and the Helmut Schmidt University of the German Armed Forces last December envisaged a scenario where the Kremlin used bogus claims of a “humanitarian crisis” in the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad to seize the Lithuanian city of Marijampole. Within days, in that war-game, an absence of US leadership and hesitancy from Nato countries allowed Moscow to gain total control over the Baltic within days, using an initial force of only 15,000 troops.
“The Russians achieved most of their goals without moving many of their own units,” Bartłomiej Kot, a Polish security analyst who acted as the Polish prime minister, told The Wall Street Journal. “What this showed to me is that once we are confronted by the escalatory narrative from the Russian side, we have it embedded in our thinking that we are the ones who should be de-escalating.”
The results of official military war-games are rarely made public. But, says a senior European diplomat who still acts as a national security adviser to a major Nato country, “these games are nothing like the real world and actually not designed to be so.” Rather, the idea of official war-games is to stress-test specific national systems, military or political – and therefore exclude outside variables that in real life would be crucial.
“What will be the effect of your diplomacy or your military actions on your adversary – this is outside the scope of the game,” says the diplomat. “Ultimately you can only test yourself.” An upcoming example of such a practical preparedness test is Britain’s Exercise Albiston Shadow in 2027, billed as the largest UK home defence exercise in several decades, with ministers and hundreds of officials testing emergency responses to hybrid attacks.
But what Sky’s The Wargame does not address is the most important question of all – how to cut through the fog of misunderstanding, rhetoric and paranoia which is the seed-bed of a brewing showdown with Russia. On the one hand, it is provably true that Russia’s security agencies have been stepping up arson and sabotage attacks on European and British soil – including the most alarming yet, a failed explosive drone attack earlier this summer on Ukrainian planes in Germany’s Leipzig airport.
On the other, intelligence chiefs in the Baltic states say that, in reality, they have no reason to believe that Russia is actually planning an armed incursion against Nato. “We don’t see indications of an imminent attack,” Normunds Mežviets, director of the VDD, Latvia’s state security service, told The Guardian last week. And Jonatan Vseviov, secretary-general of Estonia’s foreign ministry, decried “panic on social media” in recent days about a possible attack, noting that “if there is reason to fear an attack, rest assured: we will make that clear. Until then, keep calm, carry on and support Ukraine.”
One major problem is that shows like The Wargame, as well as the recent vague warnings from European leaders about rising security threats from Russia, actually serve the Kremlin’s purposes. “Scaremongering is a Kremlin psy-op,” argues Ed Lucas, founder and director of the Baltic International Security Centre. “The real attack is not on infrastructure, industry, individuals or any other physical target. It's on our decision-making.”
The Kremlin is “trying to spread FUD – Fear Uncertainty Doubt – and far too many supposedly expert voices are amplifying this,” Lucas warned on Twitter. Objectively, the Russian army has suffered catastrophic losses of up to half a million killed over the last four years and has so far failed to even take all of Donbas or more than 23% of Ukraine. Russia’s economy is twenty-five times smaller than Nato’s, and its defence spending eight times less. A war-game that pits the Kremlin’s entire strength against the comparatively tiny Baltic nations – or for that matter against Britain’s hollowed-out army and navy and dysfunctional government bureaucracy – might see a hypothetical win for Moscow within those artificial parameters. But on the bigger picture, Sikorski is right – Nato, for all its shortcomings, still remains unreservedly by far the most powerful military alliance in the world.
And while Donald Trump has insisted that Europe should pay for its own defence, the US remains, at base, strategically committed to Nato and its defensive principles. There may be a handful of old KGB men at the top of the Kremlin who are clearly badly informed and paranoid – the proximate causes of Putin’s foolish gamble on his full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – but it is unlikely that they are actually suicidal enough to imagine that attacking Nato would end in anything other than national annihilation.
Rather, what the Kremlin’s escalating hybrid war appears to be aimed at is eroding Europe’s resolve to continue to back Ukraine. This is why it is striking what it considers to be Ukrainian military-related targets inside Europe. The danger here is mutual misunderstanding. Most of the latest Russian attacks – including several bumbling plots in the UK – have been carried out by petty criminals and thugs working for hire. And these blunt instruments can and do screw up, with potentially world-changing effects.
Imagine, for instance, if the Leipzig bombers had succeeded in bringing down a cargo plane in flight over Germany, with mass civilian casualties? Or if the plot to bomb a DHL hub in Birmingham in 2024 had done the same? Ken McCallum, head of MI5, warned last October that British security services and police have disrupted "a steady stream of … plots with hostile intent" by Russian agents against their enemies on UK soil. But these are acts of thuggery and murder, not war against the UK.
Alarmist TV shows, along with equally alarmist but non-specific statements by politicians, perform one useful function in warning just how unfit for purpose Europe’s military preparedness is. But in another sense, they’re profoundly dangerous. Fear is Russia’s most effective weapon, and the Kremlin is keen to project power that it does not, in reality, possess.
Volodymyr Zelensky’s regular message that the Russian enemy is at the gates of Europe is useful for focusing governments on the need to come up with money and weapons for Ukraine. But this strategy also spurs real military preparations which Russia is taking seriously as messages of European hostility. And with neither side ready to back down or take a more realistic view of the other’s intentions, such escalation could spiral out of control.

Brazil's President Lula bans online betting ahead of presidential election
Brazil’s President Lula da Silva has signed an order to ban fixed-odds betting
RIO DE JANEIRO -- Brazil’s President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Friday signed an order banning fixed-odds betting just over a week ahead of the first round of the presidential election, in a move he said was designed to tackle the pervasive problem of families falling into debt.
The decision ends the operation, offering, intermediation and advertising of betting. The provisional executive order comes into force immediately but will need congressional approval within 120 days to remain in effect. It prohibits new deposits into accounts and gives users of betting platforms until Oct. 5 to withdraw their funds.
Lula's government has also drafted a bill to establish criminal offenses related to fixed-odds betting — the most common and dominant type of online sports betting — such as promoting them and using personal data to solicit bettors.
“I made the decision to take a hard, drastic and necessary measure,” he told journalists in Sao Paulo. “It’s like cancer, you take out the tumor, or the tumor will kill us.”
Lula had also criticized the betting industry earlier this week at the United Nations General Assembly, accusing it of “transforming addiction into profit” and of “destroying homes.”
Polls suggest a ban enjoys widespread endorsement among Brazilians. Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro, Lula's main rival in the upcoming election, accused the current leader of an “electoral measure.”
Brazil's president has sharply criticized online betting at least since April, when he called for a ban. Backlash grew during the FIFA World Cup when advertisements were ubiquitous and the number of people betting surged.
Betting and gambling are estimated to cost Brazilian society 38.8 billion reais ($7 billion) annually and increases suicide and depression, according to a 2025 study by the nonprofit Institute of Studies for Health Policies.
The country's central bank estimated last year that Brazilians spend about 30 billion reais ($5.7 billion) on bets each month. That figure included spending by beneficiaries of the cash-transfer federal welfare program Bolsa Familia (Family Grant), which was blocked from those platforms last year.
Lawmakers, including many from Flávio Bolsonaro's Liberal Party, struck down a Lula order for tax hikes on online betting and virtual casinos in October last year.
Gambling is illegal in Brazil, but the country opened the gates to online betting in 2018 during the presidency of Michel Temer. The phenomenon snowballed under the watch of former President Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio Bolsonaro's father.
In December 2023, Lula signed a law to regulate and tax betting companies for the first time. Months later, his administration blocked over 2,000 online betting websites that were designated as irregular, including some linked to criminal organizations like the First Command of the Capital from Sao Paulo and the Red Command of Rio de Janeiro. It was part of a national push to regulate the sector.
Lula and members of his administration have spoken about banning online betting as necessary to both close a drain to the country's economy and to tackle a public health issue, as many Brazilians are addicted and in financial difficulties due to spending their money on these platforms.
Business analysts say that revenues for sports betting, one of the betting models banned on Friday, are estimated at more than $4 billion per year in Brazil, one of the biggest markets in the world.
Ahead of Friday’s move, Brazil's main soccer clubs sounded the alarm after betting companies reportedly warned clubs that sponsorships will end immediately if the government bans betting.
They said the move could mean “the end of Brazilian soccer," a claim mocked by some social media users in the soccer-mad country.

Sony and Universal Music Group filed yet another suit against Suno. The labels claim its new v6 model still infringes on their copyrights because it’s trained on user outputs from previous models, which were themselves trained on unlicensed music ripped from YouTube and other sources. Sony and UMG are notable holdouts who did not sign a licensing agreement with Suno.
Sony and UMG are suing Suno again
Sony and UMG’s latest lawsuit against Suno accuses the company of ‘model laundering’
In its complaint shared with The Verge, Sony and UMG accuse Suno of “model laundering,” saying:
“Training a ‘new’ model on the outputs of an infringing model does not eliminate the infringement; it launders it, passing the value of Plaintiffs’ expression from the copied recordings into the tainted models, from those models into their outputs, and from those outputs into v6 … V6 is not a fresh start; it is the fruit of the same poisoned tree.”
When v6 launched, Suno’s Jack Brody told The Verge it was “trained from the ground up, with a new set of data,” including “user data,” but did not offer details beyond that. Suno later confirmed to Engadget that data includes “creations” from users, but would not elaborate further when reached for comment.
Sony further alleges that Suno used distillation to train v6. It claims that it was trained to replicate the results of its previous, “teacher” models, which were created using infringing data.
The complaint says that “even a model not directly trained on Plaintiffs’ recordings is informed by, and benefits from, Suno’s retained unauthorized copies.” Essentially, the labels argue that, unless Suno truly starts from scratch, its models will continue to be built on stolen data.

- Call of Duty devs revealed that they busted Cronus' North American distributor last year with a legal notice in a secret "Black Ops" operation.
- The devs released real footage of the encounter on X, showcasing Team RICOCHET handing the distributor a cease-and-desist.
- The COD devs have already issued more than 70,000 new hardware bans and 5,000 account bans for using tools like Cronus Zen and XIM Matrix.
Call of Duty devs are hunting down hackers and cheaters ahead of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’s October 23, 2026 launch, even taking a “Black Ops”-style trip to track down a major Cronus distributor last year.
According to the official Call of Duty account on X, the COD devs busted Cronus’ North American distributor to a hotel in Southeast Asia in 2025, and it’s as “Call of Duty” as it gets. But the weapon here is a cease-and-desist notice, not an assault rifle or a pocket knife.
The dev team has dropped the real footage in the latest Call of Duty X post, turning the Cronus distributor into an unexpected COD cutscene as the dramatic black-and-white video shows the team serving him a legal notice. This footage looks straight out of a Call of Duty “Black Ops” mission, except Team RICOCHET is hunting a Cronus distributor instead of terrorists.
Activision openly putting the Cronus distributor on blast suggests the company is taking its anti-cheat crackdown more seriously this time. In fact, the studio confirmed that it has already issued more than 70,000 hardware bans across the board, with 5,000 accounts banned for using tools like Cronus Zen and XIM Matrix.
The studio says that “We judge them [hackers] by what they do in a match, not by what they’re called or how they’re sold. And our enforcement doesn’t stop with the player using the device.” For those unaware, Cronus is a hardware adapter that lets Call of Duty players modify their controller inputs, use scripts, and gain unfair advantages in multiplayer.
Over the years, multiple hackers and cheaters have used Cronus Zen or CronusMax to cheat in Call of Duty games with wallhacks, aimbots, and all the knick-knacks and doodads. Some players even used them in the Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Beta, despite the RICOCHET Anti-Cheat being present.
But the Call of Duty devs are making sure that doesn’t happen in their upcoming game, busting Cronus’ North American distributor as a first step, but it certainly won’t be Team RICOCHET’s last.

The absence of a few senior leaders, including former Chief Minister Charanjit Singh Channi, from the Punjab Congress unit’s demonstration on Friday in Chandigarh against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar has again raised questions about the party’s internal cohesion.
The July 1 revamp of the Punjab Pradesh Congress Committee (PPCC) had sparked turmoil in the Punjab unit. Amarinder Singh Raja Warring was retained as the PPCC chief, and Mr. Channi, the Lok Sabha member from Jalandhar and the Congress’s most prominent Dalit face in the State, was appointed to lead the election campaign committee in the run-up to the 2027 Assembly election. Mr. Channi and a few other leaders, including Sukhjinder Singh Randhawa, Rana Gurjit and Tript Rajinder Singh Bajwa, were believed to be upset with the revamp of the party unit. Their supporters demanded that Mr. Warring be replaced as PPCC president, exposing the factional fault lines within the State unit.
PPCC revamp
With the elections approaching and differences persisting, the central leadership of the Congress brought in Sachin Pilot to replace Bhupesh Baghel, a former Chhattisgarh Chief Minister, as the general secretary in charge of the poll-bound State. Soon after taking charge, Mr. Pilot asserted that nearly all the leaders in Punjab have assured him of working collectively and unitedly.
Amid the ongoing power tussle, particularly between Mr. Channi and the PPCC president, the senior leaders showed a rare sign of unity by participating in the demonstration on September 9 against the Punjab government in Chandigarh, led by Mr. Pilot, a former Rajasthan Deputy Chief Minister.
A party source said earlier this week that a meeting regarding the State unit took place at the residence of national president Mallikarjun Kharge, where senior party leader Rahul Gandhi and Mr. Pilot were present. Mr. Pilot reportedly submitted a detailed feedback report on the affairs of the Punjab unit to the party’s top leadership.
The source added, “The situation in the State unit at present is quiet, but it could be like a calm before the storm. The party high command had asked the new in-charge to take a broad view of the PPCC’s affairs and issues and share it. The feedback has been given. I am confident the issues such as changes at the top leadership of the State unit will be resolved by next week, after which a possible bus yatra led by Mr. Gandhi to kick off the party’s election campaign could be organised.”

Bungie shares more detail about Marathon's Symbiosis update and 2027 plans
Another big overhaul to the game is now due in March.
Bungie is having a busy week. After the game studio shared its broad strategy for keeping players happy with its two main franchises, the team has gone into a little more detail about the next phase for its latest shooter, Marathon. Following on the previously announced Nightfall refresh in October, Bungie offered more insight on the new game modes coming in December and revealed that another big update is slated for March.
The team said that December's Symbiosis update will add a team deathmatch mode as well as a permanently available PvE mode. Details are still being finalized for the latter, but the goal of the PvE mode will allow people to experiment with their builds and fine-tune their skills without being attacked by other players. Bungie will also overhaul the Perimeter zone, which is the first one players see, to give it a more unique visual identity and new gameplay encounters, including a boss dubbed the Tick Queen. For the experienced players, a new shell archetype is coming. The Bishop is being billed as a "high-performance robot samurai," which certainly sounds fun. For the less experienced players, Marathon will add a social space with a firing range to help make the onboarding smoother.
Looking ahead to 2027, the March update hasn't been given a name yet, but Bungie says it will be "meaningfully larger than Symbiosis." The planned additions for that patch include "an interconnected system of permanent PvE, PvP, and PvEvP experiences," more onboarding improvements, a new zone and new alien enemies. The game will also add deeper progression to the shell system and "more focused questlines and narrative." That amounts to a pretty extensive set of changes, which Bungie says will lay a foundation for Marathon to continue growing over the course of 2027. It's a lot of big promises for a game that has already been facing a lot of scrutiny from the jump.

సౌదీ అరేబియా రాజధాని రియాద్లోని విమానాశ్రయంపై వైమానిక దాడి జరగడంతో భారీగా మంటలు, దట్టమైన నల్లటి పొగ వ్యాపించాయంటూ ఒక వీడియో (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) సోషల్ మీడియాలో ప్రచారంలో ఉంది. ఇందులో ఎంత నిజముందో ఇప్పుడు చూద్దాం.
క్లెయిమ్: సౌదీ అరేబియాలోని రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై జరిగిన వైమానిక దాడికి సంబంధించిన దృశ్యాలు.
ఫాక్ట్: ఈ వీడియో రియాద్కు చెందినది కాదు. ఇది రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జూన్ 2026లో డ్రోన్ దాడి వల్ల జరిగిన అగ్నిప్రమాదానికి సంబంధించిన వీడియో. సెప్టెంబర్ 2026లో రియాద్ విమానాశ్రయంపై హౌతీలు దాడి చేసినట్లు వార్తలు వస్తున్నప్పటికీ, వైరల్ వీడియో దానికి సంబంధించినది కాదు. కావున, పోస్టులో చేయబడిన క్లెయిమ్ తప్పుదోవ పట్టించే విధంగా ఉంది.
ముందుగా, వైరల్ వీడియోలోని దృశ్యాలను రివర్స్ ఇమేజ్ సెర్చ్ చేయగా, ఇవే దృశ్యాలను చూపుతున్న వీడియోలు (ఇక్కడ, ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) కనీసం 18 జూన్ 2026 నుంచి ఇంటర్నెట్లో అందుబాటులో ఉన్నట్లు గుర్తించాం. వీటి ప్రకారం, ఈ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోకు చెందినది. మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్పై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడి కారణంగా వ్యాపించిన మంటలను ఈ వీడియో చూపుతోంది.
వార్తా కథనాల (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) ప్రకారం, 18 జూన్ 2026న మాస్కోపై జరిగిన డ్రోన్ దాడిలో సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో మంటలు, పొగ వ్యాపించాయి. వైరల్ వీడియోలో కనిపిస్తున్న ప్రదేశాన్ని గూగుల్ స్ట్రీట్ వ్యూ ద్వారా పరిశీలించగా, అది మాస్కోలో ఉన్నట్లు స్పష్టమవుతోంది.
అయితే, 19 సెప్టెంబర్ 2026న రియాద్లోని కింగ్ ఖలీద్ అంతర్జాతీయ విమానాశ్రయంలోని ఇంధన డిపోపై తాము దాడి చేసినట్లు హౌతీలు పేర్కొన్నారంటూ పలు అంతర్జాతీయ వార్తా సంస్థలు (ఇక్కడ & ఇక్కడ) వెల్లడించాయి.
చివరిగా, వైరల్ వీడియో రష్యా రాజధాని మాస్కోలోని సాదోవోడ్ మార్కెట్లో జరిగిన ఘటనకు సంబంధించినది.

Iran said it has told Donald Trump it is willing to open the strait of Hormuz in six days, and to start talks on its nuclear program the day after, so long as the US lifts sanctions on Iran’s oil exports in return, ends the war on all fronts – including in Lebanon – and releases some of Iran’s frozen assets.
The proposal is designed to accelerate the steps first laid down in the memorandum of understanding signed by the US and Iran in June, particularly by helping the talks on Iran’s nuclear program start much more quickly than previously agreed.
Iran says a deal on the temporary route through the strait of Hormuz has been agreed with Oman, describing it as a done deal, and is ready to register the details with the International Maritime Organisation.
Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, said he was waiting to hear a response from the Americans to the proposal. He added that he had consulted on the plan with China, which fully supported the proposal.
Saudi Arabia had been expected to endorse the Oman-Iran route through the strait last week, but pulled back partly due to anger that Iranian-backed Houthis had started attacking Saudi Arabia as part of their dispute over the future of Yemen.
Iran claims it has urged the Houthis to cease the attacks on Saudi Arabia but that it does not have control over Houthi decision-making.
Araghchi, speaking to reporters in New York, said: “We have introduced a plan to the US through the mediators that if certain conditions are met, the strait will be open within seven days and talks will start.”
He said the Iranian preconditions were not new, and were contained in the Islamabad memorandum of understanding that was signed by Trump.
The advantage of the proposal, apart from opening the strait and lifting the chokehold on the world economy, would be bringing the US to the talks on Iran’s nuclear program much more quickly. Talks on the nuclear program under the MoU would not have started for 60 days. Araghchi said he was staying in New York over the weekend to await an American response, but added he was not in a hurry.
Privately, Iranian officials believe they could reach a deal with the Americans, and the Saudi hurdle over aspects of the route could be overcome, but fear Israel will use its influence to pull the US president away from the proposal.
Araghchi added he would like the deal to go through before the midterm elections, by which he meant that the strait of Hormuz could be opened and energy prices thereby reduced, something Trump badly needs for the Republican party to survive a political mauling.
For the US, there are difficulties in the plan related to forcing Israel to end the war in Lebanon. Israel may object to giving Iran such clear control over the route through which ships would travel through the strait of Hormuz. Iran also wants to retain control of shipping to prevent some US military shipping going through the strait.
Issues such as whether tolls or navigational fees could be imposed by the littoral states Oman and Iran would be settled later in the process.
Earlier in the day, the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, met Araghchi, his Iranian counterpart, for the first time in New York.
It was also the first meeting between UK and Iranian ministers for a year, and the first exchange since the UK in July proscribed the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) as a terrorist organisation, a move that has worsened the already sour relations between the two countries.
Miliband made clear that the UK was committed to freedom of navigation in the strait and wanted a diplomatic solution, also stressing support for Saudi Arabia, a UK ally in Yemen.
He warned Iran about its behaviour in the UK, including threats to Jewish communities, and called for the UK to be given consular access to the British couple sentenced to 10 years’ imprisonment in Tehran.
Araghchi and the US’s special envoy Steve Witkoff also met earlier this week on the sidelines of the general assembly to discuss Iran’s terms for reopening the strait and the speed at which that may happen, as well as the time the US had been given to respond.
A faction inside Iran is arguing that Tehran should seek to escalate the conflict with a vulnerable US president, rather than let the crisis drift in its current deadlock. Brent crude was trading at about $107 (£81) a barrel on Thursday.
Some IRGC officers have also linked the strait of Hormuz issue to the closure of the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrow waterway close to the south-west of Yemen now under control of Iranian-backed Houthis.
Maj Gen Rahim Safavi, a senior Iranian military figure, said: “If the Americans start a new war, a new front centred on the Red Sea and the Bab al-Mandab strait may open before their eyes. Are they ready to enter the battle on this front? This is a question that they should pay more attention to.”
Domestically, Pezeshkian’s defiant message to the UN general assembly on Wednesday was deemed a success overall in that it balanced a refusal to bend the knee to “the US bully” with a willingness to seek diplomatic talks.
He also proposed a new security architecture for the future in partnership with Gulf states, including those it has been bombarding in an effort to dislodge the US from its military bases.
Maj Gen Ahmad Vahidi, commander-in-chief of the IRGC, praised Pezeshkian’s speech, saying: “We are not afraid of war. It is the loud and firm call of the Iranian nation – a call that resonated from the United Nations podium, through the words of the esteemed president, and reached the ears of the world.”

Jammu and Kashmir Bank is set to issue a recruitment notification for assistant and officer-level positions within the next few days, Managing Director and CEO Amitava Chatterjee said on Tuesday.
Speaking during the bank’s 88th Annual General Meeting (AGM) at the Sher-i-Kashmir International Convention Centre (SKICC) here, Chatterjee said the bank had finalised negotiations with the agency that would conduct the recruitment examinations for Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh.
“After 2021, the bank is going for recruitment of both assistants as well as officers. The agreement for conducting the examinations for Jammu, Kashmir and Ladakh is being finalised, and the bank will come out with a notification in a few days,” Chatterjee said.
He said the recruitment would be carried out in accordance with the bank’s operational requirements and would also take into account the need for employees with proficiency in local languages.
“As far as the bank is concerned, we will do what we have done in the past. There is a requirement for people with local language proficiency, though the numbers will be limited,” he said.
Chatterjee said the bank’s presence across 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir had created a requirement for personnel familiar with local languages.
“The bank is present in 22 states outside Jammu and Kashmir, and we need people with local language proficiency to serve customers there. So, the bank may decide in future to hire a few employees to support our existing staff strength,” he said.
The recruitment announcement came during the bank’s 88th AGM, chaired by Part-time Non-Executive Chairman S. Krishnan and attended by Chatterjee, members of the Board, senior management, shareholders and other stakeholders.

“Our past gives us identity. Our present gives us strength. Our future gives us responsibility. Trust is our inheritance. Tradition is our anchor. Transformation is our obligation,” he said.
