If there is one feature that truly revolutionized because of AI, it is voice typing. Voice typing did exist way before AI, but it was very basic. It only converted the spoken audio directly into text, which included all the filler words, missing punctuation, grammar mistakes, and more. It basically turned whatever you spoke into text.
But with AI, voice typing goes through one extra step, where all your typing is fed to the AI models, which remove all filler words and format the sentence structure. It fundamentally eliminates the need for you to copy text into multiple apps, fix the grammar and sentence structure, and then copy it again to wherever you need it.
Third-party voice dictation apps went ahead and also included support for different formatting styles based on the app you are using, and they support almost every app.

Step 2: Once downloaded, install the app.
Step 3: Open the Morphe app and tap on Sources.
Step 4: Tap on the Plus icon, paste the following link in the Sources box, tap on Add this link, and tap on Add. https://github.com/jasonwu1994/Gboard-patches
Step 5: Wait for the source to load and tap on the Gboard app.
Step 6: Now tap on Yes, Help me find an APK, tap on Download APK, and download the app. Don’t install it.
Step 7: Now go back to the Morphe app, tap on Open APK file, and select the Gboard 18.0.3.954559732-release-arm64-v8a APK or later you downloaded above, and Morphe will start patching the app.
Step 8: Once patched, tap Install the app and allow Morphe to install the app on your device.
Step 9: Now open the patched Gboard and enable it. You need to set it as the default keyboard on some Android phones to use it, or you can go through the permission setup and switch to this keyboard later.
Step 10: Now open the patched Gboard and tap on Settings, scroll down, and tap on Patches.
Step 11: Tap on Advanced Voice Typing and enable the Enable Advanced Voice Typing option.
Step 12: Once enabled, go back to Voice Typing Settings and then select the Rambler feature.
Step 13: Now, to use the feature, you need to force stop the app. To do that, go to the patched Gboard app, long-press on it, tap on the i icon, then tap on the Force Stop option, and then confirm. These steps may vary depending on your smartphone brand and Android version.
Step 14: Now open any app where you can type, bring up patched Gboard, tap on the microphone icon, and start using Rambler.
This is how you can enable the Google Pixel Rambler feature on a supported Android smartphone without root. Since it is a manual process, I have included details step by step to help you understand.
If you face any issues or errors while using the Rambler feature, or if the Rambler feature is not available on your device, you can comment below. At the time of writing this article, the Google Rambler feature is officially supported on Google Pixel 11, Google Pixel 11 Pro, Google Pixel 11 Pro XL, and Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold. If you face any issues during the steps, comment below, and I will help you.
FAQs on Using Google Rambler on Non-Pixel Phones
1. Is it safe to use a patched version of Gboard with my Google account?
Yes, it is safe to install if you follow my steps exactly and only use the resources I included in this guide. For safety, I also highly recommend checking the app before installing using Google Play Protect or using third-party antivirus scanner tools like VirusTotal.
2. Will Rambler continue working after Gboard or Android gets updated?
Yes, since you are using a separate Gboard patched version, updating the original Gmail app won’t affect this patched version. However, the patched version also needs to be updated in case Google blocks access to the Rambler feature for other devices.
3. Can I switch back to the official Gboard later without losing my keyboard settings?
You won’t lose any settings; you can simply switch back to the original Gboard if you want to anytime.
4. Which languages does Rambler support for AI voice typing?
Google Rambler currently supports Arabic, English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, and a few other Indian languages,
5. Does Rambler send my voice recordings or typed text to Google for processing?
Yes, the Google Pixel Rambler feature uses cloud processing to fix sentences; however, Google says this data is not saved, stored, or shared and is deleted immediately after the processed text is delivered.

The US government is trying to get Elon Musk and his social media platform X out of a $137 million fine by the European Union in an escalation of its criticism of the bloc’s tech rules.
The US Department of Justice said it had filed an application with the help of the Department of State to support a legal challenge by Musk to annul the case in the EU’s General Court. The Luxembourg-based court will now decide whether the US has a right to intervene.
The US government is arguing that it should be involved in the case to protect American companies. The fine is precedent-setting as the bloc’s first sanction under the Digital Services Act, which requires online platforms to do more to tackle illegal and harmful content, especially the largest sites. Many of those, which include Meta’s Facebook and Instagram, Google’s YouTube, and Microsoft’s LinkedIn, are headquartered in the US and contribute significantly to the US economy, it pointed out.
“We will not tolerate the European Commission engaging in regulatory overreach to try and control American engines of innovation and economic growth,” said Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the Justice Department’s Civil Division.
The case also has “implications” for US-EU relations, it warned. The act has become a major source of tension between officials, with US President Donald Trump calling the penalties “overseas extortion.” Last year, he threatened imposing tariffs on any country implementing digital regulation, which he said were “all designed to harm, or discriminate against, American technology.” Vice President JD Vance has criticized the DS’s content moderation rules as “authoritarian censorship.”
The European Commission slapped X with the €120 million fine in December following a two-year-long investigation which found X had breached transparency obligations. Claiming users with blue checkmarks are “verified accounts” when they simply have to pay for the status is deceptive, the Commission ruled. X’s inaccessible and incomplete advertising repository and failure to provide access to public data for researchers is also hindering research into the platform’s risks, it said. In July, the Commission accepted X’s plan to fix the data access issues, which X now has six months to implement.
Both Musk and X launched appeals against the ruling on behalf of both parties in February. The EU’s investigation was “incomplete and superficial” and the interpretation of the DSA obligations “tortured,” they said. They also complained they had not been given “rights of defence … suggesting prosecutorial bias.”
Musk has also complained about the financial and administrative burden of heightened transparency requirements as governments globally try to get a better understanding of—and limit—social media platforms’ risks of harm. In July, he argued Australia’s “invasive” information-gathering powers within the country’s under-16 social media ban interfered with international law. At the time, professor of internet law at Queen Mary University of London, Julia Hörnle, told WIRED that Australian regulators were within their rights to order disclosures related to a company’s operations in that particular country.

An 18-year-old has been arrested after he was spotted allegedly moving a tub that contained a dismembered torso at an apartment in Smyrna, Georgia.
Kingston Bradley has been charged with concealing the death. He was taken into custody on Wednesday and is being held without bond at the Cobb County Jail, according to 11Alive.
Bradley was allegedly spotted moving a plastic tub through an outdoor area at the Park Valley Apartments around 8:15 p.m. on Wednesday.
When Bradley noticed that he was being watched, he allegedly dropped the tub in a dirt walkway and ran into his apartment, which is in the same complex.
Police received a missing person's report directing them to the complex. When officers arrived at the scene and opened the tub, they discovered a dismembered human torso inside.
Investigators then searched Bradley's apartment and allegedly found multiple bloodstains inside as well as a large, blood-covered saw. Police said in a report that a strong bleach smell was present in the apartment. They also allegedly found a mop, a bucket of water, and a carpet cleaner.
The victim was identified as a woman, but her name has not been released to the public. The victim's family told 11 Alive that the woman who was killed was Shanteria "Tia" Mosely.
They said they filed a missing person's report after she left home to make DoorDash deliveries and did not return home. The family members claim they tracked Mosely's phone to the apartment complex and even spoke to Bradley, who allegedly told them he had not seen the woman.
Michelle Weaver, Mosely's aunt, said she is the one who saw Bradley allegedly moving the tub.
The Smyrna Police Department is still investigating the incident.
Bradley has a previous, unresolved case that involves a fight with his father in late 2024. He was charged with two counts of terroristic threats, battery, simple battery, and criminal trespass-damage to property.
According to a warrant in that case, Bradley allegedly hit his father with an Xbox controller, breaking down his bedroom door, and then pushing "a 15-year-old male juvenile" into a window, breaking it in the process.
The terroristic threat charge comes from him allegedly "suggesting the death" of his father.
Bradley pleaded not guilty in that case in April and will face his next hearing for that matter on October 6.

Banks advise customers to complete essential transactions ahead of 3-day strike from September 28
Banks advise customers to complete essential transactions ahead of 3-day strike
Public sector banks and some old-generation private sector banks have issued advisories urging customers to complete essential banking transactions in advance to avoid inconvenience during the three-day strike from September 28 called by bank employees' unions.
The United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU), which claims to represent 90 per cent of the banking workforce, has announced a three-day strike beginning September 28, to press for a five-day banking week and other demands.
The strike, if it materialises, would coincide with the banking sector's half-yearly closing.
Deep Dive
To meet customers' banking needs before the three-day nationwide strike, the government has already instructed public sector banks to stay open on Sunday, September 27.
In its advisory to customers, SBI said that while the bank will make every effort to provide essential banking services at branches/Offices, certain services may be affected during the strike period, which may inconvenience valued customers.
"Customers are therefore requested to complete their essential banking transactions well in advance of the proposed strike dates to avoid any inconvenience. Customers are also requested to make use of ATMs/ADWMs for their cash requirements and utilise YONO, Internet/Mobile Banking, UPI and other digital channels for their banking needs, wherever possible," it said.
Another public sector lender, Bank of India, in a message to customers intimated that "due to nation-wide Bank strike on 28, 29 and 30th September 2026, we request you to use the bank's 24X7 digital channels such as Mobile Banking/ ATM/ Internet Banking/ BC Point/ UPI for your banking needs."
Besides, Regional Rural Banks are also participating in the three-day strike.
An old-generation private sector lender, Karnataka Bank, in an advisory said, "If the strike materializes, the normal functioning of the bank branches, offices, departments may be affected and the bank is taking necessary steps to ensure normal functioning."
Expected quantum of loss or damages and impact on the operations are not quantifiable, it said.
However, new generation private sector banks like ICICI Bank, HDFC Bank, Axis Bank and IndusInd Bank would continue their normal banking operations.
Earlier this week, the Finance Ministry appealed to bank employees to refrain from strikes and resolve their remaining demands through dialogue, saying most union concerns have been substantially addressed.
Other UFBU demands include updating and improving pensions, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners, and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to switch to the old pension scheme (OPS).

Over the past five years, at least three meetings involving all stakeholders were convened to address the occupational safety and health concerns faced by workers in the unorganised sector. However, despite these consultations and a plan for a dedicated policy or guidelines, a comprehensive framework to ensure their health and safety is still pending in Tamil Nadu, with health officials noting that a number of recommendations remained on paper.
With Tamil Nadu witnessing a steady increase in the migrant worker population across various sectors, the need for a comprehensive occupational safety and health (OSH) framework has become increasingly important.
What exists
On its part, the Directorate of Medical and Rural Health Services had created the Occupational, Social and Environmental Health Wing for screening, diagnosis, treatment, rehabilitation and compensation of the unorganised sector workers including micro, small and medium enterprises and inter-State migrant workers nearly a decade ago. Based on its proposal, the Health department constituted State and district-level inter department co-ordination committees and 21 disease and speciality-specific expert (technical) committees. The wing was later made into the State Nodal Centre for Occupational Health and Safety of Unorganised Workers (SNC-OSH).
Health officials said that the State Planning Commission had convened meetings on OSH of unorganised sector workers during which various aspects were discussed. A wider stakeholder consultation with trade union representatives, employers, NGOs and unorganised workers was suggested. Based on the recommendations of these meetings, the need to formulate a policy was also planned but no headway was made.
Key discussion and action points on OSH in Tamil Nadu
Key focus areas
Among the key focus areas was the health of the unorganised sector workers. Officials had raised the need for the inclusion of basic occupational health services and universal health coverage as per World Health Organization/International Labour Organization standards and mandatory health screening on job entry and regular check ups for all unorganised labourers. Maintenance of log book/health profile for all workers including inter-State migrants employed for over 30 years to track long-term illnesses like silicosis, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, noise-induced hearing loss, contact dermatitis and occupational cancers to ensure health coverage was also put forward.
One of the key action points was that all departments must provide inputs to outline OSH guidelines for unorganised sector labourers. Industrial and economic units should be required to maintain log books, ensure mandatory health screening/check ups for workers. The need to integrate OSH components into all National Health Mission programmes was another key point.
Apart from these, the need for Tamil Nadu to notify 107 diseases/hazards under OSH for unorganised workers [ILO and WHO have notified 107 diseases/hazards under occupational safety and health administration], sensitisation of workers on NCD management and conducting medical camps for NCD screening were among the other discussion points.
Independent OSH cell
A source privy to these meetings said that a series of discussions were held and one of the proposals was to have a slightly independent OSH cell. “It should have a broader perspective and a larger compass to operate on. This is an important area but least attended to. New industries are coming up and new problems will crop up. It is better to have a Standard Operating Procedure in the beginning to protect workers’ health,” he said.

Pharmacy-focused quick commerce startup Rio Health has raised $4.5 Mn (around ₹43 Cr) in a pre-Series A funding round led by Version One Ventures. Existing investors Xeed Ventures, Good Capital and Amplify also participated in the all-equity round. The startup intends to use the fresh capital to expand its presence across Delhi NCR by setting up 12 more dark stores as well as strengthen its tech abilities across ordering, inventory and delivery operations. The startup is also targeting an annual recurring revenue (ARR) of more than ₹150 Cr over the next nine to 12 months. “This funding will help us strengthen our technology, improve how we predict neighbourhood-level demand, and make reliable medicine delivery available to many more customers across Delhi NCR,” said Rio Health cofounder Ankur Agrawal. Founded by Agrawal and Amit Ahuja, Rio Health delivers medicines and healthcare essentials in Delhi NCR within 20-30 minutes. Customers can place orders by typing or speaking in Hindi, English or Hinglish, or by uploading a photograph of a prescription. The startup’s AI system identifies the medicines prescribed and creates an order, which is subsequently verified by a licensed pharmacist. Rio Health currently processes more than 30,000 orders a month, with an average order value of ₹600-700. The startup claims that nearly 80% of its orders come from repeat customers. Rio Health currently offers access to more than 20,000 SKUs, while long-tail medicines are sourced through its distributor network. Its dark stores serve a radius of around three kilometres, with neighbourhood-level demand data used to forecast medicine requirements and stock its stores accordingly. Prior to the latest round, Rio Health had raised ₹19.2 Cr across earlier funding rounds. The latest investment takes its total funding raised to ₹62.2 Cr ($6.5 Mn). The fundraise comes as quick commerce players and specialised startups are stepping up their bets on faster medicine delivery, even as the category comes with higher operational and regulatory complexities than grocery within the booming quick commerce market. Broadly, the Indian quick commerce market is expected to become a $30 Bn to $40 Bn opportunity in the next three to five years. Quick commerce players are expected to clock $68 Bn in gross merchandise value (GMV) by 2031, up from $8.3 Bn in 2026 — an almost 8X rise at a 52% CAGR. Quick commerce giants Zepto, Blinkit and Swiggy Instamart are already exploring 10-minute medicine delivery as they look beyond grocery for higher-value categories. However, unlike grocery, pharma requires licensed entities, prescription verification and tighter controls around inventory, storage and fulfilment. The complexity has also created room for specialised players. Plazza, which operates technology-enabled neighbourhood pharmacies, raised $15 Mn in July 2026 to strengthen its technology and AI-led inventory systems and expand beyond its two Bengaluru stores.

On August 17, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) announced its revamped social media team, appointing Deepak Mhaskey as the national social media convenor, and Priti Gandhi, Shivanand Dwivedi, Alok Bhatt and Arun Yadav as co-convenors.
While curiosity grew as to who these newly appointed individuals were and their past work and association with the party, social media users were quick to notice that immediately after the announcement, Gandhi, Dwivedi and Yadav made their X accounts private and there was no trace of Bhatt on the internet.
While all the other IT cell members are back to being active on X, albeit after deleting hundreds of thousands of old posts, Alok Bhatt is the only one in the group whose X handle remains inaccessible or ‘protected’ even a month after the new team was announced.
The only remnants of Bhatt’s online presence are the now-disabled X account, screenshots from his X posts and some articles in Right-wing outlets like OpIndia, Organiser and Swarajya.
Alt News found that in the past, Bhatt had been called out for controversial tweets several times. In archived screenshots of his posts from the past, the BJP functionary can be seen using sexist, Islamophobic, and derogatory language, some of which can be seen below:
Who is Alok Bhatt?
Bhatt, who claims to hail from Dehradun, has worn many hats over the course of his career. According to his LinkedIn profile, he graduated from Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University (HNBGU) in Uttarakhand and went on to work with several organisations, including NIIT University, where he served as financial controller until April 2010.
In 2010, he founded Nature Connect Outdoors — an education and adventure non-profit organisation that deals in outdoor education and skill development, including treks, camping, and rafting expeditions. According to the website’s bio, Bhatt had “shunned his corporate career” to follow his passion, which culminated in the formation of the NGO. The organisation is still functional.
According to details available on Zauba Corp, Bhatt is a Chartered Accountant (CA) and the partner of a firm of CAs called RSAC & CO LLP, incorporated in May 2021.
Bhatt has also served as the economic adviser to former Uttarakhand chief minister Trivendra Singh Rawat. However, it’s not clear when he was appointed and when exactly his tenure ended. He wrote an article for Firstpost defending the ministry of housing and urban affairs over the controversial Central Vista project. The author bio designated him as ‘Economic Advisor’ to Rawat.
In 2020, after a district officer’s press release promoting inter-caste and interfaith marriages drew criticism from social media users, Bhatt had reportedly tweeted: “No one from the government has spoken in support of promoting interfaith marriages. The Pamphlet-Savitr Analytics-Alok Bhatt Connection
In 2022, Bhatt took on a directorial role at Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation, a company that was incorporated in April 26 that year, with Bhatt and Ashish Nautiyal initially named as directors. According to documents filed with the Union ministry of corporate affairs (MCA), Bhatt holds 9,500 shares, or 95 per cent of the company, while Nautiyal holds the remaining 500 shares, or 5 per cent.
Interestingly, Nautiyal is also the founding editor of the Right-wing media outlet, The Pamphlet.
Savitr Analytics has no website or online presence. We went through its financial records filed with the MCA for the financial years 2022-23, 2023-24 and 2024-25, and found that it was registered as a Section 8 company, i.e., a non-profit. In the 2024-25 financial year, its total revenue from operations was Rs 2.7 crore.
The organisation’s revenue across all three years comes from ‘sale of services’, and the rows for ‘Grants or donations received (relevant for Sec 8 companies)’, present in the 2022-23 and 2023-24 filings, are left blank in 2022-23 and 2023-24. In 2024-25, the row does not exist.
Under ‘Corporate Information’, they state ‘Research and awareness about Indian culture and heritage…’, ‘Promotion of commerce, art, science, sports, education, research, social welfare, religion, charity, and environmental protection…’ and ‘Advancement of education, learning, and skills development…’ as their activities.
There was a category called ‘professional expenses’ in the 2022-23 filing that was later relabeled as ‘content production expenses’. Rs. 41,48,600 was spent in the first year, Rs. 95,36,600 (filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the second year, and Rs. 1,38,53,200 (also filed directly as content production expenses) was spent in the third year.
Next, we found that an individual named Ridhika Aggarwal stated on LinkedIn that she worked as a content writer for Savitr Analytics Media and Research Foundation until August 2023. We went through her X timeline (linked to her LinkedIn profile) and found that she wrote at least three articles for The Pamphlet during her tenure at Savitr. None of the articles are currently available on the website.
Ridhika is also listed as a non-official member of a steering committee formed by the Union ministry of environment, forest and climate change in 2023.
The Pamphlet, previously known as The Indian Affairs, posted for the first time on Facebook in April 2022, which is the same time when Savitr Analytics was incorporated.

It is worth noting that The Pamphlet’s website does not disclose any parent company, ownership, editorial team, funding details or board of directors. We also found that The Pamphlet had an office space from its inception in Dehradun, and it is evident from a photo posted by Nautiyal that it began with a team of at least 20 people. Bhatt, the reader would remember, also claims to be from Dehradun.
While all of this points to a connection between Bhatt and The Pamphlet, there appears to be a concerted effort to keep that relationship under wraps. Hence, we tried to dig more.
Is Bhatt Linked to The Pamphlet? We Asked The Pamphlet
We sent an email to The Pamphlet on September 3 asking them about the relationship between Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet, and whether Alok Bhatt was connected to The Pamphlet, given that he holds a 95% stake in Savitr Analytics, a company whose other directors have held senior positions at The Pamphlet. We also asked them about their funding sources, since nothing is mentioned on the website.
In reply, they asked us to send our queries to another email ID of The Pamphlet and also to Alok Bhatt, Nirwa Mehta, Ashish Nautiyal and Shiv Mishra. Interestingly, they provided us with the email IDs and phone numbers of each of these individuals. This, in itself, might be considered an indicator of some sort of link between The Pamphlet and Bhatt. It is unlikely for an organisation to provide the direct contact details of someone with whom it has no professional association.
We then sent our queries to all of them.
Nautiyal responded to us saying that his reporting manager, OpIndia editor Nupur J Sharma, “suggested” him “not to give (you) any quotes or information as a matter of policy of not engaging with entities that don’t act in good faith”. A day later, he took to X to let the world know that a woman from Alt News “with a Hindu-sounding name” had approached him with some questions.
Pamphlet editor Nirwa Mehta sent us a 1,071-word response, but did not answer any of our questions. Instead, she sent a detailed set of reciprocal questions concerning Alt News’ funding transparency, the outside associations of its founders and editor, and grants received by individuals associated with Alt News, both currently and in the past. She offered to answer Alt News’ questions in writing once Alt News answered hers first.
It is worth noting that The Pamphlet published a video on Alt News on August 16, 2026, without seeking a response from the organisation.
This correspondent responded to Mehta, stating that questions concerning Alt News’ funding should be directed to its editor, while questions concerning any of the founders’ personal assignments should be directed to the person concerned. We also reminded her that a so-called expose on Alt News’ founders had been published by The Pamphlet without either of the concerned persons being approached for a response — a violation of basic journalistic ethics.
In her final response, Mehta did not address the question of ethics. Instead, in a demand that many may find bizarre, she asked this correspondent, “as a responsible employee”, to take her questions to the Alt News directors.
At this point, we felt there was no point continuing the conversation.
We will update our article if The Pamphlet answers Alt News’ questions on whether Savitr Analytics and The Pamphlet are connected in any way, and whether Alok Bhatt, BJP’s new IT cell member who continues to remain away from X, holds a position at The Pamphlet.
Social Media Posts Answer the Question
The connection between The Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt is one of internet’s worst kept secrets, it seems. We found several instances on social media where well-known faces from the Right-wing ecosystem tagged Alok Bhatt alongside members of The Pamphlet team — whether to thank them for invitations to Delhi Shabdotsav 2026, where The Pamphlet Panchayat featured on the itinerary, or in connection with other events involving the organisation.
On January 5, 2026, Right-wing influencer Abhijit Iyer-Mitra, who was recently criticised for comparing Newslaundry journalists to prostitutes, thanked The Pamphlet team — including its editor Nirwa Mehta, anchor Shreya Arora, and Bhatt — for inviting him to speak at The Pamphlet Panchayat.
Responding to Iyer-Mitra, Nirwa Mehta and another The Pamphlet employee, Pratibha, thanked him for being a part of the session. The exchange is significant because it can be seen as an acknowledgement by the Pamphlet editor and another employee of Bhatt being a part of the organisation.
Delhi Shabdotsav 2026 was a three-day cultural and literary festival held from January 2 to January 4, 2026, organised by Suruchi Prakashan with the support of the department of art, culture and languages of the Delhi government. The Pamphlet was the digital partner at the event and hosted ‘The Pamphlet Panchayat’ at the fest. The Pamphlet team held and moderated several discussions over the three days, including those with Sanjeev Newar, Vijay Patel, and Subhi Vishwakarma. The subjects of the discussions ranged from ‘Love Jihad: factsheet’ to ‘Bharat’s Hostile Neighbourhood & Need to Regain Shatrubodh’.
We went through the images posted on Shabdotsav’s website and found that Bhatt was present at the event.
The link between Alok Bhatt and The Pamphlet becomes more apparent in another conversation on X in which Iyer-Mitra directly addressed Mehta as Pamphlet and Alok Bhatt’s ‘staff’. Iyer jokingly rebuked Mehta for liking a certain kind of car. Tagging Bhatt, he wrote, “Do @Pamphlet_in and @alok_bhatt @shreya_arora22 approve of these disgusting and extremely hateful statements by their staff?” Mehta responded to Iyer-Mitra’s post, but did not object to the ‘staff’ reference.
On June 1, 2023, a little more than a year after The Pamphlet’s inception, one @saket71 posted a picture with Ashish Nautiyal, who was working at The Pamphlet then, and called him a ‘Media Mughal’. He later tagged Alok Bhatt and Shiv Mishra, praising them for “putting a great team together.”

To sum up, what raises serious questions about the BJP’s decision to name Bhatt as its social media co-convenor is not just his past social media conduct, but also the opacity surrounding his professional associations. One organisation he appears to be associated with, The Pamphlet, does not publicly disclose its ownership, editorial team, board or funding sources. Without any apparent source of funding, it starts off as a 20-member organization. Who pays their salary? How are establishment costs met? There are no answers. Again, another corporate entity closely linked to him, Savitr Analytics, has no website or public online presence despite reporting Rs 2.7 crore in operational revenue in 2025.
Things get murkier when one takes into account the desperate efforts by Bhatt’s associates to conceal his association with The Pamphlet, evident in the organisation’s refusal to answer direct questions regarding this.

Hype merchants have a habit of overdoing it, but there’s no denying that China is making the US look more than a little antiquated when it comes to electric vehicles. Some of that is due to a deep integration of connected services and an extension of the car as part of the owner’s digital life—think additional infotainment screens and AI personal assistants, but with an Android phone-maker’s cadence of updates rather than that of a traditional car company. Other advances sound more appealing. China’s OEMs are in a battle over who can charge the fastest, and this week, Geely fired its latest salvo.
China might have a much younger driving culture than North America or Europe, but it has still been long enough to condition those drivers to how long it takes to fill a tank of gas. For all their many improvements over internal combustion engine vehicles—far greater efficiency, instant torque, very little NVH, more reliabiity, and so on—EVs do still take longer to recharge than it takes to refuel a car with a liquid.
At least until now, it seems.
Geely’s new battery can charge at up to 2.2 MW and will recharge from 10 to 70 percent in 4.5 minutes. A 10–98 percent charge takes 8 minutes and 40 seconds. Predictive thermal management is done through AI, with an average pack temperature of 55˚C and a peak temperature during charging of 65˚C, Geely said.
And while you might think pumping large amounts of energy into a battery quickly and repeatedly could harm its health, Geely says that, using AI, the system applies micro pulses of current to “reactivate lithium ions accumulated at the negative electrodes during repeated fast charging,” extending battery life by 20 percent. The pack has been tested in both the Zeekr 001 and Lynk and Co 10—maybe we’ll see a Volvo or Lotus use the same tech someday.

After a nearly monthlong delay, states are now able to order this season’s COVID-19 vaccines through a federal program that provides free immunizations to low-income children, the US health department says. Trump officials have still not provided a clear explanation for the delay, raising concerns about meddling from anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.
On Wednesday, Ars Technica reported that the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention had still not opened ordering for 2026–2027 COVID-19 vaccines through the Vaccines for Children program. That was despite the vaccines having been approved by the Food and Drug Administration in late August.
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) told Ars on Wednesday that “CDC has not yet finalized procurement decisions” for the shots. The department’s statement further suggested Trump officials were questioning whether children should receive them. “HHS and CDC are committed to responsible stewardship of taxpayer resources and to ensuring that vaccines purchased through federally funded programs are appropriate for the populations those programs serve,” the department said.
However, The Washington Post reported late Wednesday that ordering was opening. An unnamed source told the Post that part of the reason the vaccine ordering was held up was a delay in finalizing the CDC’s clinical guidance, which is written for health care professionals and public health officials. The guidance reportedly needed to be reviewed by an external expert.
Lingering questions
The Post also reported that CDC career officials had previously finished preparations for making the vaccines available. All Trump officials needed to do was essentially push a button to open ordering, sources said. Further, a spokesperson for the Minnesota Department of Health suggested to the Post that CDC leadership was behind the hold, saying the state had been told “that CDC leadership approval is needed before distribution of the vaccine can begin.”

Why Pakistan’s endless war on militants fails to break the cycle
Tactical wins and retaliatory strikes have not delivered peace, even as two separate insurgencies appear to be converging
Scores of soldiers, policemen and civilians are killed every month in Pakistan’s northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and southwestern Balochistan provinces, where near-daily attacks on security personnel, government officials and other prominent figures are carried out by militants to undermine the state’s authority and credibility.
Insurgents target patrols, checkpoints, police stations and administrative centres with roadside bombs, explosive-laden drones, coordinated ambushes, suicide attacks, large-scale raids, assassinations and kidnappings.
Pakistan’s military regularly hails the success of its counterterrorism operations, touting the eradication of hundreds of perpetrators each month. Its press releases often read like scoreboards, listing the number of insurgents “sent to hell” – with only a handful surviving to be interrogated.

This as-told-to essay is based on a conversation with Luba Patlakh Kaplun, founder of Kidology. It has been edited for length and clarity.
I used to dream of being a broadcast journalist. But my parents — Russian Jewish immigrants from Ukraine — wanted me to do something more serious, in their eyes.
I floundered for a bit, studying journalism, then opening a marketing agency. All the while, my parents were asking, "When are you going to establish yourself?"
Much of my family works in medicine, but I can't do blood and needles. I did an internet search for careers with the most security and growth potential, and found speech-language pathology. It seemed perfect: serious enough for my parents, and adjacent to the medical field, but with no blood or needles.
My language skills helped me differentiate my business
I got my master's and started working for another speech-language pathologist who had a bilingual English-Spanish clinic. I speak Russian, and when the owner realized that, they started to grow their clientele.
I realized my community was almost completely untouched. Instead of using my Russian skills to expand someone else's business, I wanted to use them to benefit my family and me. Doing that felt like a way to honor the generational trauma that my family had been through, sacrificing and working so hard to get to America.
Doing everything myself started to catch up
That's when Luba, the business owner, was born. I started going to all the Jewish clubs and churches to see students. I was juggling seeing patients with building a practice, billing insurance, and raising awareness about speech-language pathology within my Russian-speaking community.
I was constantly trying to do a little more before hiring someone. I worried I could never teach the business to another person, and that no one would treat the business — my baby — as well as I would.
Five years in, I was burned out. I realized I was missing payments because I didn't have the systems in place to track them and follow up with clients. I was good at juggling, but some of the balls were starting to drop.
Creating standard procedures helped me grow
I had just crossed into seven figures of revenue when I came across a survey asking business owners about their challenges. It was a targeted ad, but it was just what I needed. Through that company, I connected with a business course and financial management.
Those resources changed my entire business. I realized I didn't have standard operating procedures or a management structure. Once I established those, my company flourished. In 2020, we did just over $1 million in revenue. Last year, we did $4.95 million, and we're still growing.
My kids are benefiting from generations of hard work
My business is 11, and my children are 10, 8, and 4. They've been raised alongside the business. When I do community presentations, my little one loves to tell people to come talk to his mom.
My older son sees how the business's financial success has impacted his life. He used to play in a little inflatable pool; now, we have a large house with an in-ground pool. He likes to joke that his little brother doesn't remember how things used to be.
Their lives are very different from mine growing up. My family always had enough money, but we lived in apartments, and my brother and I shared a room for most of my childhood. I tell my kids that, and make sure they know everything they have come from hard work: not only mine, but my parents' and grandparents' too.

In September 2015, the Founders Fund hosted a retreat at an eco-resort in British Columbia. Most of the attendees were VCs and people from the companies the firm was backing, but they also invited a few outsiders, including computer pioneer Alan Kay, writer Neal Stephenson, and me.
One morning at breakfast I was sitting across from Kay at a long table. The man who conceived the Dynabook—basically the modern computer that we all use—was expounding on his exploits when Founders Fund leader Peter Thiel plopped down next to him. As Kay, in full raconteur mode, spun stories of optimizing the mouse and advising Steve Jobs, Thiel listened with increasingly visible incredulity. Finally, he couldn’t take it. “Who ARE you?” he demanded of Kay.
The mustachioed legend was stunned. He began stumbling out his bona fides, but quickly realized that for someone unacquainted with his résumé, it would have sounded ridiculously overblown. It was like asking Einstein or Mick Jagger to explain themselves. Kay stopped mid-sentence and sighed. “I’m just an old has-been,” he said and went back to his breakfast. Two worlds had collided, and failed to connect.
I thought back to that moment a couple of weeks ago while reading an op-ed in The New York Times headlined “Silicon Valley Was Right From the Start,” by Sharon Weinberger. The essay claimed that the portrait often painted of the Valley as driven by the counterculture and a desire to make the world better was a sham. Today’s bare-knuckled approach to accumulating massive wealth, kowtowing to an authoritarian leader, and embracing lethal military technology simply exposes the industry for what it always was. (Weinberger’s essay was promoting her new book Valley of Death: How Big Tech Is Fueling the Future of War.)
“Silicon Valley’s values haven’t changed, just its customers,” she wrote, calling the industry’s current love affair with military tech “less a story of political conversion than of market adaptation.” In that reading, all that hippie stuff about free expression and democratization during the 1980s PC revolution and the 1990s Internet boom was a mirage, an opportunistic feint by Big Tech to push its wares and garner the loot.
I disagree. The story as I see it is that beginning in the late 1970s, a new generation of technologists, identifying with the counterculture, operated with a set of values that unleashed innovation and ironically set the stage for the industry’s current wealth. Yes, that movement carried a torch from the field’s defense industry roots. But even as DOD funding kept fueling innovations (Darpa grants provided dough for the GUI, the internet, and Google Search), that new generation was characterized by idealism, a hackerish love of building things, and disdain for conventional practices.
That mindset changed not only the course of the computer industry, but the culture of American business. (Before Apple Computer, a CEO wouldn’t dare come to work in anything but a suit.) Denying the existence of that idealism is not only inaccurate, but it conveniently lets the new generation of defense contractors off the hook for their pivot toward deadly materiel.
When I shared my views with Weinberger, she acknowledged that I’d probably studied tech culture more than she had from her perch in Washington, DC. Still, she gamely defended her op-ed. “We’re all products of what we grow up in,” she says. “If you were growing up in the peace-dividend era, with defense tech jobs disappearing, the money from defense was less important, and you start to have different values.”
By that standard, the market shift from missile control modules to Macintoshes was driven not by values but by greed. Likewise, she says, the recent return to high-tech weaponry doesn’t represent a philosophical repositioning but a fortuitous opportunity to sell to a Pentagon eager to exploit the Valley’s innovations. “It's not like everybody in the workforce in Silicon Valley woke up and went, like, ‘Defense is cool,’” says Weinberger. That impulse to go where the money is, she argues, is the defining ethos of Silicon Valley. “Your prime directive is for your company to succeed,” she says. “Why didn't Apple work with the military? Because they didn't need to. They had the consumer marketplace.”
Actually, Apple and its cohorts invented the consumer marketplace for computers. And the shoulders that Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, and others stood on were not those of pocket-protector-wearing nerds clocking into jobs at Lockheed, but young and freaky computer scientists. My friend John Markoff’s book What the Dormouse Said is all about how the counterculture set the tone for the Valley during its tremendous growth years. When we spoke this week, Markoff noted that the Valley’s transition point from a defense-oriented industry to one shaped by counterculture values rose from three pivotal computer labs—AI pioneer John McCarthy’s Stanford lab, the Stanford Research Institute, which hosted Douglas Engelbart’s groundbreaking GUI innovations; and Kay’s Xerox PARC, which essentially set the foundation for the computers that we all use today.
These influential institutions were hippie havens. In fact, says Markoff, many of the researchers in those labs worked there in order to get draft deferments to avoid the Vietnam War. “Money was not the motivating factor for these people,” he says. “The Valley’s entrepreneurial culture emerged from a fusion of the counterculture hackers and engineers who believed that technology would change the world, and the more traditional semiconductor culture, which quickly escaped its military roots.”
While those labs were thriving, a ragtag group of engineers met at the Homebrew Computer Club, hosted by a political radical named Lee Felsenstein. That was the bunch that invented the personal computer industry, notably Apple. When I first became exposed to the computer world in the early 1980s, the countercultural nature of the enterprise blew my mind, and drew me into covering that world full-time. I saw for myself how, working within the infrastructure of big business, techno-idealists like the early Macintosh team built the products of their dreams.
No, the Valley did not turn from defense to consumer products because that’s where the money was. Well into the ’80s and ’90s, Apple in particular had to fight the image that their products were like toys, because they eschewed the macho industrial vibe of previous machines in favor of a friendlier look and feel. It took decades for the company to significantly break into the corporate market. (It’s ironic that the current War Bros that Weinberger writes about in her book are obsessed with masculinity.) Google was founded by iconoclasts who thumbed their noses at Wall Street even as their company pursued its IPO.
The most nuanced study of the relationship between the Valley’s military past and the counterculturists who built the modern industry is historian Margaret O’Mara’s book The Code: Silicon Valley and the Remaking of America. When I spoke to her this week, she agreed with me that the Valley's counterculture shift wasn’t a mercenary pivot but a genuine movement toward making the world better. The market’s move from defense tech to consumer, she says, was a reflection of a generational political shift. In the presidential elections of 1980 and 1984, the Valley voted decisively for Reagan. But as the Valley increasingly tilted toward the counterculture, that all changed, and for many recent cycles those tech-heavy zip codes have been tattooed in deep blue hues. While Trump-affiliated War Bros are currently getting attention, they represent only a small cohort of self-interested multibillionaires. Essentially, they’ve hijacked the values of the Valley.
“I feel like the wealth and the concentration of power has warped everything so profoundly,” says O’Mara. “When you’re in a bubble, whether you’re a president or a billionaire, you have a very hard time understanding how the rest of the world is receiving you.”
I’m sure that the War Bros themselves believe they are acting out of patriotism—though at least some of them have fetishized cool war movies and shoot-’em-up computer games to the point where they get a kick out of making products with spectacular kill functions. But for the past 40 years or so, Silicon Valley typically wanted nothing to do with killing, even though there was always money to be tapped from the Pentagon budget. Ignoring that history or, worse, denying it, takes the War Bros off the hook.
It’s too bad that Peter Thiel didn’t bother to understand what made Alan Kay tick or even know who he was. Thiel himself is a beneficiary of Kay’s idealism, as well as the ethos of countless hackers and founders. They strived for something more lofty than a Valley of Death. Don’t pretend otherwise.

Against the odds to Asian Games gold: Journey of Haryana shooters
Haryana shooters Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh clinched gold medal in the 10m air pistol mixed team event at 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan.
Haryana shooters Kamaljeet and Suruchi Singh clinched the gold medal in the 10m air pistol mixed team event at the 2026 Asian Games in Aichi-Nagoya, Japan, on Friday, securing their maiden Asian Games title.
For both shooters, however, the road to the Asian Games podium was far from easy. Both had their fair share of challenges, but their dedication to the sport was similar.
HT spoke to Kamaljeet, who said that he started his journey in shooting sports in 2019. The athlete said that the first few years were really good, with him winning several medals for the country. However, he met with an accident in 2022, was badly injured and suffered a thigh bone fracture.
Deep Dive
“It was definitely a tough time for me and my family. I had to stay away from shooting for several months and missed the National Games. Things became very difficult during that period. But deep down, I never wanted to quit shooting,” he told HT.
Recalling that difficult phase, he said there came a point when he told his family that he would not give up shooting. “Without their support, I would not have come this far. My first coach, Shaktipal, also stood by me throughout. Without all their support, I would not have been able to make a comeback,” he said.
The manner in which he bounced back was remarkable. In 2023, Kamaljeet won gold in the men’s 50m pistol individual event at the ISSF Junior World Championships in Changwon, South Korea, underlining his resilience and emerging as one of India’s promising young shooters.
Kamaljeet said the key to their success was keeping the pressure at bay and simply enjoying the final. He said the duo did not enter the contest thinking they had to win at all costs. Instead, once they reached the final, they were confident of securing a medal and focused on performing freely.
“We know that we will go back with the medal, and our focus was to give our best,” he told HT.
When asked about his future goals, Kamaljeet said representing India at the Olympics and winning a gold medal was the ultimate dream for any athlete, and that he, too, was working towards achieving it.
Meanwhile, 20-year-old Suruchi Singh had initially aspired to become a wrestler. She began training at the age of 13, but within just two-and-a-half months, she suffered a collarbone injury, forcing her to put her wrestling journey on hold.
Nishant Phogat, Singh’s brother, told HT that after this, she started looking for sports where a collarbone injury did not impact training. “Finally, she told my father that she wants to do shooting,” he said.
Their father, who had served in the Army, then took both siblings for formal shooting training, marking the beginning of Singh’s journey in the sport.
“After our classes, Singh would travel 100 kilometres to reach the Guru Dronacharya Shooting Academy. Covering 200 kilometres every day, to and fro, was a huge task for both of us, but both of us were determined to pursue shooting,” he said.
Singh’s brother, who is also an athlete, said the family faced its share of challenges, with many questioning their decision to send her into shooting.
“People would ask us why we were sending her for this sport and say that there was no future in it and that she should not pursue it. But my father was determined. He always believed that she would one day bring medals home,” he said.
For both athletes, there was disappointment as neither qualified for their individual 10m air pistol events.
“However, the hunger was still there in both of them. It simply wasn’t their day. Disappointments are part and parcel of sport. They were disappointed, but not disheartened,” national coach for the 10m air pistol event Samaresh Jung told HT.
Asked about pairing the two shooters, the national coach told HT that both are hardworking and intrinsically motivated athletes.
“There was definitely some added pressure, but both handled it differently. Singh slept through the entire night before the match, while Kamaljeet slept for a few hours before waking up,” he said.
When asked about their next target, Jung said the duo would now focus on the upcoming World Championships, with the larger goal of securing their places at the Olympics.

Perth lost its major writers' festival. Can new events fill the gap?
In 2024, the long-running Perth writers' festival announced it would be taking a break in 2025, coming back with a refreshed event in early 2026.
That never happened.
It's now unclear when it will come back, leaving Perth as the only state capital in Australia without a major writers' festival.
Literature has been a part of the Perth Festival since it was founded by the University of Western Australia in 1953, and in the 1990s the writers' component became a standalone event within the festival program, with its own manager.
By 2018, it had expanded to become Perth Writers Week, before the COVID pandemic pared it back to a single weekend that by 2024 was run jointly by peak body Writing WA and the State Library of WA.
In September that same year, Perth Festival announced a new writers' festival would begin in 2026 to "highlight literary brilliance from nations around the Indian Ocean rim, while showcasing WA's extraordinary talent to the world".
There's been no sign of it so far.
A festival spokesman said the "intent remains, with a focus on creating the right conditions for it to emerge sustainably, ensuring any new major initiative is delivered at the right time and scale," but plans have yet to be confirmed.
So what happened?
The last Perth Festival Writers Weekend, held in February 2024, was, by some accounts, a tense event.
Organisers had invited singer/songwriter Deborah Conway to appear at the festival in three events, including an opening night performance, songwriting workshop and a panel discussion about her new book.
Five months earlier, the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, and Israel's military response, which saw thousands of civilian deaths in Gaza, had sparked waves of protest.
In an interview on Radio National Breakfast on December 15, 2023 about division in the arts community over the Israel-Gaza war, host Patricia Karvelas asked Conway about the impact of Israel's military action on innocent people, including children.
Conway responded: "Well, depends on what you call kids."
Her comments triggered a strong response, and in the weeks before the festival, the organisers found themselves confronting an unexpected situation.
An open letter calling on the organisers to rescind Conway's invitation began circulating, ultimately receiving around 500 signatures.
The festival did not accede to demands to cancel Conway's appearance. Instead, it bolstered security, set up designated protest zones outside the library, added three writers of Palestinian heritage to the program and released a statement, saying it sought to foster a safe and inclusive environment.
"We are committed to ensuring our artists and audiences have a safe space to share their voices. We oppose censorship and reject bigotry, harassment and discrimination of any kind. We condemn violence and the inciting of hate or violence. We utterly reject Islamophobia and anti-Semitism," the statement said.
Literature programming becomes 'daunting'
In the years since, division in the community over Israel's invasion of Gaza has engulfed the literary sector, causing the collapse of Adelaide Writers' Week and Bendigo Writers Festival, and a mass exodus of authors from Queensland University Press over the cancellation of a children's book contract, after the illustrator was accused of anti-Semitism.
Per Henningsgaard, the current chair of Writing WA, suspects it's a daunting prospect for anyone looking to restart Perth's writers festival.
"We've seen literary programming on a national level that has been the source of significant controversy," Dr Henningsgaard said.
"I think as an entity that is responsible for arts programming, you might look at some of those examples and be a bit scared, a bit hesitant about how to proceed.
"I don't know if that is playing a role in Perth Festival's thinking around this; I have no special insight into that, but it does strike me as significant that the Perth Festival continues to program theatre, dance, visual art and yet isn't programming in the writing space at the moment."
Sisonke Msimang, who curated the festival (then known as the Literature and Ideas program) from 2019 to 2022, said the event had been navigating sensitive issues for some time, such as the Perth Festival's long running partnerships with the mining sector, including oil and gas giant Chevron, which sponsored the festival's music program.
"Writers tend to be super political. They tend to ask a lot of questions,"
"A bunch of artists were like, 'absolutely not, it's greenwashing'. That's absolutely the tension. Especially in a place like Perth, where the biggest funders of the arts are the mining companies."
Msimang said that where festival directors may have been able to tiptoe around politics in the past, the current situation in Gaza made that impossible.
"We've been so complacent for so long about freedom of speech. I think festival directors have generally been pretty tame, and they haven't been put in the spotlight because there was nothing urgent that demanded it in the same way that Gaza has," she said.
Alternative literature programming grows
In the absence of the Perth Writers Festival, a number of smaller events, many of them run largely by volunteers and supported by local councils and libraries, have flourished.
These events include the Festival of Fiction in Joondalup, Totally Lit in Fremantle, the Mandurah Writers Festival and Kalamunda Writers Festival, each run over a weekend, as well the Big Day of Books run by the ABC in its studios in Perth and a one-day event at the State Library featuring authors shortlisted for the Premier's Book Awards.
The stand-out in community festivals has been the Margaret River Writers and Readers festival (MRRF), run over three days in May, which has had considerable success in recent years attracting international and interstate authors to the wine-growing town three hours' drive south of Perth.
The festival began in 2009 and has grown significantly since 2017, when Tourism WA committed to ongoing funding for Arts Margaret River, the community organisation that runs the event.
"That really took away a lot of the stress of chasing little pockets of money everywhere to try and do something," Michelle Wright, Arts Margaret River's general manager, said.
The festival also strategically schedules its program close to, but not on the same weekends, as the Sydney and Melbourne writers' festivals, which enables them to split the costs of flying international authors to Australia and offer those authors multiple events around the country to appear at.
So successful is the MRRF that it has started exporting one-off literary events back to Perth through a partnership with the state library.
"We've made all this major, huge effort to get someone to Western Australia, because we're not exactly close, so we really try and make it as good as we can and just share the love as much as we can, touching as many people with books," Wright said
She said the festival organisers were keenly aware of the importance of free speech and had taken steps to ensure festival programming decisions were independent and could not be subject to pressure from any of the sponsors.
"We are absolutely independent of any organisation that we work with. We've done this deliberately,"
"We've got a freedom of expression statement on our website that talks about the integrity of what we do."
For now, the biggest challenge might be balancing the festival's growing popularity with its status as a community-run event in a town of fewer than 10,000 people. The festival still has just two full-time staff, as well as a handful of part-timers for part of the year and several hundred volunteers.
"We've really just got to keep hitting those same strong points before we grow or change much more, because I think sometimes, if you get too big, you dilute your message and you dilute the care," Wright said.
New festivals welcome, but gap still felt
Another small festival which has done well, according to Per Henningsgaard, is the Festival of Fiction, which was first held in late 2024 at Edith Cowan University's Joondalup campus.
"One of the reasons why I mark it out as being one of the more significant [small] festivals is because the level of ambition has been much higher and the level of funding has been much more significant," he said.
But he said, "that gap of the big major writers' festival is definitely very acutely felt".
"Many of the smaller festivals that have sprung up are run on the backs of volunteers — we love our volunteers, I'm a volunteer — but there is a real toll to volunteer work in any organisation, and certainly in the art sector, where volunteer work is relied upon a lot.
"That is really where you need a larger festival that has a full-time staff, like the Perth Festival, to be able to take some of that load off the volunteers."
The cancellation of the writers' festival has also meant a loss for audiences of a connection to stories that are easy to miss amid big name international releases, Henningsgaard said
"Literary programming, when it's done properly from the state, from your home ground, really connects with the sensibilities of that local audience and gives them access to writers from the state or writers from Australia that they wouldn't see on social media," he said.
For Msimang, the loss of Perth's writers' festival is significant.
"It's very sad. It had a fantastic children's program. For me, stuff that I loved the most was actually the huge number of children's book writers who we would platform, because they have so few other opportunities," she said.
"I think the fallout is significant. I think it's bad for literature in WA, which is already so under-resourced."

In Amish country, nurses go door to door to stop deadly spread of measles
- Published
For the past few months, nurse Dale Weiser has been making unexpected home visits.
As the state battles the deadliest measles outbreak in recent history, the clinical supervisor drives 30 miles (48.3km), sometimes daily, to a rural corner of Pennsylvania where many Amish people live.
Walking into strangers' homes, Weiser says she tries her best to be respectful and non-intrusive as she vaccinates dozens of family members against the measles, sometimes around the kitchen table.
"A lot of people that I encounter, they don't have health insurance. They don't have a lot of interaction with the health system, and they just haven't seen the need to get these vaccines," said Weiser, who works for the Chester County Health Department.
"When you start talking and you answer their questions, and build that trust, a lot of times they will make a different decision."
The at-home vaccinations are part of the county and state health departments' strategy to encourage immunisations in the county, which includes an Amish community who abstain from many aspects of modern life, including regular contact with the western medical system.
The state health department told the BBC it has administered nearly 4,300 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at pop-up clinics near the epicentre of the outbreak since it began in late April.
But even as health officials see success in their vaccine programmes, the state has reported four deaths from measles complications, marking the most deadly outbreak the US has seen since 1992.
The infections have led to tensions between state and federal health officials, including vaccine-skeptic Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr.
Those politics are back of mind in the Amish community, where people are growing fearful of more deaths as they watch their friends and family fall sick with the disease, which for decades has been eliminated in the US.
"They're not a community that's as easy to reach - we can't just put up a social media post," Weiser said. "They are suffering at the moment, and we're trying to reach out and make connections."
Amish people began coming to the US in the early 1700s, with the first community settling in Lancaster, Pennsylvania. Known as the "Plain People" for the simple clothes they wear, the Amish are a devout Christian community that does not use many forms of technology, relying on horse and buggies instead of cars.
About 90,000 Amish people live in Pennsylvania, with estimates suggesting around only a quarter of Amish people in the Lancaster area have had the MMR vaccine.
There is no particular religious text advising against vaccines, but Amish people do not have regular contact with the western medical system, or have a way to easily travel to appointments, experts said.
"A lot of people who haven't gotten vaccinated, it's not because they have a strong stance against getting vaccinated for measles. It's just that they haven't gotten around to it. It's not convenient," said Braxton Mitchell, a genetic epidemiologist with University of Maryland School of Medicine who runs a research clinic studying the Amish in Lancaster.
Amish people are extremely social, he said, so when the virus hits one church group, it affects everyone who is unvaccinated.
"Measles is rampant in the Amish community," he said. "People are concerned about it."
He added the community has been especially concerned about the dangers to babies; so far two newborns have died of measles complications, as well as an 18-year-old and a 40-year-old woman, according to state officials.
Boots on the ground
Chester County public health officials did not wait long to launch a response to the growing measles outbreak in their community, which shares a border with Lancaster County, the epicentre of the outbreak.
Jeanne Franklin, the director of the health department, said officials have been using some of the strategies they employed during the Covid pandemic - knocking on doors in the community to let them know about the outbreak and offering private settings, like people's homes, for immunisations.
Since the outbreak started, the county has given 538 MMR vaccines, 340 of which they administered in private settings.
"People have called up and said, 'I can't get to your clinic, or, I don't want people to know I've changed my mind," Franklin said. "'If you can come to us, that's a lot easier.'"
The boots-on-the-ground approach has helped the health department dispel misinformation and build trust with the community, local health officials said.
In recent years, childhood vaccination rates have fallen across the country as false theories about the safety of the measles vaccine have proliferated on social media.
Those theories have found roots even in an insulated community with limited access to computers, Weiser said. She has heard people ask if there are heavy metals in the vaccine that could make them magnetic, or if the shot has a computer chip in it.
"You're clearly getting information from that hard-core group that is promoting that misinformation and disinformation," she said.
People in this "hard-core group", who are staunchly against vaccines, are unlikely to be swayed, experts and officials themselves said.
But now, local health officials said, many affected by the Pennsylvania outbreak are seeing their neighbours fall seriously ill and asking thoughtful questions. Weiser said many are parents who are unfamiliar with the shots and are scared to make the wrong choice for their children.
"There is the classically-defined anti-vaxer, versus people who are unaware or their culture feels differently," Franklin said. "The thinking and the willingness to discuss and possibly change your mind is different between those two bookends."
Kennedy casts doubt on deaths
The ongoing measles outbreak in Pennsylvania has once again sparked political debate in the US.
After the state health department announced the first two deaths - both in infants - Kennedy, the top health official, took to social media to dispute at least one of the deaths. The BBC has contacted the Department of Health and Human Services for comment.
Democratic Governor Josh Shapiro took aim at Kennedy, saying he told the top US health official that he was spreading misinformation that was worsening the outbreak.
Lancaster County coroner Stephen Diamantoni, a Republican, has said one of the two infants died of a ruptured spleen rather than measles itself. Measles can cause the spleen to enlarge, making it more likely to rupture. Several doctors have said the measles infection made the child vulnerable.
"I think the measles very much contributed to that child's demise," said William Moss, a pediatric infectious disease specialist at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
Public health experts said a number of actions taken by Kennedy and the Trump administration have sowed doubts about vaccine safety and worsened outbreaks.
Last month, Trump passed an executive order recommending the MMR shot be split into three separate shots, a move doctors say is costly and unnecessary for a vaccine that is already safe.
"What he's doing is casting doubt," said Dr Moss. "He basically said the vaccine could be dangerous in its current combined form."
The tensions are not helpful for experts working to combat misinformation in a so-far unrelenting outbreak, they said. They worry for the start of the school year, which will provide even more opportunities for the highly contagious virus to spread.
"I think we're in this for six to 12 months. It does feel like it's spreading and accelerating," Weiser said. "We're in community transmission now. We can't stop it easily."

Family business fights rising costs to keep nasi lemak at S$2, even with rent of S$10,000
His parents see their stall’s best-known dish as a way of giving back, leaving second-generation owner Adam Danish to make the numbers work. CNA’s Money Mind finds out what the family must do.
SINGAPORE: For a food stall whose rent is nearly S$10,000 (US$7,820) a month, but still sells nasi lemak at S$2, one might think its owners did calculate the cost of selling at that price.
Certainly, that was what Adam Danish thought until he joined the family business this year. “It was messy, because there weren’t any numbers being recorded,” said the 25-year-old second-generation owner of Indonesian Selera Corner in Yishun.
Without crunching the numbers properly, it was hard to tell if sales were covering costs — and if the family can keep the dish to S$2, a price they have maintained for more than a decade.
They run their stall in a privately owned coffee shop, where rents are commercially based and can be considerably higher than at government-run hawker centres. With utilities, the family pays S$13,000 a month, before manpower and ingredient costs.
Those cost pressures are climbing too. Adam said supplies and utilities were among the stall’s biggest cost increases over the past year, and the family has already had to raise the prices of many other dishes by 50 cents.
But not the S$2 nasi lemak, which his parents began selling after an elderly customer said she wanted something smaller than their standard S$5.50 portion.
They later found the smaller serving also suited other customers, such as workers caught up in the morning rush who need to grab a quick bite to eat.
The stall now sells about 200 packets a day. For Adam’s parents, this was never meant to be a big money-maker, but rather a little something for customers including large families, low-income households and the elderly.
“I believe what we get we have to return to the public,” said his mother, Sakdiah Abdul Latiff, 53.
But can Adam and his sister, Nurangellina Hassan, 18, who goes by Angel, keep the stall going without raising the price of a dish their parents want to keep affordable?
They must get the business’ finances in order, rein in costs and find new revenue sources, Money Mind finds out.
GETTING A GRIP ON FINANCES
When Adam joined the business, its accounts were not detailed enough to show how much each dish was making.
WATCH: S$2 nasi lemak, ~S$10,000 rent — How this Gen Z hawker finds new ways to earn (7:26)
His parents had been looking at “top line numbers” instead of the bottom line, he said, referring to the amount they received from sales. This did not give them a clear view of their profit margins.
So, he began breaking down the costs. A S$2 packet of nasi lemak with rice (30 cents), fish (40 cents), egg (10 cents), sambal (20 cents) and other sides (30 cents), such as cucumber and peanuts, is worth S$1.30 in ingredients — before the other operational costs are added.
But nasi lemak is only part of a wider menu that includes epok epok (fried pastries) and nasi padang (Indonesian-style rice meal). And the latter is the stall’s main revenue earner: On average, customers spend about S$7 per order.
Adam worked out the break-even point for the stall as a whole: It needs to sell 159 plates of food every day, at S$7.40 each. This is before the family draw their salaries.
Getting the accounts in order also gave him a clear idea of what the business could pay him, which, for the first four months, was nothing.
His first pay cheque, in June, was S$1,500. And his target is a salary of S$4,000 a month, which he has yet to reach.
The family has also been looking more closely at costs — without lowering the quality of its food.
That requires “extra homework”, said Reban. For example, the family now buys fish at Jurong Fishery Port to “get the best price”, rather than from a fishmonger at the market.
Adam is looking at other operating expenses too. They spend about S$600 to S$700 a week on cooking gas and plan on switching to electric cookers, which he estimates would cut that cost by about half.
They have reduced petrol costs by, for example, making fewer trips to Jurong Fishery Port and filling up at a cheaper petrol station, paying S$190 for a full tank instead of S$220 to S$230 at the station near the stall.
But there is a limit to how much the family can save. “We can’t always look at reducing costs because things aren’t going to get cheaper,” said Adam.
“I’LL TAKE EVERY WIN”
There is room to bring in more revenue, however. Over the years, the family expanded the menu to include dishes such as nasi ambeng and nasi jenganan — both are Javanese-style rice sets — and introduced mini buffets.
More recently, Adam and Angel have taken the business online via TikTok Live, using different bundle deals and promotions to draw customers. She handles the morning livestreams, and he takes over from her in the afternoon.
With customers placing their orders via WhatsApp for pickup or delivery, the stall can reach people beyond Yishun. After about two months, said Adam, the gross revenue from the livestreams was as much as S$12,000.
Still, sales are not guaranteed. There are livestreams where they receive no orders. “It’s a new stream of revenue, so I’ll take every win,” he said. “But I believe we can do much better in the future.”
Taking orders online created a manpower challenge, however. Adam found it difficult to host a livestream while simultaneously responding to WhatsApp enquiries.
So he began using an artificial intelligence chatbot to process kitchen orders. It costs him S$50 a month, compared with the estimated S$900 it would cost to hire someone specifically for the role.
Previously, he could spend an hour and a half sorting out orders before packing them, he recalled. With the chatbot, they can be done at the same time, freeing him up to upsell to livestream viewers.
For all these changes made to the family business, its S$2 nasi lemak remains untouched. “That’s the only thing that we can (give) back to the public,” Reban said. “That’s why I say (to) my wife, we stay with it.”
