Indian devotional film “Hanuman Ansh” has grossed more than $3.5 million outside its home territory since Hombale Films took it to international audiences, and the company behind the blockbuster “K.G.F” and “Kantara” franchises has now detailed how it engineered the run.
Written and directed by Vishal Chaturvedi and adapted from his book “Divine Detour: That Changed My Life,” the film follows Lakshman Das, a boy who leaves home after his mother dies, searching for the divine. Years of wandering and meditation later, he becomes the saint Neem Karoli Baba, known to devotees as Maharaj-ji. Shobhinaw Satyaa plays the title role opposite Chandan Anand, with Vihaan Shedge as the teenage Maharaj-ji and Anil Rastogi and Purnima Tiwari in supporting roles. Chaturvedi produced with Ragini Sona, Namrata G. Singh and Anupriya A. Nagar under his Swambhu Media Network banner.
“Our strategy involved taking ownership of all global territories and collaborating with the biggest local partners in each region to ensure the best possible release footprint. By leveraging the data and learnings from our previous releases like ‘Mahavatar Narsimha,’ we were able to tap into the right locations and cinema chains. This targeted approach has yielded spectacular numbers,” says Hombale Films producer Chaluve Gowda.
Popular on Variety
The Bengaluru banner partnered with Phars in the GCC and Prathyangara in North America, and the film opened internationally on Sept. 11. It marks a first for the company.
“‘Hanuman Ansh’ is the first film outside of our own productions that we have full fledgedly distributed internationally. We truly believed in this project, as it perfectly aligns with our vision of taking Indian stories global,” Gowda says.
North America leads the overseas tally, with $1.8 million from the U.S. and Canada, according to Hombale’s territory figures. Australia and New Zealand contributed $606,716 and the Gulf Cooperation Council region $577,870, with the U.K. adding $269,837. Singapore brought in $61,334 and Europe $41,171, while the rest of the world accounted for $483,006.
Hombale previously backed the animated “Mahavatar Narsimha,” which went on to do more than INR300 crore ($31.3 million) in business.
At home, the film has been a sleeper. Made for approximately INR2 crore ($209,000), “Hanuman Ansh” opened in India on Aug. 7 on some 250 screens through Cinépolis India. Word of mouth pushed it past 2,000 screens, and it has since grossed INR340.7 crore ($35.5 million) in seven weeks.
Chaturvedi has planned the film as the first part of a trilogy.
“We will always support the makers in bringing their ultimate vision to life. These are exactly the kinds of stories we want to champion as a production house, and we will continue to back creators who dare to tell such grand stories with all their heart,” Gowda says.

Srinagar, Sept 23: PDP president Mehbooba Mufti on Wednesday warned that India could “resemble a banana republic” if electoral rolls continue to be altered according to the wishes of the ruling BJP, while praising two Election Commissioners for raising objections to decisions taken by the poll panel.
Speaking about reports that two Election Commissioners had raised objections on several occasions to decisions and positions taken by the Election Commission, Mufti said their dissent was important for the health of Indian democracy.
“Today they are trying to subvert the very fundamental of Indian democracy, which is the electoral process, by, you know, fudging the electoral rolls, which the two Election Commissioners have pointed out,” she said.
She said India and Pakistan, which she described as “sibling states”, appeared to be competing with each other in ways that harmed their own people and institutions.
“I feel that our both the sibling states, India and Pakistan, they are trying to undo each other, competing with each other — who can damage their people the most, who can damage their country the most,” Mufti said.
Referring to India’s description of itself as the world’s largest democracy, she said the country’s electoral process was central to that democratic identity.
“Our country India, which is seen as the largest democracy in the world and which our Prime Minister proudly talks about, ‘mother of democracy’, whenever he is abroad,” she said.
“But if it continues to be like this, you know, where electoral rolls — deletion and addition — happens at BJP’s will, then there are dangers that at some point of time our country, which is the largest democracy in the world, is going to resemble a banana republic.”
Mufti also contrasted the situation in India with developments in Pakistan, particularly the detention of the sisters of former Pakistan Prime Minister Imran Khan.
“At the same time, look at Pakistan, which goes around the world as a peacemaker, as mediator of peace, is crushing dissent within its country with an iron hand,” she said.
“Look at — I mean, detaining Imran Khan’s sisters, who are unarmed, who are protesting very peacefully, them detaining just because they are trying to stand up for their brother. What does it speak?”
She said the detention of women protesters was at odds with Pakistan’s international image.
“You are going around the world as a peacemaker and, in your home, inside your house, women who have no weapons in their hands, you are detaining them,” she said.
Mufti said the “only silver lining” she could see was that India still had officials willing to question those in power.
“The only silver lining I can see is that in India we still have people like the two Election Commissioners who have the courage and integrity to question the people in power,” she said.
She contrasted this with Pakistan, saying there were no comparable voices within the establishment willing to question what she described as the “arbitrary detention” of Imran Khan’s sisters.
“It’s a very, very sorry state of affairs,” she said.
Mufti also referred to the deletion of voters from draft electoral rolls, saying the scale of the changes made the independence of Election Commission officials particularly important.
“If we do not have people like the two Election Commissioners, I don’t want to take their name at this point of time. I don’t know what trouble they are going to go through,” she said.
“They will be ED raids now, Income Tax raids now. What will happen to them?”
She concluded by reiterating her warning about the consequences of continued changes to electoral rolls.
“But if we continue like this, I mean, there will be a time when we are going to resemble a banana republic. There will be no democracy,” Mufti said.

AI prescription readers can help decode hard-to-read prescriptions, medicine names, doses, and doctor notes. Tools like August AI, Prescription Reader AI, Docus AI, AI Prescription Reader, and Google Lens/Gemini can simplify medical text, but results should always be verified with a doctor or pharmacist.
I am sure you have been in a situation where you walk out of the clinic, look down at the prescription slip the doctor handed to you, only to find that you cannot understand a single word written on it. It looks less like English and more like something scribbled by a 1-year-old. For decades, deciphering a doctor’s handwriting was a superpower reserved for experienced pharmacists. But that is no longer the case. Thanks to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI) and Optical Character Recognition (OCR), the power now rests in your pockets. Here are five AI tools that you can use to your advantage to break down medical jargon and medicine names easily without needing to revisit the doctor.
Table of Contents
Best AI Prescription Readers
August AI Prescription Reader
If you are looking for something that is more than just a simple text translator for your prescriptions, then August AI is the digital health companion that you need to use. Instead of just scanning the document and showing you the raw text, August behaves like a virtual health assistant that you can actually converse with regarding the document that you have uploaded. It has a fully chat-like interface. You take a photo of your prescription (either handwritten or typed) and upload it to the chat. The AI engine then extracts the medication names, dosages, and instructions. But wait, there is more to it.
Instead of spitting raw text, it rewrites those instructions into plain, everyday language. You can then type back your questions to the virtual assistant, like “Can I take this tablet on an empty stomach?” etc., and get personalized answers. Additionally, August AI strips out medically complex jargon and also tells you what the drug will do to your body when taken. Since health data is highly sensitive, August AI uses advanced encryption to ensure medical records aren’t uploaded anywhere. The good thing is that you get this AI tool for free, and it is available for Android and iOS.
Prescription Reader AI: Meds
Another dedicated app that can help you understand what the doctor has written on your prescription is the Prescription Reader AI: Meds app, which is available on Android. This app is built by MS Productions and is arguably the most feature-packed app designed for this purpose. You open the app, point your camera at the prescription, the app takes a scan, and its smart medication recognition engine instantly detects the drug names and formatting. It converts your prescription into readable text, so that you can make informed decisions. Once the app detects a medicine, you don’t have to manually Google its uses, as the Prescription Reader AI app itself shows you the drug’s uses, precautions, and side effects.
Everything that you have searched for remains in your history, so that you can access it quickly. There is a pill reminder and alarm as well, so that you don’t miss your doses. Not only English; it supports multiple languages, supports light and dark modes, and you can also share or save the readable prescription in PDF format. The Prescription Reader AI: Meds app is available for free, but only available on Android.
Download: Android
Docus AI
While you can still apply some workarounds as mentioned above, to read prescriptions, lab reports are still the worst. A blood test report gives you a wall of numbers, acronyms, and reference ranges that are guaranteed to induce anxiety. Some numbers might look too high, while some may look too low, making a normal person confused. Docus AI helps to solve this specific problem. It is built for heavy-duty medical document analysis. You need to upload a PDF, screenshot, or photo of your lab test (blood, urine, swab, etc.). Using Docus AI’s “AI Doctor,” the app will then compare the specific numbers against standard medical guidelines to figure out exactly what is going on inside your body.
Docus AI breaks down hundreds of biomarkers like cholesterol, cortisol, or thyroid levels and lets you understand if the numbers are high or low. It goes a step further and also explains what these numbers actually mean for your health. This way, you can make necessary decisions in your lifestyle. Based on your results, this AI tool may suggest dietary changes, lifestyle adjustments, or prompt you to consult a human specialist immediately. The free version lets you access features like an AI doctor and lab test interpretation, but you can unlock full potential by paying a fee.
AI Prescription Reader
The name says it all. The AI Prescription Reader is a web tool that is good for those who don’t want an AI companion and don’t want to install an app. The AI Prescription Reader is for people who want a fast, free, no-nonsense tool that gets the job done in five seconds. The good thing about this tool is that, apart from being web-based, it is dead simple. All you need to do is upload a document, or you can take a picture with your camera and hit the Analyze button. The AI runs its OCR magic and gives you a clean, formatted text box with the detected medicine, strength, and frequency.
There is a built-in prescription dictionary as well that you can go through to understand the medical terms that doctors have mentioned in the note. You can also export the deciphered text into a PDF and send it to anyone who needs it. The best part about this tool is that it doesn’t ask you to sign up or sign in using any account. You can use it straight away by visiting its website.
Google Lens/Gemini
This list would be incomplete if we do not appreciate the powers Google Lens and now Gemini have brought to our phones. Google Lens wasn’t specifically built for medical prescriptions, but its world-class text recognition engine makes it one of the powerful tools out there. Recently, I also needed some help, and with the help of Google Lens, I was able to decipher what was written in the prescription, get it checked by the doctor, and it was 100% correct. Though this may not be the case with everyone. It is available for Android and iOS, and you probably already have the Google app on your phone.
It pulls out the medical details about the medicine it has detected and shares them with you, such as what the drug looks like, common uses, and side effects. If an elderly member of your household is using it, they can tap the Listen feature so Google Lens reads the prescription aloud.

Yes, AI is advanced, and things are going in the right direction, but it is to be taken with a quick dose of reality. AI is smart, but it is not 100% accurate. A smudge on the paper or rushed handwriting can still cause the AI to incorrectly determine the wrong medicine. It is easy to confuse 10mg with 70mg for two similarly named drugs. It is always important that you get it verified by experienced medical personnel or the doctor themselves and get the right medicine.

United Forum of Bank Unions (UFBU) has said they would go ahead with the three-day nationwide strike beginning September 28, as a conciliation meeting before the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner on Tuesday remained inconclusive.
The conciliation meeting was held a day after the Finance Ministry appealed to bank employees to refrain from resorting to strikes and resolve their remaining demands through dialogue.
UFBU, which claims to represent 90 per cent of the banking workforce, is primarily seeking 5-day banking among other demands.
The strike, if it materialises, may impact banking services for five days as the weekend before September 28 is a holiday. It would coincide with the half-yearly closing of the banking sector.
“Responding to the appeal made by the Department of Financial Services (DFS), Indian Banks’ Association (IBA), Bank managements to defer the strike, we informed them that if there is any concrete and positive development towards implementation of our demand for introduction of 5 days banking, UFBU will consider the same,” UFBU said in a statement after the meeting with the Deputy Chief Labour Commissioner.
Otherwise, it said, UFBU will be constrained to go ahead with the proposed strike on September 28, 29 and 30.
Representatives of the DFS, Ministry of Finance, informed that the Government has been taking many initiatives for the welfare of the bank employees and the issue of 5-day Banking is also under consideration as they have to take into account the views of many other stakeholders before any decision is taken, it said.
Hence, it said, they requested the UFBU to defer the strike and continue the dialogue. Bank unions under UFBU had gone on nationwide strike on September 11 over their demand.
UFBU’s other demands include an update and improvement of pension, a uniform dearness allowance formula for all pensioners and an option for employees covered under the National Pension System (NPS) to switch to the old pension scheme (OPS).
Many public sector banks have started issuing advisories to their customers to use digital channels such as Mobile Banking, ATM, Internet Banking, BC Point and UPI for banking needs if the strike materialises.
The proposed 3-day strike period also coincides with the half-yearly closing of banks on September 30, a date of particular significance for reconciliation, provisioning and treasury and market operations.
A disruption of this nature, combined with the preceding weekend, would result in an effective five-day closure of banking services at a particularly sensitive point in the financial calendar - causing considerable inconvenience to customers, businesses, Government transactions and international banking operations.
Strikes cause disruption in banking services that inconvenience the public, impact the business of the banks, and ultimately harm the interests of bank employees and there is no fruitful outcome that is achieved through strikes, the finance ministry had said on Monday.
The government assured that it remains committed to the welfare and well-being of bank employees and to addressing their genuine concerns through constructive engagement.

Under Trump, NIH funding disruptions have evolved. Here's what the numbers show
The National Institutes of Health (NIH) wields a $47.5 billion budget. More than 80% of its funds go out the door as grants to answer pressing biomedical questions. Over the decades, those grants have helped decipher the human genome, eliminate the polio virus in the U.S. and turn AIDS from a death sentence to a survivable illness.
For new discoveries, everyday mysteries and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.
But experts say this kind of fundamental science is coming up against an administration that has delayed funding and rerouted billions of dollars in research, resulting in chaos for researchers and patients alike. Trump officials say the administration's practices serve to further the agency's goals.
"NIH is committed to responsible stewardship of taxpayer dollars and to advancing rigorous, high-impact science that improves health outcomes for the American people," Emily Hilliard, a spokesperson for the Department of Health and Human Services, which oversees the NIH, wrote in an August email.
More political oversight may be coming to how those funds get dispersed, according to recent reports. For now, court cases have restored funding, and Congress has preserved it in successive budget bills. But for the scientists who have had to scrap time-sensitive experiments or have seen their labs shuttered, those top-line numbers do not tell the full story.
Here are six graphics that highlight some of the less visible impacts of changes in research funding at the NIH.
Loading...
The Trump administration proposed cutting the NIH budget by 41%, or by about $19.6 billion, for 2026. It also asked to restructure 27 institutes to eight — eliminating four outright — in its request. Congress did neither; in fact, it maintained both the existing institutes and a budget that was on par with previous years' appropriations.
But experts say that though the total amount of funding suggests that little has changed, it masks a deeper disruption in the way that money moves.
The numbers behind the numbers
Once money is appropriated by Congress, it then has to be obligated by the NIH — committing the funds to specific projects via grants. Those grants are generally doled out at a fairly consistent rate throughout the year. But since President Trump's inauguration in 2025, that process has slowed to a crawl. In fiscal year 2025, the NIH ran roughly 44 days behind the average pace of 2021 to 2024; through early July 2026, it ran 42 days behind.
Loading...
Heather Pierce tracks NIH obligations for the Association of American Medical Colleges. She pointed out that as of July — three-quarters of the way through the fiscal year — the NIH had obligated roughly half its budget, with billions of dollars still left on the table.
Jennifer Troyer, a former director of extramural operations for the NIH's National Human Genome Research Institute, oversaw billions of dollars in grants awarded over her tenure until she resigned at the end of 2025. She ticked through some of the reasons for these delays.
Grants are peer-reviewed and prepared by the NIH staff to get funded, stepping through different "statuses" in the process, says Troyer — but now, they are undergoing another level of review that she calls a "black hole."
"There's a status called Status 19 I didn't, even as the director, I did not know existed until things started getting stuck," says Troyer, "because it was something that [grants] would blip through for, like, a few minutes." Awards she had signed would go out and come back stopped, she says, flagged by the Department of Health and Human Services, by the Office of Management and Budget or by the White House "as not acceptable."
At first, she says, it was the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) doing the flagging; "and then they went away, but the other systems had been put in place to do the same function."
She says the staff members who used to process awards have also gone. Her institute went from 11 grants-management specialists (plus two assistants) down to just three specialists. Efforts to cut staff and freeze new hires exacerbated staff shortages and, in turn, further delayed funding. "We did not have the person-time to put awards out the door," she says.
With funding, timing is everything
The delays also affected grants that had already been awarded. That's because many long-term NIH grants are often awarded for multiple years and paid out annually. They not only fund lab work but also pay for employees and medical care in clinical trials. Scientists rely on that continuity to keep projects stable — which is why, prior to this administration, those renewals traditionally came in a week early, to avoid any funding gaps.
Loading...
But in the past two years, grants have regularly been renewed 90 or more days late at a rate four to six times more often than in the previous four years (3.9% in the 2025 fiscal year and 2.7% in the 2026 fiscal year, compared with 0.7% in fiscal years 2021 through 2024).
Ryan Gutenkunst is a professor and the head of the Department of Molecular and Cellular Biology at the University of Arizona. When his grant renewal got delayed, he says, "I was starting to plan who I would cut if I needed to." Fortunately, he says, his university provided bridge funding and the grant was renewed two and a half months afterward.
Not everyone experiencing these delays has been so lucky. Gutenkunst explained that researchers can sometimes get bridge funding from their institutions to keep research projects afloat, because those funds can be paid back when the grant finally renews. But that bridge funding has a 90-day window. "It's really bad if it goes past 90 days," he says — adding that these extended delays have in some cases led to lost research, loss in employment and institutions' increased hesitancy to provide bridge funding.
Loading...
The delays could be measured in roughly a third of U.S. congressional districts, and they cut across party lines: Renewals in Democratic districts went from arriving 3.4 days early to 8.4 days late; in Republican districts, they went from 3.8 days early to 8.0 days late. These widespread delays have been systemic, affecting U.S. biomedical research broadly regardless of location.
Funding winners and losers
Some disruptions — grant terminations and changes in the types of research being funded — have resulted in more than a billion dollars less for racial- and ethnic-minority health research in 2025 than in 2024 — a 29% drop. Instead, projects studying artificial intelligence, among other categories, received more funding; machine learning and AI gained $468 million, and networking and information technology $368 million — two of the five largest increases. These shifts track the administration's stated priorities; Trump's executive orders have directed agencies to end "radical" and "wasteful" diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) research, and the August 2025 NIH unified funding strategy named AI research as a priority.
Loading...
Troyer says the change in research funding happened, in part, due to the top-down control, including a new system that flagged grants with disfavored words. According to a story published by Nature, the disfavored terms include "climate change," "DEI," "gender" and "vaccine hesitancy." About half the awards going out the door, she says, had to be "renegotiated" — with the institution, the lead researcher and the program director agreeing on new language in the title, the specific aims, the abstract and "anything that was going to appear in public."
Researchers describe the same experience from their end. Mariana Stern, a professor of preventive medicine and urology at the University of Southern California's Keck School of Medicine, had to reframe her grants, her research and even her research center, which was once called the CaRE2 Health Equity Center. "We have to call it the CaRE2 Health Center now," she says — omitting the word "equity."
But for some, the shift in funding meant a loss of funds and staff. Scarlett Lin Gomez, a professor of epidemiology and biostatistics at the University of California, San Francisco, leads the Greater Bay Area Cancer Registry, which receives funding from the National Cancer Institute. That funding was cut from $5.4 million in 2024 to $4.4 million in 2025 and then $3.7 million in 2026. "We received a cut that was completely unprecedented," Gomez says. "We've not had a cut of this magnitude at all — by far." Of her roughly 50 lab employees, she had to let go about seven last year and expects she'll have to let go five or six more this year.
Loading...
Those effects also showed up in significant delays to many training grants that fund students and trainees. Some worry these and other disruptions could discourage the next generation of scientists.
"More and more students are very hesitant to go into academia because of what's happening — because they see how stressful it is for us, their mentors," Stern says. "More and more are choosing industry, because it's easier, the pay is better and they don't have to struggle with funding the way we do." Gomez sees it as worsening a preexisting problem. "We're definitely seeing an academic brain drain, and this current environment is certainly going to further hasten that."
Trump officials did not comment directly on NPR's findings, instead pointing to the merits of the administration's current strategy.
"The Unified Funding Strategy ensures that the NIH embraces transparency, scientific rigor, and unbiased, evidence-driven research," Hilliard, the Health and Human Services spokeswoman, wrote in the August email. "Under the Strategy, NIH Institute and Center Directors make final funding decisions after considering multiple factors, consistent with longstanding federal grantmaking practices."
Not everyone is critical of the NIH changes. Ian Banks, who directs science and development at the Foundation for American Innovation and has advised the White House on science policy, argues that the NIH was overdue for disruption. "I think it was clear to just about every observer, left, right, and center, that the NIH of recent decades is a very unhealthy institution and has really desperately needed substantial reform." Banks isn't for cutting funding, as he says it's well established that funding science is merited. But he does say it's time to examine whether there is a better way to allocate the funds.
Over 44% of principal investigators' time is spent on non-research activities such as filling out paperwork, per a 2018 survey, and Banks thinks it could be over 50% today. He says this is a problem that contributes to the rising time and costs for new biomedical innovations — a troubling trend named Eroom's law.
"Is a lottery a better way of allocating specific funding than the current peer review process?" asks Banks, who says he is open to any ideas that might help improve science funding. "For at least funding reforms," he says, "we don't really know what works."
The same sentiment lands with scientists too. After all, most would like to do more science and have it be easier.
"That's a legitimate debate to have," Gutenkunst, of the University of Arizona, says. "But it should be an open debate. It shouldn't be a hidden list of words that is dictating things. It should be a real discussion between the administration, the scientists and the public."
That's part of why he and other experts say they're worried about a new rule proposed by the White House's Office of Management and Budget — one that, if implemented, would give political appointees the final say on federal grantmaking. Scientists say this will likely place further restrictions on research funding and increase executive control. Its effects, if passed, remain to be seen.
Note: The information in these graphs is a snapshot of the National Institutes of Health data that was pulled from NIH ExPORTER by NPR and by Grant Witness in July 2026. That data is frequently updated retroactively on the NIH's site and is subject to change.

- Players can get the Birthday Sprite by searching chests and using Cheat Codes in and around POIs where Fortnite Cakes can be found.
- The Birthday Sprite in Fortnite gives you a chance to spawn Cake Slices when opening chests, and at max level grants a Cake Slice for each elimination.
- You can level up the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite by extracting other Sprites, searching chests/containers, entering Cheat Codes, and playing matches in general.
The Birthday Sprite was added to celebrate the ninth anniversary of Fortnite, which marks a huge milestone in how far the Battle Royale mode has come. Unlike other Sprites that take the shape of or resemble some character/creature, the Birthday Sprite is shaped like a slice of cake. If you want to know how to get the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite and what it does, here’s all the information you need.
Fortnite Birthday Sprite Locations and Where to Find It
There are two primary ways to get the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite: Searching rare chests and entering Cheat Codes. Since it is of the “Rare” rarity, it is far more common than others, such as the Klombo Sprite in Fortnite. This is great news, as it makes your search all the easier. Let’s discuss the details in depth.
Searching Rare Chests and Entering Cheat Codes
The best way to get the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite is by searching rare chests. These can be found primarily in Temple Vaults in Fortnite, located under the Mega Maze Landmark and Stone Sanctum POI. These two locations are the best places to get the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite.
We also recommend searching for the Birthday Sprite in and around Fortnite Birthday Cake locations. Since it is connected to Fortnite’s ninth anniversary, the spawn rates in these areas could be higher. Lastly, you can try your luck entering Cheat Codes in POIs that contain the Fortnite Birthday Cake to get the Sprite.
Trading Sprites with Friends and Eliminating Players
Now that we’ve covered the primary methods, let’s talk about the secondary ways to get the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite. If you have some of the rarest Sprites in Fortnite, you can trade them with friends for the Birthday Sprite at secluded locations on the island. Just be sure to have a Fortnite Extraction Gizmo ready to extract the Sprite immediately.
Another method you can try to get the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite involves combat. If you’re adept with weapons and know your way around the Fortnite loot pool, you can try eliminating players to get the Birthday Sprite. If you spot a player who has one, engage them and win the fight to claim it for yourself.
Best Search Locations for Birthday Sprite in Fortnite
As previously mentioned, searching in and around Birthday Cake locations in Fortnite is a good place to start to find the Birthday Sprite. To make your search easier, we have attached a handy map of locations we recommend searching. You may even come across some Fortnite Birthday Presents and open them to get high-tier loot. That said, here is the map.
Aside from the aforementioned marked locations, we recommend searching around the Chopped Shop POI. We’ve had great success finding other Sprites in that location; the Birthday should follow suit. Chopped Shop is also one of the locations marked on our guide for the best loot path to farm Sprites in Fortnite Chapter 7 Season 4.
Fortnite Birthday Sprite Powers Explained
Although the Birthday Sprite is just an animated slice of cake, it has a very cool ability that you should take advantage of. The Birthday Sprite in Fortnite gives you the chance to get Cake Slices when opening chests, which increase as it levels up. At maximum level, each elimination also spawns Cake Slices.
To level up the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite, you need to do tasks such as searching chests, entering Cheat Codes, and extracting other Sprites. However, if you’re using the Birthday Bounty Hunter Sprite in Fortnite, you can only level it up by eliminating other players.
Here is how the Birthday Sprite’s power increases as it levels up in Fortnite.
| Birthday Sprite Level | Chance to Spawn Cake Slice from Chests | 
|---|---|
| Level 1 | 50% | 
| Level 2 | 60% | 
| Level 3 | 70% | 
| Level 4 | 80% | 
| Level 5 | 100% | 
Looking at the Birthday Sprite’s ability and stats, it almost functions like Loot Hacks in Fortnite. Once you get it to maximum level, you won’t have to worry about healing items in the late-game, as each Birthday Cake Slice restores 20 health/shields.
All Birthday Sprite Variants in Fortnite
There are a total of five Birthday Sprite variants that you can find as of Fortnite update 42.20. This also includes the base version, which is the most common. Here’s a full list of all Birthday Sprites currently in Fortnite:
- Birthday Sprite: Lets you get Birthday Cake Slices from chests and, at maximum level, grants you a Cake Slice when you eliminate an opponent.
- Cheat Master Birthday Sprite: Base power + all inputs are correct when entering Cheat Codes found in the world.
- Gold Birthday Sprite: Base power + gain 3x bonus XP from eliminations.
- Loot Hacker Birthday Sprite: Base power + increased chances of spawning items from your Loot Hacks.
- Bounty Hunter Birthday Sprite: Base power + chance to find Sprites when eliminating opponents. Only gains Sprite XP from eliminations, unless the Sprite has special XP rules.
We could see another ‘spooky’ variant for the Birthday Sprite added during Fortnitemares 2026. There are strong rumors, but nothing concrete at the moment. Either way, Epic Games has plans to release more new Sprites in Fortnite, giving you enough to keep busy until Override ends.
How Rare Is the Birthday Sprite in Fortnite?
The Birthday Sprite is of “Rare” rarity, which means it has a pretty high spawn rate. We suspect it to be around 4% or higher for the base variant. Gold and Fortnite Cheat Master Sprite variants of the Birthday Sprite are going to be harder to find.
Find Birthday Sprites More Commonly on Fortnite Birthday Power Hour (September 26)
On a side note, with Power Hour (September 26, 2026) celebrating Fortnite’s ninth birthday, expect to find the Birthday Sprite more easily. After all, it has been created with the sole intent to celebrate this occasion. We highly recommend that you attend the upcoming Fortnite Sprite event without fail.
With there being a total of five variants to collect, you could find all of them over the weekend and get closer to completing your collection. Furthermore, if you manage to master 28 Sprite, you also get the Pixel Polli skin in Fortnite for free.
Let us know in the comments below if you have managed to get a Birthday Sprite in Fortnite and where you found it on the Chapter 7 Season 4 map.

You can get the Birthday Sprite by entering Cheat Codes and searching Rare Chests in and around Birthday Cake locations in Fortnite. Trading Sprites with friends and eliminating opponents that have the Birthday Sprite are also good options.
What does the Birthday Sprite do in Fortnite?
Lets you get Birthday Cake Slices from chests and, at maximum level, grants you a Cake Slice when you eliminate an opponent.

Keychron Thunderbolt 5 Dock review: Unusually sensible
A company that’s best known for keyboards makes a strong entry into the high-end dock world.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Keychron is best known for its mechanical keyboards that democratized higher-end customization and functionality. The company expanded that philosophy into mice with similar success. The next desk peripheral in the company's crosshairs is the PC/laptop dock. As more PCs and laptops adopt Thunderbolt 5 at the expense of broader connectivity, the appeal of a single-cable do-it-all expansion is becoming stronger.
Keychron's Thunderbolt 5 Dock is much more capable than its utilitarian name suggests. Yes, it's a dock and it delivers comprehensive connectivity, with a focus on Intel's powerful alternative to the dominant USB 3 interface. That means 80Gbps data transfers (with 120Gbps boost mode), dual 8K monitor support and 140W upstream power delivery — enough to keep most laptops running. The question is, can Keychron's success in the keyboard world translate seamlessly to other areas of productivity?
Power and ports
The Thunderbolt 5 Dock has a total of 14 different connections. On the front of the device, there are three USB 3.2 (Gen 2) ports that support 10Gbps data transfer. Two are type A and one type C. This is an okay start; at least two type C ports would have been my personal preference. There are two SD card slots, one full-size, the other MicroSD, and I'm grateful they're on the front — fumbling around for a card slot hidden on the rear or side is a frustration no one deserves.
To demonstrate this is more than a simple powered USB hub, there's also a 3.5mm jack. There's actually an audio interface inside the dock. It's not as powerful as the one built-in to my Mac or PC, but it does support inline mics for calls and other basic audio input (such as gaming), so you don't even have to plug headphones into your computer directly.
Flip the dock around and you'll find three Thunderbolt 5 ports, one upstream to your PC and two downstream for things like high-speed SSDs. There are two more USB 3.2 (Gen 2) Type A ports plus a 2.5Gb Ethernet port and a Kensington security lock. Let's not forget the two HDMI output ports for those looking for a multi-display setup.
In-use
Thunderbolt Dock 5 can support up to four displays simultaneously over both HDMI and Thunderbolt. The reality is a little more complicated. MacOS doesn't natively support multiple displays over HDMI hubs or splitters. If you plug two monitors into the HDMI ports on this hub and connect it to a Mac, your screen will be mirrored on both. You can, however, use one HDMI input, another from the Mac itself and any of the Thunderbolt ports for a true multi-display setup. Windows is a little more flexible here, with dual-HDMI support being more common.
This flexibility does introduce some other considerations. The HDMI outputs are 4K/60Hz max whatever your configuration, so if 8K or higher refresh rates are important to you, you'll be reaching for a Thunderbolt port regardless.
I do a lot of work with video, so I need reliable, fast ports for slinging gigabytes of media between cameras, SD cards and various hard drives (including the one in my Mac or Windows laptop). This dock recognized any storage I plugged into it every single time. I wish that wasn't something I had to be excited about, but it is. Transferring data always gave me maximum (or ballpark max) data speeds even when moving files from multiple sources at the same time. There's another small, but important benefit, too: weight. The Thunderbolt 5 Dock is steady enough that I can "click" a microSD card into it with one finger and the dock doesn't slide around on the desk. That's almost worth the $350 alone. My old, far cheaper, Ugreen dock, even with a Mac mini on top, couldn't promise not to move — or even register my SD card if I inserted it before waking up the computer.
The second, and more revealing, way I tested this dock is with my laptop. I have a 13-inch Asus foldable that is powerful enough to get most "desktop" tasks done, but when I'm in the office it's frustrating to work on a smaller screen and with limited inputs and outputs. This is where this dock becomes more transformative. It's not simply adding a few ports, it converts my laptop into a podcast and video studio, connected to my Rodecaster and mirrorless camera/capture card with multiple displays with full power supply — all over one cable.
The design of the dock itself is definitely "Apple-inspired" with brushed aluminum. It looks the part next to a Mac and doesn't feel out of place when I use it with my Windows laptop, either. One thing I really appreciate is that there are rubber feet on two sides so you can set it in both upright/tower or flat orientations. Rival docks make that decision for you and it's frustrating if you have a space limitation or visual/ergonomic preference. The design makes clever use of CNC-cut panels on the sides that look stylish and double as effective heatsinks. The benefit is the dock doesn't need a fan, so it runs silent.
The competition
Much of what I've talked about here can be done by many rival docks; the differences come down to connectivity, reliability and price. Popular competitors include CalDigit's TS5 dock ($399) and Razer's Thunderbolt 5 Dock Chroma ($379). The latter adds an SSD bay and (of course) RGB lighting with more type C ports. Both CalDigit and Razer ditch the HDMI connectivity though.
Anker's Prime TB5 ($399) dock closely matches Keychron's connectivity, just with a DisplayPort instead of a second HDMI and two USB-C ports on the front, but with the SD card slots on the side. Most docks in this price range are a variation on this theme. The dual HDMI ports are arguably Keychron's standout feature. You can, of course, dedicate a Thunderbolt port for a display, but then you have one less Thunderbolt port for other items.
Wrap-up
As Thunderbolt 5 docks mature as a category, your specific needs, followed by budget, will increasingly be the deciding factors. Keychron's first attempt is unusually sensible. There's no one thing that explodes the competition, but a series of smart choices and hardware experience combine into something practical and reasonably priced. An NVMe SSD slot might have elevated this dock above its rivals, but also likely the price. You might wish for 10Gb ethernet or, like me, one more USB type C port on the front, or maybe even a DisplayPort. But it's hard to argue with Keychron's crowd-pleasing offering, especially for creatives and those with a need for complex display configurations.
My personal checklist has a focus on media and creation, for which the dual HDMI ports and reliable media I/O really help. Keychron's experience with hardware is clear in the build and design, and even though the price might not seriously undercut its rivals, this dock is pitched just right to give it broad appeal to a variety of demanding users.

2026 has been the year of Robert Pattinson.
This year alone, he's appeared in "The Drama," "The Odyssey," "Primetime," and will appear in the highly anticipated "Dune: Part Three," which is scheduled for a December release.
He's come a long way since the 2000s, when he appeared in two of the biggest franchises of this century: first as the minor (but pivotal) Cedric Diggory in "Harry Potter," and then as millennials' biggest heartthrob, Edward Cullen, in "Twilight."
To celebrate the release of his latest film, "Primetime," on Friday, here's a look at how critics have rated Pattinson's movies throughout his career, from his film debut in 2005 to now.
31. "Queen of the Desert" (2017)
Based on a true story, "Queen of the Desert" follows Gertrude Bell (Nicole Kidman) as she leaves life in England behind and travels across the Middle East, forming a love affair with a British officer (James Franco) along the way. Pattinson appears as the famous archaeologist T.E. Lawrence, who was the subject of "Lawrence of Arabia."
"An emotionally empty, thematically ill-defined, and listless affair. It is never able to communicate the complexity of the woman at its center," wrote Angelica Jade Bastién for RogerEbert.com.
30 (tie). "Little Ashes" (2009)
In the period drama "Little Ashes," renowned artist Salvador Dalí (Pattinson) and poet Frederic García Lorca fall in love during the pre-Spanish Civil War era.
"The drawcard of Robert 'Twilight' Pattinson as Dalí is a mixed blessing for the filmmakers, given how ill-at-ease he is in the role. Javier Beltran, as Garcia Lorca, cast as the heroic center of the film, cuts a more confident figure," wrote Philippa Hawker for The Age.
30 (tie). "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1" (2011)
The first part of a two-part adaptation of "Breaking Dawn," the final novel in Stephenie Meyer's series, "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 1," focuses on Bella Swan (Kristen Stewart) and Edward (Pattinson) as they go from wedded bliss to chaos.
"The last twenty minutes of 'Breaking Dawn' are so harrowing that it's possible to forget that most of the acting is soap-operatic (the guy who plays Carlisle is aging to look like Liberace) and the dialogue from hunger," wrote David Edelstein for New York Magazine.
29. "Remember Me" (2010)
In the coming-of-age drama "Remember Me," Pattinson plays Tyler Hawkins, a man who struggles to connect with his father (Pierce Brosnan) following a tragic loss. He finds solace in Ally (Emilie de Ravin), but outward influences threaten the future of their relationship.
This movie's lasting legacy, though, is its twist ending — even calling it a twist feels kind of icky.
"Be warned, if you're vulnerable to outrageous, cringe-inducing implausibilities — not least the ludicrous stand-up row between Tyler and his father in the latter's Twin Towers boardroom — you'd best give this one a miss," Time Out's Wally Hammond wrote.
28. "Bel Ami" (2012)
"Bel Ami" is a drama about Georges Duroy (Pattinson), a clever traveler who rises through the ranks of Parisian society in the 1890s. As he goes from extreme poverty to settings of extravagant wealth, Duroy becomes entrenched in a world of lies and seduction.
"The women are all elegant and intelligent, they know the ways of the world, and they know Georges' history. Why do they find him attractive? We don't, and that failure is the downfall of the film," wrote Roger Ebert.
27. "The Twilight Saga: New Moon" (2009)
In the second installment of the popular "Twilight" book series, "The Twilight Saga: New Moon" begins with Edward (Pattinson) leaving Bella (Stewart) behind in an effort to protect her.
Heartbroken, Bella grows closer to her friend Jacob (Taylor Lautner) only to discover that vampires aren't the only supernatural creatures in their small town of Forks.
"If you buy into the central romance, you'll laugh, you'll cry, you'll swoon. Otherwise, the lingering glances, lip-chewing, and regular de-shirting may cause uncontrollable giggles," wrote Helen O'Hara for Empire Magazine.
26. "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse" (2010)
Upon Edward's return to Forks in "The Twilight Saga: Eclipse," Bella (Stewart) struggles to grapple with her love for him and her burgeoning attraction to Jacob (Lautner). Amid the love triangle that develops, Edward and Jacob attempt to put their feelings aside to protect Bella from a group of malevolent vampires.
"I wanted 'terrible/AWESOME' and all we got was painfully terrible. I am upset," wrote Autostraddle's Alex Vega.
25. "Twilight" (2008)
It's the one that started it all. In the first "Twilight" film, high schooler Bella Swan (Stewart) transfers to a new school in rainy Forks, Washington, and is immediately drawn to otherworldly student Edward Cullen (Pattinson). As Bella becomes more certain that Edward is a vampire, her love for him grows as well.
The New York Times' Manohla Dargis called it "a deeply sincere, outright goofy vampire romance for the hot-not-to-trot abstinence set."
24. "The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2" (2012)
In the final installment of the "Twilight" franchise, Bella (Stewart) acclimates to her new life as a vampire as she and Edward (Cullen) come together to protect their supernaturally gifted daughter, Renesmee (Mackenzie Foy), whose very existence draws the unwelcome attention of the Volturi, who are looking for any excuse to take the Cullens down.
"You're going to hear a lot about 'Breaking Dawn Part 2' being the best of the 'Twilight' movies. That's like saying a simple head cold is preferable to swine flu," wrote Peter Travers for Rolling Stone.
23. "Waiting for the Barbarians" (2020)
Based on the novel of the same name, "Waiting for the Barbarians" is about Colonel Joll (Johnny Depp), a magistrate who starts to question his loyalty to his empire as he oversees a colonial town. Pattinson portrays Officer Mandel, a sadistic warrant officer who works for Colonel Joll.
"Intermittently engrossing and always interesting, but less potent than it could have been," wrote the AP's Jocelyn Noveck.
22. "Water for Elephants" (2011)
Set in the 1930s, the drama "Water for Elephants," based on the novel of the same name, follows the romance between veterinary student Jacob (Pattinson) and star circus performer Marlena (Reese Witherspoon). Together, the two share an affection for an elephant in their traveling circus that falls under their protection.
"Beauty comes in all shapes and sizes, and 'Water for Elephants' finds immense pleasure in juxtaposing extreme dimensionality with budding emotion," wrote Glenn Heath Jr. for Slant Magazine.
21. "Maps to the Stars" (2014)
David Cronenberg's dark comedy "Maps to the Stars" tracks the unwieldy fortune of the Weiss family, headed by TV therapist Stafford Weiss (John Cusack). Pattinson appears as Jerome Fontana, a limo driver who forms a friendship with Agatha Weiss (Mia Wasikowska), Stafford's estranged daughter.
"So here's a mean, nasty little piece of work — and I have a feeling director David Cronenberg would take that as the compliment it's intended to be," wrote Flavorwire's Jason Bailey.
20. "Life" (2015)
The drama "Life" shows a snapshot look at James Dean (Dane DeHaan) through the eyes of Dennis Stock (Pattinson), the Life Magazine photographer assigned to profile him. The two men build a budding friendship as James opens up to Dennis about life in Hollywood.
"Both Pattinson and DeHaan could have used more to do, but both actors put in performances that elevate the proceedings," wrote Liz Braun for The Toronto Sun.
19. "The Devil All the Time" (2020)
In a corrupt town filled with death and darkness, one man (Tom Holland) attempts to protect himself and his family from evil, which includes a not-so-pious preacher (Pattinson).
"Don't come for sociology. Come for top actors enjoying a weekend off the leash," wrote The Irish Times' Donald Clarke.
16 (tie). "Cosmopolis" (2012)
Before "Maps to the Stars," Pattinson had collaborated with director David Cronenberg in the 2012 sci-fi drama "Cosmopolis."
Set in New York City in the near future, the film features Pattinson as Eric Packer, a privileged Wall Street financier who spends most of his life in his high-tech limousine, whose life is plunged into imminent danger when he sets foot in the real world.
"'Cosmopolis' is exhilarating in two ways. The first is that it offers up the soothing image of a billionaire capitalist brought to heel by riots. The second is that Pattinson's work as Packer, thorough enough that it looks like natural blankness, has since turned out to be one of the earliest indications of his talent," wrote Philippa Snow for The New Statesman.
16 (tie). "Damsel" (2018)
"Damsel" is a modern Western with a comedic twist, featuring Pattinson as pioneer Samuel Alabaster, a man traveling across the American Frontier to reunite with his true love, Penelope (Mia Wasikowska).
With Parson (David Zellner) by his side, Samuel's journey through the Wild West grows complicated in ways they never could have predicted.
Pajiba's Roxana Hadadi wrote, "The Zellner Brothers, Mia Wasikowska, and Robert Pattinson team up for the delightfully weird, beautifully shot, and feminist as hell 'Damsel.'"
16 (tie). "The Rover" (2014)
Set 10 years after a devastating global collapse, "Rover" is a science-fiction thriller about a loner named Eric (Guy Pearce) who does his best to survive in a lawless society. After his car is stolen by thieves, Eric forces Rey (Pattinson) into helping him retrieve his prized possession at any cost.
"Brutal as it is, 'The Rover' evolves into a strange kind of buddy movie. Squint and you might be watching a nihilistic 'Rain Man,'" wrote Danny Leigh for The Financial Times.
15. "Tenet" (2020)
In this spy film, an intelligence agent (John David Washington) goes on an epic, time-bending journey to save the world. Pattinson plays Neil, a sidekick of sorts.
"Pattinson is the best thing about the movie, bringing much-needed levity and humor. When he is not on screen, the movie doesn't feel half as fun or entertaining," wrote Jacob Sarkisian for Business Insider.
14. "The King" (2019)
The historical drama "The King" tracks the accession of King Henry V of England (Timothée Chalamet) as he inherits the throne from his deceased father. Pattinson appears in the film as the Dauphin of France, an adversary who challenges the young king's authority.
"Almost everything about 'The King' works brilliantly, from the casting (not least Robert Pattinson as a deliciously detestable Dauphin) to the generally cracking script by [David] Michôd and [Joel] Edgerton," wrote Brad Newsome for The Sydney Morning Herald.
13. "Die My Love" (2025)
Pattinson costars with Jennifer Lawrence as a married couple and new parents, Jackson and Grace, who have just moved to Montana. When Grace begins experiencing severe postpartum depression, her grasp on reality slips.
"No one burns as brightly as Lawrence. Left to her own devices by a pandering script, she alone draws the line where loneliness ends and freedom begins, keeping 'Die My Love' from plunging completely into its self-made inferno," wrote Salon's Coleman Spilde.
12. "The Drama" (2026)
In "The Drama," Pattinson plays Charlie, a museum curator who isn't sure whether he can marry his fiancée, Emma (Zendaya), after she reveals a secret from her past. The less we say about it, the better.
The Atlantic's David Sims wrote, "In 'The Drama,' Pattinson embodies Charlie as the model of tame, harmless Brit charm, and the minute the actor has built his character up, he clearly takes perverse delight in unraveling him."
11. "Mickey 17" (2025)
Director Bong Joon Ho's follow-up to best picture winner "Parasite" was "Mickey 17," a satire of capitalism starring Pattinson as Mickey, a grunt worker who volunteers to sign up as an "Expendable." Mickey is sent on dangerous jobs that will almost certainly kill him, but it's fine, because he just keeps getting cloned.
"I feel like it has the makings of a cult classic — a dystopian space comedy/adventure with shades of Terry Gilliam," wrote Baltimore Magazine's Max Weiss.
10. "High Life" (2019)
Set in the distant future, the arthouse film "High Life" follows a crew of death-row inmates as their space program unravels at the edge of the galaxy. Pattinson holds the lead role of Monte, a former prisoner who is soon left on the ship with only his young daughter at his side.
Sight & Sound's Erika Balsom wrote, "'High Life' asks us to consider the passion — and the terror — of crossing the event horizon to cast off the laws that bind us and live another day."
8 (tie). "The Lost City of Z" (2017)
Based on a true story, "The Lost City of Z" delves into the life of British explorer Percy Fawcett (Charlie Hunnam) and his journey into the depths of the Amazon. Pattinson appears as military officer Henry Costin, who assists in Percy's quest to procure evidence of an undiscovered civilization.
Karen Han of The Daily Beast called it "an exploration epic that will leave you breathless."
8 (tie). "The Batman" (2022)
Pattinson became the latest actor to wear the cape and cowl to play Bruce Wayne/Batman in "The Batman," directed by Matt Reeves. In Reeves' version of the story, Bruce is a true creature of the night, and he dedicates himself to stopping the Riddler (Paul Dano), a dangerous and brilliant serial killer.
"Robert Pattinson shuts all his haters up with a vulnerable and terrifying performance in Matt Reeves's 'The Batman,'" wrote Chicago Reader's Noëlle D. Lilley.
7. "Primetime" (2026)
Pattinson's second-to-last film of 2026 is "Primetime," in which he plays the host and creator of "To Catch a Predator," Chris Hansen. The trailer became a huge meme engine, so we can expect the movie to be too.
"On a technical and performance level, you'd be hard-pressed to find a film this year as adept at taking the internal psychopathy of its fraught subject and externalizing it as 'Primetime' does," wrote The Seattle Times' Chase Hutchinson.
6. "Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" (2005)
"Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire" is the fourth installment in the popular "Harry Potter" fantasy series, focusing on Harry's fourth year at Hogwarts School of Witchcraft and Wizardry.
Forced to contend in a magical tournament, Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) builds an unexpected friendship with Hufflepuff student and fellow champion Cedric Diggory (Pattinson).
"For those like me who are outside but sympathetic to the faith, it looks like another handsomely made, good-natured and high-spirited family movie, which is dramatically stymied through being locked within school grounds," wrote The Guardian's Peter Bradshaw.
4 (tie). "The Childhood of a Leader" (2016)
Set in Europe during World War I, "The Childhood of a Leader" is a historical drama centered on the son of an American diplomat, navigating life during wartime.
The dark coming-of-age story allows viewers to see France through Charles' eyes as he witnesses the signing of the Treaty of Versailles and the first glimpses of fascism in Europe.
Pattinson plays an investigative journalist in the film, with a second role as an older version of the protagonist later on.
Rex Reed of The Observer wrote, "'The Childhood of a Leader' is a dark and creepy work, flawed but ambitious and well worth seeing."
4 (tie). "The Lighthouse" (2019)
Horror and drama in equal measure, "The Lighthouse" tells the story of two lighthouse keepers: Thomas Wake (Willem Dafoe) and Ephraim Winslow (Pattinson). The two are driven to madness and delusion as they man their lighthouse post on a remote New England island in the 1890s.
"What is the opposite of a crowd-pleaser? A crowd-splitter, maybe? Whatever you call it, 'The Lighthouse' is one," wrote Chris Hewitt for The Minnesota Star Tribune.
3. "Good Time" (2017)
In the crime thriller "Good Time," Constantine Nikas (Pattinson) races through the nasty underbelly of New York City's criminal world in an effort to free his younger brother from jail. As Constantine desperately accrues more money to save his brother, he finds himself putting his own life on the line.
Peter Howell wrote for the Toronto Star, "Pattinson makes Connie one of the best roles of his career by turning a two-bit hood into a loyal family guy driven to help his brother. John Steinbeck would recognize these characters. So would Martin Scorsese, who is thanked in the credits."
2. "The Odyssey" (2026)
One of the biggest movies of 2026 was "The Odyssey," based on Homer's epic poem. Pattinson plays one of the film's biggest antagonists, Antinous, a suitor posted up at Ithaca, just waiting for Penelope (Anne Hathaway) to give up on her husband, Odysseus (Matt Damon), ever coming home.
Business Insider's Jason Guerrasio called Pattinson "perfect" in the role.
1. "The Boy and the Heron" (2023)
Pattinson voices the titular heron in the English dub of Hayao Miyazaki's latest (and perhaps final) film. And, as you might've guessed, he goes sicko mode voicing this creepy little bird in a vocal performance that haunts three years later.
"If this really is Miyazaki's final word, then it's a conclusion worthy of his legacy. At the same time, his imagination remains so vast, it feels like he could keep creating forever," wrote The Independent's Clarisse Loughrey.
Note: All scores were current on the date of publication and are subject to change. Films without critical ratings were not included. Films in which Pattinson had an uncredited role were also not included.

Former Liverpool, Newcastle United and England striker Andy Carroll has revealed in his autobiography that he was sexually assaulted by a man in 2021 and still struggles to deal with the ordeal.
Carroll’s autobiography, called ‘Owning It’, was published on Thursday and in it the 37-year-old Englishman details the attack at his home in Newcastle, which led to the perpetrator reportedly being jailed for three years.
“Something happened to me a few years ago that was so traumatic I only decided to include it in this book at the very last minute,” he wrote in the book, extracts of which have been published in the British press.
“I was sexually assaulted, there I said it. Scary to even think about and only a few people knew about it before now.”
Carroll was also tormented by the prospect of talking about what happened before finally deciding to include it in the book, after speaking at length with his girlfriend.
“Me and Lou spent a lot of time discussing whether to mention it in this book or not,” he said. “Scary to talk about but it’s made (me) the person I am today as much as any of the good stuff. And if me talking about it helps just one person then good, it will have been worth it.”
The mental anguish continued long after the attack, which happened after a friend of his former partner came to his home to watch a boxing match and was set to stay overnight.
Carroll details how he threw the man — who he said was a “celebrity mate” — out of the house and then “smacked him unconscious” when he tried to come back in. He then called the police.
“What happened to me affected every facet of my life. I’d think about it every day, making it difficult to focus on anything else, including football,” he said. “The trauma of what happened to me hasn’t gone away.”
Carroll cost Liverpool 35 million pounds ($46 million) when he joined from Newcastle in January 2011. Back then, he was the Premier League’s most expensive British transfer signing.
He also played for West Ham United in the Premier League, and scored twice for England, including one goal at the European Championship in 2012.
At the end of his professional career, Carroll played briefly in France with Amiens and Bordeaux before joining non-league Dagenham and Redbridge in England, scoring six goals last season.

The CEO of a Michigan credit union is no longer employed there, according to the organization, after she posted on social media what appeared to be an AI-generated image of her and her family wearing sweaters emblazoned with the Donald Trump-associated words “Lake America”.
In the statement recently announcing that Jane Smith would no longer be its CEO, Family First Credit Union also apologized “for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused”.
Smith had been the chief executive officer of the Family First Credit Union when she posed for a family photo at the Detroit airport en route to Halifax, Canada. She reportedly used ChatGPT to edit the family’s sweaters to say Lake America, which since late August has been the name that Trump ordered the US’s federal government agencies to use for Lake Ontario amid the president’s trade war with Canada.
Smith then shared the image on Facebook on 11 September – the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks in the US – along with the caption: “Like our sweatshirts? Not sure Canada will.”
The post ended with “Lol lol”. It went viral and then provoked backlash from people in Canada – where a portion of the lake is.
Those online users found it disrespectful, and the post has since been deleted according to Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) News.
Many in the comments highlighted that the post was particularly insensitive, given Halifax’s role in hosting thousands of stranded airplane passengers who were diverted there when US airspace closed on the day of the 9/11 attacks.
As the controversy intensified, Family First Credit Union – based in Saginaw, Michigan – said it was reviewing the situation. Smith, meanwhile, apologized, expressing regret, maintaining that the post was the result of poor judgment and saying that she understood why it would be offensive.
“We weren’t trying to make a political statement,” Smith told the Detroit television news station WJRT. “However, we were, you know, kind of poking fun” at the changing of the name of one of the Great Lakes.
“I understand if I was someone in Halifax and I thought a poor group of people walked in wearing those sweatshirts, it is highly offensive and I would understand why they would be so angry,” she continued in her remarks to WJRT. “I am not a person that would ever want to offend or hurt anybody.
“I do regret having any post that would make someone feel like we don’t value them as human beings.”
Despite her apology, the credit union made it clear that it had parted ways with Smith.
“Jane Smith is no longer employed by Family First Credit Union, effective immediately,” said a statement from the organization shared on social media.
After saying Smith’s interim successor would be Jason Acosta, the statement continued, “We sincerely apologize for the concern, disappointment and pain this situation has caused our members and community.
“We understand that members of our community may hold different perspectives about this decision. Our responsibility is to act in the best interest of the Credit Union, uphold the trust of our members and continue putting our community first.”
Family First Credit Union’s statement about Smith came after broader repudiation in Canada and beyond of Trump’s executive order changing Lake Ontario’s name to Lake America.
Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, explained in a post on social media that the body of water’s name comes from the language of the Indigenous Wendat people – and predates both the Canadian Confederation and the US’s declaration of independence from the UK.
“Canadians … know that naming reality means calling it Lake Ontario – then, now and always,” he wrote on X.
Several US governors in the US’s Great Lakes region also dismissed the name change. Michigan borders the Canadian province of Ontario along with four of the five Great Lakes.
The only one of the Great Lakes that Michigan does not border is Lake Ontario. New York is the only US state that Lake Ontario borders.
Trump’s order has no authority to rename Canada’s portion of the lake. It also has no power to compel Canada, international legal bodies, international mapmakers or the rest of the world to adopt a new name.

In July 2022, I fulfilled my lifelong dream of moving to Europe.
When my husband and I married in January that year, we didn't opt for the typical wedding registry. Instead, we sold, donated, or tossed almost everything we owned. Even our cars — which we sold two days before we left the US — had to go.
We headed to Germany, a country we'd never visited, with just a few suitcases and our two cats. As soon as we arrived, we noticed a lot of cultural differences.
Here are seven things that surprised us about life in Germany.
Most places don't have air conditioning.
After a tiring seven-hour flight from Boston to Frankfurt, a three-hour drive from the airport, and six flights of stairs to our apartment, we arrived in Düsseldorf and quickly learned air conditioning isn't really a thing in Germany.
The large tilt-and-turn windows in our place didn't have screens, only metal rolling shutters. This meant we couldn't open the windows fully for fear our cats would try to go outside.
Instead, we cranked the metal shutters down early in the morning to keep hot air out and rolled them up at night to let in cool air.
We also stayed hydrated, added ice cubes to the cats' water bowls, tried not to use the oven, took cool showers, and ordered a standing fan.
It blew my mind to learn that only about one in eight German households use air conditioning. Still, we had no choice but to adjust to that lifestyle.
Many apartments don't come with equipped kitchens.
When I was apartment hunting, I was surprised that many rentals didn't have kitchens stocked with a refrigerator, oven, cabinets, counters, a washing machine, or a dishwasher. Instead, there was typically only an empty room with appliance hookups.
That's because tenants in Germany often take most of their kitchen appliances with them when they leave, or they sell the major parts to whoever is moving in. This allows tenants to personalize their spaces, can help landlords save on costs, and may encourage tenants to stay longer.
Public transit is easily accessible in most major cities.
Growing up in the Massachusetts suburbs, I relied on my car and only used the train to commute to Boston. Though I got a German driver's license, I haven't driven in the past four years.
My husband and I have moved to a few different cities within Germany, and luckily, always had easy access to public transportation.
A lot of stores are closed on Sundays.
We landed in Germany on a Sunday and soon learned that most shops, including grocery stores, were closed, forcing us to use a food-delivery app.
That's because Sundays are rest days in Germany. Most people aren't supposed to work or shop, though there are a few exceptions for touristy spots and gas stations.
Carrying cash is a necessity.
To avoid fees and mitigate security concerns, many restaurants, local businesses, market stalls, and cafés only accept cash payments.
Luckily, many larger businesses, grocery stores, and malls accept credit and debit cards and forms of digital payment.
Sparkling water is preferred over still.
In Germany, restaurants automatically serve sparkling water without ice. If a customer asks for ice in their water, it signals they're an American.
There's no social expectation to tip.
In Germany, tipping is appreciated but not expected.
At restaurants, it's not common to add a tip to the receipt. Instead, people will leave a few euros on the table as a thank you.
The first time I went to pay at a hair salon, I was prepared to give a 20% tip. However, the stylist explained that although she appreciated the gesture, a 5% to 10% tip is typical. She also said some salons don't process tips by card, so cash is preferred.

ACB arrests pharma distributor Rajiv Rangila in Delhi medical procurement case
Delhi ACB arrested pharma distributor Rajiv Rangila in an alleged hospital procurement scam involving government hospitals and medical equipment.
The Delhi Anti-Corruption Branch (ACB) has arrested pharmaceutical distributor Rajiv Rangila in connection with alleged irregularities in the procurement of medicines, medical equipment and consumables worth hundreds of crores, officials said.
Rangila, 47, who allegedly fled India after an FIR was registered on June 2, is the fourth person arrested in the case. He was arrested after he returned from the United States (US) on a flight in the early hours of Thursday and surrendered before the ACB the same day, officials said.
The ACB team, which is investigating the case, produced him before a city court, which sent him to four days of custody for further investigation.
Also Read: Ex-CPA head held over alleged irregularities in DGHS procurement
Rangila was declared a proclaimed offender (PO) in the case and a look-out circular (LOC) was also issued against him, an ACB official said, requesting anonymity.
“We have already filed a charge-sheet in the case. Rangila is a mastermind in the entire multi-crore scam, as he was the prime beneficiary of the crime proceeds amounting to nearly R750 crore. He had formed four companies the owners of which were people known to him, including his employees. These four companies were awarded the contracts to supply the medical supplies. Even the basic norms were violated while awarding the contracts to the companies in question,” the official added.
ACB chief Vikramjit Singh had earlier said that Rangila was an accused in the case and multiple teams were looking for him.
Rangila allegedly played a “key link” between the companies that supplied the medical supplies and the officials from the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) and the Central Procurement Agency (CPA) involved in the alleged multi-crore cheating case, according to the official cited above.
Three people – former director-general of the DGHS Vatsala Agarwal, former head of the CPA’s office Vinod Kumar Ranga, and deputy controller of accounts (DCA) of the CPA Neeraj Chopra – have already been arrested in the case that was registered on June 2.
Also Read:Govt hospitals can now directly buy medical supplies
“Rangila has been a pharmaceutical distributor and a contractor of medical supplies in hospitals for over 25 years. His long association with the medical field helped him understand the system’s loopholes, which he allegedly exploited to commit the multi-crore scam in association with the top officials of the DGHS and the CPA,” another official said, requesting anonymity.
A resident of east Delhi’s Priyadarshini Vihar, Rangila reportedly owns multiple properties in Delhi, Uttarakhand and Haryana. He had also unsuccessfully contested the Haryana assembly elections in 2014 as an independent candidate from the Karnal assembly seat, the official said.
The ACB had registered an FIR after the Delhi government’s Directorate of Vigilance conducted searches at the CPA office and filed a complaint alleging serious irregularities in the agency’s procurement processes. The allegations relate to the procurement of portable X-ray and C-Arm radiological equipment, anaesthesia workstations, oral rehydration solution, surgical consumables, and medicines.
