US criticises Australia's proposed algorithm opt-out laws as 'censorship'
- Published
The US has criticised Australia's proposal to give users the ability to opt out of social media algorithms, saying it amounts to "censorship of protected speech".
Under Australia's draft digital duty of care laws, tech firms risk hefty fines if they fail to give users the option to turn off algorithms in a bid to protect them from harmful content.
In a rare submission to the proposed laws, the US embassy in Canberra said it had "serious concerns" and allowing the government to "enforce vague definitions of 'harm'" would lead to "viewpoint-based censorship".
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the legislation was not about giving governments control but giving it back to individuals.
"We ask that Australia clarify how exactly 'harm' and 'risks' shall be determined... ensuring these definitions do not encroach on protected speech," the US said in its submission.
The US also claimed that the proposed laws may risk "reducing the reach of independent journalists or other voices whose content touches on sensitive or controversial topics" if tech firms had to "pre-emptively demote" them.
An opt-out option would "allow regulators to impose rigid, one-size-fits-all platform design requirements" on tech firms and this could affect users outside of Australia, it said.
"Mandated platform design features, especially when applied to algorithms, may affect what users see, say, and hear not just in or from Australia, but globally."
The US also called on Australia to address industry concerns that the "biases and preferences" of government officials do not "disadvantage independent or minority-viewpoint speech".
Another worry was that the proposed laws could affect Australia's "reputation as a jurisdiction that enables innovation," the submission said.
The criticism comes during Albanese's visit to the US to speak at the UN's General Assembly about his government's tech policies.
On Tuesday, local time in New York, Albanese responded to the criticism and claims of the proposed laws being government overreach.
"It's not about giving government control," he told the media in New York.
"It's about giving people back control over what they receive on their devices."
US President Donald Trump meanwhile used his speech at the UN to play down fears about AI, rejecting proposals for guardrails on it and arguing it should be renamed "super intelligence" as "the use of the word artificial makes it sound fake".
This latest move by Australia to protect its online users from harm comes less than a year after the country introduced a social media ban for children under 16 last December.

Asian governments are rushing preparations for the most severe El Niño weather event on record, with hundreds of millions of people bracing for multiple crises at once as extreme heat, heavy rain and food shortages hit the region.
Fuelled by exceptionally warm ocean conditions across the tropical Pacific – and developing alongside the human-driven climate crisis – El Niño is virtually guaranteed to grow to a very strong intensity towards the end of this year and into 2027.
The World Food Programme has warned that about 50 million people will probably be pushed into acute hunger due to the exceptionally intense weather system, while UN secretary-general António Guterres said this month that El Niño was “being supersized before our eyes”.
Here are the steps countries in Asia are taking to prepare for El Niño:
‘Climate risk maps’ in China
In Hong Kong, authorities have already been forced to revise workplace policies, after the city experienced its hottest day on record on 9 August. During times of extreme heat, companies are expected to reschedule work, provide cooling equipment and rest breaks for their employees.
Employers in the international financial hub could even face prosecution if they fail to provide staff with support at times of sweltering heat.
In mainland China a 100-day campaign has been launched to prepare for extreme weather and help safeguard harvests against the opposing extremes of drought and intense rainfall.
Beijing has plans to upgrade early warning monitoring systems, and in July, it launched a national plan encouraging cities to draw up ‘climate risk maps’ to help identify areas most vulnerable to flooding and severe heat.
Taiwan, meanwhile, is treating the predicted extreme weather as an emergency situation, and preparing using methods similar to what it would do to train for a terrorist attack or earthquake. In early September, the island nation held a mass exercise simulating three consecutive days of temperatures above 40C. Hundreds of people took part in the field exercises, which simulated power and water disruption, rail problems, air conditioner failure and mass heatstroke.
The government has also been testing its “Cool Map” online platform, which helps to direct vulnerable people to airconditioned and cool spaces.
Sri Lanka plans to process salterwater
El Niño is already wreaking havoc across south Asia; in parts of India there has been a shortfall of monsoon rainfall of almost 50% in September, with knock-on effects on key crops such as rice, pulses, cotton and maize. Concerns are mounting that there could be a diminished harvest in the coming months, likely driving up food prices – already crippling for poor and lower middle class families.
The Indian government has taken a hyper-vigilant approach to establish what the agriculture minister, Shivraj Singh Chouhan, described as a “protective shield for farmers”.
In more than 350 vulnerable districts authorities are boosting water conservation infrastructure and water harvesting, and are encouraging farmers to plant low-water, short duration crops – such as pulses and millets.
But the most intense impact of El Niño in the area is in Sri Lanka, where the absence of rainfall and high temperatures have become so severe that the country is experiencing its worst drought in a decade. More than 160,000 people are now facing a drinking water shortage as several key reservoirs run dry.
Officials have been forced to close the tourist areas of the Yala national park, home to leopards, elephants, crocodiles and spotted deer, and have been bringing in tankers of water to fill the ponds to make sure the animals do not die. In Mullaithivu lagoon, in the north-east of Sri Lanka, thousands of fish were found dead due to the lack of fresh water.
The country’s disaster management centre is preparing for a situation in which freshwater supplies could vanish. “If water sources dry up, there will be no alternative means of obtaining water,” an official said. Colombo would then be forced to process salt water from the sea, although relying on the country’s one desalination plant is not considered workable.
Tackling an agriculture crisis in south-east Asia
In south-east Asia, El Niño is compounded by a series of ongoing crises. The Iran war has already disrupted global energy and supply chains and inflated fertiliser costs, disproportionately hitting the region. At the same time, severe haze from seasonal fires across Malaysia and Indonesia has choked cities and is damaging plants and trees.
During the 2023–2024 El Niño, south-east Asian governments successfully cushioned agricultural impacts by adjusting planting calendars and managing water, but those strategies will be insufficient to deal with the scale of the crisis, experts warn. Regional rice yields are already projected to fall by 8 to 10%.
“We can’t just assume that this El Niño is going to be the same as the last because there are so many challenges that have been stacking on top of each other,” says Elyssa Kaur Ludher, a climate and food security expert based in Singapore.
The Philippines, Malaysia and Indonesia are particularly vulnerable to food price changes, says Kaur Ludher, a visiting fellow with the Climate Change for Southeast Asia Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute in Singapore.
“In Singapore, most of our income is not spent on food. It’s under 10%. But for Indonesians, it can be up to 50% or even more as a proportion of income spent on food. So any price rise affects them disproportionately.”
With the potential for price rises to leave people desperate and angry, Kaur Ludher has argued for food security to be reframed as a national security issue. In Indonesia and the Philippines in particular, she said, social stability depends a lot on food prices. “Rice is a lifeline to this region,” she says.
To prepare, south-east Asian governments and farmer cooperatives are promoting regenerative agriculture and shifting toward biofertilisers.
“We have come to a stage where climate change is putting so much pressure on us – on our existing, already crumbling or structurally unsound, systems,” say Kaur Ludher. “Nature will force us to have a reckoning.”
South Korea overhauls its heatwave alert system
South Korea saw the driest July on record in the country’s south-east. Weeks later came a freak reversal, as a weakening storm system dragged in a deluge that dumped some of the heaviest rainfall ever recorded at a Korean weather station. The heat was so intense that farmers described spoilt potatoes as being “boiled” in the ground.
The country’s weather agency has overhauled its heatwave alert system for the first time in 18 years, adding a top tier that triggers official guidance to stop non-emergency outdoor work once feels-like temperatures hit 38C. Nationwide, phones have buzzed for weeks with government alerts urging people to stay indoors during the hottest hours.
Officials are watching out for a rough autumn, with seas around the Korean peninsula remaining unusually warm for the season and forecasters expecting the north-west Pacific to produce far more powerful storms than usual this year, since a strengthening El Niño is weakening the high pressure that has so far kept them away.
Japan prepares for ‘cruelly’ hot days and typhoons
Japan is also bracing for the arrival of so-called super-typhoons, which experts attribute to a combination of El Niño and human-induced global heating.
El Niño was once associated with slightly cooler summers in Japan. But rising sea surface temperatures mean it is having the opposite effect, blanketing many parts of the country in record-breaking heat and humidity in 2023-4, the last time the weather pattern materialised.
Japan recorded its first official “cruelly hot day” – or kokushobi – in July, just after the start of the current El Niño event. The Japanese term, introduced in April to underscore the threat to health posed by rising temperatures, refers to days when the mercury exceeds 40C.
Now, as the summer heat dissipates, the country is bracing for the arrival of potentially destructive typhoons.
The public is encouraged to take measures to protect themselves and their homes, such as heeding official evacuation warnings and stocking up on food and water. People living in apartments are urged to secure or bring inside flower pots and furniture – anything that could become a dangerous flying object during a storm.
This month the infrastructure ministry said it had identified several high-risk underpasses on national highways that would be closed preemptively during heavy rain. Underpasses – which allow cars to travel beneath other roads or railway lines – became a focus of concern last month after two trapped motorists drowned during record-breaking rain in Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo.

Opposition defence spokesperson says PM’s AI hack timing not a coincidence
Catie McLeod
The opposition’s defence spokesperson, James Paterson, has questioned the timing of the prime minister’s announcement that an AI agent hacked Medicare.
Paterson made the claim on the ABC’s 7.30 program last night after Anthony Albanese publicly disclosed that an AI agent developed by OpenAI hacked Medicare in June and that the tech giant only notified the government earlier this month using an email sent to a “public mailbox”.
Paterson told 7.30 he believed Albanese had chosen to make the announcement at the UN summit in New York, as part of his effort to stand up to “big tech” on AI.
The senator said:
The government has questions to answer about when they knew and … why the prime minister decided to disclose it in the way he did in the place he did at the time he did. But in terms of the nature of the potential of actual security breach this is the bottom end of the spectrum of seriousness.
I don’t think it was a coincidence. I think it neatly dove-tailed with the political agenda the prime minister has in New York City.
Paterson said he didn’t consider the breach to be overly serious because the data the AI agent accessed was made freely available to researchers and academics studying the health system, and was not personal or private in nature.
He said the breach was cause for “being alert but not alarmed”.
Nevertheless, he said Australians were “entitled to demand explanations and contrition” and to want high levels of confidence when entering into agreements with big tech companies such as OpenAI.

Australia’s gen Z are the generation most willing to cut their spending way back to afford a home, according to Cotality data reported by AAP.
The figures show more than 75% of all Australians were curbing their outgoings in pursuit of property, meaning we are more likely to do so than our Canadian, US and UK peers (for whom the figures sat below 70%).
Levels of discretionary spending, like eating out, owning a car, and even moving from the family home into a share house, have dropped among young adults in recent years.
But it wasn’t just first-time buyers making significant financial sacrifices to climb the ladder. Millennials – the largest buyer cohort in the world – are readily forgoing small luxuries to afford homes large enough for their families.
Prospective buyers were selling their second car or putting off holidays while their children were young, Capital Buyers Agency owner Claire Corby said.

Most Australians would not be persuaded to participate in the housing market until mortgage interest rates hit a 4.9% average, the data revealed.
The average rate for an owner-occupier in August 2026 was 6.3%, meaning the market is likely to stay quiet for some time and allowing bold buyers to swoop in.

Heartburn is commonly described as acidity and treated with antacids. But gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GERD) is not simply acidity. It occurs when the stomach contents repeatedly move into the oesophagus because the normal anti-reflux barrier does not function effectively.
“GERD is not simply a problem of producing too much acid,” said Vishnu Abishek Raju, senior consultant, medical gastroenterology, Apollo Hospitals, Greams Road, Chennai. Heartburn, therefore, is a symptom, rather than a diagnosis. Some people living with reflux have visible inflammation of the oesophagus, while others have symptoms without any visible injury.
GERD is common in India. A 2021 analysis of nine Indian studies involving 20,614 people estimated its pooled prevalence at 15.6%.
How reflux occurs
The lower oesophageal sphincter acts as a valve between the oesophagus and stomach. It can undergo brief, inappropriate relaxations, allowing stomach contents to move upwards.
A hiatal hernia can weaken the anti-reflux barrier by allowing part of the stomach to move above the diaphragm. Obesity, particularly excess abdominal fat, increases pressure within the abdomen, while delayed gastric emptying can increase the volume and pressure inside the stomach.
The oesophagus also has protective mechanisms. Saliva helps clear refluxed material, while alkaline mucus helps limit acid-related injury.
“People may have acid reflux within a stipulated period. But if that goes beyond the protective mechanisms of the body, those defensive mechanisms fail and the food pipe can ger damaged, a condition called oesophagitis,” said Arul Prakash, clinical lead and senior consultant in medical gastroenterology, SRM Prime Hospital, Chennai.
Why symptoms can be misleading
The amount of reflux does not always correspond to the severity of symptoms.
“Some people have increased sensitivity of the oesophagus, so even normal amounts of reflux can produce significant burning or chest discomfort,” Dr. Abishek Raju said. This includes reflux hypersensitivity and functional heartburn. In reflux hypersensitivity, symptoms are linked to reflux events despite normal overall reflux exposure. In functional heartburn, symptoms occur without evidence that reflux is responsible.
“These are people who may feel a burning sensation with almost anything they eat because the nerves in the food pipe are very sensitive,” Dr. Arul Prakash said.
This is one reason why simply increasing acid-suppressing medicines does not necessarily resolve persistent symptoms.
Establishing the diagnosis
A response to a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) can support a diagnosis of GERD, but it does not prove that reflux is the cause.
When symptoms continue despite appropriately used treatment, doctors may need to investigate other causes, including oesophageal motility disorders and disorders of oesophageal sensitivity.
Endoscopy is particularly important when there are alarm symptoms such as difficulty or pain while swallowing, bleeding, unexplained weight loss, persistent vomiting or anaemia. It can detect oesophagitis, ulcers, strictures and Barrett’s oesophagus.
A normal endoscopy, however, does not exclude reflux. In such cases, 24-hour pH-impedance monitoring can measure reflux episodes, distinguish acid from non-acid reflux and assess whether symptoms occur in association with reflux.
Manometry assesses pressure and movement within the oesophagus and can identify motility disorders. It is also used in selected patients before anti-reflux procedures.
Chest discomfort should not automatically be attributed to GERD because cardiac pain can have a similar presentation. Even discomfort after a heavy meal cannot by itself establish reflux. In people with cardiovascular risk factors, cardiac causes may need to be assessed first.
Lifestyle measures
Weight loss can reduce reflux symptoms in people who are overweight or obese. Avoiding food for about three hours before lying down can help, particularly with night-time symptoms.
Food triggers vary. Rather than eliminating multiple foods routinely, patients should identify those that consistently worsen their symptoms. Coffee, spicy and high-fat foods, chocolate, mint and acidic foods can trigger symptoms in some people.
For night-time reflux, raising the head end of the bed and, for some people, sleeping on the left side may help.
Complications and treatment
Persistent GERD can cause erosive oesophagitis, ulcers and strictures. It can also lead to Barrett’s oesophagus, in which the lining of the lower oesophagus changes. Barrett’s is associated with an increased risk of oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
New difficulty in swallowing, painful swallowing, unexplained weight loss, vomiting blood, black stools or persistent vomiting require medical evaluation.
For patients with objectively confirmed reflux who remain significantly symptomatic, endoscopic or surgical treatment may be considered in selected cases. Laparoscopic fundoplication is one surgical option, while endoscopic anti-reflux procedures are available for some patients.

The festive season has officially arrived, and Indian kitchens are once again coming alive with preparations of laddus, payasam, halwa, burfis, and other traditional sweets. With the rising awareness about the impact of sugar, however, some ingredients in popular sweets are being changed. Refined sugar is increasingly being replaced with jaggery, while some consumers are also experimenting with artificial sweeteners such as stevia, and of late, monk fruit sweetener.
The intention is understandable: enjoy festive food while reducing sugar use. The science behind these sweeteners however, is more nuanced. Not every alternative to sugar is nutritionally equivalent, and ‘natural’ does not automatically mean low-sugar. The important question is not simply what sweetener is being used, but how much sweetness and sugars a person consumes overall.
Jaggery counts as sugar
Jaggery has long been associated with traditional Indian cooking and is often perceived as a healthier alternative to refined sugar because it undergoes less refining and may retain small amounts of minerals. However, it remains a concentrated source of sugar.
This distinction becomes particularly important during festivals, when sweets are rarely eaten in isolation. A person may have a laddu, a serving of payasam/kheer, sweetened beverages and several savoury foods in the same day, or worse in a single meal.
The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that free sugars contribute less than 10% of total daily energy intake, with a further reduction to below 5% providing additional health benefits. For a person consuming around 2,000 calories a day, 5% is roughly 20 to 25 grams, or 4 to 5 teaspoons of sugar.
Therefore, replacing sugar with jaggery does not make a sweet sugar-free. From a doctor’s perspective, portion size and the total amount of free sugar consumed during the day remain far more important than whether the sweetener is brown or white.
Artificial sweeteners
Across the country, many people are now using low-calorie or no-calorie sweeteners. These include artificial sweeteners such as sucralose, saccharin and aspartame, as well as naturally derived sweeteners such as steviol glycosides and monk fruit extract.
Monk fruit extract, the newest addition to sweeteners in the mass market, is particularly interesting because its sweetness comes from compounds called mogrosides. Monk fruit extracts can be approximately 100 to 250 times sweeter than sugar, depending on their mogroside content. The United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has noted that the use of monk fruit extract is ‘generally recognised as safe’ under its intended conditions of use.
Artificial sweeteners work differently. They provide intense sweetness with little or no calories and are commonly used in products marketed as ‘sugar-free’, ‘light’ or ‘diet’. Approved high-intensity sweeteners are considered safe within their specified conditions of use, and several have established acceptable daily intake levels.
However, a ‘safe’ label does not necessarily mean beneficial. The World Health Organization currently advises against relying on non-sugar sweeteners as a strategy for long-term weight control. Its recommendation is conditional and is based on evidence that replacing free sugars with non-sugar sweeteners does not provide a clear long-term benefit for reducing body fat.
This is an important distinction for consumers. A sweetener can be safe to consume and still not be a reason to increase the amount of sweet food in the diet.
A better approach
The biggest misconception is that changing the sweetener automatically changes the nutritional quality of the sweet.
A jaggery laddu is still sweet. A sugar-free dessert can be calorie-dense if it contains large amounts of ghee, nuts, cream or other ingredients. Similarly, replacing sugar with monk fruit does not make an otherwise highly processed dessert a health food.
The more useful approach is for us to look at our entire festive eating pattern. One traditional sweet enjoyed occasionally is very different from consuming several servings every day throughout the season. The goal is not to find a sweetener that allows unlimited sweetness; it should be to reduce excessive sweets while retaining the cultural and social pleasure associated with festivals.
So, if a festival sweet is made with sugar, moderation matters. If it is made with jaggery, moderation still matters. Monk fruit essence or other non-sugar sweeteners do not automatically bestow a license to eat more.
The aim should be not to move from sugar to jaggery or from jaggery to monk fruit. It should be to simply learn to enjoy our favourite sweets alittle less sweet, and a little less often. This also aligns with broader dietary recommendations from the WHO that advise building diets on minimally and unprocessed foods, and restricting free sugars.
There is no need to cut out every single sweet, but do practice portion control and choose wisely. Instead of five laddus, have one and enjoy it mindfully. Keep the overall diet rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains and fibre, and let sweets remain a small part of the meal.
(Suparna Mukherjee is a dietician with Narayana Health City, Bengaluru. suparna.mukherjee@narayanahealth.org)

(Bloomberg) -- A powerful coastal storm set to slam the Eastern Seaboard is threatening New York City with damaging winds and flooding across the five boroughs through Sunday.
Up to 6 inches (15 centimeters) of rain are expected to fall in the area beginning late Friday, according to the US National Weather Service, with 50 mile-an-hour wind gusts in Manhattan. The nor’easter already is churning up large swells from the Mid-Atlantic to Maine, but the risk to New York is increasing in the latest forecasts, said weather service meteorologist Jay Engle.
As the storm track shifted, New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency for eight counties encompassing the city and suburbs. 
“We’re expecting dangerous coastal flooding, strong winds and potential power outages through the weekend,” Hochul said in a statement. “Take this storm seriously.”
Meanwhile, city workers were preparing for downed trees and clogged catch basins in anticipation of flooding, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said in a statement.
The most severe flooding along New York’s coastline is expected Saturday morning, Engle said, when up to 2 feet of water could wash ashore on top of high tide. That tide is already expected to be higher than normal due to the full moon on Saturday, known as a “Harvest Moon.” 
As of 4:20 p.m. New York time, 226 flights had been cancelled across the US, mostly at Boston’s Logan International Airport and at other airfields around Massachusetts, according to FlightAware. 
Ferry travel between downtown Boston and communities to the north and south has been canceled in anticipation of high winds and significant waves. On Thursday, droves of ferry commuters on Nantucket sought to get off the island, leading to calls to police to handle disputes about people cutting in line.
Pop star Ed Sheeran’s two concerts at Gillette Stadium outside of Boston this weekend were canceled. The shows became shadowed in controversy earlier this month after stadium owner Robert Kraft pushed Sheeran to drop opening act Macklemore over the rapper’s pro-Palestine comments at a New Jersey concert.
Other storm-related cancellations included the Global Citizens Festival in Central Park that was expected to draw 50,000 people and the All Things Go NYC at Forest Hills Stadium.

Venus has nearly the same mass, size, and structure as Earth, which has led astronomers to believe it should have a moon, but it doesn’t. It is technically possible that a moon never formed, but scientists have also come up with several scenarios to describe how Venus could have lost its satellite.
One previously presented hypothesis is that Venus’ moon was destroyed by a collision with some massive celestial body. But a recent study by researchers at the University of California, Riverside, suggests a different course of events. It posits that instead of being obliterated by some catastrophic external force, the moon was slowly pulled in by Venus’ gravity and plodding rotation until it fragmented and was completely swallowed.
“Venus didn’t require a catastrophe to arrive at what we can see today,” Steven Kane, an astrophysicist and the paper’s lead author, explained in a press release. “It turns out the gravity of the planet itself combined with the rate at which it spins naturally caused the moon to collapse on top of it.”
A planet’s rotation can either push or pull on its satellites, depending on its speed. The rotation can cause variations in gravitational strength. This is why our moon isn’t in any danger of being eaten. In fact—because our 24-hour days are rather fast in a planetary sense—our moon is currently drifting away from Earth at a rate of about 1.5 inches per year.
And when astronomers say Venus spins slowly, they really mean it. The time it takes for Venus to complete one rotation is 243 Earth days. That’s longer than Venus’ year and makes the bright planet the slowest spinner in our solar system. This protracted rotation, combined with the planet’s gravity, means that even if a moon existed, it would not be pushed outward but would instead be dragged inward.
To verify this mechanism, Kane and his research team built a computer model simulating gravitational interactions between celestial bodies. After verifying the model’s accuracy by faithfully recreating the evolution of Earth’s moon, they ran simulations varying several factors including the time it takes Venus to complete one rotation and the mass of a hypothetical moon, ranging anywhere from 0.01 to 10 times that of Earth’s natural satellite.
The outcomes showed that the moon’s fate depended on Venus’ rotation speed, the lunar mass, and the shape of its orbit. Under many conditions, the satellite spiraled inward, eventually breaking apart and succumbing to the planet’s gravity. “When I made this discovery, I was shocked,” Kane recalled. “I thought surely the broad range of scenarios I was exploring would lead to a variety of results. But it all went pretty much in the same direction.”
In a few instances—such as when the researchers artificially sped up the planet’s rotation to once every 10 to 12 hours and the moon had a mass comparable to that of Earth’s—the simulations indicated a moon could survive for up to 4.5 billion years. But that’s little more than an interesting test of the model. It’s an extremely unlikely reality given our planetary neighbor’s current lethargic speed.
This study does not, however, prove that Venus once had a moon, and finding physical evidence of its existence will not be easy. Venus’ surface is geologically young, the number of craters indicating that top layer of rock is just a few hundred million years old. The planet itself formed at the same time as the rest of our solar system, some 4.6 billion years ago, but extreme amounts of volcanic and tectonic activity have essentially remodeled the surface.
If any evidence of a moon exists, it’s been paved over and may lie deep underground. Seismological surveys penetrating far into the Earth have provided evidence of our moon’s formation—anomalous structures pointing to a massive impact. If similar measurements could be conducted on Venus, it’s possible that traces of a moon that was once absorbed might be found.
The moon’s fate could also provide clues to solving another long-standing mystery: whether Venus once had an environment capable of supporting life. Swallowing a moon would have imparted enormous energy and angular momentum to the planet, which could significantly shift its rotation, geology, and climate—altering the course of the planet’s evolution.
This is not limited to Venus. Scientists seeking to identify habitable worlds among exoplanets have often considered the presence of a moon as a factor influencing habitability. However, it remains unclear whether a large moon is essential for the existence of life.
“My feeling is there are benefits to having a moon, but it isn’t required for habitability,” Kane said. “The moon has definitely changed the way Earth has evolved through time, but we don’t fully know how important that role is.”
This finding that planets with slower rotation speeds are less likely to retain a moon offers a new perspective in the search for Earth-like exoplanets. Even if very Earth-like planets are located, if their rotation speeds are not fast enough, they might come to devour their moons.

A seven- to eight-month-old Royal Bengal tiger cub was rescued from an empty house in an Odisha village in Mayurbhanj district on Friday after heavy rain drove it out of the forest, triggering panic among residents, forest officials said.
Movement of the Cub
The cub had been moving around Khaparkhai village under the Thakurmunda forest range, adjoining the Similipal Tiger Reserve, since Thursday night.
Initial Discovery and Response
Officials said a villager first noticed the cub near his house on Thursday night, and locals soon alerted forest officials and kept watch over the animal with flashlights. A team led by Thakurmunda range officer Umakanta Behera and forester Bidyadhar Mahanta reached the village around 9 pm.
Return to Human Habitation
The cub initially moved towards the forest but returned to the habitation after heavy rain and took shelter in an unoccupied house constructed under the Pradhan Mantri Awas Yojana. On Friday morning, villagers, fearing for their safety, shut the door from outside and informed the forest department.
Rescue Operation
A senior forest team, including Karanjia DFO Ajay Kumar Sahu, ACF Prabhat Kumar Kuanr, Similipal Tiger Reserve Deputy Director ACF Phalguni Behera and ACF Ashok Kumar Das, who reached the spot, found that the cub appeared ill and required veterinary attention. Using nets and a specialised transport cage, the rescue team safely secured the animal around noon and shifted it to the Thakurmunda forest range office.
Further Actions for the Cub
Field Director of Similipal Tiger Reserve and Baripada Regional Chief Conservator of Forests Prakash Chand Gogineni said the cub was undergoing veterinary examination and treatment. “After it recovers and attains the required fitness, the cub will be shifted to a larger rehabilitation enclosure at Jamuani in the core area of the Similipal Tiger Reserve,” he said, adding that it will be kept under observation until it develops the hunting skills needed to survive independently.

Google adds creepy avatars to Gemini 3.8 live's agents
Like it or not, they may be doing customer service or sales support in the future.
Last week Google launched Gemini 3.8 Live and Live Extended Thinking models, touting them as the company's most advanced live dialogue models yet. The idea, it said, was to give "developers and enterprises... building blocks for reliable, production ready voice agents." It also made speaking back to Gemini more natural, so users can do complex tasks with voice commands.
Now, Google has added video to that formula with Gemini 3.8 Live with Live Avatar. It pairs near real-time visual presence to the live dialogue models, creating "an experience that listens, sees and speaks with a dynamic visual persona." In a nutshell, these are avatars designed to do things like sales support and customer service, so you may be interacting with them in the near future.
In several videos in the blog, Google shows both realistic and cartoon-like Avatars. They can do things like precise lip-syncing, natural expressions and "fluid turn-taking." Using them, the company says, will enable natural, multimodal conversations by allowing the avatars to communicate using facial expressions while also looking, listening and speaking. The avatars are backed by Gemini's advanced reasoning, allowing Live Avatar to trigger tool calls and fetch data in the background while continuing an active dialogue.
Google will offer a library of "diverse, preset avatars," or organizations can customize their own from high-quality reference images to preserve "reference likeness, brand styling or character identity." Those are only available through enterprise allowlisting, the company added. The Live Avatars are also built with "strict safeguards designed to respect identity and keep AI-generated content transparent," with each one watermarked using Google's SynthID.
As mentioned, Live Avatar is designed strictly for Google's Gemini Enterprise customers. However, you may see the results some day soon in the form of customer service or sales avatar appearing on your computer or phone screen. Base on what Google has shown so far, and people's distaste for AI slop, they may not be universally popular.

How Ceuta, football and Israel are shaping Morocco's election
- Published
Disillusioned young voters in Morocco were courted with viral football slogans, promises of one million jobs and anti-Israel rallying calls ahead of Wednesday's parliamentary elections.
Yet, for many young Moroccans, politics remains deeply disconnected from reality.
"I have no hope for this election. I'm ashamed of our political scene. It's a complete circus," Siham Azeroual, 32, an environmental activist who lives in the Atlas region, tells the BBC.
The outcome of the vote will decide the make-up of the next government, just weeks after 60,000 people risked their lives to cross from the North African country to the Spanish enclave of Ceuta - a sign of the lack of opportunities many young people feel they have at home.
Morocco operates as a constitutional monarchy where political parties compete for 395 seats in the House of Representatives, the legislative chamber.
Yet executive power remains closely tied to the crown. King Mohammed VI, the 63-year-old monarch, appoints the prime minister from the political party that comes first in the election, but also presides over the Council of Ministers - the country's most important policy-making body.
The current campaign also follows a wave of Gen Z protests that erupted in September 2025 over unemployment, healthcare and living costs.
Demonstrators chanted slogans like "freedom, dignity, and social justice" which escalated to "get out Akhannouch", a reference to current Prime Minister Aziz Akhannouch.
More than 2,400 people faced prosecution following the unrest. Despite the crackdown, some young activists are choosing to enter the political arena.
Hamza El Kharroubi, 29, was briefly arrested during the protests. He is now running for parliament with the little-known Environment and Sustainable Development Party, which has a green agenda.
"As a young person, I don't have much hope. I joined this party because they wanted more Gen Z faces and they are allowing us to speak freely about our demands," El Kharroubi tells the BBC.
He comes from Tetouan, just 34km (21 miles) from Fnideq beach, where the migration wave to Ceuta started in late July.
Some 60,000 people crossed, both Moroccans and other nationalities. At least 100 people died in the largest migration surge to the enclave in recent history.
"We want justice for the families of those who died crossing to Ceuta. We want compensation for their families," El Kharroubi says.
He argues that the crossing was widely linked to economic hardship and unemployment.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) estimates overall unemployment stood at 13% last year, while youth unemployment - between the ages of 15 and 24 - reached 37.3%.
El Kharroubi says his goal is not to compete with established heavyweights - but securing a voice in parliament to build toward 2031.
"As young people, we have to enter the parliament so by 2031 we have strong young politicians who can compete for a seat in the government."
Fouzi Lekjaa, head of the Royal Moroccan Football Federation and a senior politician who works in the finance ministry, has emerged as the kingdom's newest political sensation - and a definite heavyweight.
Credited with helping the Atlas Lions - as the national men's football team is known - become global contenders, Lekjaa joined the centrist Party of Authenticity and Modernity (Pam) in July.
Videos of his campaign rallies have gone viral in the football-mad nation that is jointly hosting the next World Cup along with Spain and Portugal.
The clips show crowds chanting "Sir" which means "Go" in Moroccan Arabic - the iconic catchphrase from Morocco's historic 2022 World Cup run, when it became the first Arab and African side to make it to the semi-finals.
Lekjaa has promised to make Morocco sixth in the world in education and healthcare, to match the Fifa ranking of the men's football team.
Pam is competing against 26 other parties, including Prime Minister Akhannouch's National Rally of Independents (RNI). In its bid for a second term, RNI has renewed a pledge to create one million job opportunities by 2031.
Political expert Rachid Aourraz, from the Moroccan Institute for Policy Analysis (MIPA), remains sceptical about this promise.
"The slogan 'one million jobs' has become an overused electoral slogan. There is also talk of raising the minimum wage, but what is proposed cannot withstand a structural inability to create stable net jobs," Aourraz tells the BBC.
He adds that major parties "do not compete over an alternative model", but rather over how to implement public policies set by a royal vision.
Also seeking a political comeback is the Islamist Justice and Development Party (PJD) - using anti-Israeli sentiments to woo voters.
Morocco normalised ties with Israel in December 2020 along with several other Arab countries, under the US-brokered Abraham Accords.
Led by populist former Prime Minister Abdelilah Benkirane, the PJD is campaigning heavily on a promise to end diplomatic ties with Israel. He says the normalisation was a "mistake" made by his party which led the government between 2016 and 2021.
Bilateral ties were hit during the Gaza war with weekly protests taking place in the capital, Rabat, against the Israeli diplomatic presence.
During the conflict the Israeli liaison office was closed and direct flights between the two countries were suspended.
Yet despite an outpouring of pro-Palestinian protests, with tens of thousands taking to the streets and setting ablaze the Israeli flag at the height of the war, it was announced earlier this month that Israel and Morocco had agreed to open full embassies in their respective countries.
This followed a meeting between their top diplomats and the US ambassador to the United Nations.
"We have to speak up," Benkirane told supporters at a campaign rally in Marrakesh.
"If we work hard, the king will close the Israeli embassy. The king does not like going against his own people," he added, warning of "the dangers of Israel and Zionism in Morocco".
I think young people should focus on the microscale: rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top"
More than half of Morocco's total population of roughly 38.8 million is under the age of 35 - though only 4% of the more than 15.8 million registered voters are aged between 18 and 24.
"I am not keeping up much with the campaigns - but I noticed the same faces as usual," says Hiba, a 27-year-old Moroccan living in Canada who preferred not to use her last name.
She lives in Montreal which has a large Moroccan diaspora of about 104,000 people, according to the 2016 census.
Many of last year's Gen Z protests were more vocal outside the country, where young Moroccans were able to express their anger without fear of repercussions.
Hiba, who co-organised several Gen Z protests in Montreal, says she would have considered voting had she been able to find a proxy in Morocco - which is how those in the diaspora can cast their ballot.
"Gen Z protests didn't go in vain. We achieved something. At least now we see more debates with young people on state TV," she says.
Azeroual, the environmental activist, agrees.
But having lived through both the 20 February movement in 2011 that changed the constitution and the recent Gen Z movement, she believes change must come from a multi-faceted approach.
"I think young people should focus on the microscale - rather than running for office, helping build communities and connecting with people and then building up to the top," she says.
Despite not being fully convinced by any political campaign, she says she will be heading to her local polling station to cast her ballot.

Trump's top trade envoy says U.S. 'comfortable' with state of relationship with Canada
Greer says 2 sides still talk about potential deals, but 'no urgency'
U.S. President Donald Trump is "comfortable" with where things stand with Canada — his country's once closest ally — and is in no rush to reach a new trade deal, according to his top trade envoy.
"The reality is President Trump is comfortable where we are on Canada," United States Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said in a Friday morning interview with the American network CNBC.
"They call us now and then and we have good conversations about potential deals. But there's no urgency on our side."
The two countries have been embroiled in a trade dispute since Trump was re-elected, but the relationship further soured after talks to reach a deal collapsed at the 11th hour last month.

The U.S. side maintains Canada walked away from a good deal. The Canadian side has accused the Americans of not negotiating in good faith and encroaching on Canada's sovereignty.
Greer, who mainly spoke to CNBC about new trade negotiations with Chinese President Xi Jinping, was asked about the state of the trade relationship with Canada.
"We're still getting what we need from them in terms of oil, gas, potash, all of these things. We're shipping [agricultural products] back and forth across the border, so there's still a lot of strong trade between the two countries," he said.
The U.S. slapped 50 per cent duties on roughly $28 billion of Canadian goods on Aug. 22. Canada started collecting retaliatory tariffs Sept. 8. The summer measures are on top of existing levies on Canadian steel, aluminum, autos and lumber that were imposed earlier.
Starting next week the Trump administration plans to ban the import of certain products including Canadian alcohol, motorcycles and molasses.
Trump has also ratcheted up his jabs at Canada since trade talks fell apart, including posting to social media a map of North America with the U.S. flag covering Canada and another post showing a cartoon version of himself standing over a sprawled out Prime Minister Mark Carney during a hockey game saying, "Get up, governor."
He has also signed an order to rename Lake Ontario as "Lake America."

Iran’s seven-day timetable to reopen the strait of Hormuz and start talks on its nuclear programme has been pitched as a deal that could rapidly extricate Donald Trump from a political crisis but requires the US president to make difficult concessions.
In the five days left before the proposed reopening of the strait, which is expected to relieve pressure on global energy markets, Trump would need to lift Iranian asset freezes, permit Iran to export its oil and, probably most difficult of all, order Benjamin Netanyahu to end Israel’s attacks on Hezbollah in Lebanon, thus achieving the “ceasefire on all fronts”.
Iranian diplomats in New York said they thought a three-hour meeting earlier this week with the US envoy Steve Witkoff in which they laid out the seven-day plan was productive, but were doubtful the US would deliver.
Iran nevertheless feels it has done the diplomatic spadework, taking the proposal to China for endorsement and ensuring that Oman, located on the south side of the strait, was also on board.
The foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, explained that the idea was to take the elements of the Iran-US memorandum of understanding that Trump signed in June and repackage and accelerate the process since, as they understood it, Trump had come to hate the MoU.
“The conditions we have asked the US to meet is nothing new, nothing more than what was already in the Islamabad agreement, which was signed by the US president,” Araghchi said. But what is new is the speed.
In the first four to five days under this timetable, the US would have to lift the naval blockade on Iran’s oil ports, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports, end the war on all fronts and permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets.
On the sixth day, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened by Iran, with ships using a new route designated by Oman and Iran. And on the next day, negotiations would start on the future of Iran’s civil nuclear programme, including a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium. This accelerates the point at which nuclear talks would begin, from 60 days in the June agreement to seven.
Those talks could, of course, take a long time, but from Trump’s perspective, the strait of Hormuz would be reopened before the midterm elections, a point in the political calendar that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says has never been a factor in Iranian thinking. Trump had claimed Iran was waiting until after the vote to offer a deal.
Iran, Araghchi argued at a largely off-the-record briefing with reporters – at which Pezeshkian was also present – had every reason not to negotiate with the US.
In particular, he admitted to being sceptical that Witkoff could deliver. He recounted how he had twice held talks with Trump’s special envoy, after which Witkoff had described them as “productive and good”, only for the US to bomb Iran the next day. Other Iranian diplomats say Trump’s willingness to rein in Netanyahu in Lebanon remains key. If he could do that, a deal would be feasible.
It is a difficult deal for Trump to swallow since the strait would reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters. Saudi Arabia is also concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.
Trump says he has a choice to make between the annihilation of Iran and engagement – an engagement that, he says with typical hyperbole, could make Iran one of the great countries of the world. In reality, the judgment he has to make is more prosaic. Is he prepared to go back to war with Iran after the midterms and, if not, does he believe the US can squeeze the Iranian economy so hard that the leadership will succumb.
Pezeshkian, who handed all questions about the talks to Araghchi, admitted Iranians wanted the war to end and did not deny the economic pressure, but said the public had withstood sanctions for 45 years.
He also insisted Iran’s decision-making machinery was functioning. The reclusive supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, was completely healthy, he claimed, a testimony based on spending seven hours in his presence. He did not explain why, apart from security, Khamenei had not issued a voice recording, photograph or video as proof of life.

A review found that Trump’s arch will harm DC. His appointee just ended the process
Advisory board cuts off required review process after advocates and preservationists raise major questions about Trump’s ‘military complex’

Donald Trump’s administration is abruptly ending a federally required review to determine how badly the president’s plans for a massive arch will harm the nation’s capital, already facing a flood of construction projects remaking Washington, D.C., in his image.
Last month, the National Park Service acknowledged in a lengthy report that Trump’s “triumphal” arch will unavoidably create “adverse effects” and harm historic sites, but the administration plans to go through with the plans anyway.
In a letter to local governments and advocacy groups Thursday, a Trump appointee leading an advisory board for the project said they are ending further review. “We are hereby terminating consultation,” wrote Travis Voyles, the vice chairman of the Advisory Council on Historic Preservation.
“They seem to be making up the rules as they go along,” Charles Birnbaum, president of the Cultural Landscape Foundation, told The Independent.
The advisory council will now make its own recommendations to Trump’s Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, whose agency is overseeing plans for the 250-foot-tall monument, which the president claims will also be loaded up with “large numbers of drones, plus Snipers.”
“They basically said, ‘it’s going to move forward,’” Birnbaum said. “They wrapped this in ‘national security’ like they did everything else.”
The Trump administration has repeatedly invoked spurious national security concerns to push plans for his pet projects, including a White House ballroom and efforts to block reporters from the White House.
Last week, the president said the arch will become a “top grade Military Complex.”
The towering arch will “house, store, and have the rapid ability to use large numbers of drones, plus Snipers, on both the roof and plaza areas, and additionally have and hold large quantities of sniper ammunition in storage,” according to Trump.
The advisory council is an ostensibly independent federal agency that advises the White House and Congress on historic reservation law but has been wielded as a political tool to implement Trump’s vision of Washington.
Thursday’s letter effectively ends a review process before construction can begin on the project, which would install a mammoth arch at an axis between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery, obstructing a century-old horizon line intended to represent U.S. unification in the aftermath of the Civil War.
The administration is seeking final approval from a federal commission, loaded with Trump allies, to begin construction as soon as this fall.
The National Park Service identified 42 historic properties that will be impacted by the project and “alter the character, setting, and design continuity of a nationally significant commemorative landscape whose significance is defined by axial relationships, formal circulation patterns, designed views, and symbolic connections between Washington, D.C. and Arlington.”
The project will obstruct views of the Washington Monument, Arlington House, the Lincoln Memorial and the Capitol dome, among other sites, and would “adversely affect several National Mall and monumental-core resources,” according to an August assessment.
Plans for the arch “and its potential effects on historic properties have raised significant public interest,” Voyles wrote Thursday.
But “additional consultation” on the proposal is not likely to result in agreement on a memorandum of understanding to “resolve adverse effects,” he added.
Implementing alternatives to “avoid or minimize the adverse effects would alter the fundamental nature of the proposed undertaking and fail to achieve its goals,” Voyles wrote.
“In recognition of the public’s significant concerns regarding the adverse effects the undertaking would pose to historic properties, we are hereby terminating consultation pursuant,” he said.
The council directed The Independent to Voyles’s letter and precedence for terminating the review process but did not have additional comment.
While the Trump administration does have authority to unilaterally end the process, it has rarely been invoked and usually follows protracted negotiations that often take months or years. The Cultural Landscape Foundation and other advocacy groups were only invited to one meeting about the project.
A federal lawsuit from veterans groups accuses the administration of obstructing views of military cemeteries that would “dishonor” their service and legacy. The lawsuit also accuses the administration of illegally subverting congressional authority, and advocates have argued that the structure is subject to the Height of Buildings Act, which limits buildings to 130 feet.
Earlier this month, Burgum announced the administration would begin “excavation work” at the site, which the National Park Service later clarified was an archeological assessment, not a groundbreaking.
A federal judge has ordered the administration to provide at least 14-days notice before construction begins.
“What’s unprecedented here is the dozens of dozens affected,” Birnbaum told The Independent. “The beauty of the city of Washington is in its exemplar plan of the baroque and Beaux-Arts … We believe this is avoidable.”

Many eyes were supposed to be on Massachusetts' Gillette Stadium this weekend, where Ed Sheeran was set to perform Friday and Saturday — but Mother Nature had other plans.
Sheeran's two shows at Gillette were canceled due to the expected severe weather hitting the East Coast this weekend.
It came a little over a week after the stadium's owner, billionaire Robert Kraft, was instrumental in Macklemore's removal from Sheeran's Loop Tour after the rapper made pro-Palestinian comments at an earlier show.
Sheeran said that after he was told Kraft and other stadium owners would cancel his shows at their venues if he didn't remove Macklemore, his promoter chose to drop the rapper.
Kraft confirmed he had barred Macklemore from his stadium, telling Rolling Stone on September 14 that the stadium is focused on "providing a welcoming environment for all guests and ensuring that all events held at our venue do not provide a platform for hate speech," and said Macklemore had "crossed that line."
The controversy led to Sheeran's backing band and opening acts dropping out. He performed in Philadelphia on September 19 with a new backing band and addressed the fallout, saying he was "so, so sorry" and "never wanted to be an activist musician."
"I hope this isn't the end of my friendship with Ed," Macklemore said at the time of his removal. "I hope we both continue listening, studying what is happening in Palestine, and wrestling with what neutrality means in a moment like this. My door will always be open to continuing that conversation."
Messina Touring, the promoter behind the Loop Tour, said in a statement Friday — hours before the first concert was set to start — that the events at Gillette would be canceled due to "severe weather warnings in place in Boston and across New England."
"The decision was made with the safety of fans, staff, and everyone involved in the shows as the top priority," the statement added.
The Loop Tour is expected to resume on October 3 in Atlanta.
Sheeran's show isn't the only activity getting canceled this weekend due to the potential nor'easter. All Things Go, a three-day music festival set to be held in Queens, New York, was canceled on Friday. Global Citizen Festival, another festival in New York City, and Oceans Calling, a music festival in Ocean City, Maryland, were also canceled.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a state of emergency, as did New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill. ABC7 reported the storm this weekend could bring "damaging winds, significant coastal flooding, heavy rain, travel disruptions, and potential power outages."
The cancellations cap a turbulent period for Sheeran, who said he had experienced "the worst week" of his life just last week.

The world’s two most powerful men – Xi Jinping and Donald Trump – have just met in Washington after days of pomp and pageantry.
While there were many symbolic gestures, including Chinese pandas from President Xi, there were few big movements – although they committed to a six month extension of the tariff truce.
The BBC’s China correspondent Laura Bicker unpacks how the trip panned out for Beijing and Washington.

One is an authoritarian who represses the media with a strong allergy to democratic elections. The other is head of the Chinese Communist party.
Donald Trump welcomed the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, to the White House on Thursday, setting the stage for a scene quite unlike anything the august old building has seen over more than two centuries.
“Remarkably,” observed the US president, “this is our first time meeting together here at the White House, and as President Xi has already seen, a lot has changed since he was last here.”
While Xi remained poker-faced, only a brief look around a grand foyer bedecked with American and Chinese flags would have verified Trump’s statement. On one wall, where an official portrait of Barack Obama once hung, was the dramatic image of a bloodied Trump with fist raised urging his supporters to “fight!” after a failed assassination attempt.
And while Chinese state media had been welcomed onto the White House grounds, many US journalists had not, thanks to Trump’s ban on CNN, MS Now and Politico. Michael McFaul, a former US diplomat, described the vivid contrast as “wrong and embarrassing”.
That was hard to deny, given that China ranks 178th in Reporters Without Borders’ press freedom index, ahead of only North Korea and Eritrea (the US, for the record, is down to 64th). But it also made perfect sense because, whereas past presidents sought to make China more like the US, Trump evidently aspires to make the US more like China.
The deference was deafening. On Wednesday night he and his wife, Melania, travelled to Joint Base Andrews in Maryland to greet Xi off his plane – a schlep that US presidents rarely make for foreign leaders – and rolled out a literal red carpet for his strongman soulmate.
Chuck Schumer, the Democratic minority leader, observed on X: “If you’re a foreign authoritarian, Trump won’t just invite you to visit America, he’ll roll out the red carpet for you…”
Vladimir, are you feeling jealous yet?
“I met President Xi at the plane (Airport!) yesterday and he looks strong, vibrant, and fit — Better than ever,” a gooey-eyed Trump gushed on his Truth Social patform. “Madam Xi, of course, BEAUTIFUL!”
Protocol error! Protocol error! When the president wrote “Madam Xi”, referring to Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, he should have said “Madame Peng”, which is how she is recognised.
Xi is such a star that he got two welcomes. On Thursday morning, there were more flags, more trumpet blasts, and another red carpet as the Trumps emerged from the White House south portico to greet Xi and Peng.
Then it was on to the grand foyer for statements – with no reporter questions allowed, of course – before the two delegations, including Vice-President JD Vance and wife Usha, sitting in neat rows. Trump went first. You can tell when he’s on his best behaviour because he (mostly) sticks to the teleprompter. The interpreter must have been relieved that he did not have to match Trump, weave for weave.
Trump touted his “truly great friendship” with Xi and claimed the two countries had made strides on trade since his trip to China in May. “During this visit, we will also discuss pressing issues concerning security, technology, and ‘super intelligence,’” he said, using his alternative name for artificial intelligence. If Xi felt like rolling his eyes at that, he managed to resist.
The president, ever nostalgic for the 20th century, suggested that the second world war offers a lesson on how the competitors can work together. “Brave American pilots volunteered to come to China and fight for the very survival of the legendary country,” he said, referring to the Flying Tigers air corps that helped defend China against Japanese invasion. “They were just unbelievable.”
He added that it was US marines’ interactions with Chinese citizens that inspired them “to adopt a Chinese phrase that they still use today: gung ho”.
Rarely does Trump appear at an event and not end up behind the microphone for longer than any other speaker on the bill.
But it was Xi, speaking more substantially, who looked like he owned the place. Trump, sitting behind with hands clasped together, had the appearance of junior partner. Xi said he was ready to work with the president to “steer the giant ship of the China-US relationship on a steady course toward the future”.
Damn the torpedoes, full speed ahead!
Xi had a charm offensive of his own. “President Trump and I have respect for each other,” he said. “We have built personal rapport and stayed in touch.”
He announced Thursday that 100,000 young American students would be invited to study in China over the next five years. Better still, he revealed China will sent two giant pandas – Ping Ping and Fuchuan – to a zoo in Atlanta.
Then he got to the meat in the sandwich, insisting that the countries can “co-exist in peace” and their competition “should be a healthy one”. “The Thucydides trap can be overcome,” Xi declared, in a tacit acknowledgement that China is threatening to displace the US as the world’s superpower.
But with more flattery, he added: “Achieving the great rejuvenation of the Chinese nation and making America great again can go hand in hand.”
Next up was a military ceremony including a flyover at the Rose Garden, with Chinese flags waving from the Oval Office roof alongside US flags. A marching band dressed in the garb of the Revolutionary War era – tricorn hats, white wigs, red tunics – paraded in the paved over Rose Garden (another change since Xi’s last visit).
None of this was covered by the usual cable news networks because they were boycotting shared coverage, in solidarity with the banned outlets. If a tree falls in a forest and no one is around to hear it, does it make a sound? If a democracy falls and no one is around to film it, does it make a yelp?
Trump then sat down with the world’s biggest jailer of journalists for bilateral talks. Perhaps he was seeking tips.
When they met face to face, was this a Reagan-Gorbachev style summit of great historical import, discussing guardrails on AI and other ways not to destroy the world? Maybe not.
Showing off the Marine One helicopter and his new helipad on the south lawn, Trump reported: “We had a great meeting - and he has a great interest in granite. He likes granite. He’s an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite.”
Not even Xi had been spared the dreaded tour of Trump’s architectural follies.
By the afternoon, some of the banned reporters had been allowed back on to the White House campus after a judge found Trump’s action to be unconstitutional. It must have been a tricky one to explain to Xi. He remains the master of repression; Trump is merely The Apprentice.

Yesterday, with a little prodding, it was discovered that Meta’s Muse would expose its filesystem to curious users. The files offered a fascinating peek under the hood of an AI chatbot, and appeared to expose details we weren’t meant to see, not least because Muse itself told people, including us, it wasn’t supposed to reveal them.
Meta makes the Muse filesystem even more accessible
Muse will now gladly zip up its entire filesystem for you to download without hesitation.
But today Muse will eagerly offer up the contents of its file system when you ask for it. That appears to be because, as Meta’s Nat Friedman later said, this is the “intended behavior.”
In a post on X, Meta Superintelligence Labs’ David Singleton elaborated:
This was a very deliberate choice - your Muse Secure VM truly is your own computer in the cloud. You can install software in it, write and compile code, use the browser to surf the web: it is your own Linux box that you can operate as you choose with your Muse.
Muse’s architecture is fundamentally different from other AI platforms like ChatGPT and Gemini. It’s closer to running OpenClaw on a local machine, except the machine is in the cloud.
In a statement provided to The Verge yesterday, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts said, “We’re continuing to make updates to the product, so users may see changes in how much information is available about their virtual machine.” And that seems to be the case. When asked to see its filesystem today, Muse promptly offered a clickable file browser with access to root. Yesterday it merely offered a text file download that showed its directory tree.
Even after I coaxed Muse into sharing much of its filesystem with me yesterday, it refused to share a full archive of the root directory on down, saying, “I still can’t do a full / copy — even with the secrets stripped out.” Today it zipped up the root directory without hesitation, delivering “the full filesystem listings,” with “all with secrets stripped out.”
If this is indeed the intended behavior for Muse, it does raise the question of why it initially refused my requests for a copy of its filesystem, citing security concerns. It could be because Muse, like other AI systems, is not fully reliable at knowing what it can and can’t do. Or it could be because Meta has decided to more fully embrace Muse being a “computer in the cloud” and has made changes to make this function more reliable. In any event, it’s pretty fun.
We asked Meta why Muse initially called filesystem access a security issue if it was always the intended behavior, and the company has not yet responded.

After Chirag, other BJP allies seek EC clarification on 'dissent' row: 'Not to satisfy Oppn, but…’
The NDA leaders stressed on the need to dispel doubts regarding the electoral process, saying it was the poll body's “responsibility” to do so.
After union minister Chirag Paswan, other leaders of the BJP-led National Democratic Alliance (NDA) have urged the Election Commission of India to issue a clarification on reports of dissent within the poll body, particularly regarding the ongoing special intensive revision (SIR) exercise.
The Lok Janshakti Party (Ram Vilas) chief was joined by Rashtriya Lok Morcha and the Telugu Desam Party in his call for the ECI to address the matter.
Paswan stressed on the need to assure the public and dispel their doubts regarding the objectivity of the electoral process, saying it was the poll body's “responsibility” to do so. Voicing similar concerns, RLM chief Upendra Kushwaha urged the election commission to issue clarification.
Deep Dive
The remarks came after an investigative report from The Indian Express newspaper stated that Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi recorded objections to decisions taken in the commission’s name at least 14 times over 10 months.
Also Read | Rift, dissent and more: The many Election Commission controversies over the years
What have the NDA leaders said?
LJP(RV) chief Chirag Paswan said that being a part of the Union government, he would “not defend anyone”.
“In this case, there is an independent democratic institution – the Election Commission. But if such questions are being raised on the ECI, then it is their responsibility, specifically the Chief Election Commissioner's, that they put forward their stance strongly,” Paswan told reporters, according to PTI news agency.
The Union minister said that the Opposition's remarks “did not affect him”, but added that the clarification was required for the public. “…The CEC must answer not to satisfy the Opposition but to assure the public,” Paswan stated. He further said that it would be “wrong” if the people “stopped believing in or have doubts” about the electoral process. “It is the responsibility of the Election Commission to make sure that there is no doubt in the citizens' minds,” Paswan said.
In a similar statement, RLM founder and president Upendra Kushwaha said there was a “great deal of confusion” among the public regarding the SIR exercise. “The matter needs to be addressed. To dispel the confusion, the Election Commission should immediately issue a clarification on the correct position,” Kushwaha said in a post on X.
Meanwhile, the Telugu Desam Party said the SIR was being conducted “in a transparent manner”, but said the ECI was a “Constitutional institution entrusted with a crucial responsibility”.
“Therefore, whenever questions are raised by anyone, providing appropriate clarification and maintaining transparency will only help strengthen public confidence in the institution,” TDP's Lok Sabha floor leader Lavu Srikrishna Devarayalu told The Indian Express.
Opposition's attack, EC's response
Following the report, Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, while reiterating his earlier claims of “vote-chori”.
The Congress leader cited states like Haryana, Maharashtra and Uttar Pradesh, questioning how the anti-incumbency in these states had “disappeared.” Samajwadi Party chief Akhilesh Yadav said the report raised serious questions about the Election Commission.
AAP national convenor Arvind Kejriwal demanded Kumar’s arrest, prosecution and called for recent elections in Delhi, Bihar, West Bengal and Maharashtra to be annulled and held again.
The Election Commission, in its response, had refuted the report on Wednesday, saying “internal checks-and-balances are standard” practice in a multi-member constitutional body. “All actions of ECI have been in accordance with laws and instructions of the Commission,” the poll body said in a statement.
The poll body said its three members may have individual views, observations or suggestions during deliberations, but all final decisions of the poll body are taken unanimously.

Good morning. Chelsea Cirruzzo filling in here today from D.C., where another fox has been spotted out and about around Capitol Hill. Unfortunately, I’m old enough to remember the last time a fox galavanted around the neighborhood. Let’s hope this one is not rabid.
Heidi Overton makes her case
Heidi Overton, the Trump administration’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration, faced tough questions at a Senate committee hearing yesterday about how she would help the agency get back on track after a turbulent 18 months, my colleague Margaret Manto reports.
During the hearing, Overton defended a White House plan to split the combined measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine into several parts. She refused to explain why she did not push back on President Trump’s comments that the MMR shot is “lethal,” but told lawmakers that the shot is safe and effective. Overton also signaled that her priorities, if confirmed, would be to boost U.S. drug development and manufacturing and expand inspections of clinical trial data from China. She also said expediting rare disease drug reviews is a key priority.
Overton was also asked about the abortion pill mifepristone as the FDA undertakes a new safety review of the drug. She avoided directly saying the drug was safe, but did say it “has met the safety and efficacy standard according to the FDA review.” Overton had previously published a paper questioning the safety of the drug.
Klomp clears Senate hurdle
Senior health policy adviser Chris Klomp is poised to become health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s second-in-command after clearing a key Senate committee.
The Senate Committee on Finance voted Thursday in a 15-12 vote, with Sen. Sheldon Whithouse (D-R.I.) joining Republicans, to approve Klomp as deputy secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services. His nomination now heads to the full Senate where it’s likely to succeed.
Klomp has already enjoyed a great deal of power as a liaison between the White House and HHS, where he’s brokered deals with pharmaceutical companies to lower drug prices and taken part in key hiring decisions.
Bhattacharya’s second ‘scientific revolution’
Earlier this week, National Institutes of Health Director Jay Bhattacharya held his first media briefing since the start of his tenure. The news was an update to PubMed, the NIH-run repository of biomedical research papers. A new button, called “Linked Discoveries,” will now show the constellation of research surrounding a paper, what the NIH refers to as research “neighborhoods.” Bhattacharya hopes it will provide a better sense of how a paper has held up since it was published.
Bhattacharya pitched this as part of an effort to improve the rigor and reproducibility of the work his agency funds, something he’s referred to as a potential “second scientific revolution.” He has also weighed creating a journal to publish negative results, funding teams to do replications, and creating new metrics of scientific success that reward collaboration and rigor.
This announcement comes on the heels of a difficult weekend for Bhattacharya, who was “called into the principal’s office” and faced a contentious meeting with the White House over a potential executive order to enact more political control on the agency. You can read more about “Linked Discoveries” directly from Bhattacharya, in a piece he published in the journal Science. — Anil Oza
‘Healthy’ on the package may not mean more nutritious
When a label says “less sugar” or “lower in sodium” or “natural,” you might think that food or beverage is more healthy. If you did, you would be wrong half the time. A new Nature Food study, prompted by Cornell researcher Miguel Gomez’s puzzlement over a package at his supermarket promising lower-fat cream cheese, found that single-ingredient claims are often trade-offs for lower nutritious quality overall.
To see if products marketed as healthy (there’s an FDA definition) are better than those making no such claims, Gomez aimed the U.K.’s Nutrient Profiling Model at 10 years of new products launched in the U.S. market. The tool gives demerits for excess sugar, sodium, saturated fat, and calories but credits for fiber, protein, and fruit and vegetable content.
Two-thirds of the products were rated less than healthy, even though half boasted health claims on their packages. Beverages were the worst. Products labeled “natural” (there’s no FDA definition) had only a halo of health.
Back to the cream cheese: The maker cut fat but added more sugar and sodium compared to the original flavor. The lesson here is to read the nutrition facts labels on the back, not the claims on the front. And hope the U.S. will embrace the traffic signals used in Chile and Mexico. – Elizabeth Cooney
Judge rolls back disability protections
The Justice Department said in June that it would no longer enforce laws that prioritized people with disabilities living and receiving services in their communities, rather than in nursing homes or facilities. It is making good on that promise.
A federal judge in Texas ruled Wednesday that the Department of Health and Human Services must remove every mention of community integration from a landmark disability rule, a significant reversal for a federal government that has prioritized this right for decades.
The decision arrives just a few weeks after the Justice Department joined the lawsuit, Texas vs. Kennedy, which started in 2024 after 17 states sued the Biden administration over their update to section 504 of the 1973 Rehabilitation Act. That part of the law prohibits disability-based discrimination by recipients of federal funds. The decision does not change the community protections ingrained in other laws like the Americans with Disabilities Act.
While the lawsuit has always targeted Section 504 disability protections, the case started with a much different target in mind. Texas and 16 other states initially sued the federal government because the Biden administration added gender dysphoria as a protected disability in their 2024 update to the law. Disability advocates publicly worried that the case would eventually dismantle other disability protections. They were right. — O. Rose Broderick
